guides.title: License Law & Article 12-A
guides.overview: New York's license law: Article 12-A of the Real Property Law (RPL), DOS conduct rules in 19 NYCRR Part 175, Article 12-C apartment vendors, and two seller disclosures (the PCDA and RPL §242). Three ideas matter most: salespersons act and are paid **only through their sponsoring broker**, **client money is never the broker's**, and every ad must **identify the broker**.

mustKnow: **Article 12-A** of the Real Property Law is the license law. The Department of State (DOS) licenses and disciplines; **19 NYCRR Part 175** holds the conduct rules.
A license is needed to list, sell, buy, exchange, rent, negotiate or collect rent **for another and for a fee**. Negotiating **non-residential mortgage loans** and tenant relocation count too.

Owners dealing with their own property need no license. **Exempt**: NY-admitted attorneys, people acting under a court order and public officers on duty. **Exemptions don't cover anyone they hire** (§442-f).
An attorney needs a **broker license to employ salespersons**, because salespersons may be paid only by a licensed broker.
Salesperson: age 18, **77 hours**, the state exam and a sponsoring NY broker.
Broker: age 20, **152 hours**, the broker exam and **2 years + 3,500 points** (or 3 years + 5,250). Time alone never qualifies.
An **associate broker** is broker-qualified but works under another broker, follows the salesperson rules for practice and pay, and may keep a separate broker license for her own firm.
Branches are supervised by the broker or an **office manager** (an associate broker active **2 of the past 4 years**), never by a salesperson.
Entities act through people: **each officer, partner or member who brokers needs a broker license**; a salesperson can't own voting stock in her brokerage corporation.

DOS currently has **no reciprocity** with any state; an education waiver still needs the NY exam and sponsor. Nonresidents file an **irrevocable consent** naming the Secretary of State to accept legal papers.
Salespersons and associate brokers are paid **only by their own sponsoring broker**. A client's 'gift' for a deal is **compensation** (§442-a).
Brokers may share fees only with their own licensees, other licensed brokers or brokers regularly in business in another state. Sharing a fee with an unlicensed helper is a **kickback**.
**Rebates to the buyer, seller, landlord or tenant** are legal if not paid for licensed work; cross-firm referral fees go **broker to broker**.
Make clear whom you represent. Pay from more than one party needs your **client's full knowledge and consent** (§175.7).
No lawsuit for a commission unless you were **licensed when the claim arose** (§442-d).
A licensee's listing or commission agreement **needn't be in writing** to be enforced; the writing rule exempts licensed brokers and salespersons (GOL §5-701(a)(10)).
Client money goes into a separate, special, federally insured account within **3 business days**, safeguarded until then.
Mixing client money with the broker's is **commingling**; using it for the broker is **conversion**.
Escrow interest stays out of the broker's pocket unless applied to an **earned commission with all parties' consent**; managers can't keep **secret vendor rebates** (§175.3).
**Net listings** are prohibited, and exclusive listings can't renew automatically. A broker can't buy its own listing without first making its **true position clear**.
Residential exclusives carry the DOS **exclusive-right-to-sell vs exclusive-agency** explanation in **6-point** type, signed or initialed by the homeowner.
Give signers copies of broker-prepared documents **immediately**; keep **§175.23 records 3 years** for 1–4 family, condo and co-op sales.
Never negotiate directly with an owner under another broker's **written exclusive**, and never **induce a party to break** a contract.
Supervision must be **regular, frequent and consistent**, whatever the salesperson's tax status.
**Only the broker places ads**; ads need the owner's authorization and must identify the broker. Hiding the broker makes a **blind ad**.
Banned titles: **'sales associate,' 'licensed sales agent,' 'broker' alone**. Nicknames need the full licensed name; extra phone numbers must be labeled.

**Team** names must say 'team' (not 'realty,' 'group' or 'associates'), can't include an unlicensed person's name, need 'at/of [brokerage]' unless members' full names are used, and all members share **one brokerage**.
Business cards need the **office phone**. Agent websites need the required information on **every page**; only the first email to a person needs it.
Unlicensed assistants do **clerical** work for hourly, per-task or salary pay. Showing, negotiating and **soliciting listings** need a license.
CE: **22.5 hours** per 2-year term, with every required topic **inside** the total. Extra hours don't carry over.
Required CE: fair housing 3, agency 1 (**2 in a salesperson's first term**), ethics 2.5, recent legal matters 1, cultural competency 2, implicit bias 2.
Only **NY-admitted attorneys** are CE-exempt; the 15-year broker exemption ended **July 1, 2021**.
**No grace period**: renew within 2 years of expiration but don't practice until renewed; after 2 years, retake the exam and meet current education.
Carry the **pocket card** and show it on demand. Each branch needs its own license. Moving an office without notifying DOS **suspends** the license.
When a salesperson leaves, the **old broker files the termination** and the **new broker files the change of association**; no licensed work in between.
DOS may reprimand, **fine up to $2,000**, suspend or revoke after **10 days'** notice and a hearing. Courts review by Article 78, even a refusal to discipline.
Violations are **misdemeanors** prosecuted by the Attorney General; the person aggrieved may recover **1 to 4 times** the money received.
A broker's revocation **suspends its salespersons** until they change association.
Article 12-C vendors: 1-year license (Nov 1–Oct 31); fee capped at **one month's rent**. They keep at most **$15** of an advance fee, refunding the rest within 10 days of written notice.
The **Property Condition Disclosure Statement (PCDS)** goes to the buyer **before a binding contract** on 1–4 family sales, not condos or co-ops. The $500 credit opt-out ended in 2024.
Sellers must disclose known **uncapped gas wells** before contract (RPL §242).

traps.trap: Required CE topics are added on top of the 22.5 hours.
traps.truth: They fit inside the 22.5: 12.5 specified plus 10 elective in a salesperson's first term, 11.5 plus 11 afterward.

traps.trap: A thank-you check from a happy buyer is a personal gift.
traps.truth: It is compensation for licensed work, which a salesperson may accept only from her own broker (§442-a).

traps.trap: Parking a deposit in the operating account is fine if none of it is spent.
traps.truth: Mixing the funds is commingling; spending them would be conversion.

traps.trap: 'Three days to deposit' means calendar days, and the check can sit in a drawer meanwhile.
traps.truth: Three business days, and the money must be safeguarded in a secure place until deposited.

traps.trap: An expired license has a grace period if the CE is done.
traps.truth: No licensed work until renewal; the 2-year window only avoids retesting.

traps.trap: Two years as a salesperson automatically qualifies you for a broker license.
traps.truth: You also need 3,500 points, 152 hours and a passing broker exam.

traps.trap: Brokers licensed 15+ years are CE-exempt.
traps.truth: That exemption ended July 1, 2021; only New York bar attorneys are exempt.

traps.trap: Independent-contractor salespersons need no supervision.
traps.truth: Supervision must be regular, frequent and consistent, whatever the tax status (§175.21).

traps.trap: An executor's or attorney's exemption covers the people they hire.
traps.truth: Exemptions are personal; hired help needs a license, and an attorney needs a broker license to employ salespersons.

traps.trap: Crediting part of the commission to the buyer is an illegal split.
traps.truth: Rebates to the buyer, seller, landlord or tenant are allowed unless paid for licensed work (§442).

traps.trap: DOS can jail a licensee.
traps.truth: DOS can reprimand, fine, suspend, revoke or deny; jail requires a criminal conviction in court.

traps.trap: Transaction records are kept 2 years, like the license term.
traps.truth: Keep them 3 years (§175.23).

traps.trap: 'Smith Realty Group' works as a team name.
traps.truth: Team names must use 'team'; 'realty,' 'group' and 'associates' are prohibited.

traps.trap: Any salesperson violation costs the broker its license.
traps.truth: Only if the broker knew of it or kept the profits after notice (§442-c), though weak supervision is its own violation.

traps.trap: Older textbook numbers ($1,000 fine, 75-hour course, 120 broker hours, reciprocity states, the $500 PCDS credit) still apply.
traps.truth: Now: $2,000 fine, 77 hours, 152 hours, no reciprocity, and the $500 credit is gone (2024).

traps.trap: A listing or commission agreement must be in writing to be enforceable.
traps.truth: An oral agreement with a licensee can be enforced; the writing rule for brokerage fees exempts licensed brokers and salespersons (GOL §5-701(a)(10)). The real bar: no license when the claim arose, no fee (§442-d).

traps.trap: New York has raised the broker requirement to 4 years as a salesperson.
traps.truth: Current rule: 2 years + 3,500 points. A bill for 4 consecutive years passed both houses on June 1, 2026, but wasn't signed as of October 8, 2026.

mnemonics.meaning: Salesperson: age 18 and 77 hours. Broker: age 20 and 152 hours (77 + 75).

mnemonics.meaning: Client money is deposited within 3 business days; transaction records are kept 3 years.

mnemonics.name: 10 before, 5 after, 1 year out
mnemonics.meaning: 10 days' notice before a DOS hearing; return the license and pocket card within 5 days of suspension or revocation; wait 1 year after revocation.

mnemonics.name: Money moves broker to broker
mnemonics.meaning: Pay for licensed work flows client to broker to that broker's own licensees, never to another firm's salesperson or an unlicensed helper.

formulas.name: Broker experience points
formulas.formula: Sum of (transactions × Part 179 point value); need 3,500 or 5,250

formulas.name: Civil penalty (RPL §442-e)

formulas.formula: Refund = advance fee − up to $15, within 10 days of written notice

sections.heading: Who regulates licensees in New York
sections.intro: In New York, real estate licensing is run by the state under Article 12-A and Department of State rules.
points: **Purpose**: the license law protects the public from fraud and incompetence by requiring anyone who brokers real estate for others to meet education, exam and trustworthiness standards and to work under supervision.

**Article 12-A** of the Real Property Law (RPL §§440–443-a) covers definitions, licensing, fees, discipline, commissions, the Board of Real Estate and agency disclosure. **Article 12-C** separately licenses apartment information vendors.

The **Department of State (DOS)**, through its Division of Licensing Services, issues and renews licenses, investigates complaints with subpoena power, holds hearings and disciplines licensees. It also enforces the law, including bringing prosecutions for unlicensed practice.
The **Secretary of State** heads DOS and writes the 19 NYCRR regulations: Part 175 conduct rules, Part 177 continuing education (CE) and Part 179 experience points.
The **State Board of Real Estate** has **15 members**: the Secretary of State (chair), the Superintendent of Financial Services and 13 appointees (RPL §442-i).
At least five appointees are brokers with 10+ years in New York real estate; the rest are public members. Appointees serve unpaid 2-year terms, with a 10-year lifetime limit.
The board may adopt rules, set course and exam content and school-approval rules, and recommend legislation.

Rules on commingling, client accounts, managing property for clients, a broker buying listed property, inducing breach of contract, transaction records and clients' funds are reserved to the **Secretary of State** (RPL §442-k).
The **Attorney General** prosecutes Article 12-A crimes; only a court can impose criminal punishment.

sections.heading: What requires a license, and who is exempt
sections.intro: In New York, the test is whether someone performs a brokerage act **for another and for a fee**; any valuable consideration counts.
points: **Broker activities**: listing, selling (including at auction), buying, exchanging or renting real estate, or negotiating or attempting to; collecting rent; negotiating a mortgage loan **other than a residential mortgage loan**; and acting as a tenant relocator (RPL §440).
A **tenant relocator** organizes the relocation of tenants out of a building being demolished or altered.
**Business sales** count when the real estate transferred is **not merely incidental** to the deal, unless the deal is regulated as a securities sale. Assigning only a lease doesn't count.
One prohibited act is a violation, though a fee is presumed only from repeated acts (§442-e).
**Related licenses**: residential (1–4 family) mortgage loans fall under the Banking Law, not a real estate license. **Home inspectors** are licensed under RPL Article 12-B.

**Appraisers** hold a separate DOS license or certification (Executive Law Article 6-E). So a **comparative market analysis (CMA)**, an agent's price opinion from recent sales, may never be called an appraisal.
**Owners** dealing with their own property aren't brokers at all, since they don't act 'for another.'

**Exempt**: attorneys admitted in New York; receivers, referees, executors, administrators, guardians and others appointed by or acting under a **court order**; and public officers doing official duties (RPL §442-f).
Tenant groups and nonprofits authorized by New York City to manage city-owned housing are also exempt (§440-a).

**Exemptions are personal**: the friend an executor pays to find a buyer needs a license, and a public employee's paid side deals aren't official duties. An attorney needs a **broker license to employ salespersons**, because salespersons may be paid only by a licensed broker.
An owner's own salaried employee, such as a resident superintendent showing units or taking rent for that employer, is generally treated as exempt.
A management company that **collects rent or places tenants** for client-owners needs a broker license; one doing only **maintenance** doesn't.
**REALTOR®** is a trade-association membership, not a license.

sections.heading: License types, entities and responsibilities
sections.intro: New York issues three categories of real estate license: broker, associate broker and salesperson.
points: **Broker**: runs the brokerage, owns the listings, holds client money, and supervises, employs and pays its licensees. Its duties run to the public (honesty, accounting, disclosure) and to its licensees (supervision).

**Associate broker**: licensed as a broker but working under another broker's name and supervision. She follows the salesperson rules for practice and pay, yet keeps broker status and may also hold a separate broker license for her own firm (RPL §440(2)). She owes duties to her broker and the public.

**Salesperson**: a licensee **associated with** a broker who performs brokerage acts for that broker. She can't work independently or act while unassociated. 'Associated' describes the license link only, not employee status.
**Office manager**: an associate broker who was active as one at least **2 of the 4 years** before appointment. She carries a broker's supervisory duty (RPL §440(6)).
A branch must be directly supervised by the broker, a representative broker, an LLC manager or an office manager, never a salesperson.
**Entities** (corporations, partnerships and LLCs) act through people. **Each officer, partner or member who will act as a broker needs a broker license** and must personally qualify.
No salesperson license goes to an officer, partner or member of a licensed entity. A salesperson may not own **voting stock** in her brokerage corporation (§175.22).
Trade names need DOS approval and can't be confusingly similar to another broker's (§175.18).

**Dual licensure**: one person may hold several licenses, such as an associate broker license at one firm plus a broker license for her own. A salesperson working for two brokers needs an **additional salesperson license** for each.

sections.heading: Getting licensed: education, exams and experience
sections.intro: In New York, the order is education, the school's exam, the state exam and a sponsoring broker. Only an issued license, associated with a broker, allows practice.
points: **Salesperson**: at least 18; the **77-hour** course, including the school's proctored final; the separate DOS exam; sponsorship by a NYS broker; a current NYS photo driver license or non-driver ID; and the $65 fee. No college degree is needed.
**State exam**: multiple choice, 90 minutes (2½ hours for brokers) and $15. A pass is good for **2 years**.
Results are **pass/fail** only; DOS publishes no score, question count or cutoff.
Calculators must be silent, nonprinting and without an alphabetic keyboard.

**Time limits**: an unused 77-hour course is valid for **8 years**; once used for a license it never expires. Someone with only the old 75-hour course needs an approved 2-hour fair housing and/or implicit bias course.

**Applying**: online through eAccessNY; the sponsoring broker authorizes the application, and DOS mails the license to the business address. A criminal conviction isn't an automatic bar; DOS weighs it under Correction Law Article 23-A.
**Broker**: at least 20; **152 hours** (the 77-hour course plus the 75-hour broker course); the broker exam; DOS approval of any business name; the $185 fee; and experience.

**Experience = time plus points**: **2 years** as a licensed salesperson with 3,500 points, or 3 years of general real estate experience (such as managing an employer's buildings) or a combination, with 5,250 points (19 NYCRR Part 179).
Sample point values: a residential sale 250, an exclusive sale listing 10, a rental 25, a commercial sale 400 (§179.3).
Full time means at least 35 hours a week, 50 weeks a year (§175.21(c)). False claims are grounds to deny or revoke.
**Pending bill**: S8870/A9518 would require **4 consecutive years** as a salesperson. It passed both houses on June 1, 2026.
As of October 8, 2026, the bill had not been delivered to or signed by the Governor; a 2025 version was vetoed. It would take effect 180 days after becoming law.
**Reciprocity**: DOS currently has **none** with any state. An out-of-state education waiver still requires the NY exam and a NY sponsor.
Each nonresident files an **irrevocable consent** naming the Secretary of State as agent to receive lawsuits and other legal papers (§442-g).

example.title: Worked example: counting broker experience points
steps: Step 1: Tomas has been a full-time licensed salesperson for 25 months, so he meets the 2-year rule.
Step 2: Residential sales, using the Part 179 schedule: 10 × 250 = 2,500 points.
Step 3: Exclusive sale listings: 50 × 10 = 500. An exclusive rental listing earns only 5.
Step 4: Rentals: 20 × 25 = 500.
Step 5: Total = 2,500 + 500 + 500 = 3,500 points, exactly the minimum.
Answer: He qualifies on experience but still needs 152 hours and the broker exam. With 2,100 points he wouldn't qualify, however long he'd worked.

sections.heading: Renewal and continuing education
sections.intro: Licenses run **2 years** and are renewed online. Renewal requires continuing education (CE) unless the licensee is exempt.
points: **Renewal**: opens **3 months** before expiration ($65 salesperson, $185 broker). Salespersons and associate brokers need a sponsoring broker, who authorizes the renewal. Submitting isn't approval.
**CE**: **22.5 hours** of approved courses within each 2-year term.
Required topics, all **inside** the 22.5: fair housing 3, agency 1 (2 in a salesperson's first term), ethics 2.5, recent legal matters 1, cultural competency 2 and implicit bias 2.
Sales meetings, motivation and exam-prep classes don't count.
**No carry-over** of extra hours. **Teaching** an approved course earns 2 hours per hour taught (§177.5).
A salesperson who completes an approved broker course (with its final exam) during the term gets CE credit. She must still add 2.5 hours of ethics and 1 hour of recent legal matters.
**Exempt**: only attorneys admitted to the New York bar. The 15-consecutive-year broker exemption ended **July 1, 2021**.
DOS may extend the deadline only for documented hardship (§177.6).
**Expired license**: **no grace period**. Renew within 2 years after expiration (with CE and a sponsor), but do no licensed work until renewed.
After 2 years, meet **current** education and **pass the exam** again; CE isn't required for that. Military service that prevented renewal excuses the retest.

example.title: Worked example: elective CE hours
steps: Step 1: First salesperson renewal, specified hours: 3 + 2 + 2.5 + 1 + 2 + 2 = 12.5.
Step 2: Electives: 22.5 − 12.5 = 10.
Step 3: Later renewals: agency drops to 1, so specified hours total 11.5.
Step 4: Electives: 22.5 − 11.5 = 11.
Answer: 10 hours, then 11. A choice saying required topics push the total past 22.5 is wrong.

sections.heading: Keeping a license active: offices, pocket cards and changes
sections.intro: Article 12-A attaches housekeeping duties to every license, and some lapses suspend a license automatically.
points: **Office and sign**: each broker keeps a definite place of business in New York, with an outside sign readable from the sidewalk showing its name and 'licensed real estate broker.' A qualifying nonresident broker is excepted (§442-g).
In an office or apartment building, a directory listing works. If lobby signs are banned, the sign goes on or beside the unit door (§175.26).

**Display**: the broker's license hangs conspicuously in the principal office and each branch license in its branch. Salesperson licenses are mailed to the business address and needn't be displayed. Displaying an **expired, suspended or revoked** broker license is prohibited.
**Pocket card**: the DOS-issued photo ID shows the licensee's photo, name and business address and, for a salesperson, the sponsoring broker's name and address.
Carry the pocket card and **show it on demand**. Replace a lost or damaged card through DOS ($10 plus proof), never with a copy.

**Moving**: get DOS approval before relocating an office (§175.20(c)) and notify DOS for the broker and every associated licensee ($10 each). Moving without notice **suspends the license** until DOS vacates the suspension (§441-a(5)).
**Branches**: each extra office needs its own branch office license ($185), displayed there and **owned, maintained and operated only by the broker** (§175.20).
A salesperson can't fund and run a branch for her own profit. A home isn't a branch just because its phone number is on business cards.
**Changing firms**: the broker being left files the termination within 5 days (DOS policy; no fee).
Then the **new broker files a change of association** (a new record of association, $20). No new course or exam is needed.
No licensed work in between (§442-b). The departing salesperson turns over all listing information (§175.14).

Broker's death: with surrogate's court authorization, the executor or administrator may use a sole proprietor's license up to **120 days** from the date of death to finish pending deals. DOS may add up to **120 more** for good cause.
**Convictions**: a licensee convicted of a felony or specified sex offense sends DOS a certified copy of the judgment within **5 days** after sentencing.

sections.heading: Compensation, fee splitting and suing for a fee
sections.intro: In New York, pay for licensed work moves client to broker, broker to broker, and broker to its own licensees.
points: Salespersons and associate brokers take pay for licensed work **only from their own sponsoring broker** (§442-a). A buyer's thank-you check or another firm's payment must be declined or routed through the broker.
A broker may share fees with its own licensees, any **licensed broker**, and a person **regularly in brokerage in another state**, who needs no NY license (§442).
A broker may pay an unlicensed corporation or LLC only if **every** owner is a licensed associate of that broker.
Giving an unlicensed person any part of a fee for helping with a deal is a **kickback**, whatever it's called. Hourly or salary pay for clerical work is different.

**Rebates** to the buyer, seller, landlord or tenant, such as a closing credit, are allowed if they aren't pay for licensed work. Cross-firm referral fees go **broker to broker**: Broker A pays Broker B, which pays its salesperson.
Make clear which party you represent. Take pay from more than one party only with your **client's full knowledge and consent**, given in advance (§175.7).
DOS sets no commission rates, and competing firms may not agree on rates (antitrust).

**No after-the-fact referral fees** for 'finding' a seller who already listed, a buyer whose offer was already accepted, or a property after a buyer-agency agreement is signed, absent reasonable cause (§442-l).

No one may sue for a brokerage fee without proving they were **licensed when the claim arose** (§442-d). Licensing later doesn't help, and an unlicensed finder can't collect even on a written promise.
A salesperson's commission claim is against **her own broker**, not the seller.

**No writing needed**: the statute of frauds requires a signed writing for brokerage and finder's fees. It exempts licensed brokers and salespersons, plus attorneys and auctioneers (General Obligations Law §5-701(a)(10)).
So a licensee's **oral** listing or commission agreement can be enforced. A signed agreement is still the best proof, and residential exclusives need the signed §175.24 explanation.

sections.heading: Client money, escrow and records
sections.intro: **Escrow** money is money held for others until conditions are met. In New York, entrusted money never becomes the broker's, even briefly.
points: Keep a **separate, special account** used only for client money at a federally insured bank. Deposit within **3 business days** and safeguard the money until then (§175.1).
Money-market funds, Treasury funds and other investments aren't allowed, even for a better yield.
**Commingling** is mixing client money with the broker's own, even 'just until closing' and even if unspent. A ledger entry doesn't cure it.
**Conversion** is using client money for the broker's purposes, such as paying office rent, even with a plan to repay.
**Interest** on escrowed money can't benefit the broker unless it is applied to an **earned commission with all parties' consent**.
Account to the client and **remit** unspent client money within a reasonable time (§§175.2–175.3).

A managing broker can't take a rebate or profit on the owner's spending (a vendor's secret 10%) without the owner's **full knowledge and consent**. The broker handles tenant security deposits under General Obligations Law §7-103.
**Records, kept 3 years**, for sales of 1–4 family homes and condo or co-op units; not vacant land, larger buildings or commercial leases (§175.23).

Required records: seller and buyer names and addresses; the broker-prepared contract or binder (or else the price and any deposit the broker collected); the commission; and the broker's profit if it bought for resale.
Also keep documents Article 12-A requires and the listing, commission or buyer-broker agreement. Lender files aren't required, and a broker isn't faulted for papers it never received.

example.title: Worked example: a commingling complaint, start to finish
steps: Step 1: A buyer's $20,000 deposit isn't returned when her mortgage falls through. DOS investigates and subpoenas bank records showing the deposit sat in the operating account.
Step 2: DOS serves written charges at least 10 days before the hearing; the broker may appear with a lawyer.
Step 3: A DOS administrative law judge finds commingling and untrustworthiness.
Step 4: DOS may reprimand, fine up to $2,000, suspend or revoke.
Step 5: After a suspension or revocation, the broker returns the license and pocket card within 5 days. All its salespersons are suspended until they change association (or a suspension ends).
Step 6: After revocation the broker waits 1 year to reapply. The broker, or the buyer as a person aggrieved, may seek Article 78 review.
Answer: This administrative case is separate from any criminal case by the Attorney General and from the buyer's own lawsuit for her money.

sections.heading: Part 175 rules on listings, interests and dealings
sections.intro: The Part 175 conduct rules (19 NYCRR) turn fiduciary ideals into specific rules. Scenario questions often turn on one section.
points: Don't buy a listing, directly or indirectly (an LLC counts), without first making your **true position clearly known** to the owner. Waiving the fee doesn't remove the duty (§175.4).
Disclose your ownership interest, whatever its size, to **all parties** before buying that property for a client, and to the buyer before selling it (§§175.5–175.6).

Don't negotiate directly with an owner you know has a **written exclusive** with another broker. Never **induce a party to break** a contract of sale or lease for a new principal, even for a higher price (§§175.8–175.9).

Offer property only with the **owner's authorization**, and place signs only with the owner's consent. Deliver copies of documents the broker prepared to each signer **immediately** (§§175.10–175.12).
Don't use or reward another broker's salesperson without that broker's knowledge. A departing salesperson turns over all listing information (§§175.13–175.14).
Listings get no **automatic continuation** past the fixed end date. Any extension needs the owner's separate agreement (§175.15).
**Net listings** are prohibited (§175.19).
Residential exclusives must carry the DOS explanation of the two listing types in at least **6-point type**, signed or initialed by the homeowner or the homeowner's agent (§175.24).
**Exclusive right to sell**: the owner pays even if the owner finds the buyer. **Exclusive agency**: an owner who finds the buyer owes nothing.

**Multiple listing service (MLS)**: a system where member brokers share listings and cooperate. An MLS member's residential exclusive must let the homeowner choose whether offers come through the listing broker or the selling broker (§175.24(c)).

No **blockbusting**: urging owners to sell because a protected class is moving in. Don't solicit owners who asked in writing not to be solicited or who are on the DOS list in a **cease-and-desist zone** (§175.17).
A discrimination finding is presumptive evidence of untrustworthiness.
Supervision must be **regular, frequent and consistent** and cover ads and client money; an annual meeting isn't enough (§175.21).
Part 175 doesn't decide employee or contractor status (§175.27).
Give the DOS **fair housing notice** at first substantive contact, and keep acknowledgments 3 years. Post the notice in offices, on website homepages and at open houses (§§175.28–175.29).
**Standardized operating procedures**: since April 20, 2022, brokers must date-stamp, notarize and post on their websites and apps the steps prospective homebuyers must complete (RPL §442-h(4)).

The procedures state at least whether ID, an exclusive buyer agreement and mortgage pre-approval are required. Brokers give copies on request at each office, archive each version, and post changes within 30 days.

example.title: Worked example: spotting a net listing
steps: Step 1: The seller says, 'I need to net $380,000; anything over that is yours.' The home sells for $412,000.
Step 2: The broker would keep $412,000 − $380,000 = $32,000.
Answer: Prohibited net listing under §175.19, even though the seller proposed it. A lawful alternative is a negotiated rate (5% = $20,600) plus a separate estimate of the seller's net.

sections.heading: Advertising and teams
sections.intro: In New York, **advertising** is any promotion of licensed activity, from signs and business cards to websites and email (19 NYCRR §175.25).
points: **Placement**: only the broker places ads. An associate broker, salesperson or team may advertise only property listed with or represented by their own broker, with that broker's approval.
Every property ad needs the **owner's authorization**.

**Another broker's exclusive** needs the listing broker's permission and must name that broker right after a phrase like 'Listing courtesy of.' If the licensee pays a third party for the ad, **'advertisement'** must follow the advertiser's name. Another broker's photos need the copyright holder's written permission.

**Identification**: the broker or brokerage name plus its address or phone number, including whenever an agent or team is named. An ad that leaves it out, hiding that a licensee is advertising, is a **blind ad**.
**Names and titles**: use your licensed name; a nickname needs the full licensed name shown clearly. State the license type accurately.
Banned titles: **'sales associate,' 'licensed sales agent' and 'broker' alone**.
Extra phone numbers must be labeled (cell, home, desk). An agent's logo must appear with the broker's name or logo.
**Honesty**: describe the property accurately, name the area where it actually is, and never **guarantee future profits**.
Classified and multi-property ads must identify the broker or brokerage but may omit named agents' license types. Signs must identify the broker.
**Business cards**: business address, license type, broker name and **office phone**.
**Websites**: broker-authorized and supervised, with the required information on **every page** (search-results pages included) and a homepage link to the broker's site.
**Email**: the required information goes in the **first** message to a person.
**Teams**: two or more people, at least one an associate broker or salesperson, at the **same brokerage**.
A team name must include **'team'**; 'realty,' 'group' and 'associates' are banned. It can't include an unlicensed person's name.
Without the members' full names, the team name must be followed by **'at/of [brokerage]'**. Team ads naming unlicensed people must say who is licensed.

sections.heading: Unlicensed assistants
sections.intro: DOS lets brokerages use unlicensed staff for clerical work; brokerage acts (showing, negotiating, soliciting, advising) stay with licensees.
points: **Permitted (DOS list)**: phones and messages; scheduling appointments and showings for licensees; following up on loan commitments after a contract is negotiated; assembling closing documents; drafting ads and flyers for broker approval; typing forms; computing commission checks; placing signs; ordering repairs as directed; gathering CMA or appraisal data; monitoring licenses; typing and filing.

**Not permitted**: showing property, hosting open houses, negotiating or hinting at a seller's bottom line, explaining contract terms, recommending prices, and **soliciting listings**, even with a script and hourly pay.

**Pay**: by the broker or the salesperson, **hourly, per activity or by salary**. Pay per closed deal requires a salesperson license and payment by the broker. The broker supervises assistants, and assistant time doesn't count toward broker experience.

Unlicensed assistant?

sections.heading: Discipline, penalties and court review
sections.intro: One violation can start three separate tracks: DOS discipline, a criminal case and a civil penalty suit.
points: **Grounds**: violating any part of Article 12-A; a material misstatement on the application; fraud; dishonest or misleading ads; untrustworthiness or incompetency; and Human Rights Law violations as a licensee (§441-c).
Low sales volume isn't misconduct. DOS also suspends licenses for unpaid child support on court order.
**Sanctions**: reprimand, **fine up to $2,000** (half to the anti-discrimination in housing fund), suspension or revocation, and denial of applications. Never jail.
**Process**: written charges at least **10 days** before the hearing, served in person or by certified mail (§441-e).
The licensee may be heard in person or through a lawyer. A salesperson's broker gets certified-mail notice.
DOS may suspend pending the hearing. An applicant facing denial has 30 days to request a hearing.
**After the decision**: return the license and pocket card within **5 days** of a suspension or revocation, or file an affidavit of loss.
After **revocation**, no relicensing for 1 year.
A broker's revocation or suspension **suspends every associated salesperson** until each changes association or the broker's suspension ends (§441-d).

A salesperson's violation is cause to discipline the broker only if the broker had **actual knowledge** or **kept the proceeds after notice** (§442-c). The broker's own supervision duty applies separately.
**Article 78** is the Civil Practice Law and Rules (CPLR) procedure for challenging a state or local agency's action in court (§441-f).
The applicant, the disciplined licensee or the **person aggrieved** may use Article 78, even against a refusal to discipline. The deadline is generally **4 months** (CPLR §217).
**Criminal**: every violation is a **misdemeanor**, a crime below a felony. One act is enough, and the Attorney General prosecutes (§442-e).
Older textbooks cite up to $1,000 and/or one year in jail; the Penal Law now caps a class A misdemeanor at 364 days.
**Civil penalty**: the person aggrieved may recover from a violator who was paid **at least the amount received and up to four times** it.
Unlicensed people who break cease-and-desist rules face DOS fines of $150, $500, then $1,000.

**Common violations**: commingling or conversion, unlicensed or expired-license practice, paying unlicensed people, undisclosed dual pay, net listings, blind or unauthorized ads, inducing breach, weak supervision, discrimination or blockbusting, misrepresentation, and practicing law (drafting deeds, giving legal opinions).

example.title: Worked example: an unlicensed finder collects $9,500
steps: Step 1: Negotiating a sale for another for a fee is broker activity, so a license was required.
Step 2: The unlicensed brokering is a misdemeanor the Attorney General may prosecute.
Step 3: Civil penalty: at least $9,500 and at most 4 × $9,500 = $38,000, recoverable by the person aggrieved.
Step 4: Had the fee not been paid yet, §442-d would bar any suit to collect it.
Answer: $9,500 to $38,000. The $2,000 figure is DOS's administrative fine, a different remedy.

sections.heading: Article 12-C: apartment information vendors and sharing agents
sections.intro: Article 12-C separately licenses businesses that sell rental information rather than broker leases.
points: **Apartment information vendor**: charges customers a fee for information on the location and availability of housing to rent, share or sublet.
**Apartment sharing agent**: arranges meetings, for a fee, between a customer and an occupant who wants to share.
Tenant relocation, negotiating leases and collecting rent are broker activities instead.
**License**: issued by the Secretary of State; minimum age 18; a supplemental license for each branch; a **1-year term, November 1 to October 31**.

**Trust account**: interest-bearing, at a bank with a New York office, of at least **$5,000 plus $2,500 per additional office** ($2,500 plus $1,250 for a sharing-only business); withdrawals need the Secretary's certification.
**Fees**: a DOS-approved contract must name the vendor's sources, and the fee can never exceed **one month's rent**.
From an **advance fee**, the vendor may keep at most **$15**. If the customer gives written notice that he didn't and won't rent through the vendor, the rest is refunded within 10 days.
Any amount above one month's rent is refunded even if he rents. A **sharing-only** agent may keep the whole advance fee.
**Discipline**: failing to report a change of business address or name within 10 days **forfeits** the license.
DOS may fine up to **$5,000**, order refunds, suspend or revoke. Violations are misdemeanors with the same 1×–4× civil penalty.

head: Feature
Article 12-A licensee
Article 12-C vendor
rows: Client funds in a special account within 3 business days

example.title: Worked example: refunds and trust accounts
steps: Step 1: A customer pays a $250 advance fee, finds nothing, and gives written notice. Refund = $250 − $15 = $235, within 10 days.
Step 2: A full vendor with 3 offices needs $5,000 + (2 × $2,500) = $10,000 in trust.
Step 3: A sharing-only business with 2 offices needs $2,500 + $1,250 = $3,750.
Answer: $235; $10,000; $3,750. Charging $5,000 per office ($15,000) is the classic wrong answer.

sections.heading: Seller disclosures in Subject 1: the PCDA and RPL §242
sections.intro: The syllabus places two seller-disclosure laws in this unit; the contracts and environmental chapters cover them further.
points: The **Property Condition Disclosure Act** (RPL Article 14) covers sales of **1–4 family homes**, including lease-options and installment contracts.
It doesn't cover vacant land, **condo or co-op units**, or HOA property the seller doesn't own outright.
**Seller's duty**: complete, sign and deliver the Property Condition Disclosure Statement (PCDS) to the buyer or buyer's agent **before the buyer signs a binding contract**.
A copy signed by both is attached to the contract. Answers reflect the seller's **actual knowledge**; no inspection is required.

**Changes**: the **$500 credit opt-out was eliminated** effective March 20, 2024; the form added flood questions, and DOS's revised form (with a septic-system information note) has been required since July 1, 2025.
**Revisions**: give a revised PCDS as soon as practicable if new knowledge makes it materially inaccurate. This isn't required after closing or the buyer's occupancy.
**Liability**: the seller owes actual damages only for a **willful** failure; other remedies remain.

**Exempt transfers** include court-ordered, foreclosure, fiduciary (estate, trust, guardianship), co-owner, family and divorce transfers, government and sheriff's sales, partitions, and **never-occupied new construction**.

**Agent's duty**: the listing agent tells the seller about the seller's obligations. The buyer's agent (or the seller's agent dealing with an unrepresented buyer) tells the buyer about the buyer's rights before a binding contract (§466).
Telling them ends the agent's PCDA liability. Agents shouldn't fill out the form.
A seller who **knows** of **uncapped natural gas wells** on the property must tell the purchaser before the contract (RPL §242).

**Written notice** is also required, before accepting an offer, if there's no utility electric service, a utility surcharge for a line extension, or a Green Jobs–Green New York on-bill recovery charge (RPL §242).

guides.title: Law of Agency
guides.overview: This chapter answers one question: whose interests must this licensee protect? It covers how agency is created and ended, the six fiduciary duties (OLD CAR), duties to customers, every New York agent role, disclosure forms, stigmatized property, misrepresentation, liability, fees and antitrust. The exam hits hardest on **client vs. customer**, **dual agency consent** and **§443 disclosure timing**.

mustKnow: **Client** = the represented principal, owed fiduciary duties; **customer** = a party served but not represented.
Agency sits at the **broker (firm) level**: salespersons act for the broker, and listings belong to the broker.
**Who pays does not decide who is represented**; the agency agreement and disclosed role do.
**OLD CAR** duties (obedience, loyalty, disclosure, confidentiality, accounting, reasonable care) are owed to the client only.
**Obedience** covers lawful instructions only: refuse to discriminate, lie or hide defects.
**Confidentiality** covers the client's private information (price limits, motivation, finances) and **survives termination**. It never covers a known defect.
Customers get **honesty, fair dealing and reasonable care**, plus disclosure of known material facts. 'Not my client' never excuses a lie.
Seller's agent to buyer: known facts affecting **value or desirability**. Buyer's agent to seller: known facts affecting the buyer's **ability or willingness to perform**.
Authority runs universal > general > special. A listing broker is a **special agent** and can't sign the sale contract without separate authority; a property manager is a **general agent**.
Agency arises by express agreement, implied conduct, **ratification** (later approval) or **estoppel** (reliance on apparent authority).
**Gratuitous agency** (no fee) carries full fiduciary duties.
**Puffing** is opinion; a false verifiable statement is **misrepresentation**.
Knowing falsity or active concealment, plus reliance and damage, is **fraud**.
Principals can be **vicariously liable** for agents and subagents acting within the agency. Brokers can be civilly liable for their salespersons.
A client has no vicarious liability for a **broker's agent**; the engaging agent directs it and is liable.
A **broker's agent** always works for a **different firm** from the agent who engaged it.
A **subagent** owes the seller full duties; a buyer working only with one is an **unrepresented customer**.
There is no **blanket unilateral offer of subagency** anymore. Sellers may reject subagency to limit liability.
**Dual agency** needs **informed written consent of both** parties. Both give up undivided loyalty, not confidentiality.
**Advance informed consent** to dual agency (with or without designated sales agents) is an optional box on the form.
**Designated sales agents** are salespersons or associate brokers, never the supervising broker. They advocate, but the **broker stays a dual agent**.
**Undisclosed dual agency** means DOS discipline, possible loss of commission and damages. A smooth closing doesn't cure it.
Always make your role clear. Pay from more than one party needs the **broker's client's** full knowledge and consent (§175.7).
The agency disclosure form covers **1–4 family** homes and **condo/co-op units** (any building size), for sales and rentals, but not vacant land or commercial property (RPL §443).
Give the form to your own client **before the agency agreement** (listing, buyer or tenant). Give it to the other side at **first substantive contact**.
**First substantive contact**: talk moves past basic listing facts to the consumer's needs, finances or motivation, or to seeing or offering on a specific property.
Greetings, a register signature, or an availability-and-asking-price question are not first substantive contact.
The form says **'THIS IS NOT A CONTRACT'**: signing acknowledges receipt only.
Give the signer a copy and keep one **3 years**. If the consumer refuses to sign, make a **written declaration under oath or affirmation** and keep it 3 years.
HIV/AIDS, a death, or a felony at the property is **not a material fact**. Silence brings no lawsuit and no discipline (§443-a).
A buyer's **written inquiry** about stigma goes through the seller's agent. The **seller decides** whether to answer, and nobody may lie (§443-a).
The stigma law covers **sales and leases** regardless of units and **preempts** local law. Physical damage from a crime is not stigma (§443-a).
Agency ends by performance, expiration, mutual agreement, revocation, renunciation, or **operation of law** (death, incapacity, bankruptcy, destruction, license loss).
Fees are **always negotiable**. No price fixing, boycotts, market allocation or tie-ins.
**Net listings** and automatic extensions of exclusive listings are banned.

traps.trap: Whoever pays the commission is the client.
traps.truth: Representation comes from the agreement and disclosed role; a buyer's agent paid from the seller's proceeds still represents only the buyer.

traps.trap: Signing the disclosure form hires the broker.
traps.truth: The form says 'THIS IS NOT A CONTRACT'; the signature only acknowledges receipt.

traps.trap: Designated sales agents end the dual agency.
traps.truth: In New York the broker stays a dual agent and designees cannot give undivided loyalty, whatever other states do.

traps.trap: Consenting to dual agency waives confidentiality.
traps.truth: Only undivided loyalty is given up; a dual agent never reveals either side's price or other confidences.

traps.trap: Confidentiality lets the agent hide a leak the seller wants kept quiet.
traps.truth: Confidentiality covers bargaining information, not defects; an instruction to conceal is unlawful.

traps.trap: Any licensee helping the listing agent is a broker's agent.
traps.truth: A broker's agent works for a different firm; an in-house salesperson acts within the seller's agency.

traps.trap: The seller is liable for a broker's agent just as for a subagent.
traps.truth: The engaging agent, not the seller, is liable for a broker's agent (§443). The seller can be liable for a subagent.

traps.trap: If a buyer won't sign the acknowledgment, the agent must stop working with her.
traps.truth: Make a written declaration of the refusal under oath or affirmation, keep it 3 years, and continue.

traps.trap: The agency disclosure form is required for all residential property.
traps.truth: Only 1–4 family homes and condo/co-op units are covered (§443). An 8-unit rental building and vacant land are out, though the fair housing notice still applies.

traps.trap: A death isn't material, so the agent may say no one died there.
traps.truth: The law removes the duty to volunteer, not the duty of honesty (§443-a). Point the buyer to the written inquiry.

traps.trap: The stigma law, like the disclosure law, covers only 1–4 family sales.
traps.truth: The stigma law covers property offered for sale or lease, regardless of the number of units (§443-a).

traps.trap: A broker paid by both sides needs every party's consent.
traps.truth: Only the broker's client must give full knowledge and consent (§175.7). Older textbooks say 'all parties'; current law says the client.

traps.trap: The listing moves with the salesperson who took it.
traps.truth: It is the broker's contract and stays with the broker.

traps.trap: A listing broker can sign the sale contract for the seller.
traps.truth: A special agent cannot bind the seller without separate authority.

traps.trap: A no-fee favor creates no fiduciary duty.
traps.truth: Gratuitous agency is still agency; consent, not payment, creates the duties.

sections.heading: Agency basics: parties, the firm, and authority
sections.intro: Start every agency question by naming the client, then ask what the licensee owes everyone else.
points: **Agency**: a principal authorizes an agent to act on its behalf, and the agent accepts.
Agency is **fiduciary**: the client's interests come before everyone else's, including the agent's own.
A **client** is the represented principal and is owed fiduciary duties.
A **customer** is a party the agent works with but does not represent, such as an unrepresented buyer viewing a listing. A **third party** is anyone outside the relationship.
An **agent** is a licensed broker, associate broker or salesperson acting in a fiduciary capacity (RPL §443).
Agency is created at the **firm level**: listings and buyer agreements are the broker's contracts. Salespersons act for the broker as subagents of its clients.
**Brokerage is not the same as agency.** Brokerage is the licensed business; agency is representation.
MLS membership, cooperating on a deal, helping a customer or paying the fee does not decide whom an agent represents.
A salesperson may be paid for licensed work **only by her sponsoring broker** (RPL §442-a), never directly by a buyer, seller or customer.
A **power of attorney** is only as broad as its terms: one limited to selling one condo creates special agency, not universal agency.
The principal owes the agent **cooperation** and agreed **compensation**.
The principal also owes **indemnification** if the agent is held liable because the principal hid facts or lied.

sections.heading: How agency is created
sections.intro: Agency rests on consent, which can be stated, inferred from conduct, given after the fact, or imposed by law to protect someone who relied on it.
points: **Express agency**: created by words, written or oral, such as a signed listing or buyer agency agreement. Writing is strongly preferred because it proves duties, term and fee.
**Implied agency**: inferred from conduct. A seller's agent who coaches an open-house visitor on bidding and inspection leverage can create an implied buyer agency.
On top of the listing, that implied buyer agency is **undisclosed dual agency**.
**Ratification**: the principal approves an unauthorized act after the fact. Example: the seller signs a contract including the dining set the agent promised without authority.
**Estoppel** (ostensible or apparent authority): the principal's conduct or silence leads a third party to reasonably believe an agency exists, so the principal cannot deny it.
Ratification turns on later approval; estoppel turns on reliance. Neither needs a signed writing.
**Gratuitous agency**: acting without a fee still creates full fiduciary duties.
Factual help to a customer, such as filling in an offer form or describing the home, does not create buyer agency; advocacy and negotiating advice can. Explain your role early.

head: Method
How it arises
Exam clue
rows: Agent acts as the consumer's advocate
Later approval of an unauthorized act
Third party relies on the principal's conduct or silence
Owner never corrects a false claim of agency

sections.heading: Fiduciary duties: OLD CAR
sections.intro: The DOS forms list a client's six duties as reasonable care, undivided loyalty, confidentiality, full disclosure, obedience and duty to account. OLD CAR puts them in memorable order.
points: **Obedience**: follow lawful instructions, such as showing hours, notice before showings or no lawn sign.

Obedience never covers unlawful acts. Refusing families with children is familial-status discrimination; calling a 25-year-old roof new is misrepresentation. Refuse, and withdraw if the client insists.
**Loyalty**: the client's interests come before the agent's commission.
Loyalty breaches include undisclosed **self-dealing** (buying the listing through a spouse or LLC) and steering a buyer toward homes paying a higher fee.
**Disclosure**: tell the client every material fact, including every offer and the agent's conflicts. The client decides whether to reject an offer.
A buyer's agent shares facts that help the buyer, such as public records showing the seller is in foreclosure.
**Confidentiality**: protect the client's price limits, motivation, deadlines and finances, even after the agency ends. It never covers hiding a material defect.
**Accounting** (accountability): safeguard and account for money, keys and documents. Deposit escrow promptly and never **commingle** it with business funds. This duty also survives termination.
**Reasonable care**: act competently, verify what you say, and refer legal, tax and engineering questions (such as an easement's effect) to professionals.
Spot the duty from the facts: no instruction means it isn't obedience; a withheld offer is disclosure; leaked information is confidentiality; money or keys is accounting.

head: Duty
Classic breach
rows: Showing on 1 hour's notice when the seller required 24
Secretly buying the listing through a spouse's LLC
Telling the listing agent the buyer is preapproved for more
Deposit left in a drawer, then put in the operating account
Assuring a buyer an easement won't block a garage

sections.heading: Duties to customers: honesty without advocacy
sections.intro: Everyone in the transaction is owed honesty. The DOS forms spell out what each agent owes the party it does not represent.
points: A **seller's or landlord's agent** dealing with the other side must use reasonable skill and care, deal honestly, fairly and in good faith, and disclose known facts **materially affecting value or desirability**, except as law provides.

A **buyer's or tenant's agent** owes the seller the same care and honesty and discloses known facts materially affecting the **buyer's ability and/or willingness to perform**, consistent with its duties to the buyer.

A **material fact** would likely change a reasonable party's decision: a leaking basement, failed septic, flood history. A known defect must be disclosed however the agent learned of it, even from an earlier buyer's inspection.

Bargaining information is not a property fact owed to the other side. The seller's price floor, reason for moving and deadline, the landlord's minimum rent, and the buyer's top price all stay confidential.
Decline to answer; never lie. If you don't know whether the septic ever failed, say so and find out.
A client's instruction to lie is no defense. 'She's only a customer' never excuses a false flood-zone answer.

example.title: Worked example: protecting the price without lying
steps: Facts: A buyer customer asks the listing agent, 'Will the seller take $20,000 less?' The seller has privately said yes.
Step 1: The seller is the client; the buyer is owed honesty, not confidentiality.
Step 2: The price floor is confidential bargaining information, not a property fact.
Step 3: Saying 'Yes' breaches confidentiality.
Step 4: Saying 'Not a penny less' is a misrepresentation.
Answer: 'I can't share the seller's position; submit your best offer and I'll present it.'

sections.heading: Misrepresentation, puffing, and fraud
sections.intro: **Misrepresentation** is a false statement or concealment of a material fact that someone relies on. The agent's state of mind decides how serious it is.
points: **Puffing** is exaggerated opinion a reasonable buyer wouldn't treat as fact ('best light on the block'). Anything verifiable (taxes, zoning, roof age, square footage, sewer, flood zone, other offers) is a statement of fact.

**Negligent misrepresentation**: the agent should have known, such as posting the seller's 2,400 square foot guess when records show 1,850. Repeating the seller's figure is no defense when the agent had reason to check.
**Fraud** needs a knowingly false statement or concealment of a material fact, made to induce reliance, plus justifiable reliance and damage.
**Active concealment**, like painting over a leak stain, is fraud without words. Staging may not hide a known defect.

**Self-dealing** requires disclosure first. A broker may not buy a listed property, directly or indirectly, without making his position clear to the owner (19 NYCRR §175.4), and must disclose his interest when buying for a client or selling his own property (§§175.5–175.6).
Consequences: damages, **rescission**, lost commission, and DOS discipline under RPL §441-c (reprimand, fine up to **$2,000**, suspension or revocation).

sections.heading: Vicarious liability
sections.intro: **Vicarious liability** makes a person answer for wrongs committed by those acting with authority on that person's behalf.
points: A **principal is vicariously liable** for its agents and **subagents** acting within the agency: a seller can be sued over a cooperating subagent's false school-district claim.
A sponsoring **broker** can be civilly liable for a salesperson's acts on firm business, in addition to the salesperson's own liability.

License discipline is narrower. A salesperson's violation can cost the broker's license only if the broker had **actual knowledge** or **kept the benefits** after notice of the misconduct (RPL §442-c).
The broker's own failure to supervise is a separate violation (§175.21).
**Broker's agent rule**: the seller or buyer has no direct relationship with a broker's agent and cannot instruct it. So neither has **vicarious liability** for its acts (§443).
The listing or buyer's agent that engaged and directs the broker's agent is liable. A seller passes instructions through the listing agent.
To widen cooperation while limiting exposure, a seller authorizes **buyer's agents and broker's agents** and **rejects subagency**.

head: Who misstated
Who else may be liable
rows: The engaging agent, not the seller
Its own broker and possibly the buyer; not the seller

sections.heading: Agent roles, subagency, and buyer agency
sections.intro: New York's forms name the roles a licensee can play. Know whom each represents and how cooperating agents fit in.
points: **Seller's agent**: engaged by the seller to find a buyer on the seller's terms.
The term also includes the listing agent, an agent cooperating with it, a seller's subagent, and a broker's agent finding a buyer (§443).
**Landlord's agent** and **tenant's agent** are the rental versions. They appear only on DOS-1735.
**Buyer's agent**: engaged by the buyer to locate property and negotiate for the buyer. It gives the buyer loyalty, confidentiality and advice on price and terms.
The buyer, the seller or the listing broker's split may pay a buyer's agent; it still represents only the buyer.
Not everyone needs an agent: a buyer may proceed as a customer, often with an attorney.
**Subagent**: an agent of the agent, owing the seller full fiduciary duties. In-house salespersons are subagents of the firm's clients.
Another firm becomes a subagent only by accepting an offer of subagency that the seller and listing broker authorized. A buyer working only with a subagent is an **unrepresented customer**.
The old **blanket unilateral offer of subagency** made every MLS member automatically the seller's subagent. It no longer exists.
The seller decides in the listing agreement whether to allow subagents, buyer's agents and broker's agents. Brokerage works fine without subagency.
**Broker's agent**: engaged by or cooperating with a listing, buyer's or tenant's agent but working for a **different firm**.
Example: a Rochester licensee engaged by a Buffalo buyer's agent to find homes for that buyer is a broker's agent for the buyer. A salesperson in the listing firm never is.
**Single agency**: the firm represents one party in a transaction, never both. Some firms practice it exclusively (seller-only or buyer-only), so they never act as dual agents.
A **cooperating agent** from another firm must disclose whether it is a subagent, buyer's agent or broker's agent. Its actual agreement decides, not who called first.
A listing-firm salesperson showing to unrepresented buyers represents the seller. New York forms have no 'facilitator' role.
In NYC rentals, the fee of a broker representing the landlord, such as the listing agent, cannot be passed to the tenant, even by lease clause.
That rule is the **FARE Act**, effective **June 11, 2025**. The Second Circuit upheld it on July 13, 2026.

sections.heading: Dual agency and designated sales agents
sections.intro: A **dual agent** represents both buyer and seller (or tenant and landlord) in one transaction. New York allows it only with informed written consent, and it always costs undivided loyalty.
points: Most dual agency arises from **in-house sales**: a firm's buyer client wants the firm's own listing.
Because agency sits at the firm level, the firm is a dual agent even if different salespersons handle each side. This is **broker dual agency**.
One salesperson representing both sides (**single-licensee dual agency**) is also allowed with consent.
**Informed consent**: each party understands that the agent also acts for the other side, and what that costs, then agrees **in writing**. Oral, one-sided or payer-only consent fails.
The risk is built in: the seller wants the highest price and the buyer the lowest.
Both parties **give up undivided loyalty** but keep honesty, reasonable care, accounting and confidentiality. Neither side's price goes to the other.
**Advance informed consent** (since Jan 1, 2011) is an optional box on the form. If it's left blank, dual agency needs later written consent, and the listing stays valid.
Even with advance consent, DOS guidance says the showing licensee must notify the seller, or the seller's designated agent, once an in-house showing produces real interest.

**Designated sales agents**: with both parties' informed written consent, the broker assigns one salesperson or associate broker to each side. Each advocates for its own party and keeps that party's confidences, but the **broker remains a dual agent** and no designee gives undivided loyalty.

The supervising broker cannot be a designee, and one person cannot be the designee for both sides. Advance consent with designated agents names the consenting party's own designee; the other side's need not be known yet.
If either party refuses consent, the firm cannot represent both; it may keep one client while the other seeks separate representation.

**Undisclosed dual agency**, including an implied agency from coaching a customer, brings DOS discipline, possible loss of commission, damages and rescission. A good price or smooth closing doesn't cure it.
Firm policy sets the options: seller agency only, buyer agency only, consensual dual agency for in-house sales, or designated agents.

head: Feature

rows: Each designee advocates for its party

example.title: Worked example: an in-house sale
steps: Facts: Kim of ABC Realty represents buyer Lee, who wants a house listed by ABC salesperson Ortiz. The seller gave advance consent to dual agency with designated sales agents, naming Ortiz.
Step 1: ABC represents both sides, so ABC is a dual agent.
Step 2: The seller's written consent is on file; Lee must also consent in writing, after Kim explains that neither side gets undivided loyalty.
Step 3: With both consents, Kim is designated for Lee and Ortiz for the seller; ABC's broker supervises.
Answer: Lawful once Lee consents. Kim may negotiate hard for Lee, neither designee shares confidences, and ABC remains the dual agent.

sections.heading: RPL §443 agency disclosure: scope, timing, and paperwork
sections.intro: New York requires a state-written disclosure in residential deals so consumers know whom each licensee represents before sharing confidences. It adds a form to a broader rule for every transaction, commercial and vacant land included: always make clear which party you represent (19 NYCRR §175.7).
points: **Scope**: property improved by a 1–4 family dwelling or by condo or co-op apartments in a building of any size, for sales and rentals.
**Excluded**: unimproved land (even if a home will be built), 5+ unit rental buildings that aren't condos or co-ops, and commercial property such as a retail lease.
**DOS-1736** covers buyers and sellers (including co-op share sales); **DOS-1735** covers landlords and tenants (including renting a co-op unit).
**Timing**: the listing agent gives it to the seller or landlord before the listing agreement. A buyer's or tenant's agent gives it to its client before the agency agreement.
Each agent gives it to the **other side at first substantive contact**, including a for-sale-by-owner seller.
**First substantive contact**: talk moves past a greeting or basic listing facts into the consumer's needs, finances or motivation, or into seeing or offering on a specific property.

Counts: a walk-in asking to see three listings, or a visitor discussing her budget. Doesn't count: a guest-register signature, a single fact question (year built), or an availability-and-asking-price call.
A phone or email exchange can become substantive; the form can then be emailed or faxed.
Make your role clear first and explain the form; don't just collect a signature. A seller's agent who claims to be 'neutral' misrepresents her role, and what the buyer reveals belongs to her seller.
**Acknowledgment**: the consumer signs for receipt. The licensee prints name and firm and checks the role box; no notary is needed.
A buyer's agent may get the seller-side signature from the seller or the listing agent.
Give the signer a copy and keep one **3 years**. Nothing is filed with DOS.
**Refusal**: the agent signs a **written declaration of the facts under oath or affirmation** (an initialed note won't do), keeps it 3 years, and may keep working with the person.
**'THIS IS NOT A CONTRACT'**: the form sets no fee or term. It gives no dual-agency consent unless an advance box is checked.
The form warns that each assisting agent may give its own form, refers legal and tax questions to professionals, and has no facilitator box.

Only licensees acting as agents give it; an owner renting directly gives none. Licensees working by agreement in a non-agent capacity are exempt (§443(5)), and the common law of agency still applies (§443(6)).
A role change (such as buyer's agent to dual agent) requires a new explanation, disclosure and consent.

**Pre-2011 vs. now**: condo/co-op units in buildings over four units were excluded, and dual-agency consent was allowed only once a specific deal existed. Since Jan 1, 2011, all condo/co-op units are covered and advance consent is available.
The fair housing notice (DOS-2156, §175.28) is a separate document. It applies to all real property, including commercial and vacant land.
The Property Condition Disclosure Statement covers most 1–4 family home sales and has had no $500 opt-out since 2024. Neither document replaces the agency form.

example.title: Worked example: disclosure moments on one listing
steps: Step 1: Ana explains DOS-1736 to the sellers and gets their acknowledgment before they sign the listing agreement.
Step 2: An open-house visitor signs in, asks the year built and leaves: no form yet.
Step 3: Another visitor starts discussing her budget and moving deadline: Ana says she represents the sellers and gives the form.
Step 4: That visitor refuses to sign: Ana prepares a sworn or affirmed declaration and keeps it 3 years.
Answer: Before the listing, then at each first substantive contact; copies to signers, 3-year retention.

sections.heading: RPL §443-a: stigmatized property
sections.intro: A **stigmatized property** carries a psychological taint rather than a physical defect. New York's stigma law says which stigmas are not material facts (RPL §443-a).
points: **Not a material fact**: an owner or occupant has, had or was suspected of having HIV/AIDS or another disease highly unlikely to spread through occupancy.
Also **not a material fact**: the property was the site of a homicide, suicide or other death (accidental or natural), or of any felony.
Nondisclosure creates **no cause of action** against owners or agents and is **not grounds for DOS discipline**.
**Written inquiry**: a buyer who cares may submit a written question through the seller's agent (or to the seller if none) when negotiating or making a bona fide offer.
The **seller decides whether to answer**. The agent relays an answer only with the seller's consent and subject to privacy laws.
No duty to volunteer is not permission to lie. Asked casually whether anyone died there, the agent must not answer falsely and should explain the written-inquiry route.
The law covers property offered for **sale or lease**, including residential property regardless of the number of units (§443-a). It **preempts** inconsistent local laws.
Only the event is stigma. Known physical conditions it left, such as drug-lab chemical residue, must be disclosed.

**Stambovsky v. Ackley** (1991): the seller had publicized her house as haunted, then stayed silent with an out-of-town buyer. She could not rely on buyer-beware, and the court let the buyer seek rescission of the contract.

**Glazer v. LoPreste** (2000): sellers and brokers had no duty to volunteer that a convicted sex offender lived nearby, since the information was publicly available. Buyers can check the registry themselves.

sections.heading: Compensation, listing agreements, and antitrust
sections.intro: The listing or buyer agreement, not the disclosure form, sets the fee, the term and when the fee is earned. Every fee is negotiable.
points: There is **no standard or legal commission rate**. A fee is typically earned when the broker produces a **ready, willing and able** buyer on the client's terms, or as the agreement says.

A broker must make clear which party it acts for. It may be paid by **more than one party** only with the **full knowledge and consent of the broker's client** (§175.7). Older textbooks say 'all parties'; current law requires only the client.
Federal **RESPA §8** separately bars kickbacks for referring buyers to lenders or mortgage brokers on federally related loans; consent doesn't cure them.
A seller's broker who also acts as the buyer's mortgage broker must give the separate Department of Financial Services (DFS) dual agency disclosure (3 NYCRR §38.12).
**Net listings** are prohibited (§175.19), and exclusive listings may not **automatically continue** past their end date (§175.15).

Exclusive residential listings must include the DOS explanation of exclusive right to sell versus exclusive agency, signed or initialed by the owner (§175.24), and signers get copies immediately (§175.12).
**Antitrust** (Sherman Act; New York's Donnelly Act): competing firms may not agree on price fixing, group boycotts (shunning a discount firm) or market allocation (dividing territories).
No firm may impose **tie-ins**, such as requiring a certain lender as a condition of service.
Sherman Act violations are felonies: up to **10 years** and $1 million for individuals, and **$100 million** for corporations.

example.title: Worked example: following the money
steps: Facts: $500,000 sale, negotiated 5% commission split 50/50 between firms; the buyer's salesperson gets 60% of her firm's side.
Step 2: $25,000 × 0.50 = $12,500 to the buyer's firm.
Step 3: $12,500 × 0.60 = $7,500, paid by her own broker.
Answer: $7,500. Seller-funded, yet the buyer's agent still represents only the buyer.

sections.heading: Terminating agency
sections.intro: Agency ends by the parties' acts or automatically by operation of law. Some duties outlive it.
points: By the parties: performance (the sale closes), expiration of the term, mutual agreement, **revocation** by the principal, or **renunciation** by the agent. Example of renunciation: withdrawing because the seller insists on hiding a defect.
A principal has the **power** to revoke at any time, unless the agency is coupled with an interest, but not always the **right**.
Revoking an exclusive listing early without cause ends the agency, but the seller may owe damages. The broker then stops marketing (MLS, signs, lockbox).

**Operation of law** ends agency with no notice needed: death or incapacity of the principal or of an individual agent (such as a sole-proprietor broker), bankruptcy, **destruction** or condemnation of the property, or loss of the broker's license.
If the house burns, the listing ends; selling the land needs a new agreement.
A salesperson's death or departure does not end a listing; it stays with the broker, and the departing salesperson must turn over all listing information (§175.14).
**Agency coupled with an interest** (the agent has its own stake in the property) cannot be revoked by the principal and survives the principal's death.
**Confidentiality** and **accounting** survive: never reveal a former client's bottom line, and return all keys and funds.

head: Way it ends

rows: No automatic renewal of exclusive listings

sections.heading: Independent contractor or employee
sections.intro: Most salespersons are independent contractors for tax purposes, but only if federal and state tests are met. Classification never ends the agency relationship or the broker's duty to supervise.
points: **Statutory nonemployee** (federal tax law, Internal Revenue Code §3508): a licensed agent whose pay is substantially all tied to sales or output, not hours, with a **written contract** saying the agent won't be treated as an employee for tax purposes.

**New York test** (Labor Law and Workers' Compensation Law rules dating to 1986): pay must be output-based, and the written contract must have been signed **within the past 12 to 15 months**, not under duress.
The contract must state that the salesperson is an independent contractor, paid commissions without tax deductions and nothing for hours.
It must also state that she may work any hours, from home or the office, and take outside work, and that she pays her own expenses (the broker may supply office space).
Finally, it must state that both will follow the license law (RPL Article 12-A) and that either party may end the arrangement at any time on notice.
**Substance over form**: if the broker pays hourly or sets mandatory hours, the contract won't save the classification. The broker **supervises** but does not direct and control the details.

If the test fails, salespersons are **employees**: the broker owes unemployment insurance, workers' compensation and disability coverage and must withhold income and Social Security taxes; the salesperson loses Schedule C expense deductions.
Either way, brokers must give **regular, frequent and consistent** supervision (§175.21) and keep transaction records **3 years** (§175.23).

guides.title: Legal Issues & Land Title
guides.overview: How New York ownership changes hands: deeds, delivery, recording, title searches and insurance, legal descriptions, adverse possession, inheritance, escheat, and eminent domain. The exam hits three ideas hardest: **title passes on delivery**, not recording; a later buyer wins only as a good-faith purchaser for value who **records first**; and deed forms differ in what they promise.
