mustKnow: **Title** is ownership; a **deed** is the writing that transfers it. The grantor conveys and the grantee receives.

A valid deed needs a writing, a competent grantor, a living, identifiable grantee, words of conveyance, a consideration recital, a legal description, the grantor's signature, and **delivery and acceptance**.
Only the **grantor** must sign. Grantees need no capacity, but a deed to a grantee who **died before delivery** is void.
A **minor's** deed (under 18) is **voidable**, not void, and recording doesn't cure it.
Deeds need no witnesses. **Acknowledgment** is needed only to **record**, not for validity.
**Title passes on delivery and acceptance**, not at signing and not at recording.
**Delivery** means giving up control with **present intent**. A deed kept in the grantor's safe, or held by her own attorney until she decides, isn't delivered.
Acceptance is presumed for a beneficial deed, but an **express refusal** defeats it. Destroying or returning a delivered deed **doesn't reconvey** the land.
**Recording** gives constructive notice and priority. It can't pass title, cure non-delivery, or validate a **forged deed**.
New York is a **race-notice** state: a later buyer wins only as a good-faith purchaser for value who **records first** (RPL §291).
Donees and heirs can't use the recording act to defeat an earlier unrecorded deed. **Mortgagees for value** can.
Someone other than the seller **in possession** gives **inquiry notice**.
Record with the **county clerk** where the land lies. Most of NYC records with the City Register through **ACRIS**.
Deed strength: **full covenant and warranty > bargain and sale with covenant > bargain and sale without covenants > quitclaim**.
The five covenants: **seisin, quiet enjoyment, against encumbrances, further assurances, warranty**. Seisin and against encumbrances are **present** covenants.
The **bargain and sale deed with covenant against grantor's acts** is the usual NY residential deed; it covers only the **seller's own** acts.
A **quitclaim** passes whatever interest the grantor has, with no warranties. It's the standard way to clear a **cloud on title**.
**Referee's deed** = foreclosure or partition sale.
**Executor's deed** = estate with a will; **administrator's deed** = estate without one.
**Granting clause** = words of conveyance; **habendum** ('to have and to hold') = the estate granted.
An **exception** keeps land out of the deed; a **reservation** keeps a new right such as an easement. 'Subject to' lists encumbrances the buyer accepts.
NY deeds usually recite nominal consideration. The real price goes on the **TP-584**, which both parties sign, and the **RP-5217**.
The RP-5217 gives sale data to assessors and ORPTS, the state Office of Real Property Tax Services.
NYS transfer tax: **$2 per $500 or fraction**, units rounded up, paid by the **seller**.
**Chain of title** = owner-to-owner links; abstract = summary of every recorded document; **marketable title** = free of reasonable doubt.
An **owner's policy** covers the buyer and heirs while they own; a **lender's policy** covers only the lender, up to the loan balance. NY buyers customarily pay for both, once, at closing.
Title insurance covers **hidden defects existing on the policy date**. Survey matters and **parties in possession** are standard exceptions.
**Metes and bounds** starts and ends at the point of beginning, and **monuments beat distances**.
Bearings run from N or S toward E or W. Reversing a line **flips both letters** (N 60° E becomes S 60° W).
NY uses metes and bounds, filed maps, and tax maps, not the **rectangular survey**. **1 acre = 43,560 sq ft**.
**Adverse possession** takes **10 years** of hostile, actual, open and notorious, exclusive, continuous possession under claim of right. Paying taxes isn't required, and tacking is allowed.
Since 2008, **claim of right** means a reasonable basis to believe you own the land.
Since 2008, de minimis fences, hedges, and sheds, plus mowing, are **permissive**.
A **quiet title** judgment makes an adverse possessor's title marketable.
Intestate with spouse and issue: the spouse gets **$50,000 + half the rest**. With no issue, the spouse takes **everything**.
The **elective share** is the greater of **$50,000 or ⅓**.
A will needs a testator 18+, a signature **at the end**, and **two witnesses** signing within 30 days. Holographic wills count only for wartime military and mariners at sea.
**Devise** = real property by will; **bequest** = personal property; probate = the Surrogate's Court proving the will.
**Escheat** happens only if **no distributee** survives.
**Eminent domain** requires **just compensation**, plus severance damages after a partial taking.

traps.trap: Title passes when the deed is recorded.
traps.truth: Title passes on delivery and acceptance; recording only gives notice and priority.

traps.trap: A deed that isn't notarized or witnessed is invalid.
traps.truth: The deed is valid between the parties; NY requires no witnesses for validity. Without an acknowledgment, or proof by a subscribing witness, it can't be recorded.

traps.trap: Whoever records first always wins.
traps.truth: Only a good-faith purchaser for value who records first wins. A donee, or a buyer with notice, loses even after recording first.

traps.trap: Recording a forged deed protects the innocent buyer who records.
traps.truth: A forged deed is void, and recording can't fix that. Title insurance is the protection.

traps.trap: A quitclaim conveys nothing, or only a defective title.
traps.truth: A quitclaim conveys whatever the grantor owns, possibly full title. It just carries no warranties.

traps.trap: A bargain and sale deed without covenants is the same as a quitclaim.
traps.truth: The quitclaim is weaker. The bargain and sale deed's granting words imply the grantor has title; a quitclaim implies nothing.

traps.trap: A bargain and sale deed with covenant protects against an earlier owner's liens.
traps.truth: Its covenant covers only what the grantor did or allowed. Only the full covenant deed reaches older defects.

traps.trap: The lender's title policy protects the buyer too.
traps.truth: It protects only the lender. The buyer needs an owner's policy, and the seller's old policy doesn't pass to the buyer.

traps.trap: Title insurance covers title problems that arise after closing.
traps.truth: A standard policy covers only defects that existed on the policy date, subject to its exceptions. Only enhanced homeowner's policies add a few later risks, such as post-closing forgery.

traps.trap: Ten years of using a neighbor's strip automatically gives title.
traps.truth: Every element must be proven, including claim of right. Mowing and de minimis fences, hedges, and sheds are permissive. Paying the taxes is neither required nor enough.

traps.trap: Dying without a will sends property to the state.
traps.truth: Escheat happens only if no distributee survives; even a first cousin inherits ahead of the state.

traps.trap: A spouse with no children shares the estate with the decedent's parents.
traps.truth: With no issue, the spouse takes everything; parents inherit only if there's no spouse and no issue.

traps.trap: A signed, handwritten will is valid, especially if notarized.
traps.truth: Everyone except wartime military and mariners at sea needs two witnesses, and notarizing can't replace them. Only those groups can use unwitnessed handwritten wills.

traps.trap: The court appoints an executor when there's no will.
traps.truth: With no will, the court appoints an administrator. An executor is named in a will.

traps.trap: One acre is 48,400 square feet.
traps.truth: One acre is 43,560 sq ft (4,840 sq yd).

sections.heading: What makes a deed valid
sections.intro: A **deed** is the written instrument that transfers **title** (ownership) of real property. The sale contract promises a conveyance; the deed delivered at closing makes it.
points: The **grantor** ('party of the first part' on NY forms) conveys. The **grantee** ('party of the second part') receives.
A **conveyance** is the transfer or the document that makes it. **Alienation** is any transfer of ownership.
A conveyance must be **in writing and subscribed by the grantor**, or by an agent authorized in writing such as an attorney-in-fact (General Obligations Law §5-703).
A **minor's** deed is **voidable**: it stands unless the minor disaffirms it. A grantor who lacked mental capacity can have the deed set aside. Recording cures neither.
The **grantee** must be identifiable and **alive at delivery**; an entity grantee must already exist. A deed to someone already dead is void. Minors can be grantees.

Unstated shares are presumed equal. Co-grantees take as **tenants in common** unless the deed expressly creates a joint tenancy. Spouses take as **tenants by the entirety** unless the deed says otherwise (EPTL §6-2.2).
A grantor conveys only what she owns. If one of two tenants in common signs a deed for 'the property,' the buyer gets only her undivided share.
Validity needs no **witnesses** and no grantee's signature. A grantee signs only to take on a duty, such as assuming the seller's mortgage (GOL §5-705).
**Acknowledgment** matters only for recording.

sections.intro: Questions often quote deed language and ask which clause it is.
points: NY deeds usually recite **nominal consideration**. The real price is reported on the TP-584 and RP-5217.
A **gift deed** is valid. But a donee isn't a purchaser for value, so the recording act protects a donee less.
**Exception:** that piece never passes, and the grantor keeps owning it. **Reservation:** the land passes, but the grantor keeps a new right in it, usually an easement.
'**Subject to**' language lets the buyer take title burdened by the listed encumbrances without a covenant claim against the grantor. It neither creates nor ends them.
Discriminatory restrictions in old deeds are unenforceable.
A **correction deed** from the same grantor to the same grantee fixes clerical errors, such as a misspelled name or a transposed lot number, without a new sale.

head: Clause
Typical wording
Effect
rows: 'does hereby grant and release unto the party of the second part'
'ten dollars and other good and valuable consideration'
'to have and to hold ... forever' or 'for and during her natural life'
Fee simple, or a life estate
'subject to a utility easement of record'
'except the two-acre homesite in the northeast corner'
Keeps that land out of the deed
'reserving to the grantor a right of way'
Seller holds the proceeds as a trust fund to pay first for improvements
Protects the title against mechanic's liens for recent work (Lien Law §13(5))

sections.heading: Covenants in a full covenant and warranty deed
sections.intro: A **covenant** is a promise in the deed. New York's statutory full covenant and warranty deed has five (RPL §§253, 258). Books that count six split 'right to convey' out of seisin.
points: **Present** covenants (seisin, against encumbrances) are breached at delivery or never.
**Future** covenants (quiet enjoyment, further assurances, warranty) are breached later, when a superior claim surfaces.
Only this deed warrants against defects from **any period**, including those created before the grantor owned the land.
The **covenant against grantor's acts** says the grantor 'has not done or suffered anything' to encumber the land. It isn't one of the five.
It's the only title covenant in the bargain and sale deed with covenant and in the statutory executor's deed.

head: Covenant
The grantor promises
Type
rows: I own this estate and may convey it
No liens or encumbrances except those listed
No one with better title will disturb you
I'll sign anything else needed to perfect your title
I'll forever defend your title against all lawful claims

sections.heading: Forms of deeds, ranked by protection
sections.intro: New York's statutory deed forms are optional (RPL §258). The sale contract decides which one the seller must deliver.
points: The **bargain and sale deed with covenant** is the usual New York residential deed. Other states call the closest equivalent a special warranty deed.
A judgment lien against an earlier owner falls outside its covenant. Title insurance handles that.
A **bargain and sale deed without covenants** says 'grant and release,' which implies the grantor has title.
A **quitclaim** ('remise, release and quitclaim') implies nothing, so it's the weakest deed. It still passes full title if the grantor has it.
A quitclaim is the standard cure for a **cloud on title**, such as a possible claim by an heir or ex-spouse.
**Court and fiduciary deeds** carry no full warranties.
NY residential foreclosures are court cases, so the winning bidder gets a **referee's deed**. A court-ordered partition sale between co-owners ends the same way.

head: Deed
What the grantor promises
Typical use
rows: All five covenants, against claims from any era
Implied title; grantor did nothing to encumber it
Whatever interest the grantor has, if any
Clearing clouds; family and divorce transfers
Customarily the covenant against grantor's acts only
Customarily the covenant against grantor's acts only
Administrator sells for an intestate estate

sections.heading: Delivery and acceptance
sections.intro: Title passes at delivery and acceptance, so these questions turn on whether the grantor truly let go.
points: **Delivery** means the grantor gives up control with the **intent that title pass now**. The deed goes to the grantee or the grantee's agent, such as an attorney or title company.
**Not delivered:** a deed kept in the grantor's own safe-deposit box, held by the grantor's own attorney until she decides, or found after death.
Delivery must happen **during the grantor's life**.
An **escrow** agent holding the deed under **irrevocable instructions** is different. The grantor can't recall it, so delivery can be valid.
**Acceptance** is presumed when the deed benefits the grantee. An **express refusal**, such as mailing back a deed to a contaminated lot, means title never passed.
After delivery, returning or tearing up the deed **doesn't reconvey** the land.
Recording raises a presumption of delivery but **can't cure non-delivery**.
Sequence: grantor signs → acknowledges → delivers, grantee accepts (title passes) → grantee records.

sections.heading: Acknowledgment and recording (race-notice)
sections.intro: Acknowledgment makes a deed recordable. Recording gives the world notice and gives the grantee priority.
points: **Acknowledgment:** the grantor declares before a notary or other authorized officer that the signature is genuine and voluntary (RPL §298). It makes the deed **recordable**.
Acknowledgment doesn't pass title or give notice.
An unacknowledged deed is **valid between the parties** but **can't be recorded** unless proved by a subscribing witness. So it gives no constructive notice.
Record with the **county clerk** where the land lies. An Albany house goes to the Albany County Clerk, not the assessor.

In NYC, Manhattan, the Bronx, Brooklyn, and Queens record with the **City Register** through ACRIS, the Automated City Register Information System. Staten Island records with the **Richmond County Clerk**.
**Race-notice:** an unrecorded deed is void against a later buyer who takes in good faith (no notice), for value, and **records first** (RPL §291).
A pure race statute would ignore notice. A pure notice statute would ignore who records first.
Protected: buyers and **mortgagees** who give value. A mortgage counts as a conveyance (RPL §290).
Not protected: **donees**, heirs, and anyone with notice.
Recording can't validate a **forged** or void deed, cure non-delivery or incapacity, or guarantee title.
A recorded **notice of pendency (lis pendens)** warns of a lawsuit affecting title but decides nothing.
'First recorded wins' isn't absolute: real estate tax liens take priority anyway.

head: Notice
Meaning
Example
rows: Seller mentions the earlier unrecorded deed
The law presumes knowledge of the record
A properly recorded deed or mortgage
Facts a prudent buyer would investigate
Someone other than the seller lives there

example.title: Worked example: who wins under race-notice?
steps: Owner sells a lot to Ana, who doesn't record, then sells the same lot to Ben.
Step 1, good faith: if Ben knew of Ana's deed, or Ana was visibly living there, Ben loses regardless of recording.
Step 2, value: if Ben received the lot as a gift, he can't defeat Ana.
Step 3, the race: Ben paid value without notice. If he records before Ana, he wins, and Ana sues Owner.
Step 4: if Ana records first, Ana wins.
Answer: the later buyer wins only with all three: good faith, value, and recording first.

sections.heading: Transfer forms and the transfer tax
sections.intro: Tax and reporting forms are filed along with the deed.
points: **NYS transfer tax:** $2 per $500 of consideration or fraction thereof, paid by the **seller**. The buyer is liable if the seller doesn't pay or is exempt (Tax Law §§1402, 1404).
The TP-584 also reports the **1% mansion tax**. The **buyer** pays it on residential sales of $1 million or more, on the full price.
In NYC, the seller also pays the city transfer tax. Residential rates: 1% at $500,000 or less; 1.425% of the full price above that.
Big sales owe extra state tax. The base rate rises to $3.25 per $500 at residential $3 million+ (other property $2 million+).
The buyer's mansion tax climbs in steps from 1.25% at residential $2 million+ to 3.9% at $25 million+.
The **RP-5217** is required to record a deed (RPL §333(1-e)). Mortgage recording tax is a separate tax on the loan.
**ACRIS** is NYC's land-records system. eAccessNY is the DOS licensing portal, unrelated to deeds.

head: Form
What it is
Who signs or uses it
rows: Combined NYS transfer tax return (with the seller's income tax exemption certification)
Grantor and grantee both sign; the seller alone signs the income tax certification
Real Property Transfer Report of price and sale conditions
Assessors and the State Office of Real Property Tax Services (ORPTS)
Estimated income tax payment by a nonresident seller
NYC's online deed, transfer tax, and RP-5217NYC preparation

example.title: Worked example: NYS transfer tax
steps: A house outside NYC sells for $512,300.
Step 2: Any fraction counts as a full unit: 1,025 units.
Answer: $2,050, paid by the seller. Distractors: $2,049.20 (no round-up), $2,048 (rounded down), $5,123 (1%).

sections.heading: Title search, chain of title, and clouds
sections.intro: A **title search** of the public records confirms the seller owns what's being sold and finds liens and encumbrances.
points: The **title report** (commitment) lists what must be paid off or cleared before closing and what the insurer won't cover.
**Chain of title** is the sequence of ownership transfers. An **abstract of title** is a condensed summary of every recorded instrument: deeds, mortgages, liens, easements.
A missing link in the chain is a **gap**. Any claim casting doubt on ownership is a **cloud**.
**Marketable title** is free from reasonable doubt, acceptable to a prudent, informed buyer.
Marketability is measured against the contract. An easement the buyer agreed to take subject to doesn't make title unmarketable.

Records can't reveal a forged deed, or rights created without any document: a **prescriptive easement**, adverse possession, someone in possession. Inspection, a survey, and title insurance fill those gaps.

head: Problem
Example
Usual cure
rows: No recorded deed from Baker to Cole
Record the missing deed, get a quitclaim, or sue to quiet title (a court ruling on ownership)
Paid off, but no satisfaction recorded
An heir or ex-spouse might claim an interest
Heirs can't be found to sign
Misspelled name or wrong lot number
Quiet title judgment, then record it

sections.heading: Title insurance
sections.intro: **Title insurance** covers losses from title defects that existed on the policy date, except listed exceptions. The premium is paid once, at closing. The Department of Financial Services regulates it (Insurance Law Article 64).
points: **Covered:** forgery, a past grantor's incapacity, missing heirs, indexing errors. The insurer **defends the title** and pays covered losses up to the policy amount.
**Not covered** by a standard policy: defects arising **after** the policy date (a neighbor's shed built later), listed exceptions, and physical damage.
An enhanced homeowner's policy adds a few post-closing risks, such as later forgery or a neighbor's later-built structure other than a fence or wall.
Unless a question says the policy is enhanced, apply the standard rule.
**Standard exceptions:** survey matters such as encroachments, and **parties in possession**.
A **survey reading** compares a survey with the deed description and swaps the general survey exception for specific ones. So 'never covers encroachments' is too broad.
With a $500,000 price and a $400,000 loan, the lender's policy is $400,000 and protects only the bank.
An owner's policy never passes to the next buyer.

head: Feature
Owner's policy
Lender's policy
rows: While insured or heirs hold an interest
Shrinks with the loan; ends at payoff

sections.heading: Legal descriptions, surveys, and acreage
sections.intro: A **legal description** lets a surveyor find the exact parcel. New York deeds use metes and bounds, filed-map references, or both, often alongside tax map numbers.
points: **Metes** are distances and **bounds** are directions.
A description starts at the **point of beginning (POB)** and must return to it.
**Bearings** start at north or south and turn up to 90° toward east or west. S 30° W means face south, then turn 30° west.
Reverse a line by **flipping both letters**: N 60° E becomes S 60° W.
**Monuments** (an iron pipe, a stone wall, a stream) **control over distances**. 'North 200 feet to an iron pipe' with the pipe at 204 feet means the pipe wins.
A **filed plat** reference: 'Lot 14 on the map of Maple Ridge Estates, filed as Map No. 3127.' In NYC, 'Block 1450, Lot 22' comes from the **tax map**.
A **survey** by a licensed land surveyor locates boundaries, improvements, encroachments, and easements.
A **datum** is the base level for elevations, such as mean sea level. A **benchmark** is a marker of known elevation.
Area: rectangle = length × width; triangle = ½ × base × height. **1 acre = 43,560 sq ft**; 1 square mile = 640 acres.

head: Method
How it works
Used in NY?
rows: Courses and distances from a POB and back
Lot on a subdivision map filed with the county clerk
Section, block, and lot (borough, block, and lot in NYC)
Yes, usually with a full description

example.title: Worked example: acreage of an irregular lot
steps: A parcel is a 400 ft × 217.8 ft rectangle plus a right triangle with legs of 200 ft and 217.8 ft. Land sells for $36,000 per acre.
Step 1: Rectangle = 400 × 217.8 = 87,120 sq ft.
Step 2: Triangle = ½ × 200 × 217.8 = 21,780 sq ft.
Step 3: Total = 108,900 sq ft ÷ 43,560 = 2.5 acres.
Answer: 2.5 acres, worth $90,000.

sections.heading: Adverse possession in New York
sections.intro: **Adverse possession** gives title to someone who meets every element for **10 years** (CPLR 212(a); RPAPL Article 5). It's involuntary alienation, tightened in 2008.
points: **2008 amendments** (effective July 7, 2008): someone who knowingly takes an identifiable neighbor's land has no claim of right. Minor encroachments and mowing are permissive.
If the 10 years ended before July 7, 2008, title already vested under the old law.
Paying **taxes** isn't required.
**Tacking:** possessors in privity, such as seller and buyer, add their time together (6 + 5 = 11 years).
Title **vests automatically** at 10 years. A **quiet title** judgment makes it recordable and marketable (RPAPL Article 15).
Government land held for a **public use** (streets, parks) can't be adversely possessed.
A **prescriptive easement** is a 10-year **use** right, such as driving across a side yard. It isn't ownership, and it won't show up in a records search.

head: Element
Meaning
NY detail
rows: Reasonable basis to believe you own it
Excused if the owner can't be found in county records or by reasonable means (RPAPL §501(3))
De minimis fences, hedges, shrubs, sheds, and mowing are permissive (RPAPL §543)
Using the land as an owner would
If not under a written instrument: acts open enough to notify a diligent owner, or a substantial enclosure (RPAPL §522)

sections.heading: Transfers at death: wills, intestacy, and escheat
sections.intro: Property passes under a will (**testate**) or under the intestacy statute (**intestate**). In New York, the Surrogate's Court supervises both.
points: **Testate:** probate proves the will, and the court issues letters testamentary to the **executor** named in it. The executor sells with an executor's deed.
**Intestate:** the court appoints an **administrator** and issues letters of administration. The administrator signs an administrator's deed.
A **testator** makes a will, and a **codicil** amends it. Testatrix, executrix, and administratrix are older female forms.
A **devise** is real property by will, to a devisee. A **bequest** or legacy is personal property.
Heirs under intestacy are **distributees**, and they take **title by descent**.
**Executing a will:** the testator must be 18+ and of sound mind. The will must be in writing, **signed at the end**, and declared to be the will.
A will needs **two attesting witnesses** who sign within one 30-day period. No notary is needed (EPTL §§3-1.1, 3-2.1).

**Holographic** (handwritten, unwitnessed) and oral wills are valid only for armed forces members in war or armed conflict, those accompanying them, and mariners at sea. They also expire (EPTL §3-2.2).
**Elective share:** a disinherited spouse can elect the greater of **$50,000 or ⅓ of the net estate** (EPTL §5-1.1-A). A $600,000 estate left to charity lets the wife elect $200,000.
**Escheat** happens only if **no distributee** survives; a first cousin still inherits.
Books split on whether descent is voluntary or involuntary, but escheat is always involuntary.

head: Survivors (intestate)
Who takes (EPTL §4-1.1)
rows: Spouse: $50,000 + ½ of the rest; issue: the balance
Siblings or their descendants (no one closer)
Siblings and their descendants (nieces, nephews), by representation
Grandparents, aunts, uncles, first cousins (no one closer)
Half to each side of the family (all to one side if the other has no one)
First cousins once removed (no one closer)
Half to each side, per capita

example.title: Worked example: intestate shares
steps: A New Yorker dies intestate with a $450,000 net estate, a spouse, and two children.
Step 1: The spouse takes $50,000, leaving $400,000.
Step 2: The spouse takes half of that: $200,000.
Step 3: The children split $200,000: $100,000 each.
Answer: spouse $250,000, each child $100,000. With no children, the spouse takes all $450,000.

sections.heading: Voluntary and involuntary alienation
sections.intro: **Voluntary alienation** is a transfer the owner chooses; **involuntary alienation** happens by operation of law.
points: **Eminent domain** is the power to take private property for public use; **condemnation** is the process.
Just compensation, usually market value, is required, so eminent domain is involuntary but paid (U.S. Const. 5th Amend.; NY Const. art. I §7; Eminent Domain Procedure Law).
A partial taking pays for the part taken plus **severance damages** to the remainder.
**Inverse condemnation** is the owner's suit when government effectively takes property without condemning it, such as by repeated sewer flooding.
**PETE:** police power (zoning regulates use without compensation or title transfer), eminent domain, taxation, escheat.
**Accession:** **accretion** adds soil gradually, and the added soil is alluvion. Reliction exposes land as water recedes.
**Avulsion** is a sudden loss to a flood or river change. It generally leaves the legal boundary, and the owner's title, where they were.
**Quiet title** settles competing ownership claims; **partition** divides co-owned land or forces a sale.

head: Transfer
Type
How
rows: Gift of land to the public, such as subdivision streets; by deed, it's dedication by deed
Government conveys land by a land patent
Court divides co-owned land or orders a sale
Accretion or reliction adds land; gradual erosion removes it (a sudden avulsion doesn't move the boundary)

guides.title: Estates & Encumbrances
guides.overview: This chapter covers what can be owned in New York real estate and what can burden it: property rights, fixtures, estates, co-ownership, liens, easements, licenses, encroachments and deed restrictions. Expect classification questions (freehold or leasehold, general or specific lien, easement or license) and New York numbers: 4 and 8 months, 1 year, 3 years and 10 years.

numbers.label: Mechanic's lien filing deadline: single-family dwelling, after the last work or materials
Mechanic's lien filing deadline: all other property, including a two-family house
Days before and after filing to serve the owner with the notice of lien
Deadline after filing to file proof of service, or the lien terminates
Life of a filed mechanic's lien unless foreclosed (with a lis pendens) or extended
Bond that discharges a mechanic's lien from the property
Docketed judgment's lien on the debtor's real property in that county
Lis pendens (notice of pendency) life; a court may extend it for good cause
New York period for adverse possession (title) or a prescriptive easement (use)
Unities: PITT for a joint tenancy, plus marriage for a tenancy by the entirety
Written notice to end a tenancy at will or at sufferance (RPL §228)
Residential notice: non-renewal or 5%+ increase; tenancy under 1, 1–2, 2+ years (RPL §226-c)
New York abolished dower and curtesy (RPL §§189–190)
Surviving spouse's elective share of the net estate (EPTL §5-1.1-A)
Non-residential lease a broker must procure (written agreement) to file a commission mechanic's lien
Wall encroachment that becomes an easement unless the neighbor sues in time (RPAPL §611)

mustKnow: **Real property** = land + permanent improvements + the **bundle of rights**; movable, unattached items are personal property.
A **fixture** passes with the deed; test it with **MARIA**, where a specific written agreement outweighs every other factor.
**Trade fixtures** stay the commercial tenant's property if removed by the end of the lease; items left behind go to the landlord by **accession**.
Trees and perennials are real property; annual crops (**emblements**) are personal property a tenant may return to harvest if its tenancy ends through no fault of its own.
**Riparian** rights = flowing water; **littoral** rights = lakes and seas. Air and mineral rights can be sold, leased or reserved separately.
Accretion and reliction add land gradually and erosion removes it; a sudden **avulsion** generally doesn't move the boundary.
**Freehold** = indefinite duration (fee simple, life estate); every **leasehold** is personal property (a chattel real), whatever its length.
'So long as' creates a **fee simple determinable** (ends automatically; possibility of reverter); 'but if' creates a **fee on condition subsequent** (right of re-entry; the grantor must act).
After a life estate, a named third party takes a **remainder**; otherwise the grantor keeps a **reversion**.
A life estate **pur autre vie** is measured by someone else's life.
A life tenant may lease, mortgage or sell only the life estate, pays taxes and ordinary repairs, and must not commit **waste**.
New York **abolished dower and curtesy**; a surviving spouse has a **right of election**.
The **homestead exemption** only shields some home equity from judgment creditors.
**Estate for years** = fixed dates (even six months); **periodic tenancy** = renews until notice.
**Tenancy at will** = consent, ends at either party's death; **at sufferance** = holdover without consent.
A New York landlord who **accepts rent from a holdover** creates a **month-to-month** tenancy (RPL §232-c), not a new term.
**Severalty** = one owner, even a corporation with many shareholders.
New York default: co-grantees are **tenants in common** unless joint tenancy is expressly declared; spouses are **tenants by the entirety** unless the deed says otherwise (EPTL §6-2.2).
**Joint tenancy** needs PITT; **survivorship** beats any will; a conveyance by one joint tenant severs that share into a tenancy in common.
Tenancy by the entirety: one spouse can't sell the whole or force **partition**, and **divorce** converts it to a tenancy in common.
Tenants in common may hold **unequal** shares and pass them by will; **partition** ends co-ownership by division or sale.
The **trustee** holds legal title for the beneficiary; an **LLC** shields members who manage; a joint venture is one project.
Every **lien** is an **encumbrance**, but easements, deed restrictions and encroachments are encumbrances that secure no debt.
Mortgage = **voluntary, specific**; judgment and federal tax lien = **involuntary, general**; property tax, special assessment and mechanic's lien = involuntary, specific.

**Property tax and special assessment liens** come first regardless of date; otherwise the first lien recorded, docketed or filed generally wins, unless a **subordination agreement** changes the order.
File a mechanic's lien within **4 months** (single-family dwelling) or **8 months** (other property).
A filed mechanic's lien lasts **1 year** unless foreclosed or extended; its priority runs from **filing**.
A **110% bond** moves a mechanic's lien off the land; advance lien waivers and willfully exaggerated liens are void.
A **docketed judgment** liens all of the debtor's real property in that county, including later purchases, for **10 years**.
A **lis pendens** binds later buyers to the outcome of a pending lawsuit over title or possession and lasts **3 years** unless extended.
**Appurtenant** easement: the dominant parcel benefits, the servient parcel is burdened, and it runs with both; an easement **in gross** benefits a person or company, such as a utility.
**Prescription** = 10 years of open, notorious, continuous, hostile use and gives use, not title; nonuse alone doesn't end an easement created by grant.
A **license** is revocable permission, not an interest in land; it ends at revocation, death or sale, and permissive use never ripens into a prescriptive easement.
**Encroachments** show up on a **survey**, not a title search; New York deems de minimis fences, hedges and sheds over the line permissive (RPAPL §543).
When zoning and a **deed restriction** both apply, the **stricter** one controls.

traps.trap: The lien recorded first always gets paid first.
traps.truth: Property tax and special assessment liens go first regardless of date, even ahead of an older mortgage, and a subordination agreement can reorder the rest.

traps.trap: An owner-occupied two-family house gets the 4-month mechanic's lien deadline.
traps.truth: Only a single-family dwelling gets 4 months; all other property gets 8, owner-occupied or not.

traps.trap: A mechanic's lien relates back to the day work began.
traps.truth: New York ranks it from the filing of the notice of lien (Lien Law §13), so a mortgage recorded before that filing generally stays ahead.

traps.trap: A filed mechanic's lien lasts 4 or 8 months (or 10 years).
traps.truth: A filed lien lasts 1 year unless enforced or extended. 4 and 8 months are filing deadlines, and 10 years is the judgment-lien period.

traps.trap: Two names on a deed means a joint tenancy with survivorship.
traps.truth: New York presumes a tenancy in common unless joint tenancy is expressly declared; the main exception is spouses, who take as tenants by the entirety.

traps.trap: A joint tenant can leave her share by will.
traps.truth: Survivorship takes effect at death, so the share never enters her estate. She would have to sever, and record the severance, while alive.

traps.trap: Severalty means ownership by several people.
traps.truth: Severalty is sole ownership; a corporation with 500 shareholders owns in severalty.

traps.trap: 'So long as' and 'but if' deeds both end automatically on breach.
traps.truth: Only the fee simple determinable ('so long as') ends automatically; after a 'but if' breach the grantee keeps title until the grantor re-enters.

traps.trap: A New York widow gets dower, a life estate in one-third of her husband's land.
traps.truth: Dower and curtesy were abolished in 1930; the spouse's protection is the right of election (the greater of $50,000 or one-third of the net estate).

traps.trap: Accepting a holdover's rent renews the lease for another year.
traps.truth: In New York it creates a month-to-month tenancy (RPL §232-c) unless the parties agree otherwise.

traps.trap: A recorded easement ends after years of nonuse.
traps.truth: Nonuse alone never ends an easement created by grant; abandonment needs intent shown by clear acts.

traps.trap: Twelve years of using a neighbor's path with permission creates an easement.
traps.truth: Permissive use is a license, not hostile use, so it never ripens into a prescriptive easement.

traps.trap: A lis pendens is a money lien or a judgment.
traps.truth: It is only notice that a lawsuit affecting title to or possession of a specific property is pending. It creates no debt, but later buyers are bound by the outcome.

traps.trap: A federal tax lien beats every other lien.
traps.truth: A mortgage recorded before the notice of federal tax lien was filed stays ahead, and local property tax liens outrank it even when they arise later.

mnemonics.meaning: Fixture tests: Method of annexation, Adaptability, Relationship of the parties, Intention, Agreement

formulas.formula: File by: last work + 4 months (single-family) or + 8 months (other). Lien ends: filing date + 1 year
formulas.example: Single-family job done March 2 → file by July 2; filed May 12, 2026 → ends May 12, 2027

formulas.name: Joint tenancy survivorship
formulas.formula: Survivor's share = own share + (deceased's share ÷ number of surviving joint tenants)
formulas.example: Three joint tenants at 1/3; one dies → 1/3 + (1/3 ÷ 2) = 1/2 each

sections.heading: Land, real estate and real property
sections.intro: Start every question by identifying what is being owned and which rights in the bundle are involved.
points: **Land** is the earth's surface plus its natural attachments (soil, trees, minerals), extending below ground and into the airspace.
**Real estate** adds permanent improvements such as buildings, and **real property** adds the legal rights of ownership.
**Personal property** (chattels) is movable and transfers by bill of sale, not deed.
**Severance** turns realty into personalty (a cut tree becomes logs); **annexation** does the reverse (lumber built into a wall).
The **bundle of rights** is possession, control, enjoyment, exclusion and disposition.
A lease transfers possession for the term, while the owner keeps title and can still sell.
**Escheat** is a government power (PETE), not an owner's right.
**Appurtenances** pass automatically with the land, such as an appurtenant easement or unsevered air, water and mineral rights.
**Possessory** interests (estates) include occupancy; **non-possessory** interests (easements, profits, liens) don't.
A license is mere permission, not an interest in land.
Real property is immobile, indestructible and unique. Its value is shaped by scarcity, improvements, permanence of investment and location, and it is illiquid.
Uses are residential, commercial, industrial, agricultural and **special purpose** (churches, schools, cemeteries). Special purpose property is costly to convert and rarely sells.
A **parcel** is an identifiable piece of land.

head: Term
What it includes
Exam angle
rows: Surface, subsurface, airspace and natural attachments
A growing tree is realty; once cut, it is personal property
Real estate plus the bundle of rights
Movable items; a lease is a chattel real

sections.heading: Fixtures, trade fixtures and crops
sections.intro: A **fixture** is former personal property that has become part of the real estate, so it conveys with the deed unless the contract excludes it.
points: Courts weigh the **MARIA** factors, but a **specific written agreement** carries the most weight.
A signed exclusion lets a seller remove even a wired-in chandelier, leaving the wiring safely capped.
When the contract is silent, attached or custom-fitted items generally convey: built-in bookcases, chandeliers, a furnace, and custom storm windows even if stored in the basement at closing.
Freestanding items such as a plug-in refrigerator usually don't convey, so list them as inclusions.
**Relationship of the parties**: an owner's improvements are presumed permanent, while a tenant is presumed to intend removal.
So an identical air conditioner can be a fixture for an owner and personal property for a tenant.
**Trade fixtures** (a commercial tenant's ovens, display cases, shelving) stay the tenant's personal property even when bolted down.
The tenant may remove trade fixtures before the lease ends, repairing any damage. Items left behind become the landlord's by **accession**.
Trees and perennials (**fructus naturales**) are real property.
Annual crops such as wheat or corn (fructus industriales, or **emblements**) are personal property.
A tenant whose estate ends through no fault of its own before harvest may come back for the crop it planted.
If a life tenant dies in July, her estate, not the remainderman, takes that harvest.

head: MARIA factor
Question it asks
Example
rows: Was it made or fitted for this building?
Custom storm windows stored in the basement
Was it meant to be permanent?
A safe bolted into a concrete floor
What does the signed contract say?

sections.heading: Air, subsurface and water rights
sections.intro: Ownership can be split vertically into air, surface and subsurface rights, and land that touches water carries rights of its own.
points: **Air rights** can be sold or leased separately, as when a railroad sells the right to build an office tower over tracks it keeps using.
In New York City, unused development rights are often transferred to neighboring lots.
A seller can reserve the **subsurface (mineral) rights** and convey only the surface.
**Riparian rights** attach to land along flowing water, such as rivers and streams.
**Littoral rights** attach to land along stationary water, such as lakes and seas (a house on Lake George).
New York follows the riparian reasonable-use approach, not the western prior-appropriation system.
Generally the state owns the beds of navigable waters, while an owner along a non-navigable stream usually owns to its center.
Groundwater (**percolating water**) may be used reasonably, but runoff may not be piped or ditched onto a neighbor's land.
Gradual changes (accretion, reliction, erosion) move the legal boundary with the water.
A sudden **avulsion** generally does not, so the owner who lost land can still claim it.

head: Term
What happens
Effect on the owner
rows: Sudden loss, such as a flood cutting a new channel

sections.heading: Freehold and leasehold estates
sections.intro: An **estate** is a possessory interest classified by how long it lasts: freehold (ownership of indefinite length) or leasehold (a tenancy).
points: **Freehold** estates (fee simple and life estates) last an indefinite time. Duration, not inheritability, is the test.
**Leaseholds** give possession without title, and a lease of any length is a **chattel real** (personal property).
**Fee simple absolute** is the largest estate, freely transferable and inheritable, but still subject to zoning, taxes and recorded restrictions. The seller keeps no right of re-entry.
A **fee simple determinable** (also called a qualified fee) uses words of duration: 'so long as,' 'while,' 'until.'
A fee simple determinable ends **automatically** on breach through the possibility of reverter.
A **fee on condition subsequent** uses 'but if' or 'provided that.' A breach gives the grantor a **right of re-entry**, and the grantee keeps title until the grantor acts.
Both are **defeasible** fees.
'Forever' signals a fee simple absolute. 'For the life of' or 'for as long as [a person] lives' signals a life estate, because an estate that must end at a death is not a fee.
An **estate for years** has definite start and end dates, even if shorter than a year.
A New York residential landlord who won't renew, or will raise the rent 5% or more, must still give **30, 60 or 90 days'** written notice based on occupancy or lease length (RPL §226-c).
A **tenancy at will** (consent, no fixed term or period) ends at either party's death. Estates for years and periodic tenancies survive death.
A New York landlord can end a tenancy at will or at sufferance with **30 days'** written notice (RPL §228).
A **tenant at sufferance** entered lawfully and stayed without consent, unlike a trespasser.
If the landlord accepts rent after expiration, the tenancy becomes **month-to-month** (RPL §232-c).
Removing a residential holdover takes a court proceeding; **self-help eviction is illegal** (RPAPL §768).

head: Estate
Type

rows: Passes by sale, will or inheritance

sections.heading: Life estates, remainders and reversions
sections.intro: A **life estate** lasts for a measuring life and is usually created by deed or will.
points: An **ordinary life estate** is measured by the life tenant's own life.
An estate **pur autre vie** is measured by someone else's life ('to Dana for the life of Eli'). If Dana dies first, her heirs or devisees hold it until Eli dies.
A named third party who takes next holds a **remainder** and is called the remainderman. If no one is named, the grantor keeps a **reversion**.
The remainderman's future interest can be sold or mortgaged now but brings no possession until the life estate ends.
The life tenant may occupy, collect rents, and lease, mortgage or sell the life estate.
Every transfer **ends with the measuring life**: if Grace sells to Hal, Hal's estate ends when Grace dies.
A life tenant can't convey the fee or leave an ordinary life estate by will.
The life tenant pays property taxes and ordinary repairs and must not commit **waste**.
Waste can be **voluntary** (demolishing a sound barn, clear-cutting timber) or **permissive** (neglect, such as letting the roof leak until the framing rots).
New York **abolished dower and curtesy in 1930**. A surviving spouse instead has a **right of election** against the will: the greater of $50,000 or one-third of the net estate (EPTL §5-1.1-A).
The **homestead exemption** shields a limited, county-based amount of principal-residence equity from judgment creditors (CPLR §5206).
The homestead exemption is not a life estate or the STAR program, and it doesn't stop foreclosure of a mortgage the owner signed.

head: Deed language
Present estate
Future interest
rows: 'To Beth for life, then to Carlos'
'To my sister for life' and nothing more
Reversion to the grantor or heirs
'To Dana for the life of Eli'
Pur autre vie; Dana's heirs hold if she dies first
Reversion unless a remainder is named
'To Ira for as long as Ira's mother lives'
Pur autre vie, not a determinable fee

sections.heading: Severalty and co-ownership
sections.intro: **Severalty** is ownership by one person or entity. Co-owners each hold an **undivided interest**: a share of the whole, not a particular room or acre.
points: **Tenancy in common**: shares may be unequal, and each owner may possess the whole and may sell, mortgage or will its share. There is no survivorship.
**Joint tenancy** requires PITT: equal interests, same deed, same time, equal possession.
Joint tenancy carries **survivorship**: a deceased joint tenant's share passes to the survivors outside the will.
A conveyance by one joint tenant severs that share into a tenancy in common.
A New York joint tenant can also sever alone by a written declaration.
A one-sided severance, such as a deed to an outsider or a declaration, cuts off the other joint tenants' survivorship only if **recorded before the severing tenant dies** (RPL §240-c).
**Tenancy by the entirety** is for legally married spouses only (PITT plus marriage), regardless of who paid or whether it is their home.
In a tenancy by the entirety, one spouse can't convey the whole, defeat survivorship or force partition.
A creditor of one spouse takes subject to the other spouse's survivorship, and **divorce** makes it a tenancy in common.
New York default: co-grantees take as **tenants in common** unless joint tenancy is expressly declared (EPTL §6-2.2).
Spouses take **by the entirety**, including co-op shares since 1996.
Unmarried grantees described as spouses, and co-executors or co-trustees, take as joint tenants. Heirs without a will take as tenants in common.
**Partition** lets a tenant in common or joint tenant have a court divide the land or order a sale and split the proceeds (RPAPL Article 9).
New York is not a **community property** state. In those states, most property acquired during marriage belongs equally to both spouses.

head: Feature
Tenancy in common
Joint tenancy
Tenancy by the entirety
rows: Equal; the couple owns the whole
Free; the buyer is a tenant in common
Co-grantees, unless joint tenancy is stated
Spouses, unless the deed says otherwise

example.title: Worked example: severance, then survivorship
steps: Step 1: Eva, Finn and Gia are joint tenants, 1/3 each.
Step 2: Eva sells to Hugo and the deed is recorded, severing her 1/3 (RPL §240-c).
Step 3: Hugo is a tenant in common; Finn and Gia remain joint tenants as to the other 2/3.
Step 4: Finn dies, and survivorship gives his 1/3 to Gia: 1/3 + 1/3 = 2/3.
Answer: Gia owns 2/3 and Hugo 1/3, as tenants in common; Finn's heirs take nothing.

sections.heading: Trusts, entities, condos and co-ops
sections.intro: The form of ownership decides who holds title and who is personally liable.
points: In a **trust**, the trustor (settlor) creates it, the **trustee** holds legal title and manages, and the beneficiary receives the benefits.
An executor handles a decedent's estate, not a trust.
A **corporation** owns in **severalty**; its shareholders own stock, not real estate.
General partners share management and unlimited liability. Limited partners are passive and risk only their investment.
New York's Partnership Law lets property be titled in the partnership's name. Co-investors who take title in their own names hold as tenants in common by default.
An **LLC** lets members manage while generally shielding their personal assets.
A **syndicate** pools many investors, and its interests are generally securities.
A **joint venture** handles one project and then disbands; a **REIT** is an ongoing company owning many properties.
A **condo** owner holds a deed to the unit plus an undivided share of the common elements, which can include the land.
A **co-op** buyer gets shares (personal property) and a **proprietary lease**.

head: Form
Title held by
Key feature
rows: General partners fully liable; limited partners passive
Members manage with a liability shield
Unit plus share of the common elements
Buyer gets shares and a proprietary lease

sections.heading: Encumbrances and lien classification
sections.intro: An **encumbrance** is any interest held by someone else that burdens title or limits use; liens are the money kind.
points: A **lien** secures a debt and can be foreclosed. Every lien is an encumbrance, but easements, deed restrictions and encroachments are encumbrances that secure no debt.
**Voluntary** liens are chosen by the owner, such as a mortgage or home-equity loan. The foreclosure remedy doesn't make them involuntary.
**Involuntary** liens arise by law: taxes, judgments, mechanic's liens.
**Specific** liens attach to one parcel; **general** liens reach all of the debtor's property within their scope.
General liens include docketed judgments, federal and state tax liens, estate and inheritance taxes, a decedent's debts and unpaid corporate franchise taxes.
A **special assessment** for sidewalks or sewers is involuntary and specific, and it shares property-tax priority.
Specific liens follow the property, so they are paid from the seller's proceeds at closing and a **satisfaction** is recorded.
A New York lender must arrange for its satisfaction to be presented for recording within **30 days** of payoff (RPAPL §1921).

head: Lien

rows: General: real property in that county

sections.heading: Lien priority, judgments and lis pendens
sections.intro: In a forced sale, proceeds pay liens in order of priority, and a junior lienholder collects only from what is left.
points: **Real property taxes and special assessments come first.** After that, first in time generally wins: mortgages by recording, judgments by docketing, mechanic's liens by filing.
The size of a debt is irrelevant to priority.
A **subordination agreement** lets a lienholder voluntarily take a lower position, such as a home-equity lender staying behind a refinance.

A **federal tax lien** is not valid against an earlier mortgagee until its notice is filed, so a mortgage recorded first stays ahead. Local property taxes outrank it even when they arise later (26 U.S.C. §6323).
A **docketed judgment** is a general lien on the debtor's real property in that county, including later acquisitions, for **10 years** (CPLR §5203).
To reach another county, the creditor dockets a transcript there.
A **writ of execution** enforces a judgment; an **attachment** holds property before judgment.
A **lis pendens** (notice of pendency) warns that a lawsuit affecting title or possession is pending.
A lis pendens is **constructive notice**: it binds later buyers and lenders to the outcome even without actual knowledge (CPLR §6501).
It lasts **3 years**, extendable by court order for good cause (CPLR §6513).

example.title: Worked example: paying liens from a foreclosure sale
steps: Step 1: The sale nets $300,000 after the costs of sale. Liens: a 2019 mortgage of $240,000, a 2021 docketed judgment of $50,000 and unpaid 2026 property taxes of $12,000.
Step 2: Taxes are paid first regardless of date: $300,000 − $12,000 = $288,000.
Step 3: The mortgage was recorded before the judgment was docketed: $288,000 − $240,000 = $48,000.
Step 4: The judgment creditor receives $48,000 and can pursue the $2,000 shortfall from the debtor's other assets.
Answer: taxes $12,000, mortgage $240,000, judgment $48,000.

sections.heading: New York mechanic's liens
sections.intro: A **mechanic's lien** is an involuntary, specific lien securing payment for labor or materials that improved real property (Lien Law Article 2).
points: Contractors, subcontractors, laborers, suppliers, architects, engineers and surveyors may file.
A real estate broker can file only for procuring a **non-residential lease longer than 3 years** under a written agreement.
The work must be done with the owner's consent or at its request.
If a tenant orders work the landlord never consented to, the lien reaches only the **tenant's leasehold**.
A **subcontractor's lien** can't exceed the amount earned and unpaid on the owner's contract when the notice is filed, plus any amount earned later (Lien Law §4).

An **advance waiver** of lien rights is void, though a written waiver at or after payment is allowed. A **willfully exaggerated** lien is also void and can expose the lienor to damages (Lien Law §§34, 39, 39-a).
A lien is discharged by a satisfaction filed by the lienor, lapse, a deposit with the county clerk, a **110% bond**, or a court order.
With a bond, the claim shifts to the bond and the land is freed.
A discharging court order can follow the owner's notice under Lien Law §59, requiring the lienor to sue within at least 30 days.
Priority runs from the **filing** of the notice (Lien Law §13).
Mechanic's liens share equally among themselves whatever their filing order, except that daily or weekly wage laborers are paid first.
A mortgage recorded after work starts keeps priority for advances made before a lien is filed only with the Lien Law **trust fund** covenant. New York deeds and mortgages recite that covenant.

Deadline
Lien Law
rows: Within 4 months after the last work or materials

example.title: Worked example: mechanic's lien dates and amounts
steps: Step 1: A single-family kitchen job ends March 2, 2026, so the notice must be filed by July 2, 2026.
Step 2: For a two-family house, the deadline would be November 2, 2026.
Step 3: Filed May 12, 2026, the lien ends May 12, 2027 unless foreclosure with a lis pendens starts or a court extends it.
Step 5: The owner's contract is $40,000, the job is finished, and $34,000 was paid in good faith before a subcontractor filed for $10,000: cap = $40,000 − $34,000 = $6,000.

sections.heading: Easements and profits
sections.intro: An **easement** is a non-possessory right to use another's land for a limited purpose. It is an interest in land, so an express easement must be in writing.
points: **Appurtenant**: the **dominant** parcel benefits and the servient parcel is burdened, as with a driveway right-of-way.
An appurtenant easement runs with both parcels when either is sold and can't be sold separately.
**In gross**: the easement benefits a person or company (utility lines) with no dominant parcel. Commercial ones are usually assignable interests in land.

Easements are created by grant, reservation (a seller keeps a right over the land sold), implication (an apparent, continuous use when one owner divides land), necessity (a landlocked parcel), prescription, condemnation or dedication.
**Prescription** in New York: **10 years** of open, notorious, continuous, hostile use gives a right of use.
Adverse possession also requires exclusive possession and gives title. Permissive use never qualifies for either.
A **negative easement**, such as an easement for light and air, restricts what the servient owner may do. New York gives no natural right to light or a view.
A **party wall** is shared by two buildings; each owner owns its part, with cross-easements for support.
A **profit** (profit à prendre) is the right to take timber, gravel or minerals from another's land; it is an interest in land and transferable.
An easement ends by recorded release, merger (no revival after a later split), end of the necessity, abandonment, expiration, condemnation, or the servient owner's adverse blocking for 10 years.
**Abandonment** needs intent shown by clear acts; **nonuse alone** isn't enough.

sections.heading: Licenses, encroachments and deed restrictions
sections.intro: Ask whether you are looking at permission, a physical intrusion or a recorded limit on use.
points: A **license** is revocable personal permission, such as letting a neighbor fish or park a boat.
A license is not an interest in land, can be oral, can't be assigned, and ends on revocation, either party's death or sale of the land.
An **encroachment** is an improvement that crosses the line without permission, such as a garage or fence.
An encroachment is found by a **survey**, not a title search, so title policies typically except it. The owner can sue for removal or damages.
New York deems **de minimis non-structural encroachments** (fences, hedges, plantings, sheds) and mowing across the line permissive and non-adverse (RPAPL §543).

If a building's exterior wall encroaches **6 inches or less** and the neighbor's building abuts it, the neighbor must sue to recover the strip within 1 year of the wall's completion, or for damages within 1 more year.
Paying that damages judgment transfers the strip. After that, the wall's owner holds an easement while the wall stands (RPAPL §611).
**Adverse possession** gives title after 10 years of adverse, open and notorious, continuous, exclusive and actual possession under a **claim of right** (RPAPL §501).
**Deed restrictions** (restrictive covenants) are recorded private limits on use that run with the land.
Owners under the same subdivision plan can enforce deed restrictions by **injunction**, and breach doesn't forfeit title.
When zoning and a deed restriction both apply, the **stricter** one controls, and a building permit doesn't override a restriction.
**Racially restrictive covenants** are unenforceable (Shelley v. Kraemer, 1948; Fair Housing Act).

guides.title: Real Estate Contracts
guides.overview: How contracts are formed, classified, enforced, and broken, plus the contracts licensees handle: listings, buyer agency agreements, binders, the New York contract of sale, options, rights of first refusal, and installment land contracts. The exam hits hardest on **void vs. voidable**, the **statute of frauds** (GOL §5-703), and **option vs. right of first refusal**.

numbers.label: Age of contractual capacity; a minor's contract is voidable by the minor
Longest lease that may be oral; longer ones need a signed writing (GOL §5-703)
Statute of limitations for breach of contract (CPLR §213)
Customary downstate down payment; generally kept as liquidated damages on a buyer's willful default
Broker deposits trust money into a separate escrow account (§175.1)
Common attorney-approval window, counted from the day after full execution
Minimum size of the §175.24 explanation, signed or initialed by the homeowner
Residential property covered by §175.24 and RPL §443 (not vacant land)
Exclusive agency when another broker finds the buyer: selling broker plus listing broker
No automatic continuation of an exclusive listing past its end date
Risk of loss stays with the seller until title or possession passes
Housing covered by lead-paint disclosure; buyer gets a 10-day inspection opportunity
Landlord's written reminder window for an automatic-renewal lease clause (GOL §5-905)

mustKnow: Valid contract: **competent parties, mutual agreement, lawful objective, consideration**, plus a **signed writing** for land sales and leases over one year; recording is not required.
**Void** = no legal effect (illegal purpose, party already adjudicated incompetent); **voidable** = valid until the protected party cancels (minor, fraud, duress, undue influence).
**Bilateral** = promise for a promise (contract of sale); **unilateral** = promise for an act (option, open listing).
A **counteroffer** kills the original offer; an acceptance is effective when sent, a revocation when received.
**Forbearance** is consideration; **past consideration** is not; earnest money is customary, not required.
**Statute of frauds**: land sale contracts and leases over one year need a writing signed by the **party to be charged** or an agent with written authority (GOL §5-703).
**Parol evidence rule**: earlier oral side deals can't contradict a complete signed writing; fraud can still be proved.
Contract suits: **6 years**; **laches** can bar equitable relief sooner.
Remedies: **specific performance** (land is unique); **rescission** cancels and restores; reformation corrects a drafting error.
**Liquidated damages** can't be a penalty; NY sellers generally keep a down payment up to **10%** on a buyer's willful default.
**Exclusive right to sell**: broker paid whoever finds the buyer. Exclusive agency: the owner's own sale owes nothing. Open listing: only the **procuring cause** is paid.
Exclusive residential listings carry the DOS explanation, printed on or attached, in at least **6-point** type, **signed or initialed** by the homeowner (§175.24).
If the broker is in an MLS, the listing must let the owner route offers through the **listing or the selling broker** (§175.24).
Automatic listing renewals are banned (§175.15), but a **protection clause** is allowed. **Net listings** are illegal (§175.19).
Listings belong to the **broker** and end at the owner's death. A signed contract of sale **binds the estate**.
A broker earns the fee by producing a **ready, willing, and able** buyer on the listing terms, unless payment depends on closing.
**Who pays does not decide who is represented**; pay from more than one party needs the **client's** consent (§175.7).
A binder **“subject to a formal contract”** binds no one; licensees fill in **facts only**, since drafting clauses is the unauthorized practice of law.
**Attorney approval clause**: a timely disapproval for **any reason** ends the deal (Moran v. Erk); silence makes it binding.
**Downstate**: the seller's attorney drafts, the **buyer signs first** and pays 10% to the seller's attorney as escrowee, and the seller signs last.
Broker escrow: separate account within **3 business days**; no **commingling** or conversion. Disputed money waits for joint instructions or a court order.
A **mortgage contingency** needs a prompt good-faith application and timely notice; the protected party may **waive** it.
**Option**: only the optionor is bound and the price is fixed; **right of first refusal**: the holder can only match a bona fide offer.
**Installment land contract**: vendee has possession and equitable title, vendor keeps legal title; NY may require **foreclosure**, not forfeiture.
Before title or possession passes, a material loss lets the buyer **cancel**; an immaterial loss means a **price abatement** (GOL §5-1311).
No **time of the essence** clause: a reasonable adjournment is allowed; time can be made of the essence later by clear notice setting a reasonable date.
The **PCDS** goes to the buyer before she signs a binding contract; lead disclosure applies to **pre-1978** housing.

traps.trap: “Executed” means signed.
traps.truth: In classification it means fully performed; a signed contract is executory until closing.

traps.trap: A minor's contract is void.
traps.truth: It is voidable, and only by the minor; the adult stays bound.

traps.trap: An oral contract to sell a house is void or illegal.
traps.truth: It is unenforceable (GOL §5-703); part performance can still support specific performance.

traps.trap: Changing only the closing date is still an acceptance.
traps.truth: Any change is a counteroffer that rejects the original offer.

traps.trap: A signed binder with a deposit locks in the sale.
traps.truth: A binder “subject to a formal contract” binds no one; the seller may take a higher offer.

traps.trap: Under exclusive agency, the owner pays only if the listing broker finds the buyer.
traps.truth: She escapes only on her own sale; if another broker finds the buyer, she owes both brokers.

traps.trap: An exclusive listing may auto-renew if the seller initials the clause.
traps.truth: Automatic continuation is banned (§175.15); only a separate extension or a protection clause is allowed.

traps.trap: The attorney needs a good reason to disapprove.
traps.truth: A timely disapproval can be for any reason or none (Moran v. Erk).

traps.trap: Risk of loss shifts to the buyer at signing.
traps.truth: The seller keeps the risk until title or possession passes, unless the contract says otherwise (GOL §5-1311).

traps.trap: Missing an “on or about” closing date by a few days is a default.
traps.truth: Without time of the essence, either side gets a reasonable adjournment.

traps.trap: A right of first refusal lets the tenant buy at a preset price.
traps.truth: That is an option; a right of first refusal only lets the holder match a bona fide offer.

traps.trap: Assigning the contract releases the original buyer.
traps.truth: The assignor stays liable; only a novation releases her.

traps.trap: Lead-paint rules cover homes built after 1978.
traps.truth: The federal rule covers housing built **before 1978**; the syllabus wording has it backwards.

traps.trap: A seller may give a $500 credit instead of the PCDS.
traps.truth: That opt-out ended in 2024; deliver the statement before the buyer signs.

mnemonics.name: Accept on dispatch, revoke on receipt
mnemonics.meaning: Mailbox rule: an acceptance counts when sent; a revocation only when received.

mnemonics.name: Optionor is obligated; optionee opts
mnemonics.meaning: Only the owner (optionor) is bound; the buyer (optionee) chooses whether to buy.

mnemonics.name: EA = except the owner
mnemonics.meaning: Exclusive agency pays the broker on every sale except the owner's own; exclusive right to sell has no exception.
