sections.heading: Land-use basics and the four government powers
sections.intro: Ownership gives the bundle of rights (possess, use, exclude, transfer), but every right yields to public regulation and valid private restrictions. For any project, ask: Does zoning allow it? Do other government approvals allow it? Do private restrictions allow it?
points: **Police power** lets government regulate property to protect public health, safety, morals and general welfare. New York delegates it to cities, towns and villages for zoning, building codes and subdivision rules. The State uses it for rules such as rent regulation. A valid regulation owes **no compensation**, even if value drops.
**Eminent domain** takes property for public use with **just compensation**, through condemnation.
**Taxation** includes property taxes and **special assessments** on land that a local improvement, such as a sewer, benefits. Unpaid taxes end in tax foreclosure.
**Escheat** passes property to the State when an owner dies with no will and no heirs. Any qualifying relative, even a first cousin, prevents it.
An **as-of-right** use meets the zoning without a variance or special permit. It still needs a building permit.
New York requires zoning rules to be **uniform** for each kind of building within a district (Town Law §262).

head: Power
What it does
Owner paid?
Example
rows: Regulates use for health, safety and welfare
No, unless it becomes a taking
Raises revenue; liens and tax foreclosure
Takes property with no owner or heir

sections.heading: Planning and the bodies that regulate land use
sections.intro: In New York, land use is mostly local: the elected legislative body makes the rules, appointed boards (the planning board and the zoning board of appeals, or ZBA) apply them, and county and state agencies add layers.
points: The **comprehensive plan** (master plan) sets long-range goals for land use, housing, transportation, utilities and open space.
The plan draws on demography (population statistics), census tracts (small Census Bureau statistical areas), topography (land contours) and infrastructure (roads, water, sewer, schools).
The planning board may draft the plan, but the **legislative body adopts it** (Town Law §272-a).

Zoning must be **in accordance with a comprehensive plan** (Town Law §263). The plan is only a guide: if it calls for shops but the map still says single-family, the **current zoning controls** until the legislative body rezones.

The **official map** shows existing and proposed streets, parks and drainage. In towns, a building permit generally requires access from a street on the official map, an existing public highway or an approved plat (Town Law §280-a).
**Capital budgeting** schedules and funds public improvements.

The **Open Meetings Law** (Sunshine Law) opens planning board, ZBA and legislative meetings to the public, including ZBA deliberations. The **Freedom of Information Law (FOIL)** covers records. Both are New York State laws.
Enforcement runs through the building department or code enforcement officer, the board of health, professional consultants (engineers, surveyors, planners) and the courts.
**Federal Housing Administration (FHA) approval** of homes for FHA-insured loans is a separate federal track.
In NYC, zoning map changes go through the **Uniform Land Use Review Procedure (ULURP)**. The 2025 Charter amendments created the faster **ELURP** for modest housing rezonings.

head: Body
Land-use job
Exam angle
rows: Town board, village board of trustees or city council (elected)
Adopts and amends zoning and the comprehensive plan; imposes moratoriums
Subdivision plats, site plans, cluster plans, often special permits; advises on the plan
Zoning board of appeals (appointed; usually 3 or 5 members)
Appeals from the zoning officer, interpretations, use and area variances
Building department or code enforcement officer
Building permits, inspections, certificates of occupancy (COs), violations
Reviews zoning actions within 500 feet of municipal lines, state or county roads and parks
Acting against its disapproval or modification takes a majority plus one
NYC: City Council, City Planning Commission, Board of Standards and Appeals (BSA), Department of Buildings (DOB)
Map changes go through ULURP or the faster ELURP; BSA grants variances; DOB issues permits and COs

sections.heading: Zoning districts, bulk rules and key terms
sections.intro: **Zoning** divides a municipality into districts, each with permitted uses and dimensional rules. Towns zone under the Town Law, villages under the Village Law and cities under the General City Law; New York City's 1916 resolution was the nation's first comprehensive zoning code.
points: A zoning law has a **map** (district lines) and **text** (permitted, specially permitted and prohibited uses, plus dimensional rules).
Village of Euclid v. Ambler Realty (1926) upheld use-district zoning as police power, hence the name **Euclidean zoning**.
Classifications include residential, commercial, industrial, agricultural, institutional (schools, hospitals), open space, parks and recreation, vacant land and conservation land.
**Bulk rules** set lot area, frontage, setbacks (minimum distances from lot lines), height, lot coverage, density (units per acre) and parking.
**Floor area ratio (FAR)** = gross floor area ÷ lot area.
**Family** is defined locally. But New York's highest court struck down a definition that excluded households functioning as a family (McMinn v. Town of Oyster Bay, 1985).

A licensed community residence for up to 14 people with mental disabilities counts as a **family unit** (Padavan Law, Mental Hygiene Law §41.34). The municipality has 40 days to approve the site, suggest another or object to over-concentration.

Listing on the State or National Register does not by itself restrict a private owner using private funds; a local landmarks law can. In New York, the **Office of Parks, Recreation and Historic Preservation (OPRHP)** handles listings.

head: Term
Meaning
rows: Incidental to the main use on the lot, such as a garage or shed
Second, smaller unit with a single-family home, where the ordinance allows
A resident's business inside the dwelling with little outward sign
Residence for unrelated people who need support; often treated as a family
Right to use another's land for a limited purpose
Easement or strip of land for passage
Dead-end street ending in a turnaround
Right to use the space above land; can be sold separately
Measures boundaries and locates improvements and encroachments

example.title: Worked example: floor area ratio
steps: A 10,000 sq ft lot allows a maximum FAR of 2.0.
Maximum floor area = 10,000 × 2.0 = 20,000 sq ft.
That could be 4 stories of 5,000 sq ft, if height rules allow.
Answer: 20,000 sq ft of floor area.

sections.heading: Zoning techniques
sections.intro: Exam questions describe a flexible zoning tool and ask for its name.
points: **Cluster development**: if the town board authorizes it, the planning board may shrink lots to preserve open space. Total units may **not exceed** a conventional layout (Town Law §278).
A **planned unit development (PUD)** goes further, mixing housing types and commercial uses under one master plan.
**Incentive zoning** trades bonus density or floor area for amenities (Town Law §261-b).
**Transfer of development rights (TDR)** lets owners of preserved land, such as farms or landmarks, sell unused rights for use in a receiving area (Town Law §261-a).
**Inclusionary zoning** requires or rewards affordable units.
**Exclusionary zoning**, such as huge minimum lots, keeps lower-income households out. New York requires zoning to weigh regional housing needs (Berenson v. Town of New Castle, 1975).
**Downzoning** (lowering allowed density) is valid without compensation unless it becomes a taking.

head: Technique
Key idea
rows: Higher uses allowed in lower districts, so a house in a light-industrial zone is fine
Only listed uses, so homes can be barred from industrial zones
Extra rules (historic, flood) laid over base districts; base uses unchanged
In the text but unmapped until applied to a qualifying parcel (Rodgers v. Village of Tarrytown, 1951)
Same density, smaller lots, open space
Mixed uses under one master plan
Development rights moved from a sending to a receiving area

example.title: Worked example: density bonus and affordable split
steps: Base density: 30 acres × 2 units per acre = 60 units.
20% incentive bonus for a park: 60 × 0.20 = 12 extra units.
Total = 60 + 12 = 72 units, not 60 + 20 = 80.
Inclusionary rule: 25% of a 120-unit building = 30 affordable units.
Market-rate units = 120 − 30 = 90.
Answer: 72 units; 90 market-rate units.

sections.heading: Rezoning, spot zoning and moratoriums
sections.intro: Changing the zoning map or text is a **legislative** act of the elected board, taken after a public hearing with at least 10 days' published notice.
points: A rezoning passes by simple majority unless owners file a written **protest**. Qualifying owners hold 20% of the land being changed, or of land within 100 feet of it (adjacent or directly opposite).
After a valid protest, the rezoning needs **three-fourths** of the whole town board (Town Law §265).
Zoning actions within **500 feet** of a municipal boundary, or of a state or county road or park, go to the county planning agency (General Municipal Law §239-m).
If the county recommends disapproval or modification, acting against it takes a **majority plus one** of all members.
**Spot zoning** singles out a small parcel for a different use, mainly for its owner and against the comprehensive plan. It is invalid. A small rezoning that **implements the plan** is valid.
A hardship shared by a whole area, such as highway noise on every lot, calls for **rezoning**, not individual use variances.
A **moratorium** temporarily halts specified development while the town plans or adds capacity; a reasonable one is valid police power and not automatically a taking.

example.title: Worked example: protest-petition vote
steps: A seven-member town board receives a valid protest.
7 × 3/4 = 5.25, rounded up to 6.
Answer: 6 yes votes (a simple majority would be 4).

sections.heading: Variances and special use permits
sections.intro: A **variance** lets one parcel depart from the zoning rules. The ZBA grants two kinds, with different tests (Town Law §267-b). Villages and cities use the same tests. A **special use permit** is not a variance.
points: Classify first. A **use variance** allows a prohibited use, such as a store in a residential zone or a two-family house in a one-family district.

An **area variance** relaxes a dimensional rule for a permitted use: setback, height, lot size, frontage, coverage or parking. Examples: a deck 6 feet into a rear yard, or a house on a 9,000 sq ft lot where 10,000 is required.
**Use variance**: the applicant must prove **unnecessary hardship**, which has four elements.

(1) No reasonable return from **each and every** permitted use, shown by competent financial evidence. Proof that another use would earn more is not enough. The syllabus phrases this as being deprived of all economic use.
(2) The hardship is **unique**, not shared by much of the district. (3) The use won't change the neighborhood's essential character.
(4) The hardship is **not self-created**. Buying with knowledge of the zoning is self-created.

**Area variance**: the ZBA balances benefit to the applicant against detriment to the community. It weighs (1) undesirable change or harm to neighbors, (2) a feasible alternative, (3) substantiality, (4) physical or environmental effects and (5) self-created difficulty.
For an area variance, self-created difficulty counts but is **not fatal**. The syllabus's older label for this test is practical difficulty.

The ZBA grants the **minimum variance** necessary and may impose reasonable, land-related conditions. A variance **runs with the land**, so a condition ending it on sale is invalid (St. Onge v. Donovan, 1988).
A **special use permit** (special exception, conditional use) approves a use the ordinance already lists for the district, once stated standards are met. **No hardship** showing is needed.
The legislative body chooses the issuing board, often the planning board. That board holds a public hearing within 62 days and may add reasonable conditions (Town Law §274-b).

example.title: Worked example: how substantial is an area variance?
steps: A 20-foot side yard is required; the addition would leave 15 feet.
A side yard is a dimensional rule, so this needs an area variance.
Relief = 20 − 15 = 5 feet.
Substantiality = 5 ÷ 20 = 25%. Dividing 5 ÷ 15 = 33% uses the wrong base.
Answer: a 25% area variance, weighed with the other factors.

sections.heading: Nonconforming uses
sections.intro: A **lawful nonconforming use** (grandfathered) was legal before the zoning changed. An **illegal use** was never lawful and gains no protection with age.
points: Nonconforming uses may **continue but not grow**; the goal is to phase them out over time.
Where an ordinance sets a discontinuance period, the right ends when the period runs, **regardless of intent** to reopen (Toys "R" Us v. Silva, 1996).
In NYC the period is **2 continuous years** (Zoning Resolution §52-61).
**Amortization** ends a use after a reasonable period to recover the investment (Harbison v. City of Buffalo, 1958); billboards are typical targets.

head: Situation
General rule
rows: Use continues; it runs with the land
Not allowed on nonconforming status alone
Rebuilding limited by the local ordinance

sections.heading: ZBA procedure and Article 78 review
sections.intro: The ZBA is **administrative and quasi-judicial**: it applies legal standards to individual cases and makes no policy. Its power is mainly **appellate**, so an applicant usually needs a ruling from the zoning officer first.
points: Town and village ZBAs have **3 or 5 members**. A town ZBA that already had 7 when the current law took effect may keep them until the town board reduces it.
Legislative board members cannot serve. Members need **4 hours of training** a year unless the town board waives it.

Any **aggrieved** person may appeal the zoning officer's order or interpretation. The ZBA acts as the ordinance's **interpreter**, for example deciding whether a garage apartment is a prohibited second dwelling.
Every ZBA action needs a **majority of all members**; absences and vacancies count against it. A rehearing instead needs a unanimous vote of the members present.
On an appeal, missing that majority within 62 days is a **default denial**.

**Article 78** of the Civil Practice Law and Rules is the court challenge, brought in State Supreme Court. File within **30 days** after the ZBA decision is filed with the town clerk; the general 4-month Article 78 limit does not apply.
The court upholds a decision with a **rational basis**. It overturns only illegal or **arbitrary and capricious** action.
In NYC the **Board of Standards and Appeals (BSA)** grants variances and hears appeals from DOB zoning rulings.

head: Step
Deadline or rule
rows: 60 days after the zoning officer's determination is filed
Decision filed with the town clerk
Against a county disapproval or modification

example.title: Worked example: counting ZBA votes
steps: A seven-member ZBA; five attend and vote 3–2 to grant.
Needed: a majority of 7 = 4 (5 if the county recommended disapproval or modification).
Answer: not granted, because 3 is a majority of those present, not of the board.

sections.heading: Subdivisions, site plans and land-sale disclosure laws
sections.intro: A **subdivision** divides land into lots for sale or development. When the town board authorizes it, the **planning board** reviews subdivisions (Town Law §§276–278).
points: The developer submits a **plat**: a map of lots, streets, easements, utilities and drainage. It is usually preliminary, then final, with public hearings coordinated with SEQR environmental review.
Final approval is the authorized officer's **signature**; the owner must **file the plat with the county clerk within 62 days** or the approval expires.
Streets, drains and water lines must be built or guaranteed by a **performance bond**. The bond term is up to 3 years unless the board extends it.
If the plat needs recreation land but has no suitable site, the board may require a **fee in lieu of parkland**, held for recreation.
**Site plan review** covers the layout of a permitted use on a site: parking, access, lighting, landscaping and drainage (Town Law §274-a).
**Development costs** (roads, utilities, fees) usually fall on the developer.

Consumer laws apply on top of plat approval: the federal **Interstate Land Sales Full Disclosure Act (ILSFDA)** and New York's **Real Property Law Article 9-A**. The Department of State (DOS) administers Article 9-A.
Since 1997, Article 9-A ads need not be filed with DOS. They must state that the filing is not DOS approval.

head: Law
Covers
Requirement
Buyer's right
rows: Public Health Law §§1115–1116 (water); ECL Art. 17, Title 15 (sewage)
Realty subdivision: 5 or more residential lots of 5 acres or less, sold or offered within 3 years
Health department approves water and sewage plans before sale
No cooling-off period; lots can't be sold until approved
Vacant subdivided land, wherever located, sold or leased to NY residents on installment plans
Filing and offering statements with DOS
Unimproved lots sold across state lines; under 25 lots exempt
Registration and property report for 100+ lots
Revoke within 7 days; 2 years if no report

example.title: Worked example: maximum lot yield
steps: 30 acres; 25% goes to improvements; 2-acre minimum lots.
Usable land = 30 × 0.75 = 22.5 acres.
Answer: 11 lots. Round down; 30 ÷ 2 = 15 ignores the improvements.

sections.heading: Building codes, permits and certificates of occupancy
sections.intro: Zoning decides what may be built where; **building codes** decide how it must be built. Zoning relief never waives code rules.
points: Outside NYC, the **Uniform Fire Prevention and Building Code** sets statewide **minimums** (Executive Law Article 18). The Energy Code does too. Localities enforce them, or the county or DOS does if a locality opts out.
Stricter local construction standards need State Code Council approval (Executive Law §379). A **code variance** comes from a DOS **regional board of review**, not the ZBA.
**NYC** has its own Construction Codes, enforced by the Department of Buildings (DOB).

A **building permit** authorizes construction before work starts. A **certificate of occupancy (CO)** follows final inspection and permits occupancy for the stated use. It is not a title guarantee or a no-defect warranty.
A CO fixes the legal use and unit count. Converting a two-family to a three-family needs a **new or amended CO**; an extra unit is illegal even if long rented.
NYC began requiring COs in **1938**. Older unchanged buildings may have none, and DOB can issue a Letter of No Objection.

sections.heading: SEQR environmental review
sections.intro: The **State Environmental Quality Review Act (SEQR)** makes state and local agencies weigh environmental impacts before approving, funding or undertaking a **discretionary** action, such as a rezoning, subdivision or variance (ECL Article 8; 6 NYCRR Part 617).
points: Review sometimes requires an **environmental impact statement (EIS)**. The Department of Environmental Conservation (DEC) writes the rules. NYC's version is City Environmental Quality Review (CEQR).
**Ministerial** acts, such as a routine building permit issued once fixed standards are met, are outside SEQR (the rules also list them as Type II).

**Type I** actions require the Full EAF (environmental assessment form) and are likelier to need an EIS. Examples: adopting a comprehensive plan or a first comprehensive zoning law, use changes affecting 25+ acres, and a nonresidential project physically altering 10+ acres.
**Type II** actions need no review. All other actions are **Unlisted**.
A **lead agency** coordinates review. If agencies cannot agree on one within 30 days, the DEC Commissioner picks it.
The lead agency issues a negative declaration (no EIS), a conditioned negative declaration (Unlisted actions only) or a **positive declaration** (EIS required).
Amendments effective **June 12, 2026** added environmental-justice review. They also made certain multifamily buildings of up to 10,000 sq ft Type II.
The May 2026 state budget also exempts many housing projects on previously disturbed sites with public water and sewer. Check current rules for a live project.

head: Category
Examples
Result
rows: Comprehensive plan adoption; use changes affecting 25+ acres
Anything not Type I or II
1–3 family home on an approved lot; deck or garage; setback variance; multifamily up to 10,000 sq ft (2026)

example.title: Worked example: SEQR steps in order
steps: The lead agency reviews the EAF.
It issues a positive declaration.
Scoping sets the issues the EIS must cover.
A draft EIS gets at least 30 days of public comment.
A final EIS answers the comments.
At least 10 days later, each agency adopts a findings statement and decides.
Answer: EAF, draft EIS, final EIS, findings.

sections.heading: Wetlands, flood zones, coasts and the Adirondacks
sections.intro: State and federal programs regulate land regardless of local zoning, and they often overlap. Get a **current jurisdictional determination** instead of assuming.
points: **Freshwater wetlands**: DEC regulates the wetland plus a **100-foot adjacent area** (ECL Article 24). Inside the Adirondack Park, the Adirondack Park Agency (APA) regulates wetlands instead.
An April 8, 2026 court decision annulled DEC's 2025 wetland rules. DEC now requires permits for wetlands of **12.4 acres** or more (7.4 acres from 2028) and wetlands it mapped before 2025.

**Tidal wetlands**, such as Long Island salt marshes, need DEC permits (ECL Article 25). The regulated **adjacent area** runs up to 300 feet landward, or 150 feet in NYC, unless a 10-foot contour or a road ends it sooner.
The **U.S. Army Corps of Engineers** issues permits to fill federally regulated wetlands (Clean Water Act §404).
**Coastal Erosion Hazard Areas** need a DEC or approved local permit (ECL Article 34).
A FEMA **Special Flood Hazard Area** (100-year floodplain) has a **1% flood chance every year**.
A mortgage in a flood zone from a federally regulated lender, or a federally backed loan, requires **flood insurance** for the life of the loan. Homeowners policies exclude flood.
The **Adirondack Park Agency** classifies private land in the Park (Executive Law Article 27).

APA classes: **Hamlet** (no density limit), Moderate Intensity (about 1.3 acres per principal building), Low Intensity (3.2), Rural Use (8.5), **Resource Management** (15 buildings per square mile: 640 ÷ 15 ≈ 42.7 acres each) and Industrial Use.

**Forest Preserve** land in the Adirondacks and Catskills is **forever wild**. It cannot be sold, leased or exchanged (NY Constitution Article XIV). The Catskills have no APA; local zoning, DEC and NYC watershed rules apply.

example.title: Worked example: flood risk over a mortgage
steps: Annual flood chance 1%; 30-year mortgage.
No flood in 30 years = 0.99^30 ≈ 0.74.
At least one flood = 1 − 0.74 = 0.26.
Answer: about 26% (not 30%).

sections.heading: Eminent domain, condemnation and takings
sections.intro: The Fifth Amendment and New York Constitution Article I, §7 allow takings only for **public use** with **just compensation**. Takings follow New York's Eminent Domain Procedure Law (EDPL).
points: Condemnors include the State, municipalities, school districts, public authorities and some utilities. No owner consent is needed; refusing an offer affects only the payment.
An owner can challenge the condemnor's published public-use **determination and findings**. The owner must petition the **Appellate Division within 30 days** (EDPL §207).
The condemnor's written offer must be at least its highest approved appraisal (EDPL §303). The owner may take it as an **advance payment** and still claim more (EDPL §304).
A claim against the State goes to the Court of Claims within **3 years** of vesting or the notice of acquisition, whichever is later (EDPL §503). Other condemnors are generally sued in Supreme Court.
**Just compensation** is **fair market value** at highest and best use, not purchase price or assessed value.
A **partial taking** adds **severance damages** for the remainder's lost value.
**Inverse condemnation** is the owner's suit when government effectively takes property without condemning it, such as permanent flooding or constant low flights.

A rule that destroys **all** economic use is generally a taking (Lucas, 1992). Otherwise courts balance impact and expectations. For example, NYC's landmarks law was upheld for Grand Central (Penn Central, 1978).
Kelo v. City of New London (2005) accepted economic development as a public use.

example.title: Worked example: partial taking
steps: Value before $500,000; after $380,000; the strip alone is worth $90,000.
Answer: $120,000; paying only $90,000 ignores the remainder's loss.

sections.heading: Private land-use controls
sections.intro: Private restrictions apply alongside zoning. The owner must satisfy both, so the **stricter** rule controls.
points: A **deed restriction** or restrictive covenant is a recorded limit on use, such as single-family only, setbacks or design approval. Subdivisions often record **covenants, conditions and restrictions (CC&Rs)**, enforced by a homeowners association (HOA).
Recording gives **constructive notice**, so later owners are bound even if they never read the restrictions.
Covenant breach brings an **injunction or damages** from benefited owners.
A deed **condition** with a right of re-entry (fee simple subject to a condition subsequent) can cost the owner **title**.
A ZBA variance or building permit **does not release** a covenant: the municipality enforces zoning, while private parties enforce covenants.
Covenants end by expiration, release, merger, or a court finding of no real benefit because of **changed conditions** (RPAPL §1951).
Under the **doctrine of laches**, owners who unreasonably delay enforcement may lose the right.
**Discriminatory covenants** are unenforceable (**Shelley v. Kraemer**, 1948) and banned by fair housing laws, however old the deed.

guides.title: Construction & Environment
guides.overview: How a house is built and how its systems work, then the hazards and disclosure laws that affect a sale. The exam hits hardest on vocabulary (framing members, roofs, house styles), quick math (roof pitch, R-values, tons, amps) and the lead, radon, CERCLA and PCDS rules. The theme: spot warning signs, disclose what you know and refer testing to professionals.

Buyer's lead inspection opportunity (not tenants); can be changed or waived in writing
Keep signed lead disclosure forms
EPA radon action level (consider fixing at 2–4)
RRP minor repair: interior per room / exterior
One ton of cooling
Typical 120/240-volt service; 60 amps is usually inadequate

New-home warranty: workmanship / systems / material defects
Owner can cancel a home improvement contract
Report a petroleum spill to the DEC Spill Hotline

mustKnow: **Footing** = wide concrete base below the frost line that spreads the load; **sill plate** = first wood member, bolted to the foundation.
**Platform framing** builds one story at a time and is today's standard.
**Balloon framing** runs studs from sill to roof and needs firestops; **post-and-beam** uses heavy, widely spaced timbers.
**Joists** are horizontal, studs vertical and **rafters** sloped.
**Girders** carry the joists, often resting on **lally columns**.
**Headers** span openings; the masonry version is a **lintel**.
Interior walls can be **bearing walls**. Never cut a **truss** member without an engineer's design; structural changes need an engineer or architect.
A 2×4 is a **nominal** size; it actually measures about 1½ × 3½ inches.
**Gable** = 2 slopes; **hip** = 4.
**Gambrel** = 2 pitches on 2 sides (Dutch Colonial); **mansard** = 2 pitches on 4 sides (Second Empire).
**Roof pitch** = inches of rise per 12 inches of run; on a symmetrical gable or hip roof the run is half the span.
**Cape Cod** = 1½ stories with dormers; **Colonial** = 2 symmetrical stories.
**Raised ranch** = entry between levels; **split-level** = 3+ staggered levels.
**R-value**: higher is better and layers add; compressed batts lose R. **U-factor**: lower is better (U = 1 ÷ R).
A **BTU** heats 1 pound of water 1°F; **1 ton** of cooling = 12,000 BTU/hr.
For the AFUE (furnace) and SEER (cooling) efficiency ratings, **higher is better**.
**Forced air** = furnace, blower, ducts; **hydronic** = boiler, circulator, baseboards.
**Steam** heat needs no circulator pump; a **heat pump** moves heat and reverses to cool.
**Supply** lines are pressurized; **drain-waste-vent** lines use gravity.
The **trap** seals out sewer gas; the **vent** keeps traps from siphoning.
The **T&P valve** (temperature and pressure relief) keeps a water heater from bursting.
**Amps = watts ÷ volts.** Breakers trip on overload; service amps are capacity, while usage is billed in kWh.
**GFCI** = shock protection near water; **AFCI** = arc (fire) protection in bedrooms and most other living areas.
NY **home inspectors** are licensed: report within **5 business days**, confidential to the client, no referral fees to agents, no engineering.
**New-home warranty**: 1 year workmanship, 2 years systems, 6 years material defects (GBL §777-a).
**Amanda's Law**: carbon monoxide (CO) alarms wherever there's a fuel-burning appliance or attached garage.
Sellers of a 1–2 family home, condo or co-op give a **smoke alarm affidavit** at closing; the buyer has 10 days to report dead alarms, and the seller pays.
**Lead disclosure** (pre-1978): pamphlet, known lead and reports, warning statement; buyers get **10 days**; no testing or removal required.
**RRP** is separate: certified contractors, lead-safe work and the Renovate Right pamphlet; window replacement is never minor repair.
**Radon**: test the lowest lived-in level; fix at **4 pCi/L** or more (sub-slab depressurization); NY requires no test or mitigation at sale, but the PCDS asks.
**Friable** asbestos crumbles to powder under hand pressure and releases fibers; leave intact material alone and never sample it yourself.
**Mold**: fix the moisture first; there are no federal limits.
NY mold jobs over **10 sq ft** need a DOL-licensed assessor and a different licensed remediator; owners working on their own home are exempt.
**UFFI** emits formaldehyde that declines with age; **PCBs** are in old transformers, capacitors and fluorescent ballasts.
**Oil spills**: strict liability under NY's Navigation Law and a **2-hour** report to DEC, registered tank or not.
The **Safe Drinking Water Act** covers public systems only, so well owners test their own water; a **perc test** measures how fast soil absorbs water.
Filling a wetland can require both a **Clean Water Act §404** permit (Army Corps) and a NYS DEC permit.
**CERCLA** liability is strict, joint and several, and retroactive; defenses require **all appropriate inquiries**; lenders that don't manage the site are exempt.
**Phase I** = records, site visit, interviews (no sampling); **Phase II** = sampling; Phase III = cleanup; Phase IV = monitoring.
**PCDS**: 1–4 family homes (not condos or co-ops), delivered before a binding contract, actual knowledge, not a warranty; the $500 credit is gone.
Licensees **disclose known material defects** and refer testing; concealing a defect on the seller's instruction is misrepresentation.

traps.trap: Joists are the sloped roof members.
traps.truth: Rafters slope from ridge to eaves; joists are horizontal floor and ceiling members.

traps.trap: Any interior wall can come out.
traps.truth: A wall where joists end or overlap is probably load-bearing. Removing it needs an engineered beam and usually a permit.

traps.trap: Pitch = rise ÷ full span × 12.
traps.truth: Use the run (half the span): 8 ÷ 16 × 12 = 6 in 12, not 3 in 12.

traps.trap: A bigger rating number is always better.
traps.truth: A lower U-factor is better. Higher is better only for R-value, AFUE and SEER.

traps.trap: The lead rule makes sellers test or remove lead.
traps.truth: No testing or abatement is required. The rule requires disclosure of known lead and reports, the pamphlet, the warning statement and the buyer's 10 days.

traps.trap: Tenants get the 10-day lead inspection too.
traps.truth: Only buyers do; landlords still give the pamphlet, disclosures and warning statement.

traps.trap: Sellers hand buyers the Renovate Right pamphlet.
traps.truth: Sellers and landlords give Protect Your Family From Lead in Your Home; Renovate Right is the contractor's RRP pamphlet.

traps.trap: Radon under 4 pCi/L means no radon risk.
traps.truth: No level is known to be safe; EPA suggests considering mitigation between 2 and 4.

traps.trap: Old asbestos is harmless because it was banned, but it still has to come out before a sale.
traps.truth: No ban date clears a house, and no rule requires removal before a sale. Intact material is often best left alone.

traps.trap: An unregistered home oil tank creates no cleanup liability.
traps.truth: Registration and liability are separate. Liability is strict, and spills must be reported within 2 hours and cleaned up.

traps.trap: If I didn't pollute, I'm automatically safe under CERCLA.
traps.truth: Liability is strict, so not polluting isn't enough. Defenses require all appropriate inquiries; a buyer who knew may still be a bona fide prospective purchaser.

traps.trap: A Phase I includes sampling and lasts five years.
traps.truth: A Phase I has no sampling; that's Phase II. For AAI it must be within 1 year of purchase, with key parts within 180 days.

traps.trap: A 100-year floodplain floods once a century.
traps.truth: It has a 1% chance of flooding every year.

traps.trap: A seller can still give a $500 credit instead of the PCDS.
traps.truth: Covered sellers must deliver the PCDS before the buyer signs; the credit ended March 20, 2024.

sections.heading: Codes, permits, inspections and warranties
sections.intro: Plans lead to a permit, code inspections and a certificate of occupancy; buyers add their own inspections.
points: **Plans** (blueprints) show the design; **specifications** spell out materials and workmanship.
The **Uniform Fire Prevention and Building Code** applies statewide except in New York City, which has its own codes.
The **Energy Code** sets minimums for insulation and windows.
Inspectors check footings, framing and rough-in plumbing, electrical and HVAC before the walls close, then the final work.
Electrical work is checked against the **National Electrical Code**.
A **certificate of occupancy** follows a passed final inspection. A change of use needs a new one.
Neither a certificate of occupancy nor a permit guarantees there are no defects or private restrictions.
Site review covers NYS DOH well and septic rules, drainage and grading, landscaping, shading, walks, appurtenances (rights such as easements) and zoning.
**Home inspectors** are licensed by NYS DOS. They need 140 hours of training, including 40 supervised field hours, plus an exam.
The inspector's duty runs to the client. The license number goes on every report and ad, and the report must list the systems observed.
An inspector may not pay referral fees or kickbacks to the seller or either agent, or inspect a property in which he or a relative has an interest.
An inspector also may not charge to repair what he inspected before closing, or take a fee contingent on findings or a closing.
Inspectors can't practice engineering, so structural concerns go to an engineer.
The **new-home warranty** covers single-family homes and condo or co-op units in buildings of five stories or less. It starts at first title transfer or occupancy.
A builder can exclude the new-home warranty only by offering a qualifying written limited warranty (GBL §777-b).
**Home improvement contracts** over **$500** must be in writing and include a mechanic's lien notice. Advance payments go into escrow unless the contractor posts a bond or letter of credit.
Every 1–2 family home and condo or co-op unit needs a working smoke alarm. Battery-only alarms sold since April 1, 2019 must have sealed 10-year batteries.
**Amanda's Law** adds carbon monoxide (CO) alarms wherever there is a fuel-burning appliance or an attached garage.

sections.heading: Foundations, drainage and moisture
sections.intro: The foundation carries the load to the soil, and most foundation problems start with water.
points: The **footing** is the wide concrete base under walls and columns. It spreads the load over more soil and sits below the frost line so frost can't heave it.
**Foundation walls** rest on the footings. They are poured concrete, block, or in older homes stone or brick.
Wall height decides basement versus crawl space. Full basements are the most common foundation in New York.
A **monolithic** slab is poured together with its footing; a **floating** slab is poured separately.

Keep water out: ground sloping away (about 6 inches of drop in the first 10 feet), working gutters, footing drains, a sump pump, dampproofed walls and vapor barriers under slabs and over crawl-space soil.
Red flags: **efflorescence** (a white mineral crust left by water moving through masonry), musty basements, and horizontal cracks or bowing in block walls.

Description
Exam clue
rows: Walls enclose a full below-grade story
Shallow open area under the first floor

sections.heading: Framing methods and structural members
sections.intro: Loads flow from rafters or trusses through joists, studs, bearing walls, girders and columns down to the footings.
points: **Platform framing** builds each story on its own deck, which acts as a firestop. It is the standard method.
**Balloon framing** runs studs from sill to rafters, so the open cavities spread fire unless **firestops** are added.
**Post-and-beam** uses heavy, widely spaced timbers, allowing open rooms and exposed beams.
Studs sit 16 or 24 inches **on center**.
Lumber goes by **nominal size**: a 2×4 is about 1½ × 3½ inches, a 2×6 about 1½ × 5½.
Cutting a bearing wall, girder or truss needs a fix designed by an engineer or architect, and usually a permit.
Some texts call the double top plate a flitch beam. A true **flitch beam** is a steel plate bolted between wood members.

head: Member
What it does
Exam angle
rows: First wood member, anchor-bolted to the foundation; joists rest on it
Horizontal members carrying floors and ceilings
Concrete-filled steel post under a girder
Vertical wall members between sole and top plates
Spans a door or window opening
Sloped members from ridge to eaves
Never cut a member without an engineer's design
Plywood or OSB (oriented strand board) over studs and rafters

sections.heading: Roofs, exterior and interior finish
sections.intro: Roof questions come down to counting slopes and sides.
points: **Ridge** = the peak; **eaves** = the lower edges that overhang the walls.
**Soffit** = the underside of the overhang; **fascia** = the trim board on the roof edge.
**Flashing** = metal or membrane that seals joints at chimneys, valleys and walls.
Asphalt shingles are the most common roofing, and slate lasts longest. Flat roofs use membrane or built-up roofing.
Attic ventilation (soffit and ridge vents), together with insulation and air sealing, helps prevent **ice dams**.
The PCDS asks the roof type, its age and any transferable warranty.
Outside: sheathing, house wrap, then **siding** and roofing.
Inside: after rough-ins pass inspection come insulation and **drywall** (gypsum wallboard or plasterboard). Older homes have plaster on lath.
Older textbooks may state pitch as rise ÷ span (8 ÷ 32 = ¼ pitch). That is the same roof as 6 in 12. Answer pitch questions as rise per 12 inches of run.

head: Roof
Shape
Clue
rows: Two slopes with triangular end walls
Slopes on all four sides; no gable walls
Two pitches on each of two sides
Two pitches on all four sides

example.title: Worked example: roof pitch
steps: A gable roof spans 32 feet and the ridge rises 8 feet above the walls.
Step 1: Run = 32 ÷ 2 = 16 feet.
Answer: 6 in 12. Using the full span gives the wrong 3 in 12.

sections.heading: Architectural styles
sections.intro: Questions describe a house and ask for its style.
points: Symmetry signals Colonial, Federal or Greek Revival; asymmetry, towers and ornate trim signal Victorian.
Count stories: ranch 1, Cape Cod 1½, Colonial 2, split-level 3 or more staggered levels.
The roof can name the style: gambrel = Dutch Colonial, mansard = Second Empire, long rear slope = saltbox.

head: Style
Signature features

Two full stories, symmetrical facade, center entry
Long rear roof slope over a one-story back

Three or more levels offset by half-flights

sections.heading: Insulation, windows and ventilation
sections.intro: The building envelope separates conditioned space from the outdoors.
points: **R-value** (R-factor) is resistance to heat flow. Higher is better, and layers add.
Typical R-values: R-13 to R-15 in 2×4 walls, R-19 to R-21 in 2×6 walls, and about R-38 to R-60 in attics.
Insulate wherever heated space meets unheated space: attics, exterior walls, floors over crawl spaces or garages, foundation walls and slab edges.
**Compressed**, gapped or wet insulation underperforms. Air sealing is a separate job.
In New York's cold climate a **vapor retarder**, where used, goes on the warm (interior) side.
The **U-factor** rates a window's heat flow; lower is better. Fog between panes means the seal failed.
**Double-hung** sashes slide vertically. Casements are side-hinged and crank out, awnings are top-hinged and swing out at the bottom, and hoppers tilt in.
Ventilation controls moisture: kitchen and bath exhaust, heat or energy recovery ventilators (HRVs or ERVs) in tight homes, and attic and crawl-space vents.
Fuel-burning equipment also needs combustion air and a flue.

head: Insulation
Typical use
About R per inch
rows: Walls, rim joists, roof lines; seals air
Attics; reflects heat across an air gap
Pumped into existing walls in the 1970s

example.title: Worked example: adding attic insulation
steps: An R-11 attic gets 8 inches of cellulose rated R-3.5 per inch.
Step 1: New layer = 8 × 3.5 = R-28.
Step 2: Total = 11 + 28 = R-39.
Step 3: U = 1 ÷ R. Before: 1 ÷ 11 ≈ 0.091.
Step 5: Heat loss = U × area × temperature difference. For 1,000 sq ft and 40°F, that is about 3,640 BTU/hr before.
Step 6: After, it is about 1,030 BTU/hr.
Answer: R-39, cutting ceiling heat loss about 72%. Traps: R-28, R-14.5, R-88.

sections.heading: Heating, cooling and heat pumps
sections.intro: Separate the distribution system (air, water, steam) from the fuel (oil, gas, electricity).
points: One **BTU** raises 1 pound of water 1°F.
Capacity is rated in BTU per hour. Air conditioners are rated in **tons** (12,000 BTU/hr each).
Size equipment from a load calculation (area, insulation, windows, foundation, ventilation), not from room count.
**AFUE** (annual fuel utilization efficiency) is the share of fuel delivered as heat.
**SEER** (now SEER2) rates cooling, and HSPF rates heat-pump heating. For all three ratings, higher is better.
Condensing furnaces (90%+) vent through PVC pipe.
Fuels are gas or propane, oil (in an aboveground or underground tank) and electricity.
Electric resistance heat needs no flue but is costly to run in New York.
Central AC has an outdoor **compressor** and condenser and an indoor **evaporator coil**. Integral systems share the furnace's ducts.
Homes use air-cooled condensers; big buildings may use water-cooled ones.
**Heat pumps** move heat with refrigerant and reverse to cool. Air-to-air is most common; water-source and geothermal units also exist.
Modern cold-climate heat pumps heat well below 32°F; older ones relied on backup heat.
**Freon (R-22)** is no longer made. Refrigerant must be recovered, not vented (Clean Air Act).
Rough lifespans: furnace 15–20 years, boiler 15–30+, AC or heat pump 10–15, tank water heater 10–15.

head: System
Key parts
Clue
rows: Furnace, blower, supply ducts, return registers, filter
Boiler, circulator pump, baseboards or radiators, expansion tank
Boiler, pipes, radiators; no circulator pump
Tubing or cables in floors or ceilings

example.title: Worked example: tons and AFUE
steps: Step 1: A cooling load of 42,000 BTU/hr ÷ 12,000 = 3.5 tons. Dividing by 10,000 gives the wrong 4.2.
Step 2: A furnace with 90,000 BTU/hr input at 80% AFUE delivers 90,000 × 0.80 = 72,000 BTU/hr.
Step 3: The other 18,000 BTU/hr is lost.
Step 4: Electric heat: 1 watt = 3.412 BTU/hr, so a 1,500-watt heater gives about 5,100 BTU/hr.
Answer: 3.5 tons and 72,000 BTU/hr. The trap 112,500 wrongly divides by 0.80.

sections.heading: Plumbing, wells and septic systems
sections.intro: Two separate systems: pressurized supply in, gravity drainage out.
points: **Supply** lines run under pressure, about 40–80 psi. Pressure above 80 calls for a pressure-reducing valve. Undersized or clogged pipes cut the flow.
**Drain-waste-vent** lines slope (typically ¼ inch per foot) so waste drains by gravity to the soil stack and on to the sewer or septic system.
Each fixture has a **trap** holding a water seal against sewer gas.
**Vents** through the roof admit air so traps aren't siphoned. A blocked vent causes gurgling and sewer odor.
Water heaters: gas, electric or oil tanks (often 40–60 gallons), tankless units, or indirect tanks and tankless coils run off the boiler.
The **T&P relief valve** (temperature and pressure) releases water if temperature or pressure gets too high.
The **thermocouple** shuts off the gas when the pilot goes out.
Bacteria are the top drinking-water threat. Hardness causes scale, not illness. Acidic (low-pH) water corrodes pipes and can leach lead.
Private **wells** are the owner's job; the Safe Drinking Water Act (SDWA) covers public systems only.
EPA suggests yearly well tests at a NYS DOH-certified lab for coliform bacteria, nitrates, dissolved solids and pH.
NY has no statewide test-at-sale rule for wells, though some counties (Westchester, for one) require one.
**Septic** system: house sewer, then the **septic tank** (solids settle), distribution box, and absorption field or seepage pit.
The tank is sized by bedrooms and the field by the **perc test** (10 NYCRR Appendix 75-A). Conventional fields need **1–60 minutes per inch**.
A NY-licensed engineer or architect designs the system. The health department approves it and keeps the as-built drawings.
The septic tank needs periodic pumping.

Notes

Long-lasting; old joints may have lead solder

PEX is flexible, needs few fittings

example.title: Worked example: NY septic sizing
steps: Rule: 1–3 bedrooms need a 1,000-gallon tank; add 250 gallons per added bedroom.
Step 1: A garbage grinder counts as one more bedroom, so a 4-bedroom house with a disposal is sized as 5.
Step 3: Place the tank at least 50 feet and the absorption field at least 100 feet from the well.
Answer: 1,500 gallons.

sections.heading: Electrical systems
sections.intro: Voltage pushes, amperage flows and watts measure power.
points: Power comes overhead (**service drop**) or underground (**service lateral**). The owner is generally responsible for the service equipment and all wiring inside.
Homes get **120/240 volts** (older texts say 110/220): 120 for lights and outlets, 240 for ranges, dryers and central AC.
**Service size** is capacity: 100–200 amps today, and 60 is usually inadequate. Usage is billed in kWh.
The service-entrance cables, not the number of fuses or breakers, are the sure sign of service size.
The PCDS asks the amperage and whether the panel has breakers or fuses.
**Fuses** melt and must be replaced; **breakers** trip and reset. Branch circuits are usually 15 or 20 amps.
Copper is the standard conductor. **Aluminum branch wiring** (about 1965–1973) can overheat at connections.
Knob-and-tube wiring (pre-1940s) is ungrounded.
Refer wiring concerns to a licensed electrician; never open a panel.

head: Term
Meaning
Exam angle
rows: Ground-fault circuit interrupter; cuts power on a ground fault
Arc-fault circuit interrupter; detects arcing in damaged wiring
Fire protection: bedrooms and most living areas
Adopted through the NY Uniform Code

example.title: Worked example: amps and service capacity
steps: A 1,500 W heater and a 1,200 W microwave share a 120-volt, 20-amp circuit.
Step 1: Total load = 1,500 + 1,200 = 2,700 W.
Step 2: 2,700 ÷ 120 = 22.5 amps. That's over 20, so the breaker trips.
Step 3: Continuous loads should stay at or under 80% of the rating (16 amps on 20).
Step 4: Service capacity = volts × amps: 200 × 240 = 48,000 W.
Step 5: A 60-amp service gives 14,400 W.
Answer: 22.5 amps. Dividing by 240 (11.25) or 100 (27) are the traps.

sections.heading: Environmental hazards at a glance
sections.intro: Know each hazard's source, risk and response, then refer to qualified testers.
points: **Asbestos** can't be identified by sight. It causes asbestosis, lung cancer and **mesothelioma** decades after exposure.
Asbestos testing uses bulk, air and wipe sampling. The fixes are **encapsulation** (sealing), **enclosure** (covering) or removal.
NY's Department of Labor licenses asbestos contractors and generally requires a survey before demolition or renovation permits.
**Radon** is an odorless, invisible radioactive gas. It enters through cracks, sumps, drains and well water, and tight new homes can trap it.
Radon is the **leading cause of lung cancer in nonsmokers**. EPA estimates 1 in 15 homes run high.
Short-term radon tests take 2–90 days with the house closed.
Radon-resistant construction uses gravel, plastic sheeting, sealing and a vent pipe.
**Lead** comes from pre-1978 paint and dust, soil, lead service lines and lead solder (banned in 1986).
Lead causes lasting brain and nerve damage in **children under 6**. Adults risk high blood pressure and kidney damage.
**Sick building syndrome** means symptoms tied to time in a building with no identifiable cause; a building-related illness has one.
**Wood-destroying insects**: termites build mud tubes and eat wood. Carpenter ants nest in wood and leave coarse frass but don't eat it.
Powderpost beetles leave tiny holes and fine powder; carpenter bees bore ½-inch holes.
**EMFs** (electromagnetic fields) have no federal standard and no proven harm.
NY's Public Service Commission caps new transmission lines at **200 milligauss** at the edge of the right-of-way.

head: Hazard

rows: Test, remove; report spills in 2 hrs

sections.heading: Lead-based paint: disclosure vs. RRP
sections.intro: The disclosure rule governs information in sales and leases (Title X §1018, EPA and HUD, 1996). The Renovation, Repair and Painting (RRP) rule governs paid work that disturbs paint.
points: **Target housing** = built before 1978. Elderly or disabled housing and zero-bedroom units are exempt unless a child under 6 lives or is expected to live there.
Co-op sales and sales to investors are covered.
Before a buyer or tenant is bound, they must get the pamphlet, known lead information and reports, and the **Lead Warning Statement**, and sign acknowledgments.
Only buyers get **10 days** to inspect, which can be changed or waived in writing. Keep records **3 years**.
Agents must inform the seller and ensure compliance, and must refuse to hide a known lead report.
An agent who complied isn't liable for facts the seller hid. A buyer's agent paid only by the buyer isn't covered.
Exempt: foreclosure sales, leases of 100 days or less with no renewal, leases of certified lead-free units, and renewals after full disclosure.
Knowing violators face penalties and **triple damages**.

sections.heading: Environmental laws, tanks, wetlands and flood zones
sections.intro: Match each law to its job, then learn New York's tank and wetland rules.
points: **Tanks**: a fill or vent pipe, or oil lines through a wall, signals a tank even in a gas-heated house.
Get closure records and a professional evaluation (tank sweep, tightness test, soil test). Pulling the pipes to dodge questions is **concealment**.
The Department of Environmental Conservation (DEC) says a buried tank 10–15 years old probably isn't leaking, but the risk rises with age.
Most home oil tanks (under 1,100 gallons) aren't registered with DEC, though Nassau, Suffolk and Westchester have their own rules.
Liability under the **Navigation Law** is still strict, and spills go to DEC within **2 hours**.
The only exception: a known spill under 5 gallons that is contained, stays off land and water, and is cleaned up within 2 hours.
Retired tanks must be emptied, cleaned and purged. DEC prefers removal; closing in place means filling with sand or similar.
Homeowners policies often exclude pollution cleanup.
**Wetlands**: filling federal waters needs a Clean Water Act **§404 permit** from the Army Corps, with EPA oversight.
New York regulates tidal (ECL Art. 25) and freshwater (ECL Art. 24) wetlands, and towns may add rules.
NY freshwater wetlands of **12.4 acres** or more are regulated whether mapped or not. The threshold drops to 7.4 acres on Jan 1, 2028.
Wetlands DEC mapped before Jan 1, 2025 are also regulated, and protection extends to a **100-foot adjacent area**.
On April 8, 2026 the Albany County Supreme Court annulled DEC's 2025 wetland regulations (6 NYCRR Part 664) but upheld the 2022 law.
DEC now requires permits only for previously mapped wetlands and those of 12.4 acres or more.
Get a current jurisdictional determination. The Adirondack Park Agency handles the park.
**Flood**: the Special Flood Hazard Area (100-year floodplain) has a **1% annual chance** of flooding; the 500-year zone has 0.2%.
Federally backed lenders require flood insurance there, and homeowners policies exclude flood.

sections.heading: CERCLA (Superfund) and site assessments
sections.intro: CERCLA can make an owner pay for pollution it never caused, so commercial buyers and lenders do due diligence first.
points: CERCLA (1980) created the **Superfund**. NY's Love Canal disaster helped prompt it.
**Potentially responsible parties** pay: current owners and operators, owners at the time of disposal, and arrangers and transporters who chose the site.
Liability is **strict** (no fault needed) and retroactive.
Liability is also **joint and several**: one party can owe the whole bill.
**Innocent landowner defense** (Superfund Amendments and Reauthorization Act, SARA, 1986): all appropriate inquiries (AAI) before purchase, and no knowledge or reason to know.
Title insurance, as-is clauses and seller indemnities don't create the innocent landowner defense.
**Bona fide prospective purchaser** (2002): a buyer who knows of contamination is protected if it did AAI, isn't affiliated with a liable party, doesn't worsen it and meets continuing obligations.
**Secured creditors** that don't manage the site are exempt.
AAI is usually a **Phase I** (ASTM E1527-21) done within **1 year** before purchase.
The Phase I interviews, lien search, records review and site visit must fall within **180 days**.
A **brownfield** is property whose reuse is complicated by possible contamination, such as an old dry cleaner or gas station.
NY's Brownfield Cleanup Program offers tax credits.

Exam angle
rows: Records, site walk, interviews; no sampling
Asbestos, lead, radon and mold are add-ons

sections.heading: Property condition disclosure and the licensee's role
sections.intro: The Property Condition Disclosure Statement (PCDS) is the seller's disclosure for houses (RPL Article 14).
points: The form has **56 questions** covering general, environmental, structural and mechanical items.
Environmental questions cover flood zones, flood insurance and claims, wetlands, landfill, fuel tanks, asbestos, lead plumbing, radon tests, spills and mold tests.
Structural questions cover rot, pests and the roof. Mechanical questions cover water, sewage and electric.
The seller answers from **actual knowledge**, may check unknown, fills it out personally and need not investigate.
An as-is sale is still allowed.
A seller's agent must disclose known facts that materially affect value or desirability.
Hiding a defect on the seller's instruction is **misrepresentation**, with fines up to **$2,000** (RPL §441-c). If the seller insists, withdraw.
Stigma facts, such as a death on the premises, aren't physical defects and needn't be volunteered (RPL §443-a).
Spot red flags, state only what you know, and recommend inspectors and testers.
Never sample, diagnose or promise safety.

The PCDS exempts 14 transfers: court order, deed in lieu, deed of trust, foreclosure, power of sale, lender resale after foreclosure, fiduciary, co-owner to co-owner, spouse or lineal relative, divorce, government, never-inhabited new construction, sheriff and partition (RPL §463).

guides.title: Valuation & Market Analysis
guides.overview: This chapter covers value vs. price vs. cost, the principles of value, highest and best use, the appraisal process, New York appraiser licensing, and pricing a listing with a comparative market analysis (CMA). The exam hits hardest: adjust the comparable, never the subject; capitalize NOI, not cash flow; and in New York a CMA is never an appraisal.

numbers.label: Elements of value: demand, utility, scarcity, transferability (DUST)
Highest-and-best-use tests, in order: legally permissible, physically possible, financially feasible, maximally productive
Approaches to value: sales comparison, cost, income
Kinds of accrued depreciation: physical deterioration, functional obsolescence, external obsolescence
Neighborhood life-cycle stages: growth, stability, decline, revitalization
DOS syllabus look-back for comparable sales in a CMA
Minimum closed comparable sales in a Fannie Mae appraisal; 3 to 6 is typical
NY Executive Law article under which DOS licenses and certifies appraisers
NY appraiser credentials: assistant, licensed residential, certified residential, certified general
Minimum time a supervisor must be state-certified; max 3 trainees at once
NY appraiser credential term
Continuing education per renewal: 7-hour USPAP plus valuation bias and fair housing course
Experience hours: licensed residential / certified residential / certified general. Assistants: none, no exam
Reg B appraisal copy: on completion or 3 business days pre-closing, whichever is earlier
Federal bank appraisal threshold for home loans since 2019; older books say $250,000

mustKnow: **Appraisal**: an unbiased, supported opinion of the value of defined rights as of an **effective date**. Federally related loans require a state licensed or certified appraiser.
**Valuation** is the process of estimating value; an **evaluation** studies utility or feasibility without necessarily estimating value.
In New York a **CMA** is an opinion of value and by law may never be called an **appraisal**; a real estate license carries no appraiser credential.
**Market value** is the **most probable** price, not the highest, after reasonable exposure, in cash or its equivalent, between informed parties under no duress, in an arm's-length sale.
**Price** is what a buyer actually paid; **cost** is what it takes to build; either can differ from value.
**Direct (hard) costs** are labor and materials; **indirect (soft) costs** are fees, permits, financing and administration.
**DUST**: demand (desire plus purchasing power), utility, scarcity and transferability must all exist.
**Substitution**: buyers pay no more than an equally desirable substitute costs; it drives the sales comparison approach.
**Regression** pulls the best house on the block down; **progression** pulls a modest house among better ones up.
**Contribution**: a feature is worth what it adds to value, not what it cost.
**Anticipation** (value is the present worth of future benefits) underlies the income approach; **change** ties every value to a date.
**Highest and best use**: legally permissible, physically possible, financially feasible, maximally productive. Analyze it as vacant and as improved.
Appraisal process: define the problem, set the scope of work, collect data, analyze (including highest and best use), value the land, apply the approaches, **reconcile**, report.
DOS licenses appraisers under **Executive Law Article 6-E**.

**Certified general** covers all property; certified residential covers 1–4 units of any value; licensed residential is capped by value and complexity; an assistant works only under a certified supervisor.
**USPAP** bans fees contingent on the value reported and requires competence. The Appraisal Standards Board of The Appraisal Foundation writes it.
**Appraiser independence**: no one may pressure an appraiser toward a value; asking through the lender to consider more comps or correct errors is allowed.
A **BPO** is a broker's price estimate for lenders (foreclosures, short sales); it can't be the primary basis of value for a mortgage to buy a principal home.
CMA data: solds show what buyers paid, **actives** show the competition, **expireds** show prices the market rejected.
Adjust the **comparable**, never the subject: comp better, subtract; comp poorer, add.
Transaction adjustments (financing, concessions, time) come before physical ones; use only **arm's-length** sales; the comp with the smallest **gross** adjustment usually gets the most weight.
Cost approach: **land + (cost new − accrued depreciation)**; land is never depreciated.
**Reproduction** cost = exact replica; **replacement** cost = equal utility with modern materials, the usual choice for older buildings.
Depreciation: physical (wear), **functional** (design or features inside the property, including overimprovement), **external** (outside the property, almost always incurable).
**Curable** means the cure costs no more than the value it adds.
**Age-life**: depreciation = cost new × effective age ÷ total economic life; use **effective**, not calendar, age.
PGI − vacancy and collection loss + other income = EGI; EGI − operating expenses = **NOI**; **value = NOI ÷ cap rate**.
NOI excludes **debt service**, tax depreciation, income taxes and capital improvements, but includes a market management fee and reserves for replacement.
Higher risk means a higher cap rate and a **lower** value.
**GRM** = price ÷ monthly rent; **GIM** = price ÷ annual gross income. Some questions give an annual GRM for annual rent. Match the periods; multipliers ignore vacancy and expenses.
**Reconciliation** weighs the indications rather than simply averaging them: sales comparison for homes, income for investment property, cost for new or special-purpose buildings.

traps.trap: A salesperson may call a CMA an appraisal if no fee is charged.
traps.truth: A CMA is never an appraisal, paid or free, so 'free home appraisal' flyers are improper. Only credential holders may use the state appraiser titles (Exec. Law §160-b).

traps.trap: When the comparable has a feature the subject lacks, add its value.
traps.truth: Subtract, because the comp is superior: a $350,000 comp with a $15,000 garage the subject lacks adjusts to $335,000. Adjust the comp, never the subject.

traps.trap: Depreciate the whole property, land included.
traps.truth: Depreciation comes off the cost new of the improvements only; land is added back at full value.

traps.trap: Mortgage payments are an operating expense.
traps.truth: Debt service is excluded from NOI. NOI − debt service is before-tax cash flow; the income approach capitalizes NOI, not cash flow, to value the property.

traps.trap: Curable means the defect can physically be repaired.
traps.truth: Curable is an economic test: the cure costs no more than the value it adds. An $85,000 foundation repair that adds $30,000 is incurable.

traps.trap: A poor floor plan is external obsolescence.
traps.truth: Problems inside the property are functional obsolescence. External obsolescence comes from outside, such as a landfill or a plant closing.

traps.trap: Market value is the highest price a buyer might pay.
traps.truth: Market value is the most probable price. One specially motivated buyer's higher figure is investment value.

traps.trap: The age-life method uses the building's actual age.
traps.truth: Age-life uses effective age, which reflects condition and renovation. A gutted and rebuilt 45-year-old house might have an effective age of 15.

traps.trap: Reconciliation averages the three approaches.
traps.truth: Reconciliation weighs each indication by reliability and relevance. A simple average gives weak data an equal say.

traps.trap: A higher cap rate means a higher value.
traps.truth: A higher cap rate means a lower value: $120,000 of NOI is worth $2,000,000 at 6% but only $1,500,000 at 8%.

traps.trap: A monthly GRM can be applied to annual rent.
traps.truth: Match the periods: monthly GRM × monthly rent, annual GIM × annual income. Otherwise the answer is off by a factor of 12.

traps.trap: Comps must be under 6 months old, and every year of age knocks $1,000 off value.
traps.truth: The DOS outline uses a 12-month look-back, and every adjustment must come from market evidence. Neither the 6-month nor the $1,000 figure is a rule.

traps.trap: Any licensed appraiser can supervise an appraiser assistant.
traps.truth: The supervisor must be state-certified for at least 3 years and approved by DOS, with no more than 3 trainees at a time. A licensed residential appraiser can't supervise.

traps.trap: Plottage means combining parcels.
traps.truth: Combining parcels is assemblage; plottage is the extra value the combined parcel has.

mnemonics.name: DUST
mnemonics.meaning: Demand, Utility, Scarcity, Transferability: the four elements of value

mnemonics.name: PEGS
mnemonics.meaning: Physical, Economic, Governmental, Social: the four forces that affect value

mnemonics.name: CBS / CPA
mnemonics.meaning: Comp Better, Subtract; Comp Poorer, Add

mnemonics.name: IRV
mnemonics.meaning: Income = Rate × Value, so V = I ÷ R and R = I ÷ V

formulas.name: Adjusted comparable price
formulas.formula: Comp price − comp's extra features + subject features the comp lacks

formulas.name: Market-conditions (time) adjustment
formulas.formula: Comp price × (1 + monthly rate × months since sale)

formulas.name: Cost approach
formulas.formula: Land + cost new − accrued depreciation

formulas.name: Age-life depreciation
formulas.formula: Cost new × effective age ÷ total economic life

formulas.name: Index method
formulas.formula: Original cost × current index ÷ original index

formulas.name: NOI
formulas.formula: PGI − vacancy and collection loss + other income − operating expenses

formulas.name: Value (income approach)

formulas.formula: GRM = price ÷ monthly rent; value = monthly rent × GRM

formulas.name: Gross income multiplier
formulas.formula: Value = annual gross income × GIM

formulas.formula: Sum of each indication × its weight

sections.heading: Appraisal, valuation, evaluation, price and cost
sections.intro: Many questions turn on picking the right word, so start with the Department of State (DOS) vocabulary.
points: An **appraisal** is an unbiased, supported estimate of the value of an identified interest in real estate as of a stated date. It can also address the property's nature, quality or utility.
Federally related loans require a state licensed or certified appraiser.
**Valuation** is the process of estimating value as of a given date. An appraisal is one kind of valuation; a CMA is a less formal one.

An **evaluation** studies utility, feasibility, marketability or highest and best use without necessarily producing a value. Bank regulators also use 'evaluation' for a simplified estimate on some smaller loans; on the exam, use the syllabus meaning.

**Price** is what one buyer and seller agreed to in one deal. **Cost** is the total outlay to build, including the contractor's and developer's overhead and profit. Either can sit above or below value.

head: Term
What it is
Exam clue
rows: Unbiased, supported opinion of value as of an effective date
Credentialed appraisers follow the Uniform Standards of Professional Appraisal Practice (USPAP)
The builder could build it today for $380,000
Architect, engineering, appraisal and legal fees; permits; construction-loan interest; lease-up; administration

sections.heading: Market value and other types of value
points: DOS defines **market value** as the most probable price, as of a specific date, in cash or its equivalent, for which the specified property rights should sell after reasonable exposure in a competitive market.
The sale must meet all conditions requisite to a fair sale: buyer and seller act prudently, knowledgeably and in their own interest, and neither is under undue duress.
Key pieces: **probable**, not the highest price or the first offer; a specific date; and **cash equivalent**, so special financing and concessions are adjusted out.
The value is for the specified rights after **reasonable exposure** before the sale. Marketing time is the separate estimate of how long a sale would take afterward.
Fair-sale conditions: a broad market, wide publicity, time, knowledge and no duress.
It assumes an **arm's-length** sale between unrelated parties; family, related-company and forced sales are poor evidence.
**Market price** is what a property actually sold for, which may or may not equal market value.

head: Type of value
Meaning
Exam clue
rows: Most probable price to a typical informed buyer
Value to one investor, based on that investor's own goals
A neighbor who can share a lobby pays more; needing 10% on $50,000 of income means paying at most $500,000
Value to a particular user for a particular purpose
A plant built around one manufacturer's process
Cost to rebuild what a loss could destroy
Tax-roll value used to compute property tax
May be a fraction of market value; doesn't cap the price
Conservative; lenders often use the lower of price or appraisal
Must sell within 30 days; not market value

sections.heading: Elements, forces and principles of value
sections.intro: Principle questions usually tell a short story and ask which principle it shows.
points: All four **elements of value** (DUST) must exist: demand, utility, scarcity and transferability. Immobility, indestructibility and uniqueness describe land itself, not value.
Demand means **effective demand**: desire backed by purchasing power.

Four **forces** affect value (PEGS): physical (location, topography, access), economic (jobs, incomes, interest rates), governmental (zoning, taxes, codes) and social (population, household size, tastes).

The protected traits of a neighborhood's residents are never a value factor. The federal Fair Housing Act expressly covers appraising, and New York's Human Rights Law bars discrimination in real estate transactions.
Under the principle of change, neighborhoods follow a **life cycle**: growth, stability, decline, and sometimes revitalization.

head: Principle
Meaning
Exam clue
rows: No one pays more than an equally desirable substitute costs
Won't pay $520,000 when near-twins sell for $490,000
Excess supply lowers prices; excess demand raises them
300 new condos, same buyers, prices fall
Fitting in with the neighbors maximizes value
A superior property is pulled down by lesser neighbors
An inferior property is pulled up by better neighbors
A cottage on a street of large, expensive homes
A part is worth what it adds, not what it cost
Value is the present worth of expected benefits
Prices fall on news of a plant closing
Conditions change, so value is tied to a date
A March appraisal is stale by September
Influences outside the property raise or lower value
A rail station raises values; a landfill lowers them
Land and improvements in proportion maximize value
A mansion squeezed onto a tiny lot
Improvements pay off up to a point, then add less than they cost
A second bath pays; a fifth may not

sections.heading: Highest and best use and site valuation
points: **Highest and best use** is the reasonably probable use that is legally permissible, physically possible, financially feasible and maximally productive, **tested in that order**.
A use barred by zoning fails no matter how profitable. Among uses passing the first three tests, the highest-value one wins.
Test it **as vacant** and as improved. If the site's value as vacant, minus demolition cost, exceeds the property's value as improved, the existing building is an **interim use**.
**Site valuation**: land is usually valued by comparing vacant-land sales, adjusted for location, size, shape, frontage, topography, utilities and zoning. Usable area matters more than gross acreage.
Other land methods: **allocation** applies a typical land-to-total ratio; **extraction** takes the sale price minus the depreciated improvements.
**Assemblage** is combining parcels; **plottage** is the extra value the combined parcel has.

example.title: Worked example: as vacant vs. as improved
steps: An old house on a lot rezoned for apartments is worth $680,000 as improved.
The cleared lot would sell for $900,000, and demolition costs $60,000, so it nets $840,000 as vacant.
Answer: $840,000 beats $680,000, so the house is an interim use and redevelopment is the highest and best use.

sections.heading: The appraisal process
sections.intro: Expect questions on the first step and on the order of the steps.
points: Step one is **defining the problem**: client and intended use, the property and the rights appraised, the type of value, the **effective date** and any assumptions.
Rights matter. **Fee simple** is ownership free of leases.
The **leased fee** is the landlord's interest in leased property; the **leasehold** is the tenant's. A building locked into a below-market lease can be worth less as a leased fee.
The **effective date** is the date the value applies to. Values go stale as markets change; New York law sets no expiration date, though lenders and agencies limit how old an appraisal may be.

USPAP's report options are the **Appraisal Report** and the **Restricted Appraisal Report**; home loans typically use forms such as the Uniform Residential Appraisal Report (URAR). An appraisal is not a home inspection.

example.title: Worked example: the steps in order for a leased office building
steps: Define the problem: lender client, leased fee interest, market value, effective date June 1.
Set the scope of work: inspection, lease review, sales and rent comparables.
Collect general data (region, neighborhood, trends) and specific data (the subject and the comparables).
Analyze the market and highest and best use, as vacant and as improved.
Value the land from vacant-site sales.
Apply the approaches: income first, supported by sales comparison and cost.
Reconcile, giving the income approach the most weight.
Answer: the last step is the report, signed with the appraiser's credential title and number.

sections.heading: Appraiser licensing, standards and independence
sections.intro: Real estate licensees and appraisers are separate professions under separate laws.
points: The Department of State licenses and certifies New York appraisers under **Executive Law Article 6-E**, with the **State Board of Real Estate Appraisal**.
A broker or salesperson license under Real Property Law Article 12-A is not an appraiser credential.

Only credential holders may use the titles 'state certified real estate appraiser', 'state licensed real estate appraiser' or 'state licensed real estate appraiser assistant', or call an appraisal 'certified' or 'licensed' (Exec. Law §160-b).
Article 6-E is a title law. It doesn't bar uncredentialed appraising (§160-b(2)), but federally related loans need a credentialed appraiser, and a licensee's CMA may never be called an appraisal.
Reports must show the credential title and number (§160-r).
**FIRREA** requires credentialed appraisers for federally related loans above set thresholds (Title XI of the Financial Institutions Reform, Recovery, and Enforcement Act, 1989).
FIRREA makes **USPAP** the standard. USPAP is written by the Appraisal Standards Board of The Appraisal Foundation.
The federal bank appraisal threshold for home loans is **$400,000** since 2019; older books say $250,000. Fannie Mae, Freddie Mac, FHA and VA keep their own appraisal rules.
USPAP **Ethics Rule**: be impartial and never discriminate. Never take a fee contingent on a predetermined result, the value reported or the loan closing.
Disclosure doesn't cure a contingent fee, and New York bans such fees too (Exec. Law §160-y).
USPAP **Competency Rule**: be competent. If not, disclose the gap to the client before accepting, become competent and describe how in the report; or decline.
Holding the right credential doesn't by itself prove competence for an unfamiliar property type.

**Appraiser independence**: on a loan secured by a consumer's principal dwelling, no lender, broker, agent or other interested person may pressure the appraiser toward a value, even unsuccessfully (Truth in Lending Act §129E; Regulation Z §1026.42).
Allowed: asking through the lender to consider more comps, explain the conclusion or correct errors.

**Regulation B**: on a first-lien dwelling loan the applicant gets a free copy of each appraisal promptly on completion or 3 business days before closing, whichever is earlier, unless the applicant waives the timing. The lender orders the appraisal; the buyer usually pays for it.

After a **low appraisal**, the buyer adds cash, the price is renegotiated, the lender is asked to reconsider with better comps, or the buyer uses an appraisal or mortgage contingency if the contract has one.
Since January 1, 2026, New York appraisers must take a Valuation Bias and Fair Housing Laws and Regulations course.
That course is 8 hours in qualifying education, at least 7 hours for the first renewal and 4 for later renewals.
DOS doesn't count a licensee's CMAs as appraisal experience.
