example.title: Worked example: a Brooklyn two-family sale at $1,150,000
steps: Step 1: NYS transfer tax = $1,150,000 ÷ $500 = 2,300 units × $2 = $4,600 (seller).
Step 2: NYC RPTT: residential and over $500,000, so 1.425% × $1,150,000 = $16,387.50 (seller).
Step 3: Mansion tax: residential and at least $1 million, so 1% × $1,150,000 = $11,500 (buyer).
Step 4: The price is under $2 million, so neither NYC extra applies.
Step 5: Seller's transfer taxes = $4,600 + $16,387.50 = $20,987.50.
Trap: 1.425% of only the $650,000 above $500,000 ($9,262.50), or 1% of only the $150,000 above $1 million ($1,500), treats cliff taxes as marginal.
Answer: seller $20,987.50; buyer $11,500 (plus mortgage recording tax on any loan).

sections.heading: Loan math: LTV, points, interest and amortization
sections.intro: Loan problems move from price to loan to costs to payments. Once the loan amount is set, it is the base for everything that follows.
points: **Loan-to-value (LTV)** uses the **lower of price or appraisal**. A low appraisal shrinks the loan and the buyer covers the gap; a high one doesn't enlarge it.
**Down payment** = price − loan. **Combined LTV** = (first + second mortgage) ÷ value.
**Points charged** = point cost ÷ loan ($5,700 ÷ $380,000 = 1.5).
**Discount points** are prepaid interest that buy a lower rate; an **origination fee** pays for making the loan. No fixed rule says how much rate a point buys.
**Interest** runs on the **current balance**, not the original loan. Working backward, balance = monthly interest × 12 ÷ rate ($1,300 × 12 ÷ 0.065 = $240,000).
Interest is paid in **arrears**, so the June 1 payment covers May's interest.
**Prepaid (per diem) interest** = loan × rate ÷ 365 (or 360) × days.
Per diem example: $365,000 at 6% accrues $60 a day. A June 22 closing collects June 22–30, 9 days counting the closing day = $540.
**Amortization**: the payment stays level while the interest share falls and the principal share grows. Escrow never reduces the balance.
**Annual debt service** is principal and interest (P&I) only: monthly P&I × 12.
**Interest-only**: payment = balance × rate ÷ 12 ($300,000 at 6% = $1,500), and the balance doesn't fall.
A **loan constant** = annual P&I ÷ loan. From a payment factor, loan = P&I ÷ factor × 1,000.
**Private mortgage insurance (PMI)** is usually required on a conventional loan above 80% of value.
Under the federal Homeowners Protection Act, a borrower in good standing may ask to cancel PMI at **80%** of original value. Original value is the lower of price or appraisal at origination.
PMI ends automatically at **78%** on schedule. On a $400,000 purchase appraised at $410,000, those balances are $320,000 and $312,000.

example.title: Worked example: from price to the second payment
steps: Facts: price $600,000; appraisal $590,000; the lender lends 80% of the lower value at 6.3% for 30 years (P&I $2,921.55) and charges 1.5 discount points.
Step 5: Month 1 principal = $2,921.55 − $2,478.00 = $443.55, so the new balance is $471,556.45.
Step 7: Month 2 principal = $2,921.55 − $2,475.67 = $445.88, so the balance is $471,110.57.
Trap: points on the price ($9,000), a loan based on the $600,000 price, or subtracting the whole payment from the balance.
Answer: loan $472,000; down payment $128,000; points $7,080; balance $471,110.57.

sections.heading: Qualifying ratios
sections.intro: Lenders compare monthly obligations with gross monthly income. Ratios such as 28% and 36% are lender guidelines stated in the question, not New York law.
points: **Gross monthly income** = annual gross income ÷ 12, combining co-borrowers. Ratios use gross (before-tax) income, not take-home pay.
**Housing expense** is **PITI** plus PMI and condo common charges or HOA dues when the lender counts them.
**Recurring debts** for the back-end ratio are obligations such as car loans, student loans and minimum card payments; groceries, utilities and phone bills don't count.
The **lower** payment limit controls because the borrower must pass both tests.
**Minimum income** is the higher of housing ÷ front-end limit and (housing + debts) ÷ back-end limit.
Minimum-income example: $2,240 of PITI and $700 of debts at 28/36 give $8,000 and $8,166.67, so $8,166.67 a month is needed.
**From payment to loan**: subtract monthly taxes, insurance and other escrows from the maximum PITI to get the P&I, then divide by the payment factor per $1,000.
Paying off a debt raises the maximum payment only when the back-end test is the one that binds.

example.title: Worked example: maximum payment and loan
steps: Facts: co-borrowers earn $102,000 a year combined; other debts total $830 a month; limits are 28% and 36%; taxes and insurance will be $610 a month; the lender's factor is $6.32 per $1,000.
Step 1: Gross monthly income = $102,000 ÷ 12 = $8,500.
Step 2: Front-end cap = $8,500 × 28% = $2,380.
Step 3: Back-end cap = $8,500 × 36% = $3,060, minus $830 of debts = $2,230.
Step 4: The lower figure, $2,230, is the maximum PITI.
Answer: maximum PITI $2,230; maximum loan about $256,329.

sections.heading: Area, volume, acres and front feet
sections.intro: Sketch the lot, split odd shapes into rectangles and triangles, keep every dimension in feet, and convert to acres or yards last.
points: **Triangle** height is measured at a right angle to the base, never along a slanted side.
A **trapezoid** has two parallel sides: average them and multiply by the perpendicular distance between them.
**Irregular shapes**: split an L into two rectangles and add them, or take the outer rectangle and subtract the cutout. Multiplying an L's outside dimensions counts space that isn't there.
**Perimeter** (the sum of the sides) prices fencing, not area: a 120 × 80 ft lot has 400 ft, so fencing at $25 a foot costs $10,000.
**Acres**: a square one-acre lot is about 208.7 ft on a side, the square root of 43,560.
**Lots from a tract** = (total area − road land) ÷ lot size. Example: 10 acres less 25% for roads = 326,700 sq ft ÷ 21,780 = 15 half-acre lots.
**Volume** = length × width × height in feet (4 in = 1/3 ft). Concrete, fill and topsoil are priced per cubic yard.
The cubic-foot cost method multiplies a building's volume by a cost per cubic foot.
**Coverage** = cubic feet ÷ depth: 10 cu yd (270 cu ft) spread 6 in deep covers 540 sq ft.
**Front foot**: in a lot described as 90 × 140 ft, 90 is the street frontage. Depth doesn't enter a front-foot price.
**Price per front foot** = price ÷ frontage. Depth = area ÷ frontage: 21,780 sq ft with 121 ft of frontage is 180 ft deep.
**Price per square foot** = price ÷ square feet. It can rank lots differently from front-foot price.
To value a house from comps, average their price per square foot and multiply by the subject's size. Count only the space the comps counted, such as above-grade living area.

example.title: Worked example: a trapezoid lot priced two ways
steps: Facts: the front and rear lot lines are parallel, 200 ft and 240 ft long, and 297 ft apart; the 200-ft line is the street frontage. Offers: $62,000 per acre or $450 per front foot.
Step 2: Acres = 65,340 ÷ 43,560 = 1.5 acres.
Step 3: Per-acre offer = 1.5 × $62,000 = $93,000.
Step 4: Per-front-foot offer = 200 × $450 = $90,000 (depth is ignored).
Trap: adding the parallel sides without halving gives 130,680 sq ft (3 acres).
Answer: 1.5 acres; the per-acre offer is $3,000 higher.

sections.heading: Property tax, mills and equalization
sections.intro: In New York, real property taxes are levied by counties, cities, towns, villages, school districts and special districts; the state itself levies none.
points: **Taxable assessed value** = assessed value − partial exemptions (for example, veterans' and senior citizens' exemptions). Market value and sale price are not the base.
**Levy** = budget − non-property-tax revenue. Wholly exempt property (houses of worship, government land) is left out of the taxable total, which raises everyone else's rate.
**Level of assessment**: New York assessors may assess at a uniform percentage of market value rather than 100%, so assessed value = market value × that percentage (RPTL §305).
The state's **equalization rate** lets county and school taxes be shared fairly among towns that assess at different levels.
**Revaluation**: reassessing at full value raises assessments and lowers the rate.
With the same levy, a bill changes only if the owner's share of total value changes, so compute both bills.
**Tax periods** for prorations: school taxes typically run July 1–June 30, town and county taxes usually the calendar year, and NYC's tax year July 1–June 30. Use the period the question gives.

example.title: Worked example: a village rate and one owner's bill
steps: Facts: the village budget is $4,850,000 with $1,250,000 of other revenue; total taxable assessed value is $150,000,000. A home is assessed at $210,000 with a $15,000 exemption.
Step 3: Taxable assessed value = $210,000 − $15,000 = $195,000.
Step 5: If the village's equalization rate is 60%, the home's full value = $210,000 ÷ 0.60 = $350,000.
Trap: taxing market value ($350,000 × 0.024 = $8,400) or skipping the exemption ($5,040).
Answer: 24 mills; annual tax $4,680.

sections.heading: Prorations
sections.intro: A proration divides a bill or income item between seller and buyer by days. Three facts decide most answers: the day-count method, who owns the closing day, and whether the item was paid in advance or is still owed.
points: **Day counts**: ÷ 360 (twelve 30-day months) or ÷ 365 (actual days; 366 in a leap year if stated); monthly items use ÷ 30 or the month's actual days. Use only the method stated.
**Count days inclusively** and give the closing day to whoever owns it: a seller who owns an August 14 closing day has 7 × 30 + 14 = 224 days with 30-day months, or 226 actual days.
**Who owns the closing day?** The widely used bar-association residential contract in New York apportions items as of midnight of the day before closing, so the buyer owns closing day.
Some textbooks charge the closing day to the seller. Exam questions state the rule.
**Prorate over the bill's own period**: a July 1–June 30 school tax counts from July 1, not January 1, and a half-year installment is spread over that half-year's days.
**Rent**: prorate only rent actually collected; unpaid rent isn't apportioned unless the contract says so.
**Security deposits** transfer to the buyer in full and aren't prorated (GOL §7-105).
Fuel oil isn't prorated by days: gallons left × price, credited to the seller.
Every proration is a **double entry**: the same amount is a debit to one party and a credit to the other.

head: Item
Seller
Buyer
rows: Taxes the seller prepaid past the closing date
Taxes unpaid for the seller's days (buyer pays the bill later)
Rent the seller collected for the closing month
Accrued interest on a mortgage the buyer assumes
Fuel oil left in the tank

example.title: Worked example: prepaid taxes under both day counts
steps: Facts: closing is September 18 in a non-leap year; the seller prepaid the $8,760 calendar-year taxes; the buyer owns the closing day.
Step 1 (365-day method): daily rate = $8,760 ÷ 365 = $24.
Step 2: Buyer's days = Sept 18–30 (13) + Oct (31) + Nov (30) + Dec (31) = 105; the seller has the other 260.
Step 3: Buyer's share = 105 × $24 = $2,520: credit seller, debit buyer, because the seller paid the whole year.
Step 4 (360-day method): buyer's days = 13 + 90 = 103.
Step 5: Buyer's share = 103 × $8,760 ÷ 360 = $2,506.33 (keep the $24.333… daily rate unrounded).
Trap: giving the seller the closing day leaves the buyer 104 days ($2,496), and debiting the seller reverses the direction.
Answer: credit seller and debit buyer $2,520 (actual days) or $2,506.33 (360-day year).

sections.heading: Income property: NOI, cap rate and GRM
sections.intro: The income approach turns a year of net operating income into a value. Build NOI in order, then apply IRV.
points: **Gross income** is income before expenses; **net income** is what remains after them.
**PGI** (potential gross income) = every unit at full rent for a year.
**EGI** (effective gross income) = PGI − vacancy and collection loss + other income (laundry, parking, storage). Vacancy is a percentage of PGI unless stated otherwise.
**NOI** (net operating income) = EGI − operating expenses; the table below shows what counts.
Value moves opposite the cap rate: $90,000 of NOI is worth $1,500,000 at 6% but $1,200,000 at 7.5%.
**After-tax cash flow**: loan principal isn't deductible, and depreciation is deductible even though it isn't a cash expense.
**Gross rent multiplier (GRM)**: a monthly GRM is 12 times the annual GRM for the same property, so the size of the multiplier tells you which rent to use.
A **gross income multiplier (GIM)** uses total gross income, including other income. Build the comparable's multiplier and apply it to the subject on the same basis.

head: Item
Operating expense?
Why
rows: Utilities, repairs, management, reserves for replacement
Depreciation and the owner's income tax
Capital spending, not an annual expense

example.title: Worked example: a 10-unit building
steps: Facts: 10 units at $2,100 a month; 5% vacancy and collection loss; $3,600 of laundry income; $85,500 of operating expenses; $108,000 of annual debt service; 7% cap rate; $550,000 of cash invested.
Trap: capitalizing the cash flow after debt service ($49,500 ÷ 0.07 = $707,142.86) confuses cash flow with NOI.
Answer: indicated value $2,250,000.

sections.heading: Percentage leases
sections.intro: Retail tenants often pay a fixed base rent plus a percentage of gross sales above a breakpoint.
points: The percentage applies to **gross sales** (receipts), not profit.
The **natural breakpoint** is the sales level at which the percentage just equals the base rent. A lease may set a different, negotiated breakpoint, so use the one the question gives.
With a natural breakpoint, total rent equals the **larger** of the base rent or rate × total sales. Below the breakpoint the tenant pays base rent only; a shortfall doesn't reduce the base rent.
**Annualize first**: base rent is often quoted monthly, so multiply by 12 before dividing it by the rate or comparing it with annual sales.
**Working backward** to sales: sales above the breakpoint = (total rent − base rent) ÷ rate; total sales = breakpoint + that amount.

example.title: Worked example: rent with a natural breakpoint
steps: Facts: base rent is $7,500 a month plus 6% of annual gross sales above the natural breakpoint; this year's sales are $1,820,000.
Step 1: Annual base rent = $7,500 × 12 = $90,000.
Step 2: Natural breakpoint = $90,000 ÷ 0.06 = $1,500,000.
Trap: a breakpoint built from the monthly base ($7,500 ÷ 0.06 = $125,000), or 6% of all sales added on top of the base ($199,200).
Answer: $109,200 for the year.

sections.heading: Loss factor, add-on factor and rentable area
sections.intro: Office rent is quoted per rentable square foot, but the tenant occupies usable square feet. The factor linking them can be stated two ways, with different denominators.
points: **Usable area** is the space a tenant occupies exclusively. **Rentable area** adds the tenant's share of common areas (lobbies, corridors, restrooms).
**Carpetable area** is the unobstructed floor inside the usable space.
**Building efficiency** = usable ÷ rentable = 1 − loss factor.
**Which factor?** The standard loss factor is measured against rentable area, so divide by (1 − loss factor). The NYREPL formula list uses this definition.
The NYREPL annual-rent formula, (usable × loss factor + usable) × rate, marks usable area up instead. That is the add-on method, and it gives less rentable area for the same percentage.
'Add-on' or 'add X% to usable area' means multiply; a loss factor measured on rentable area means divide.
**Annual rent** = rentable sq ft × annual rate per rentable sq ft; divide by 12 for monthly rent. Confirm whether the quoted rate is annual or monthly.
Compare spaces on **total rent** for the usable area you need, not on the quoted rate: a lower rate with a bigger loss factor can cost more.

example.title: Worked example: rent for a usable-area requirement
steps: Facts: a tenant needs 7,200 usable sq ft; the building quotes $52 per rentable sq ft per year and a 20% loss factor (common area as a share of rentable area).
Step 1: Rentable area = 7,200 ÷ (1 − 0.20) = 9,000 sq ft.
Step 5: For contrast, a 20% add-on factor would mean 7,200 × 1.20 = 8,640 rentable sq ft and $449,280 a year.
Trap: pricing only the usable area ($374,400), or using the add-on method when the question defines a loss factor.
Answer: $468,000 a year ($39,000 a month).

sections.heading: Depreciation in appraisal and for taxes
sections.intro: Depreciation means two different things on the exam: lost value in the cost approach, and a tax deduction for investment property. Land is never depreciated in either.
points: **Cost approach**: use the improvements' replacement (or reproduction) cost new, and add depreciated site improvements if they are listed separately.
**Age-life (straight-line) method**: the annual rate is 1 ÷ economic life (a 50-year life = 2% a year).
**Effective age** reflects condition and renovation and can be lower or higher than actual age; use it when given.

**Three kinds of accrued depreciation**: physical deterioration (wear and tear), functional obsolescence (outdated design or layout) and external obsolescence (caused outside the property, such as a nearby nuisance). Subtract every one the question lists.
**Land value by extraction** = sale price − depreciated building value.
**Tax depreciation (cost recovery)** applies to rental and business property; a personal residence isn't depreciated.
Tax depreciation example: a $770,000 rental house with $220,000 of land gives $550,000 ÷ 27.5 = $20,000 a year.
**Adjusted basis** keeps the land: a $1,000,000 office building with $220,000 of land, after 6 years at $20,000, has an adjusted basis of $880,000.

head: Feature
Appraisal (cost approach)
Tax (cost recovery)
rows: Not depreciated, but stays in the basis

example.title: Worked example: cost approach with effective age
steps: Facts: a 2,600 sq ft house costs $240 per sq ft to replace; actual age 22 years, effective age 15 years, economic life 60 years; the land is worth $185,000.
Step 2: Accrued depreciation = $624,000 × 15 ÷ 60 = $156,000 (25%).
Step 3: Depreciated improvements = $624,000 − $156,000 = $468,000.
Trap: using actual age (22 ÷ 60 gives $228,800 of depreciation and a $580,200 value) or depreciating the land too.

sections.heading: Appreciation, profit and percent change
sections.intro: All of these are percent-change problems. The base is the starting value or the cost, not the ending value, unless the question names another base.
points: **Simple annual rate** = total percent change ÷ number of years.
**Compound growth**: future value = present value × (1 + rate)^years. At 5% a year for 3 years, $400,000 grows to $463,050 compounded, versus $460,000 with simple growth.
**Successive changes multiply**: a 20% loss then a 20% gain leaves 0.80 × 1.20 = 96% of the start.
Two sales at the same price, one at a 20% gain and one at a 20% loss on cost, produce a net loss. The loss is figured on the larger cost.
**Profit percentage** = profit ÷ total investment (price + capital improvements) unless another base is named.
Profit = net proceeds (price − commission − selling costs) − total investment.
**Percentage points vs. percent**: a rate rising from 4% to 5% is up 1 percentage point, which is a 25% increase in the rate.
**Home sale exclusion**: a seller who meets the ownership and use tests (2 of the last 5 years) may exclude up to $250,000 of gain, or $500,000 for most married couples filing jointly.

example.title: Worked example: an investor's profit percentage
steps: Facts: bought for $300,000; spent $60,000 on improvements; sold for $420,000 with a 5% commission and $3,000 of other selling costs.
Step 2: Net proceeds = $420,000 − $21,000 commission − $3,000 = $396,000.
Step 4: Profit percentage = $36,000 ÷ $360,000 = 10%.
Trap: ignoring the selling costs ($60,000 ÷ $360,000 = 16.67%) or dividing by the sale price ($36,000 ÷ $420,000 = 8.57%).
Answer: 10%.

guides.title: Municipal Agencies
guides.overview: How New York's counties, cities, towns and villages split land-use power, which board or office does each job, and how NYC agencies and ULURP work. The exam hits hardest on agency-to-function matching, the planning board, ZBA and Article 78 rules, and one theme: **elected bodies make the rules, appointed boards apply them, and advisory bodies only advise**.

numbers.label: County referral distance (GML §239-m) and neighbor-notice distance (§239-nn)
County's time to respond after a full statement; then the board may act
Votes of all members to override a county disapproval or modification (5 members: 4)
All-member town board vote to rezone after a 20% owner protest petition
Published notice of a town zoning hearing; §239-nn notice to a neighboring clerk
Published notice of a ZBA hearing; ZBA decision filed within 5 business days

ZBA decision deadline after its hearing; deadline to file a signed final plat
Article 78 deadline after a ZBA or planning board filing (general limit: 4 months)
Yearly training for planning board and ZBA members

FOIL response; appeal a denial within 30 days, decided in 10 business days
ULURP days: community board, borough president, City Planning Commission, City Council = 200
Mayoral veto window; Council override window and vote (34 of 51 members)
CPC: 7 mayoral (incl. chair), 1 per borough president, 1 public advocate; 7 approve
ELURP and Fast Track: community board and borough president 60 together, CPC 30, final
Minimum age for NYC landmark designation
NYC buildings finished before 1938 need no CO unless use, egress or occupancy changed
Discontinuance that ends an NYC nonconforming use (ZR §52-61)
Well to absorption field; tank 50, seepage pit 150, upgrade in drainage path 200

mustKnow: The elected **legislative body** (city council, town board, village board of trustees) adopts local laws, zoning, **rezonings**, the comprehensive plan, the budget and the tax levy.
The **planning board** (appointed, 5 or 7 members) reviews **subdivision plats** and site plans and advises; it doesn't adopt the plan or grant variances.
The **ZBA** (appointed, 3 or 5 members) is quasi-judicial: appeals, interpretations, **use and area variances**, and some special permits. It can't rezone.
Town board members can't serve on the town ZBA or planning board; village trustees can't serve on the village ZBA or planning board.
Town zoning covers only land **outside incorporated villages**; villages zone their own land; New York counties generally don't zone.
The town **supervisor** presides over the town board and votes; a village board is the **mayor plus four trustees** by default.
Zoning must be **in accordance with the comprehensive plan**, which the legislative body adopts.
**Cluster development**: the planning board, if authorized by the town board, groups homes to save open space without raising density.
**Use variance**: **unnecessary hardship**, meaning no reasonable return from any permitted use (financial proof), a unique hardship, no change in neighborhood character, and not self-created.
**Area variance**: the owner's benefit is weighed against detriment to the neighborhood using five factors; self-created difficulty doesn't automatically bar it.
A **special use permit** is for a use the zoning already lists for the district; meet its standards, no hardship needed.

Votes count **all members**, not those present: ZBA and planning board majorities, the §239-m majority plus one, and protest-petition three-fourths. Exception: a ZBA rehearing needs **unanimity of members present**.
Building inspector's zoning ruling → ZBA appeal within **60 days** → Article 78 within **30 days** after the ZBA decision is filed.
Article 78 asks only whether the decision was illegal, **arbitrary and capricious** or irrational; the court doesn't rehear the case.
**ARB** approval covers appearance only; a building permit is still required.
The **CAC** inventories open space and wetlands and advises; it can become a **conservation board**. Neither issues DEC permits.
**Building department**: permits, inspections, **certificates of occupancy**, violations. A permit authorizes work; the CO confirms it.
The **assessor** values; the **legislative body** sets the levy and rate; the receiver of taxes collects; the board of assessment review hears grievances.
The **county health department** approves septic systems, wells, and water and sewer plans for **realty subdivisions** (5 or more lots of 5 acres or less within 3 years).
**County referral**: plans, zoning changes, special permits, site plans and variances within **500 feet** of listed features go to the county before final action (GML §239-m).
County disapproval or modification → the board needs a **majority plus one of all members** and must report its reasons to the county within 30 days.
A SEQR **lead agency** must be an **involved agency**; an interested agency only comments; the DEC Commissioner settles lead-agency disputes after 30 days.
SEQR: **Type I** is likely significant (Full EAF); **Type II** needs no review (such as ministerial building permits); Unlisted is everything else.
A **negative declaration** means no EIS; a positive declaration means an EIS. A **conditioned negative declaration** is for Unlisted actions only.
**Open Meetings Law**: 72-hour notice for meetings set a week ahead; executive session only for listed subjects, by a majority of the total membership; **ZBA** deliberations must be public.
**FOIL** covers records: 5 business days to respond; 30 days to appeal a denial.
NYC: DOB issues permits and COs; the **BSA** grants variances and hears DOB appeals; DCP and the CPC handle zoning changes and ULURP; the **LPC** handles landmarks.
NYC: **HPD** enforces the housing code and registration; DEP runs water and sewer; **DOF** handles assessments, taxes and ACRIS; OATH decides summonses.
**ULURP**: certification → community board 60 → borough president 30 → CPC 60 → Council 50 → mayor 5 → override 10. Community board and borough president votes are **advisory**.

Zoning **map** changes go through ULURP; zoning **text** amendments and BSA variances don't (text changes still get CPC and Council review). Since 2025, modest qualifying map changes can use ELURP instead.
**Recent update (2025 NYC Charter; may not be tested yet)**: ELURP and the Affordable Housing Fast Track end at the CPC in about 90 days. Standard ULURP still ends with the Council.

Also new in 2025: the BSA can fast-track publicly financed affordable housing, and the **Affordable Housing Appeals Board** (2 of 3 votes) can reverse Council denials or modifications of qualifying affordable-housing applications.
The 2025 proposal to move NYC elections to even years failed.

traps.trap: The ZBA can rezone an area if enough owners want it.
traps.truth: Rezoning is a legislative act of the town board, city council or village board. The ZBA gives relief to single parcels and interprets the law.

traps.trap: The planning board adopts the comprehensive plan and zoning.
traps.truth: The legislative body adopts both; the planning board prepares, reviews and recommends.

traps.trap: A majority of the members present is enough.
traps.truth: ZBA and planning board actions need a majority of all members; a §239-m override needs a majority plus one of all members; a protest petition needs three-fourths of all board members.

traps.trap: If the county ignores a §239-m referral, the project is disapproved.
traps.truth: After 30 days of silence the board may act without the report. Only a disapproval or modification recommendation (even a late one received at least 2 days before final action) triggers majority plus one.

traps.trap: A ZBA is quasi-judicial, so it may deliberate in private.
traps.truth: The Open Meetings Law exempts quasi-judicial proceedings except those of zoning boards of appeals. A ZBA deliberates and votes in public.

traps.trap: 72 hours is the FOIL response time.
traps.truth: 72 hours is the Open Meetings Law notice period; FOIL requires a response within 5 business days.

traps.trap: A neighbor has 4 months to sue over a town ZBA variance.
traps.truth: Town Law allows 30 days after the decision is filed with the town clerk; 4 months is the general Article 78 limit.

traps.trap: The town board can overrule its ZBA.
traps.truth: ZBA decisions go to State Supreme Court by Article 78. The town board, Department of State and county clerk can't reverse them.

traps.trap: An issued building permit means the work is approved.
traps.truth: A permit only authorizes work. A final inspection and a CO or certificate of compliance show completion; an old open permit isn't grandfathered.

traps.trap: If the assessor's record card lists an apartment, it's legal.
traps.truth: The assessor records features for taxes. Legality depends on zoning and the building department's permits and CO.

traps.trap: A conservation advisory council member can confirm a wet area isn't a regulated wetland.
traps.truth: The CAC only advises. Get a written jurisdictional determination from DEC and check federal and local rules.

traps.trap: A community board or borough president 'no' kills a ULURP application.
traps.truth: Their recommendations are advisory; the City Planning Commission and City Council decide.

traps.trap: Every NYC zoning, variance and landmark matter goes through ULURP.
traps.truth: BSA variances, LPC actions and zoning text amendments have their own procedures. ULURP covers zoning map changes, CPC special permits, city property deals and similar actions.

traps.trap: ULURP takes 240 days because each step gets 60.
traps.truth: 60 + 30 + 60 + 50 = 200 days; a veto and override can add 15 more.

traps.trap: Any old building is a landmark, and State Register listing blocks changes.
traps.truth: Only LPC or local landmark-commission designation restricts alterations; NYC landmarks must be at least 30 years old. State or National Register listing restricts private work only when state or federal funding, licenses or permits are involved.

traps.trap: Since the 2025 Charter changes, NYC rezonings no longer go to the City Council.
traps.truth: Standard ULURP rezonings still get a Council vote and possible mayoral veto. Only qualifying ELURP and Affordable Housing Fast Track applications end at the CPC, and the exam may not test these new tracks yet.

mnemonics.name: Make it, plan it, bend it
mnemonics.meaning: The legislative body makes the rules (zoning, rezoning, budget, tax rate); the planning board plans and reviews layouts (master plan, plats, site plans); the ZBA bends the rules for one parcel (variances, interpretations).

mnemonics.name: ULURP 60-30-60-50
mnemonics.meaning: Community board 60, borough president 30, City Planning Commission 60, City Council 50 = 200 days; then mayor 5 and override 10.

mnemonics.name: Lead must be involved
mnemonics.meaning: A SEQR lead agency must have power to fund, approve or undertake the action; an interested agency, such as a CAC, can only comment.

formulas.name: Majority plus one (GML §239-m)
formulas.formula: Majority = (all members ÷ 2, rounded down) + 1; override = majority + 1

formulas.name: Protest-petition vote (Town Law §265)
formulas.formula: Votes needed = all board members × 3/4, rounded up

formulas.name: Unused floor area (FAR)
formulas.formula: Maximum floor area = lot area × FAR; unused = maximum − existing

sections.heading: How local government is organized in New York
sections.intro: Every parcel is in a county and in either a city or a town; some town land is also inside a village. The layer decides who zones and taxes it.
points: **Counties** run regional services: the county clerk records deeds and plats, the county health department approves septic and water systems, and the county planning agency reviews §239-m referrals. Counties generally don't zone.
**Cities** run under their own charters, with an elected council and a mayor (a strong mayor with a veto, a weak mayor, or a council-appointed city manager).
**Towns** cover all land outside cities (and Indian reservations), but town zoning applies only **outside incorporated villages** (Town Law §261).
**Villages** sit inside towns. Village residents pay town taxes too, but the village board of trustees zones village land, so check for a village before reading any zoning map.
**Home rule** lets local governments pass local laws consistent with state law. School and special districts (fire, water, sewer) tax but never zone.
**New York City** is one city of five boroughs, each also a county, with no towns or villages. It uses its Charter, Zoning Resolution and own agencies instead of the Town and Village Law.

Elected legislative body

Generally none; its planning agency reviews referrals

Mayor, plus five elected borough presidents
Zoning Resolution, via CPC, Council and BSA

sections.heading: The legislative body: council, town board, village board
sections.intro: If a question asks who changes the law, the zoning map, the budget or the tax rate, the answer is the elected legislative body.
points: Powers: local laws, the zoning ordinance and map and their amendments (**rezoning**), the comprehensive plan and official map, the **budget and tax levy** (which produces the rate), cluster authorization, moratoria, and eminent domain decisions.
It creates and fills the appointed boards (planning board, ZBA, CAC, ARB, landmark commission). In a village, the mayor appoints planning board and ZBA members with trustee approval.
The **town board** is the elected supervisor, who presides and votes, plus council members. The **village board of trustees** is the mayor plus four trustees by default.
Town rezoning steps: a hearing after at least **10 days'** published notice, a §239-m county referral, and SEQR review.
The town also sends written notice at least 10 days ahead to the clerk of any city, village, town or county whose boundary is within **500 feet**.
Notice also goes to the state park commission or housing authority when a state park, parkway or public housing project is within 500 feet.

**Protest petition** (Town Law §265): if owners of 20% of the land in the change, or of the land within 100 feet adjacent or directly opposite, file a written protest, passage needs **three-fourths of all board members**. Villages match this (two-thirds on a three-member board).
The legislative body is not an appeals court for the ZBA; ZBA decisions are challenged in court.

example.title: Worked example: a protest-petition vote
steps: Owners of 25% of the land within 100 feet of a proposed rezoning file a written protest with a 5-member town board.
25% is at least 20%, so the three-fourths vote applies.
Round up, since there are no partial votes: 4 yes votes.
A 7-member board would need 7 × 3/4 = 5.25, rounded up to 6.
Answer: 4 of 5 (6 of 7). Without a protest, 3 of 5 would pass it.

sections.heading: The planning board and planning staff
sections.intro: The planning board is the appointed land-use reviewer and adviser. It reviews how land is divided and laid out; it doesn't legislate or grant variances.
points: A town board may create one by local law with **5 or 7** members, whom it appoints; staggered terms last as many years as the board has members. Town board members are ineligible, and alternates can fill in for conflicts.
Members need **4 hours of training a year** unless waived. Skipping it can cost reappointment, but no board decision is voided.

**Subdivision**: it reviews preliminary and final plats and may require improvements or a performance bond, plus parkland or a fee in lieu. The signed final plat must be filed with the county clerk within **62 days** or approval expires.
**Site plan review** covers parking, access, lighting, drainage and landscaping for a **permitted** use. If the use isn't permitted, the applicant first needs a use variance or rezoning.
It prepares or reviews the **comprehensive (master) plan** and advises other boards; the legislative body adopts the plan.
**Cluster development** (Town Law §278): with town board authorization, it may allow smaller lots that group homes and preserve open space, with no more units than a conventional layout.
A **planning department** is professional staff that advises but doesn't vote. In NYC, the Department of City Planning serves the City Planning Commission.

head: Request
Who decides
Key point
rows: File the signed plat within 62 days

sections.heading: The zoning board of appeals and Article 78
sections.intro: The ZBA is zoning's safety valve: an appointed, administrative and quasi-judicial body that applies legal standards to one property at a time. It interprets the ordinance but doesn't make policy.
points: **Membership**: 3 or 5 members appointed by the legislative body (in a village, by the mayor with trustee approval), staggered terms equal to the board size, and 4 hours of training a year. Legislative-body members are ineligible.

**Appellate jurisdiction**: it hears appeals from the zoning officer's or building inspector's orders, interpretations and determinations, filed within **60 days**. An appeal usually stays enforcement.
**Procedure**: the ZBA holds a hearing on at least **5 days'** published notice, with mailed notice to the parties and, when §239-m applies, to the county.
The ZBA decides within **62 days** after the hearing and files the decision with the clerk within 5 business days.
**Votes**: a majority of **all members**, regardless of absences; an appeal that falls short is denied by default. A rehearing needs a unanimous vote of the members present.
It must grant the **minimum variance** needed, and any conditions must relate to the land and its use, because a variance runs with the land. It can't waive private deed covenants.
**Article 78** (CPLR) is the court challenge in State Supreme Court. It's due within **30 days** after a ZBA or planning board decision is filed with the town clerk; the general limit is 4 months.
The court asks whether the decision was illegal, arbitrary and capricious or irrational; it doesn't rehear the case. The town board can't reverse a ZBA.

example.title: Worked example: a ZBA deadline chain
steps: The building inspector's permit denial is filed March 2, so the owner's ZBA appeal is due within 60 days: by May 1.
The ZBA holds its hearing May 20 and must decide within 62 days: by July 21.
It grants a variance July 15 and files the decision with the town clerk July 17.
A neighbor's Article 78 petition is due 30 days after filing: by August 16.
Answer: 60 days to appeal, 62 days to decide, 30 days to sue.

sections.heading: Who does what: the other local offices
sections.intro: Exam questions often describe a problem and ask which office handles it. Match the function, then confirm locally, because titles and delegated powers vary.
points: Approvals don't substitute for each other. Converting a barn into a restaurant can need zoning (use, site plan or special permit), building (code, CO), health (septic, food service) and engineering (access, drainage) sign-offs.
Rely on written answers from the office with authority, not a board member's remark, a seller's story or a neighbor's experience.
Permitted uses come from the current zoning text and map; the assessor's property class code is a tax label that grants no development rights.

sections.heading: Building permits, certificates of occupancy and code enforcement
sections.intro: Outside NYC, the NYS Uniform Fire Prevention and Building Code applies everywhere and is usually enforced by the city, town or village (see the opt-out chain below). NYC has its own Construction Codes, enforced by its Department of Buildings.
points: A **building permit** authorizes work, and inspections follow.
A **certificate of occupancy** (new buildings, changes of use) or certificate of compliance (other work) confirms compliance. A temporary CO can allow occupancy of finished, safe portions.
An **open permit** (issued but never finaled) is a red flag; age doesn't grandfather it, and the seller usually must close it out.

**Opt-out chain** (Executive Law §381): if a city, town or village opts out of enforcing the Uniform Code, the county enforces it; if the county opts out too, the **Department of State** does. The code always applies.
Stricter local construction standards need State Code Council approval, and Uniform Code variances come from Department of State regional boards of review, not the ZBA.
A building permit for a conforming house is **ministerial** (no discretion), so it's Type II under SEQR and isn't referred to the county.
A unit is legal only if zoning allows it and the building file supports it; tax records, rental history and listing descriptions don't legalize it.

sections.heading: Health, water and environmental approvals
sections.intro: Rural and suburban deals often turn on wells, septic systems and wetlands. Those approvals come from health and environmental agencies, not zoning boards.
points: The **county health department** (or a State Health Department office where the county has none) approves septic designs and private water supplies; local sanitary codes may be stricter than state minimums.

**Realty subdivision** (Public Health Law §1115): a tract divided into **5 or more residential lots of 5 acres or less** within any 3 years needs health department approval of water and sewage plans before lots are sold, leased or offered.
Reliable well-water results come from a lab certified under the State Health Department's **ELAP** program, not a home kit or the seller's disclosure.
**Wetlands**: DEC regulates freshwater wetlands of **12.4 acres** or more (7.4 acres from January 1, 2028), plus a 100-foot adjacent area.
DEC also regulates wetlands it mapped before January 1, 2025, including mapped wetlands of unusual local importance. The Adirondack Park Agency covers the Adirondack Park.
DEC narrowed its reach after an April 8, 2026 Albany County Supreme Court decision on its wetland rules. Get DEC's written **jurisdictional determination** and check Army Corps and local rules.
A CAC or local wetlands commission studies and advises (or runs a local permit law); it can't replace DEC.

head: Wastewater component
Minimum distance from a private well
rows: Any system upgrade in the drainage path to the well

sections.heading: County planning referral: GML §239-m, §239-n and §239-nn
sections.intro: Some local decisions affect people beyond town lines, so state law routes them past the county planning agency before final action.
points: **What** (§239-m): adopting or amending a comprehensive plan or zoning law, special use permits, site plans, use or area variances, and other zoning authorizations. Subdivision plats go under **§239-n**.

**Where**: land within **500 feet** of a city, town or village boundary; a county or state park; a county or state road, parkway or expressway; a county drainage channel; county or state land with a public building; or a farm in an agricultural district (not for area variances).
Schools, churches and private golf courses don't count.
Not referred: ministerial acts such as a building permit for a conforming house, or actions the county agrees in writing are of local concern only.
The county has **30 days** after receiving a full statement (application plus environmental assessment form) to recommend approval, modification or disapproval.
If the county misses that deadline, the board may act. A late report received at least **2 days** before final action still counts.

After a disapproval or modification recommendation, the board can act contrary only by a **majority plus one of all its members**. It must report its final action and reasons to the county within 30 days. Skipping a required referral can void the approval.

**Neighbor notice**: a hearing on a special use permit, use variance, site plan or subdivision within 500 feet of an adjacent municipality requires notice to that municipality's clerk at least **10 days** before (§239-nn). The neighbor may be heard, but its consent isn't needed. NYC is excluded.

example.title: Worked example: overriding the county
steps: A 5-member ZBA refers a use variance for land 300 feet from a county road, and the county recommends disapproval within 30 days.
Majority of all 5 = 3, so majority plus one = 4.
Only 4 members attend and vote 3–1 to grant. It fails, because the count uses all members, not those present.
Answer: 4 yes votes, plus a report of reasons to the county within 30 days.

sections.heading: SEQR: who reviews environmental impacts
sections.intro: The State Environmental Quality Review Act (ECL Article 8; 6 NYCRR Part 617) makes state and local agencies weigh environmental impacts before approving, funding or carrying out a discretionary action.
points: **Type I** actions are listed as likely to be significant, for example adopting a comprehensive plan or first zoning law, or changing allowed uses on 25 or more acres.
Type I actions need a Full Environmental Assessment Form (EAF) and, when several agencies are involved, coordinated review.
**Type II** actions need no review: ministerial building permits, area variances for 1–3 family homes, and a 1–3 family home on an approved lot. Everything else is **Unlisted**.
A **negative declaration** means no significant adverse impact and no environmental impact statement (EIS); a positive declaration requires an EIS.
A **conditioned negative declaration** is only for Unlisted actions, with mitigation conditions and a comment period of at least 30 days.

EIS path: required **scoping** → draft EIS → public comment (at least 30 days, and at least 10 days after any hearing) → final EIS → written **findings** by each involved agency → decision. No involved agency may approve before SEQR is complete.
Typical involved agencies: the town board for a rezoning, the planning board for a site plan or subdivision, the ZBA for a use variance, DEC for a state permit. A CAC is usually an interested agency.
**Recent update (May 2026; the exam may not test it yet)**: the FY2027 state budget, signed May 27, 2026, exempts many housing projects from SEQR, including NYC's CEQR.
The exemption covers projects on previously disturbed land connected to existing water and sewer, up to unit caps.
Unit caps: NYC 250 citywide, or 500 in medium- and high-density areas; 300 in other urbanized areas; 100 in non-urbanized areas; 20 where there's no zoning.
The budget also sets a 2-year deadline to finish an EIS. Zoning, permits and other environmental rules still apply.
NYC applies SEQR through **CEQR**, with a city agency such as DCP as lead agency for land-use applications.

sections.heading: Open Meetings Law and FOIL
sections.intro: Two separate laws open local government: the Open Meetings Law, or Sunshine Law (Public Officers Law Article 7), covers meetings; the Freedom of Information Law (Article 6) covers records.
points: **Executive session** subjects are limited: public safety, law-enforcement matters, litigation, collective bargaining, exams, and a particular person's medical, financial or employment history (or hiring, discipline or firing).

Executive session also covers the **proposed acquisition, sale or lease of real property** (or securities) when publicity would substantially affect its value. No formal vote to spend public money may be taken there.

Exempt from the Open Meetings Law: judicial and quasi-judicial proceedings **except zoning boards of appeals** (and the Public Service Commission), political caucuses, and matters made confidential by law.
**Minutes** are due within **2 weeks**; minutes of a vote taken in executive session are due within 1 week.
A public hearing (comments) differs from a meeting (deliberation). An open meeting doesn't guarantee a right to speak.
FOIL lets a licensee request a town's permit file, violation history or ZBA decisions, but privacy, security and internal pre-decision memos may be withheld.

sections.heading: New York City agencies
sections.intro: NYC has no town boards or village ZBAs. Its land-use and building functions are split among agencies created by the City Charter.
points: **HPD registration**: every multiple dwelling (3 or more units) and every 1–2 family home where neither the owner nor an immediate family member lives must register yearly; an unregistered owner can't bring a nonpayment case. HPD doesn't issue COs.

**HPD violation classes**: A is non-hazardous (90 days to correct), B is hazardous (30 days), and C is immediately hazardous (generally 24 hours). Class C has a few exceptions, such as 21 days for lead paint. No heat in heat season is Class C. There is no Class D.
**LPC permits**: staff issue a Certificate of No Effect for DOB-permitted work that doesn't affect protected features, and a Permit for Minor Work for rule-compliant work that does.
Work outside LPC's rules, such as a visible rooftop addition, demolition or new construction, needs a **Certificate of Appropriateness** from the full Commission after a public hearing.

**Landmarks** may be individual, interior, scenic or historic districts and must be at least **30 years** old. Interior landmarks must be customarily open or accessible to the public, so a private apartment doesn't qualify.

**BSA variance findings**: unique physical conditions, no reasonable return (not required for nonprofits), no harm to neighborhood character, hardship not created by the owner or a predecessor, and the **minimum variance** (ZR §72-21).
Taxes: DOF mails the Notice of Property Value each January; the separate **NYC Tax Commission** hears assessment appeals; the **City Council** fixes tax rates.
ACRIS covers Manhattan, the Bronx, Brooklyn and Queens; Staten Island records go to the Richmond County Clerk.

sections.heading: NYC zoning and building records to check
sections.intro: Most NYC deal problems show up in DOB, HPD, DEP and DOF records. Know what each document proves.
points: The **certificate of occupancy** fixes legal use and unit count; an extra unit is illegal until DOB amends the CO.
Buildings finished **before 1938** generally need no CO unless use, egress or occupancy changed. DOB can issue a Letter of No Objection confirming use.

An owner can't collect rent or sue for nonpayment for periods a multiple dwelling is occupied without the required residential CO (Multiple Dwelling Law §§301–302). Compliant Loft Law units are excepted.
**Districts**: R (residence), C (commercial), M (manufacturing). **C1 and C2 overlays** on residential blocks allow local retail; overlays are zoning, not landmark, designations.

**Nonconforming use**: stop substantially all of it for **2 continuous years** and only conforming uses may follow, whatever the owner intended (ZR §52-61). City of Yes for Economic Opportunity (2024) lets some vacant ground-floor storefronts in residential districts reopen for local retail or offices, but it doesn't revive uses like auto repair.
**FISP (Local Law 11)**: buildings over **6 stories** need facade inspections every 5 years.
**Local Law 97** caps carbon emissions for most buildings over **25,000 square feet**. Both FISP and Local Law 97 can mean big co-op or condo costs.
Paying an OATH penalty doesn't clear a DOB violation; the owner must certify correction.
Unpaid **DEP water and sewer charges** are liens, so they're paid or escrowed at closing.
**FAR** = floor area ÷ lot area; unused floor area is marketed as **air rights**.

example.title: Worked example: unused floor area (air rights)
steps: Lot: 25 × 100 = 2,500 square feet; district maximum FAR 3.0.
Maximum floor area = 2,500 × 3.0 = 7,500 square feet.
Unused = 7,500 − 5,500 existing = 2,000 square feet.
Answer: 2,000 square feet. Traps: 7,500 ignores the building; 2,500 is the lot area.

sections.heading: ULURP step by step
sections.intro: The Uniform Land Use Review Procedure (NYC Charter §§197-c and 197-d) is the city's fixed-clock public review for major land-use actions: advisory reviews first, binding votes last.
points: ULURP covers zoning **map** changes, CPC special permits, City Map changes, city facility sites, city property acquisitions and dispositions, housing and urban renewal plans, franchises and revocable consents, landfills and subdivision mapping.

Not ULURP: zoning **text** amendments (CPC hearing and vote with community and borough comment, then Council review), **BSA** variances and special permits, and LPC designations and permits. Since 2025, some qualifying actions use ELURP instead (next section).
Community board and borough president recommendations are **advisory**; if either fails to act or waives review, the application moves on.
If the CPC misses its deadline, the application is generally deemed denied; if the Council misses its 50 days, the CPC decision stands.

example.title: Worked example: the ULURP clock
steps: Community board 60 + borough president 30 = 90 days of advisory review.
CPC 60 brings the total to 150.
City Council 50 brings it to 200.
Mayoral veto 5 + override 10 = 215 days at most.
Answer: the four sequential review periods total 200 days, about seven months.

sections.heading: The 2025 NYC Charter changes and recent updates
sections.intro: The state exam is built on the DOS syllabus and may not test these 2025 changes yet. **All of this is recent**, so answer an ordinary ULURP question with the classic steps.
points: On November 4, 2025, NYC voters approved four Charter Revision Commission proposals (Questions 2–5). Three reshape land-use review for housing (two fast tracks, ELURP and an appeals board); one creates a digital City Map.
A fifth proposal, Question 6, would have moved city elections to even years. It failed.
Unchanged: ULURP still governs most rezonings, community boards keep a 60-day review in every track, and the Charter changes don't alter environmental review or landmark protections.
Separately, the 2026 state SEQR exemptions can remove environmental review for some housing.
**Exam angle**: the classic answer, in the syllabus and older books, is that an NYC rezoning ends with a Council vote and a possible mayoral veto. That's still true for standard ULURP.

The new exceptions: qualifying ELURP and Fast Track applications end at the CPC, and BSA fast-track approvals skip ULURP. The Affordable Housing Appeals Board can reverse Council denials or modifications of qualifying affordable housing.

Earlier Charter changes still in force: **2018** community board term limits (4 consecutive 2-year terms); **2019** a project summary 30 days before ULURP certification and longer community board review for June (90 days) and July 1–15 (75 days) certifications.

**ELURP** (§197-e) rezonings must be modest: to districts with a standard height of 45 feet or less in lower-density areas, or up to 30% more residential floor area in medium- and high-density districts. Nothing that needs an EIS qualifies.
Under ELURP, the CPC holds a hearing and votes within 30 days, and its decision is final. Exception: city land sales to low-income housing companies (HDFCs) skip the CPC and go to the Council.

**BSA fast track** (§666-a): a 60-day community board review comes first, then a BSA hearing about 30 days later. The BSA must find no harm to neighborhood character and a real need for the relief, not variance hardship.

**Affordable Housing Appeals Board** (§197-g): it acts if the applicant appeals or the board calls the case up. It covers single-borough ULURP applications or text amendments that directly facilitate affordable housing, replacing the mayoral veto and Council override for them.

example.title: Worked example: ULURP vs ELURP timeline
steps: ELURP: 60 (community board and borough president together) + 30 (CPC) = 90 days.
Savings: 200 − 90 = 110 days, about 3.6 months, with no Council vote.
A Fast Track rezoning that needs an EIS: 60 + 45 = 105 days.
Answer: about 90 days, with the CPC as final decision-maker.

guides.title: Property Insurance
guides.overview: Property insurance shifts the risk of physical loss and liability to an insurer. This chapter covers policy types, HO forms, Coverages A–F, perils, valuation, coinsurance, deductibles, flood insurance, hard-to-insure homes, cancellation and the licensee's role. The exam hits hardest on matching the occupant to the **HO form**, computing **ACV and coinsurance** payouts, and knowing that standard policies **exclude flood**.

mustKnow: **Property insurance** pays for damage to your own property; **liability insurance** pays others your negligence injures.
A **package policy** (homeowners, tenants) bundles property, liability, theft and medical payments; a **monoline policy** covers one line.
**HO-1 (basic)** and **HO-2 (broad)** are named-peril; HO-2 adds falling objects, weight of ice, snow or sleet, and accidental discharge of water from plumbing or heating.

**HO-3 (special)** is the most widely used form and the lenders' favorite: open-peril on the dwelling, named-peril on personal property. **HO-5 (comprehensive)** makes personal property open-peril too.

**HO-4** = tenants and co-op owners (per the NY syllabus and DFS): contents, liability, loss of use, no building. **HO-6** = condo unit owners: interior improvements, contents, liability, loss assessment.
**HO-8 (market value)** = older home whose rebuilding cost exceeds market value; a modified HO-1 paying cash value or repair with common modern materials.
Coverages: A dwelling and attached structures, B detached structures, C personal property, D loss of use, E personal liability, F medical payments to others.
**Named-peril**: covered only if a listed cause did it, and the insured must show that. **Open-peril**: covered unless excluded, and the insurer must prove the exclusion.

**ACV** = replacement cost − depreciation. **Replacement cost** repairs or replaces with like kind and quality, with no depreciation. Insure the cost to rebuild the structure, not land, price or market value.
**Coinsurance**: carry at least **80%** of replacement cost or a partial loss pays only (carried ÷ required) × loss, never more than the limit.
A **deductible** is the insured's share of each covered loss; raising it lowers the premium but adds no limits or perils.
NY **hurricane deductibles** are usually a percentage of Coverage A and must appear in dollars on the declarations page (Insurance Law §3445, Regulation 159).
A NY hurricane deductible applies only to wind damage from a hurricane with **New York landfall**, within the 12-hour window.
**Endorsements (riders)** add to or change the policy: scheduled personal property, inflation guard, ordinance or law, water backup, loss assessment, increased liability limits, earthquake.
**Flood is excluded** from homeowners, renters and condo policies. Buy flood coverage from the NFIP, run by FEMA and often sold by Write Your Own insurers, or from a private insurer.
Flood insurance is **mandatory** for a federally backed or regulated loan on a building in a Special Flood Hazard Area (Zones A and V), for the life of the loan.
Required flood coverage is at least the **lesser of the loan balance or the NFIP maximum**.
**NYPIUA**, New York's FAIR plan, is the insurer of last resort: limited property coverage, generally ACV, higher premiums, and **no liability, theft or flood**.
**C-MAP**, run by NYPIUA, helps coastal owner-occupants after a cancellation or nonrenewal, often adding a voluntary wraparound policy.
A **CLUE** report shows up to 7 years of claims on the property and owner; the owner, not a buyer, can order it.
**E&O** (errors and omissions) covers a licensee's negligent professional mistakes, not fraud or bodily injury. An open-house fall is general liability. NY doesn't require licensees to carry E&O.
**Insurable interest** must exist at the time of loss: a seller who keeps her policy after closing can't collect for a later fire (Insurance Law §3401).

Lenders require hazard insurance with a **mortgagee clause** (claim checks payable jointly). A NY lender closing a 1–4 family loan **must accept a binder** from a licensed insurer (Insurance Law §3404(h)).
**Escrow**: the lender collects 1/12 of the yearly premium and property taxes with each payment (**PITI**) and pays the bills.
**Cash sale**: no lender requires coverage, but the buyer bears the loss once title or possession passes, so the policy must start then (General Obligations Law §5-1311).
Landlords use **dwelling (DP) forms**: building plus **fair rental value**, no liability unless added, nothing for tenants' belongings.
**Subrogation**: after paying a claim, the insurer can sue whoever caused the loss.

traps.trap: Open-peril ('all risk') coverage has no exclusions.
traps.truth: Open-peril policies still exclude flood, earth movement, sewer backup, wear and tear, neglect, war and intentional loss.

traps.trap: An HO-3 covers my belongings open-peril, so a paint spill that ruins the rug is covered.
traps.truth: HO-3 contents are named-peril, and a spill isn't listed; an HO-5 or special personal property endorsement fixes that.

traps.trap: Insuring to 80% of replacement cost means a total loss is paid in full.
traps.truth: 80% only avoids the partial-loss penalty. Payment stops at the limit, leaving a 20% gap on a total loss.

traps.trap: Coinsurance means the insurer pays 80% of each loss, and the fraction divides by full replacement cost.
traps.truth: Meeting the requirement pays partial losses in full, less the deductible. Divide by the required amount, not full replacement cost.

traps.trap: A 2% hurricane deductible is 2% of the damage.
traps.truth: It is 2% of the Coverage A limit: $9,000 on a $450,000 limit, whatever the size of the claim.

traps.trap: A home outside the 100-year floodplain is safe, and a 100-year flood comes once a century.
traps.truth: A 100-year flood has a 1% chance every year, about 26% over 30 years. Outside a Special Flood Hazard Area, flood insurance is optional but available; the HO-3 still excludes flood.

traps.trap: I can buy an NFIP policy when the storm shows up in the forecast.
traps.truth: NFIP coverage generally starts 30 days after purchase. Exceptions: a loan closing (no wait) and a recent map revision (1 day).

traps.trap: Sewer or sump backup counts as accidental discharge from plumbing, or is covered by flood insurance.
traps.truth: Sewer and drain backup is a separate exclusion, fixed by a water backup endorsement. Accidental discharge means water escaping from your own plumbing or heating.

traps.trap: The condo master policy covers everything inside my unit.
traps.truth: A bare-walls master policy stops at the structure; the HO-6 must cover cabinets, fixtures, flooring and improvements.

traps.trap: A co-op shareholder needs an HO-6, just like a condo owner.
traps.truth: Answer HO-4: the NY syllabus and DFS pair co-op owners with HO-4, though some insurers use a unit-owners form.

traps.trap: An umbrella pays for flood damage to my house once my HO-3 limit runs out.
traps.truth: An umbrella is excess liability only; it never pays the insured's own property loss.

traps.trap: Medical payments (Coverage F) pays only if the owner was negligent.
traps.truth: Med pay (Coverage F) covers guests' reasonable medical bills regardless of fault, up to a small limit. Coverage E requires legal liability.

traps.trap: If I buy the coverage my lender requires, I'm fully insured.
traps.truth: The lender's requirement protects its loan. The owner needs enough to rebuild at today's costs, which can far exceed the loan balance.

mnemonics.name: Did over Should
mnemonics.meaning: Coinsurance pay = (insurance you DID carry ÷ insurance you SHOULD carry) × loss, minus the deductible; never more than the limit.

mnemonics.name: Title looks back, hazard looks forward
mnemonics.meaning: Title insurance covers defects existing on the policy date, for a one-time premium; hazard insurance covers later physical loss, with renewed premiums.

mnemonics.name: Section I is me, Section II is them
mnemonics.meaning: Coverages A–D pay for the insured's own property and living costs; E–F pay other people.

mnemonics.name: Name it to claim it
mnemonics.meaning: Under named-peril the loss must come from a listed cause; under open-peril it's covered unless the insurer points to an exclusion.

formulas.name: Actual cash value
formulas.formula: ACV = Replacement cost − Depreciation

formulas.name: Straight-line depreciation
formulas.formula: Depreciation = Replacement cost × (Age ÷ Useful life)

formulas.name: Coinsurance requirement
formulas.formula: Required insurance = Replacement cost × Coinsurance %

formulas.name: Coinsurance recovery
formulas.formula: Payment = (Carried ÷ Required) × Loss − Deductible, capped at the limit

formulas.name: Percentage deductible
formulas.formula: Deductible = % × Coverage A limit; Payment = Loss − Deductible

formulas.name: Replacement cost holdback
formulas.formula: Holdback = Replacement cost − ACV paid first

formulas.name: Mandatory flood coverage
formulas.formula: Required = lesser of loan balance or NFIP maximum (never above insurable value)

formulas.name: Umbrella payment
formulas.formula: Umbrella pays = Covered judgment − Underlying limit, up to the umbrella limit

formulas.name: Escrow deposit and cushion
formulas.formula: Monthly escrow = (Annual taxes + Annual premium) ÷ 12; RESPA cushion ≤ 1/6 of annual escrow

sections.heading: Insurance basics and who sells it
sections.intro: Insurance is a contract: the insurer accepts a defined risk for a premium.
points: **Property insurance** (hazard, fire or homeowners insurance) pays for direct physical loss to insured property, plus some indirect loss such as extra living costs.
Homeowners policies have **Section I** (property) and **Section II** (liability).

**Indemnity** restores the pre-loss position without profit. So a claimant needs an **insurable interest** at the time of loss: a lawful and substantial economic interest in the property (Insurance Law §3401). Owners, lenders and tenants (for their belongings) have one.
A **peril** causes loss (fire, wind, theft). A **hazard** makes loss likelier or worse.
Three kinds of hazard: physical (frayed wiring), **moral** (dishonesty, such as arson for profit) and **morale** (carelessness because 'I'm insured').
The **declarations page** shows the named insured, policy period, address, mortgagee, limits, deductibles, endorsements and premium.
An endorsement (rider) changes the policy. A **binder** is temporary written evidence of coverage until the policy issues.
A **package policy** combines lines such as property and liability and generally costs less than separate **monoline** policies.

NY fire policies must be at least as favorable to the insured as the **standard fire insurance policy of the state of New York** (Insurance Law §3404). Under it, concealment or fraud voids the policy, and the policy can't be **assigned** to a buyer without the insurer's written consent.
The **Department of Financial Services (DFS)** regulates insurers, agents and brokers; the Department of State licenses real estate licensees, not insurance sellers.

head: Seller

rows: One or more insurers that appoint the agent

sections.heading: Perils: named-peril, open-peril and exclusions
sections.intro: Some forms list the covered perils; others cover everything not excluded.
points: **Named-peril** coverage pays only if a listed peril caused the loss, and the insured must show it. **Open-peril** coverage (special form, once 'all risk') pays any direct physical loss unless excluded, and the insurer must prove the exclusion.

**Basic perils** (HO-1, per DFS): fire, lightning and smoke; windstorm and hail; explosion; riot and civil commotion; vehicles and aircraft; vandalism and malicious mischief; burglary and theft; glass breakage.

**Broad perils** (HO-2 adds): falling objects; weight of ice, snow or sleet; accidental discharge or overflow of water or steam from plumbing, heating, air-conditioning or sprinkler systems; sudden cracking of heating systems and water heaters; freezing of plumbing; electrical damage to appliances.

**Exclusions**, even open-peril: flood and surface water, earth movement, sewer or drain backup, wear and tear, mechanical breakdown, mold, vermin, neglect, off-premises power failure, war, nuclear hazard and intentional loss. Earthquake, water backup and power interruption can be **bought back** by endorsement; flood needs a flood policy.
Insurance covers **sudden and accidental** loss. A 30-year-old roof that finally leaks is excluded wear and tear, even under an HO-3; calling it windstorm damage fails when no storm occurred.

**Vacancy**: the NY standard fire policy suspends coverage after 60 consecutive days vacant or unoccupied unless the policy says otherwise, and homeowners forms exclude vandalism after 60 days vacant. Business use and claims history also affect coverage.

sections.heading: Homeowners and dwelling policy forms (HO-1 to HO-8)
sections.intro: Match the occupant and property to the form. Insurers may use trade names, so read the description, not the label.
points: **HO-3** is the default for an owner-occupied house and the form lenders want. DFS says homeowners forms fit people who own and live in a one- or two-family house, so an owner living in half of a two-family home qualifies.
**HO-8** solves the 'white elephant': an 1890s Victorian worth $350,000 that would cost $700,000 to reproduce. It doesn't simply pay the sale price.
The syllabus calls HO-8 a modified HO-1 paying cash value instead of replacement cost. DFS adds that payment can't exceed repair with materials of like kind and quality, not exact originals.
**Dwelling policies** (DP-1 basic, DP-2 broad, DP-3 special) insure buildings the owner doesn't occupy, such as a rented house.
DP-1 is named-peril and often ACV; DP-3 is open-peril on the building. Dwelling policies are property-only: liability needs an endorsement or a separate policy.

sections.heading: Coverages A through F
sections.intro: Section I (A–D) protects the insured's own property and living costs; Section II (E–F) protects other people.
points: Coverage A includes **attached** structures; Coverage B covers **separated** ones. Each has its own limit, so a loss above the B limit isn't paid from room under A.

Coverage C **special limits** (DFS's typical figures): money $200; securities and deeds $1,500; theft of jewelry, watches and furs $1,500; theft of silverware or guns $2,500; business property $2,500 at home, $500 away. Raising Coverage A doesn't raise them.
Coverage D pays only the **increase** over normal costs: if groceries normally cost $800 a month and $1,400 while displaced, D pays $600 plus the hotel.

Liability **exclusions**: injury the insured expected or intended, business and professional activities, most motor vehicles, injury to the insured's household, and damage to the insured's own property.
NY bars refusing, canceling, surcharging or limiting homeowners coverage based solely on **dog breed**. Insurers may act on a dog legally designated dangerous (Insurance Law §3421).

A NY homeowners policy with personal liability on an owner-occupied 1–4 family home must include **workers' compensation** for household employees working under 40 hours a week (DFS); full-time household workers need separate coverage.

example.title: Worked example: hitting the Coverage B limit
steps: Coverage A is $380,000, and Coverage B is 10% of A: 10% × $380,000 = $38,000.
A covered fire does $45,000 of damage to the detached garage, a separate structure, so only Coverage B applies.
Answer: $38,000 (ignoring the deductible); the owner absorbs the $7,000 shortfall. Taking 80% of the loss ($36,000) is a distractor.

sections.heading: Replacement cost vs. actual cash value
sections.intro: The valuation method decides what the owner collects; questions usually add a deductible.
points: **Replacement cost (RC)** is today's cost to repair or replace with materials of like kind and quality, with no deduction for depreciation.
**Actual cash value (ACV)** is RC minus depreciation. Insurers' schedules vary, but exam questions use straight-line depreciation (age ÷ useful life).
Many RC policies pay ACV first and **hold back** the depreciation until the owner repairs or replaces, within a deadline the policy sets.
**Land is not insured.** Coverage A should match the cost to rebuild the structure, which may be above or below price or market value. Revisit limits after renovations and keep a contents inventory.

The NY standard fire policy pays the lesser of ACV, the cost to repair or replace with like kind and quality, or the limit, never more than the insured's interest; homeowners forms may be more generous, not less.

head: Feature
Replacement cost
Actual cash value
rows: The structure on most homeowners forms when insured to at least 80%
Contents (unless a replacement cost endorsement is added), HO-8 dwellings, DP-1 forms, NYPIUA policies
Owner rebuilds without paying for depreciation

example.title: Worked example: ACV, deductibles and the holdback
steps: Furniture: replacement cost $3,000 − depreciation $1,800 = ACV of $1,200.
Furniture payment = $1,200 − $500 deductible = $700.
Roof: 20-year useful life, 15 years old, $24,000 to replace. Depreciation = $24,000 × 15/20 = $18,000.
Roof payment = $6,000 − $1,000 deductible = $5,000.
Holdback: cabinets cost $12,000 to replace, and depreciation is $4,000. The insurer first pays ACV of $8,000.
After replacement, the insurer releases the $4,000 holdback.
Wrong answers: the deductible taken off replacement cost ($2,500 or $23,000), or the depreciation less the deductible ($17,000).
Answer: furniture $700; roof $5,000; cabinets $8,000 now plus $4,000 after replacement.

sections.heading: Coinsurance and the 80% rule
sections.intro: The coinsurance (replacement cost) condition penalizes underinsurance on partial losses.
points: **Required insurance = replacement cost × coinsurance percentage.** 80% is standard for homes; 90% and 100% clauses appear mostly in commercial policies.

**Meet** the requirement and a partial loss is paid in full, less the deductible. **Fall short** and payment = (carried ÷ required) × loss. Payment never exceeds the limit, so insuring to 100% of replacement cost is the safer advice.
Additions and construction inflation raise replacement cost, so a home that met 80% last year may fall short today; an **inflation guard** endorsement raises Coverage A automatically.

ISO drafts the standard forms most insurers use. Real ISO forms are kinder: below 80%, the insurer pays the **greater** of ACV or the proportional amount. Exams use the proportional formula, and the NYREPL math guide subtracts any deductible from the result.
The 80% coinsurance rule has nothing to do with an 80% loan-to-value ratio or 20% equity.

example.title: Worked example: coinsurance in five situations
steps: Underinsured: replacement cost $500,000, 80% clause, carried $300,000, loss $60,000. Required = $400,000.
Requirement met: replacement cost $400,000, carried $320,000, which equals the requirement. A $50,000 loss is paid in full, not $40,000.
But payment stops at the $240,000 limit.
Keeping up: replacement cost rises from $350,000 to $425,000; carried $300,000. Required = 80% × $425,000 = $340,000.
The owner needs $40,000 more coverage.
90% clause: replacement cost $400,000, carried $300,000, loss $36,000. Required = $360,000.
Answer: $45,000; $50,000 in full; $240,000 (the limit); $40,000 more coverage; $30,000.

sections.heading: Deductibles and New York's hurricane rules
sections.intro: New York regulates how windstorm and hurricane deductibles are disclosed and triggered.
points: DFS lists three types of deductible: a **standard (all-peril)** flat deductible, such as $500 or $1,000; an optional windstorm deductible; and a hurricane deductible, usually insurer-mandated near the coast.
Windstorm and hurricane deductibles commonly run **1% to 5%** of the dwelling's value or Coverage A amount, so the dollar figure moves with the limit.
Many insurers require hurricane deductibles in the five NYC boroughs, Nassau, Suffolk and coastal Westchester.
The insurer must show DFS enough hurricane exposure, and the deductible may vary by county or distance from the shore (DFS **Regulation 159**, 11 NYCRR Part 74).

Every new and renewal policy must come with a plain-language notice of the deductible's amount and trigger. The declarations page must show a hurricane deductible as a percentage and in dollars (Insurance Law §3445, Regulation 159).

For policies issued or renewed since Feb. 2, 2026, a hurricane deductible is triggered only when the National Weather Service finds the hurricane made **landfall in New York**. The policy states which hurricane category triggers it.
It applies only to wind damage from **12 hours before landfall to 12 hours after** the last NY hurricane watch or warning is canceled.

All covered losses from the storm count toward one hurricane deductible. It can't apply to loss-of-use coverage. When several deductibles could apply to a loss, only one does, and the insurer may choose the higher.
Earthquake coverage, by endorsement or separate policy, usually has a large percentage deductible (DFS cites 10% to 25%).

example.title: Worked example: percentage deductibles
steps: A Long Island home has a $450,000 Coverage A limit and a 2% hurricane deductible; a qualifying hurricane causes $28,000 of covered wind damage.
Deductible = 2% × $450,000 = $9,000, based on the limit, not the loss.
DFS's illustration: a home insured for $150,000 with a 5% hurricane deductible bears the first $7,500. On a $10,000 loss the insurer pays $2,500.
Trap: taking 2% of the $28,000 loss ($560) and paying $27,440.
Answer: the insurer pays $19,000.

sections.heading: Endorsements: adding to the basic policy
sections.intro: Endorsements (riders) change the policy for an added premium; the syllabus stresses increased liability limits and insuring more personal property and other structures.
points: Raising Coverage A doesn't lift a Coverage C special limit: an $18,000 engagement ring needs a scheduled personal property endorsement or a personal articles floater.
DFS notes that neither a flood policy nor a homeowners policy alone is likely to cover a sump failure caused by a flood.
Endorsements can also narrow coverage, such as removing off-premises theft, for a lower premium (DFS).
