sections.heading: Flood insurance and the NFIP
sections.intro: Flood is excluded from homeowners, renters and condo policies; the National Flood Insurance Program (NFIP), created in 1968 and run by FEMA, fills the gap.
points: NFIP coverage is sold only in **participating** communities that enforce floodplain management rules (most NY towns, villages and cities). **Write Your Own** insurers sell and service NFIP policies under their own names; the federal program sets rates and carries the risk.

**Limits**: $250,000 on a 1–4 family building and $100,000 on contents, bought separately with separate deductibles. Renters can buy **contents-only** coverage; a landlord's building policy doesn't cover tenants' belongings.

**Settlement**: contents at ACV; the building at replacement cost only for a single-family principal residence insured to at least 80% of replacement cost (or the maximum). Basement coverage is limited, and the NFIP pays no additional living expenses.

**Waiting period**: generally 30 days; none when the purchase is tied to making, increasing, extending or renewing a loan (coverage starts at closing); 1 day if bought within 13 months after a map revision puts the building in a high-risk zone.

**Mandatory purchase**: a building in a Special Flood Hazard Area that secures a loan made, insured or guaranteed by a federal agency (FHA, VA, USDA), or made by a federally regulated lender, must stay insured for the life of the loan (Flood Disaster Protection Act of 1973).

**Lapse**: if the borrower doesn't replace coverage within **45 days** of the lender's or servicer's notice, the lender must force-place it and may charge him. Regulated lenders generally must escrow flood premiums too.
**Private flood insurance** also exists. Federally regulated lenders must accept qualifying private policies, which keep working if the NFIP lapses.
Congress extends the NFIP in short reauthorizations, currently through Dec. 11, 2026. During a lapse, FEMA can't sell or renew policies but still pays claims.

An NFIP building policy can be **assigned** in writing to a buyer. A seller whose property got federal flood disaster aid conditioned on keeping flood insurance must tell the buyer in writing of that duty.
**NY flood notice**: insurers must give homeowners and dwelling fire policyholders an annual notice that the policy excludes flood and mudslide and that NFIP coverage exists (Insurance Law §3444).
**Leases**: residential leases must disclose FEMA floodplain status, known flood damage and the availability of NFIP renter coverage (Real Property Law §231-b).
The **Property Condition Disclosure Statement** asks about flood zones, flood insurance, flood claims and federal flood aid.
FEMA disaster aid is no substitute: it is limited, needs a federal disaster declaration and can require buying flood insurance.

example.title: Worked example: how much flood insurance must the lender require?
steps: A buyer takes a $320,000 federally backed mortgage on a single-family home in Zone AE. Insurable value is $400,000; the NFIP building maximum is $250,000.
Required = the lesser of the loan balance ($320,000) or the NFIP maximum ($250,000), never above insurable value.
Requiring $320,000 ignores the program cap; $256,000 (80% of the loan) is invented. Private excess flood coverage can insure the rest.
Risk check: 1 − 0.99^30 ≈ 0.26, about a 26% chance of at least one 100-year flood over the 30-year loan.
Answer: the lender must require $250,000.

sections.heading: Condos, co-ops, renters and landlords
sections.intro: The building's owner insures the structure; each occupant insures what that policy leaves out.
points: **Condo master policies** range from **bare walls** (structure only; the owner insures cabinets, fixtures, flooring and finishes) to single entity (original fixtures) to all-in (improvements too).

The board insures the building when the declaration, bylaws or a majority of owners require it. It gives owners written notice of the coverage and any change, and charges premiums as common expenses. Owners may still insure their own units (Real Property Law §339-bb).

HO-6 **loss assessment** coverage pays the owner's share of an association assessment from a covered loss to common property, such as roof repairs above the master limit or a large master-policy deductible. Basic limits are low.
Injuries **inside a unit** fall on the owner's HO-6 (or HO-4) liability; the master policy's liability coverage targets common areas.

**Co-op**: the corporation insures the building; the shareholder insures her belongings, liability and her own improvements (a $60,000 kitchen renovation may not be covered by the building policy). Check the proprietary lease.

**Renters**: a tenant whose candle starts a fire relies on HO-4 **personal liability**. The landlord's insurer can pay and then pursue her through subrogation. HO-4 loss of use pays the hotel if a neighbor's fire makes her unit unlivable.

**Landlords**: an investor renting out a house he doesn't occupy needs a dwelling (DP) policy, whose **fair rental value** coverage replaces lost rent during repairs. A DP-3 without a liability endorsement leaves him uninsured if a tenant's visitor falls on a broken step.

**Building staff**: NY employers must carry **workers' compensation**, including co-op and condo boards or managing agents that employ supers and porters. It pays medical costs and lost wages regardless of fault and is generally the worker's exclusive remedy.
A building permit requires proof of the contractor's workers' comp (Workers' Compensation Law §57); owners should also get proof of the contractor's liability coverage.

sections.heading: Liability, umbrella, E&O and commercial policies
sections.intro: Liability insurance pays other people; the exam tests which policy answers which claim.
points: An **umbrella** (personal excess) policy adds liability limits, typically $1 million or more, above homeowners, renters and auto policies. It pays only after the underlying limit is exhausted.
Insurers usually require minimum underlying limits. Umbrellas often cover extra offenses such as libel, slander and false arrest, but never the insured's own property loss.

**E&O (errors and omissions)** is professional liability coverage for licensees and firms. It pays economic-harm claims from negligent mistakes, such as advertising 2,400 square feet for a 1,900-square-foot home, subject to limits and deductibles.
E&O excludes intentional fraud, bodily injury and property damage. NY doesn't require licensees to carry it.

**Commercial general liability (CGL)** covers bodily injury and property damage claims against a business. A visitor who slips on spilled coffee at an open house is a CGL (or seller's homeowners liability) claim, not E&O.
A **businessowners policy (BOP)** packages commercial property, general liability and business income for small businesses, without automatic E&O.
Commercial property can be written on a **specific** policy (one building or class) or a **blanket** policy (several under one limit).
If a brokerage's sales associates are deemed employees rather than independent contractors, the broker must provide workers' compensation, disability and unemployment insurance.

example.title: Worked example: umbrella over a homeowners policy
steps: An owner has $300,000 of homeowners liability and a $1,000,000 umbrella; a guest wins a covered $1,100,000 judgment.
The homeowners insurer pays first, up to its $300,000 limit.
The umbrella pays the excess: $1,100,000 − $300,000 = $800,000, within its $1,000,000 limit.
Traps: assuming the umbrella pays its full $1,000,000, or computing $1,000,000 − $300,000 = $700,000.
Answer: the umbrella pays $800,000.

sections.heading: Hard-to-insure homes: NYPIUA, C-MAP, excess lines and CLUE
sections.intro: The syllabus topic 'problems in obtaining insurance' covers NYPIUA, the NFIP and coastal residents assistance: DFS help, windstorm deductible disclosure and C-MAP. Insurance agents should try the voluntary market first.
points: **NYPIUA**, the New York Property Insurance Underwriting Association, is an association of all insurers selling fire insurance in New York. It is the state's FAIR plan and **insurer of last resort** (Insurance Law Article 54).

NYPIUA's **Basic form** covers fire, extended coverage perils (wind including hurricane, hail, explosion, riot, aircraft, vehicles, smoke) and vandalism. The **Broad form** adds falling objects, weight of ice and snow, water discharge and more.
NYPIUA policies are generally **ACV**, cost more and include **no liability, theft or flood**. Broad form policies in the seven downstate coastal counties carry a 2% hurricane deductible.

**C-MAP** (Coastal Market Assistance Program) is a voluntary network of insurers and producers run by NYPIUA. It serves **owner-occupied** 1–4 family homes, apartments and condo units near the shore in the Bronx, Brooklyn, Queens, Staten Island, Nassau, Suffolk and Westchester.
C-MAP reaches 1 mile from shore on Long Island's south shore and forks, Brooklyn, Queens and Staten Island, and 2,500 feet from shore on Long Island's north shore, the Bronx and Westchester.
To qualify, the owner must have received a cancellation, nonrenewal or conditional renewal for a reason other than nonpayment. A new buyer names the prior owner's insurer.
A voluntary **wraparound** policy adds liability, contents and theft and can make replacement cost available.
Cancellation and nonrenewal notices on homes in a market-assistance area must explain possible C-MAP or NYPIUA eligibility and how to apply (Insurance Law §3425(e)).

**Excess line market**: after at least three licensed insurers decline, an owner may buy from an unlicensed insurer through a licensed excess line broker. These policies skip NY rate and form approval, and the Property/Casualty Insurance Security Fund won't protect the owner if the insurer fails.

A **CLUE report** (Comprehensive Loss Underwriting Exchange, run by LexisNexis) lists claims on the property and owner for up to seven years, including reported but unpaid losses. Water claims can raise premiums or block coverage.
A CLUE report is a Fair Credit Reporting Act consumer report, not a public record. The owner gets a free copy each year and can share it before listing; a buyer can't pull one on someone else's home.

sections.heading: Premiums, cancellation and nonrenewal in New York
sections.intro: Premiums vary by insurer, property and person, and New York limits when an insurer can drop a homeowners or tenants policy.
points: **Cost factors**: location, construction, age and condition, coverage amounts, deductible, claims history and discounts.
Location means the rating territory and the community's public fire protection class, which runs from 1, the best, to 10, unprotected. For construction, brick resists fire better than frame.
**Discounts** (Insurance Law §2346): **required** for hurricane or storm shutters and hurricane-resistant laminated glass windows and doors.
Discounts are **permitted** for smoke detectors, sprinklers, fire extinguishers, deadbolts and an approved disaster-preparedness course (good for three years).
**First 60 days**: an insurer may cancel a new policy, but the notice must state the **specific reason** (Insurance Law §3425(b)).

**After 60 days**, or from the start of a renewal, an insurer may cancel only for: nonpayment of premium; conviction of a crime arising from acts that increase the hazard insured against; fraud or material misrepresentation in obtaining the policy or presenting a claim.

The other grounds after 60 days: willful or reckless acts or omissions that increase the hazard; physical changes that make the property uninsurable; or a DFS determination that continuing the policy would violate the law.

**Nonpayment**: the notice must state the amount due, and paying within **15 days** after it is mailed is timely. If premiums come from a mortgage escrow account, the notice must go to both homeowner and lender or it has no effect.
**Nonrenewal**: homeowners policies have a **three-year required policy period**, and nonrenewal inside it needs a ground that would justify cancellation.
Notice of nonrenewal or conditional renewal, with specific reasons, must be mailed **45 to 60 days** before the policy period ends. Otherwise the insured may renew by paying the premium.
An insurer may not refuse to issue or renew solely because of the applicant's **advanced age** (Insurance Law §3425(i)).

sections.heading: The licensee's role: lenders, escrow, closing, and title vs. hazard
sections.intro: Licensees explain insurance's purpose and cost, the lender's interest, escrow and cash-sale timing, then refer; they don't sell or bind insurance unless separately licensed.
points: **Purpose and cost**: insurance is an ongoing cost of ownership. Urge coverage for the cost to **rebuild**, and refer buyers to a licensed agent or broker.
Selling insurance, or being paid for placing it, requires a NY insurance license. RESPA treats hazard and flood insurance as settlement services, so referral kickbacks are illegal.

**Lender's interest**: the house is collateral, so lenders require hazard insurance, plus flood insurance in a Special Flood Hazard Area (SFHA), with a **mortgagee clause**, also called a standard mortgage clause.
The mortgagee clause means joint claim checks, a lender claim that can survive the owner's denial, and separate written notice to the lender before cancellation.
If coverage lapses, the lender can **force-place** a pricier policy at the borrower's cost.

**Proof at closing**: a policy or an **insurance binder**. A NY lender making a 1–4 family loan can't refuse a licensed insurer's binder as evidence of hazard insurance, though it may also ask for a premium receipt (Insurance Law §3404(h)).

**Escrow**: lenders often collect 1/12 of the annual premium and property taxes with each monthly payment, making up **PITI** (principal, interest, taxes, insurance). They commonly require escrow when the buyer puts down less than 20%.
RESPA caps the escrow cushion at one-sixth of the year's escrow payments. At closing the buyer usually prepays the first year's premium and funds the initial escrow deposit.

**Cash sale**: nobody forces the buyer to insure. The seller bears the risk of loss until legal title or possession passes; then the buyer must pay even if the house burns (Uniform Vendor and Purchaser Risk Act, General Obligations Law §5-1311).
Start the buyer's policy at closing or move-in, whichever comes first.

**Seller's side**: the seller insures until closing, then cancels for a refund of unearned premium. After the deed passes she has no insurable interest, and her policy can't go to the buyer without the insurer's written consent.
**After a loss**: notify the insurer promptly; written notice to its licensed agent counts. Make reasonable temporary repairs, keep damaged items for the adjuster and document everything.

A sworn **proof of loss** is due within 60 days after the insurer's written request and blank forms (Insurance Law §3407); the standard fire policy allows 24 months to sue. Never promise a claim will be paid.

example.title: Worked example: building the monthly PITI payment
steps: Annual homeowners premium $2,400 + annual property taxes $9,600 = $12,000 of escrow items.
Monthly escrow deposit = $12,000 ÷ 12 = $1,000 (insurance $200 + taxes $800).
Maximum cushion RESPA allows = $12,000 ÷ 6 = $2,000.
PITI = $2,500 principal and interest + $1,000 escrow = $3,500.
Answer: PITI is $3,500 a month, of which $200 is the insurance escrow.

guides.title: Taxes & Assessments
guides.overview: How New York property taxes are set, cut by exemptions such as STAR, challenged and collected; the taxes due at a sale; and federal income tax: deductions, gain, §121, depreciation and 1031. The exam hits hardest: **tax = taxable assessed value × rate**, **full value = assessed value ÷ equalization rate**, the grievance calendar, and who pays each closing tax.

Foreign seller (FIRPTA): gross price / buyer-occupied home at $300,001–$1,000,000; $300,000 or less: none
§121 home-sale exclusion: single / joint
Depreciation: residential rental / nonresidential
Top rate on unrecaptured §1250 gain (from past depreciation)
1031: identify / acquire, both counted from the sale
Deductible mortgage debt cap (loans after Dec 15, 2017); permanent since 2025
SALT cap, 2025 / 2026; phased down above $500,000 / $505,000 MAGI; floor $10,000
Holding period for long-term capital gain

mustKnow: **Tax = taxable assessed value × rate**; rate = levy ÷ total taxable assessed value; levy = budget − other revenue. **New York State levies no property tax.**
Outside NYC and Nassau, every parcel is assessed at one **uniform percentage** of value (RPTL §305).
**Full value = assessed value ÷ equalization rate.** The ORPTS rate apportions county and school levies and can exceed 100%.
Town calendar: March 1 taxable status date → May 1 tentative roll → **Grievance Day** (4th Tuesday in May) → July 1 final roll → **30 days** to start SCAR or certiorari.
**Welcome stranger** assessing (raising only homes that just sold) is illegal and supports an unequal claim.
A **special assessment** charges only benefited parcels, often by front foot; a special district levy is by value.
**Property tax liens** outrank private liens, even earlier mortgages. A **tax lien sale** sells only the right to collect.
**In rem** foreclosure follows a redemption period of about 2 years. Since Tyler v. Hennepin County (2023) and NY's 2024 law, surplus goes to lienholders, then the former owner.
**STAR** cuts school taxes on a primary residence only. **Enhanced STAR** needs one resident owner 65 by December 31 and a lower income limit.
New owners since 2016 get the **STAR credit**; switching from the exemption to the credit is **irreversible**.
Exemptions are **personal**. Nonprofits need **exempt ownership and use**.
Senior exemption: up to **50%**, local option, combinable with Enhanced STAR (§467). Alternative veterans: **15% + 10% combat + half the disability rating**.
Farmland converted within 5 years (8 outside an ag district) owes a **conversion payment**.
**Tax cap**: levy growth is limited to 2% or inflation. A school budget over it needs **60%**, and one bill can still rise more.
**Homestead option**: two tax rates. **NYC class 1** (1–3 family): 6% ratio; caps of 6% a year, 20% over five.
Grievance grounds: **excessive, unequal, unlawful, misclassified**. The RP-524 must be **received** by Grievance Day; the Board of Assessment Review (BAR) can't raise an assessment.
**SCAR** (owner-occupied 1–3 family): 30 days, $30. Other property uses **Article 7 certiorari**. NYC: Tax Commission; Nassau: Assessment Review Commission.
**NYS transfer tax**: $2 per $500 or fraction, paid by the **seller** (the buyer if the seller doesn't pay).
**Mansion tax**: 1% of the whole price at $1,000,000+, paid by the **buyer**.
**NYC RPTT**: 1% up to $500,000, and **1.425% of the whole price** above.
**Mortgage recording tax** is on the **loan**: none for cash buyers or co-op share loans; a CEMA taxes only new money.
**FIRPTA**: the buyer withholds **15% of the gross price** from a foreign seller; 10% for a buyer-occupied home at $300,001–$1,000,000; none at $300,000 or less.
Nonresident sellers pay NY estimated tax on **IT-2663**.
Mortgage interest and property taxes help only **itemizers**. Interest counts on debt up to **$750,000**, now permanent.
Property taxes fall under the **SALT cap**: $40,000 for 2025, $40,400 for 2026.
Home-equity interest counts only if the loan buys, builds or improves the home. **Mortgage insurance** is deductible again from 2026.
**§121**: exclude $250,000/$500,000 after owning and using the home **2 of the last 5 years**; once every 2 years, any age.
**Gain** = amount realized − adjusted basis; a mortgage payoff is irrelevant.
**Depreciation**: buildings only, never land or a personal home; **27.5 years** residential rental, 39 nonresidential. Gain from past depreciation is taxed at up to 25%.
**1031**: investment real estate for investment real estate; **45 / 180 days**, both from the sale. A qualified intermediary holds the cash; boot is taxed; gain is deferred.
Inherited property gets a **stepped-up** basis; a gift keeps the donor's basis. Long-term means held **more than 1 year**.

traps.trap: To get full value, multiply the assessment by the equalization rate.
traps.truth: Divide: $84,000 ÷ 0.35 = $240,000. Multiplying gives a meaningless $29,400.

traps.trap: An equalization rate can never top 100%.
traps.truth: It can, when values fall and assessments aren't lowered. Older study guides say otherwise.

traps.trap: Grievance Day is March 1.
traps.truth: March 1 is the taxable status date; Grievance Day in most towns is the fourth Tuesday in May.

traps.trap: A grievance mailed by Grievance Day is on time, and owners can skip it and sue or stop paying.
traps.truth: The RP-524 must be received by Grievance Day and is required before SCAR or certiorari. Withholding taxes only adds a lien and penalties.

traps.trap: A mortgage recorded first beats a later tax lien.
traps.truth: Property tax liens outrank private liens regardless of date, which is why lenders escrow taxes.

traps.trap: The buyer keeps the seller's STAR, senior or veterans exemption.
traps.truth: Exemptions are personal; the buyer must qualify and apply on her own.

traps.trap: Enhanced STAR requires both spouses, or all owners, to be 65.
traps.truth: Since 2026, one resident owner 65 by December 31 is enough, whatever the owners' relationship. The older all-owners rule is outdated.

traps.trap: The 2% tax cap means no bill can rise more than 2%.
traps.truth: It limits the total levy (with a 60% override). One bill can rise more after a reassessment or a lost exemption.

traps.trap: NYC RPTT on a $750,000 condo is 1% on the first $500,000 and 1.425% on the rest.
traps.truth: It isn't tiered: 1.425% × $750,000 = $10,687.50. The mansion tax likewise hits the whole price.

traps.trap: The state transfer tax starts above $25,000 and is exactly 0.4%.
traps.truth: It applies above $500 at $2 per $500 or fraction, rounding up. $25,000 is the NYC RPTT floor.

traps.trap: Mortgage recording tax is a percentage of the price, and co-op buyers pay it too.
traps.truth: It is figured on the recorded loan; cash buyers and co-op share loans pay none.

traps.trap: The home-sale exclusion is a one-time break for sellers 55+ who buy a pricier home.
traps.truth: That ended in 1997. Anyone meeting the 2-of-5-year tests can exclude $250,000 or $500,000 once every 2 years, without reinvesting.

traps.trap: Paying off the mortgage at closing reduces the taxable gain.
traps.truth: Gain = amount realized − adjusted basis. The payoff only reduces the seller's cash.

traps.trap: FIRPTA withholding is 15% of the seller's profit.
traps.truth: It is 15% of the gross amount realized, and a buyer who fails to withhold can be liable.

traps.trap: A 1031 exchange is tax-free, and the 180 days start after the 45 days end.
traps.truth: It defers gain (the replacement takes a lower basis), and both clocks start at the sale. Homes and dealer property don't qualify.

traps.trap: The SALT cap is still $10,000, and mortgage insurance is never deductible.
traps.truth: The 2025 law set $40,000 for 2025 and $40,400 for 2026 (phased down at high incomes, never below $10,000), and mortgage insurance is deductible again from 2026.

sections.heading: How property taxes work
sections.intro: Property taxes are the main source of local revenue. First identify who levies a charge and what kind it is.
points: Property taxes fund local services: schools (usually the largest share), police, fire, roads, libraries and parks. **Taxation** is the T in PETE.
Counties, cities, towns, villages, school districts and special districts levy them. **New York State levies none.**
Real estate is taxed because it is a predictable base, hard to conceal or move, and historically tied to wealth and land productivity.
**Ad valorem** means 'according to value': taxable assessed value × rate on every taxable parcel. A transfer tax is due only on a conveyance.

An **assessing unit**, usually a city or town, keeps the **assessment roll**. Nassau and Tompkins counties assess countywide. School and other districts, whose lines can cross town lines, levy from the roll.
Wholly **exempt property** (government, religious, charitable, educational) pays no general tax, shifting the burden to other owners.
A **special assessment** charges only benefited parcels (a special assessment district) for one improvement, such as sidewalks or a sewer line. It is usually figured by front footage.
A special assessment is a **specific lien**, often paid in installments. It adds to basis rather than being deducted.
A **special district** (fire, water, sewer, lighting) levies by value inside its boundaries.

head: Charge

Based on
Exam angle

example.title: Worked example: special assessment by front foot
steps: New curbs cost $96,000 along a street with 1,600 total front feet. A lot is 60 feet wide (frontage) and 120 feet deep.
Step 1: Cost per front foot = $96,000 ÷ 1,600 = $60.
Answer: $3,600, a specific lien until paid. Using the 120-foot depth ($7,200) is the trap.

sections.heading: Assessment, the assessment calendar, and reassessment
sections.intro: The assessor values property and fixes factual errors; the receiver of taxes collects; the governing body (and school voters) adopts the budget.
points: **Market (full) value** is the likely sale price; **assessed value** is the roll figure.
**Taxable assessed value** is assessed value minus exemptions. It can differ for county, town and school taxes.
**Uniform percentage**: outside NYC and Nassau, every parcel is assessed at one percentage of value, 100% or any fraction (RPTL §305). Only those two use class percentages.
**Level of assessment** = assessed value ÷ market value. With no required reassessment cycle, many towns sit far below 100%.
Town calendar: the **valuation date** is July 1 of the prior year. It fixes market conditions.
The **taxable status date** is March 1. It fixes condition, ownership and exemption eligibility; exemption applications are due.
Then: tentative roll May 1 → **Grievance Day**, the fourth Tuesday in May → final roll July 1 → **30 days** to start SCAR or certiorari.
Assessments drift because values change unevenly. **New construction** enters at current value while older homes keep stale values.
**Undeclared improvements** stay off the roll until building permits alert the assessor.
A **community-wide reassessment** redistributes the levy but doesn't raise it: when total assessed value rises and the levy doesn't, the rate falls.

Raising only homes that just sold (**welcome stranger** assessing) is illegal and supports an **unequal** grievance; a town-wide revaluation, adding a newly found improvement or correcting an error is legal.
**Back taxes** are limited. Property omitted from the prior year's roll is added at that year's rate (RPTL §551). There's no general ten-year rule.
Exempt property bought by a non-exempt owner is taxed at once, prorated (RPTL §520; STAR excepted).

example.title: Worked example: a revaluation with the levy unchanged
steps: A $3,000,000 levy on $60,000,000 of taxable value is $50 per $1,000; owners A and B, each assessed at $24,000, pay $1,200.
Step 1: A revaluation raises the total to $240,000,000, so the rate falls to $12.50 per $1,000.
Step 2: A rises 4 times, like the town, to $96,000: still $1,200.
Step 3: Under-assessed B rises 5 times, to $120,000: $1,500.
Answer: the levy didn't grow; the burden shifted to B. Keeping the old $50 rate is the trap.

sections.heading: Equalization rates and the residential assessment ratio
sections.intro: Equalization puts towns that assess at different percentages on a common full-value basis.
points: The **state equalization rate** = a municipality's total assessed value ÷ total market value.
ORPTS (Department of Taxation and Finance) sets it from sales data, such as the **RP-5217** filed with each deed.
Its main job is **apportioning county and school levies**: convert each town's assessed value to full value, then split the levy by share of full value.
**Full value = assessed value ÷ equalization rate**; never multiply.
The rate can **exceed 100%** when values fall; a falling rate with unchanged assessments means values rose. It describes a whole municipality, not anyone's bill.

The **residential assessment ratio (RAR)** compares residential assessments with residential market values. At the BAR or in SCAR, a home whose assessment ÷ market value exceeds the RAR is unequally assessed.

example.title: Worked example: apportioning a county levy
steps: A county must raise $9,000,000. Town A: $60,000,000 assessed, rate 40%. Town B: $210,000,000, rate 70%.
Answer: A pays $3,000,000; B pays $6,000,000. Splitting by raw assessed value (60 ÷ 270) is the trap: it charges A only $2,000,000, rewarding the town that assesses lower.

sections.heading: From budget to tax bill
sections.intro: Assessments set each owner's share; the budget sets how much there is to share.
points: An **appropriation** authorizes spending; the budget totals them. **Levy** = budget − other revenue (state aid, sales tax share, fees).
**Rate** = levy ÷ total taxable assessed value. Leaving exempt property out raises everyone else's rate.
Rates appear as decimals, percents, dollars per $100 or $1,000, or **mills**. To compare, convert to per $1,000 (per $100 × 10; percent × 10).
**Tax = taxable assessed value × rate**, never market value × rate. Each bill line (county, town, school, village, district) has its own rate and exemptions.
**Agent duty**: compute taxes from the current roll and rates, and note which exemptions the bill reflects. Never present the seller's bill as the buyer's future tax.

example.title: Worked example: from budget to one owner's tax
steps: Budget $14,200,000; state aid and fees $5,200,000; roll $320,000,000, including $20,000,000 wholly exempt.
Step 3: Taxable assessed value = $150,000 − a $10,000 exemption = $140,000.

sections.heading: Exemptions: STAR, seniors, veterans, farmland, and nonprofits
sections.intro: Exemptions lower taxable assessed value (the STAR credit is a check instead). Most need an application by the taxable status date and belong to the owner: a buyer must qualify and apply anew.
points: **Wholly exempt**: government property and nonprofit religious, charitable, educational and hospital property with **exempt ownership and exempt use** (RPTL §420-a). A floor a church leases to a for-profit firm is taxable.
**STAR** cuts school taxes only, on a primary residence only.
**Basic STAR**: no age test. Income up to $500,000 for the credit or $250,000 for the exemption.
**Enhanced STAR**: one resident owner **65 by December 31** of the benefit year. Since 2026, the owners' relationship doesn't matter. Upgrades to Enhanced are automatic.
Enhanced STAR income limit: resident owners' and spouses' income of $110,750 or less for 2026, and $113,550 for 2027.
**Credit vs exemption**: new homeowners since 2016 register with the Tax Department for the STAR credit, paid by check or direct deposit. The school-bill exemption is closed to newcomers.
Switching from exemption to credit is **irreversible**. Only the credit can grow, up to 2% a year.
**Senior citizens exemption**: up to **50%** off for owners 65+ under the local income limit (RPTL §467). An added option reaches 65% at the lowest incomes.
The senior exemption is a local option for each county, city, town, village and school district. It combines with Enhanced STAR.
All owners must be 65 unless they are spouses or siblings; then one is enough. They must have owned the home 12 months.

**Alternative veterans exemption**: 15% wartime + 10% combat zone + half the service-connected disability rating, under local caps (§458-a; local option, schools included). It gives no special district relief.
**Cold War** and **eligible funds** exemptions are separate.

Where adopted, VA-rated **permanently and totally disabled** veterans get a full exemption on their primary residence, special levies and assessments included. It starts with rolls whose taxable status dates fall on or after **October 1, 2026** (§458-a(11)).
**Disabilities and limited incomes**: up to 50% by local option (§459-c). Owners eligible for this and the senior exemption choose one.
**Agricultural assessment** taxes farmland at farm value (Agriculture and Markets Law §305). Idling the land triggers nothing.
Converting farmland within **5 years** (**8** outside an agricultural district) triggers a conversion payment: five times the last year's savings plus interest.

example.title: Worked example: a veterans exemption, then a sale
steps: A combat-zone wartime veteran rated 40% disabled owns a home assessed at $200,000; the town rate is 24 mills and caps aren't reached.
Step 4: A non-veteran buyer pays on the full $200,000: $200,000 × 24 ÷ 1,000 = $4,800.
Answer: the veteran pays $2,640; the buyer pays $4,800, because the exemption is personal.

sections.heading: Tax cap, homestead option, and NYC and Nassau classes
sections.intro: The levy cap, the two-rate homestead option, and the NYC and Nassau class systems change how the tax burden is divided.
points: The **property tax cap** limits levy growth to **2% or inflation**, whichever is less, with adjustments (General Municipal Law §3-c; Education Law §2023-a). It has been permanent since 2019.
A school budget above the cap needs 60% voter approval. A local government overrides it by a local law passed by 60% of its board. NYC isn't covered.
**Homestead option**: an approved assessing unit that completed a state-recognized revaluation may tax homestead (mostly 1–3 family) and non-homestead property at different rates (RPTL Article 19).
The homestead option keeps homeowners from absorbing more after a revaluation. Assessments stay uniform.
NYC and Nassau are **special assessing units** with classes, each with its own ratio and rate (RPTL Article 18).
NYC assesses class 1 at **6%** of market value and the rest at 45%. Its tax year runs July 1–June 30.

NYC caps market-driven class 1 increases at **6% a year and 20% over five years**, and class 2 buildings of 10 or fewer units at 8% and 30%; larger class 2 and class 4 phase changes in over five years. Physical improvements aren't capped.
Co-op owners pay through maintenance (the building is one class 2 parcel); condo units are assessed individually.

head: NYC class
Includes
Ratio
Increase limits
rows: 1–3 family homes, most condos of three stories or fewer, most residential vacant land
Other residential: rentals of 4+ units, co-ops, most condos
10 or fewer units: 8% / 30%; larger: five-year phase-in
Not under the class 1 and 2 caps
Commercial and industrial: offices, stores, hotels, factories

example.title: Worked example: the NYC class 1 cap
steps: A Staten Island two-family house was assessed at $28,000 last year; 6% of Finance's new market value is $36,000, with no physical change.
Answer: $29,680. The small class 2 cap (8%) gives $30,240; the 20% five-year cap in one year gives $33,600. Both are traps. A new addition would be added outside the cap.

sections.heading: Challenging an assessment: grievance, SCAR, and certiorari
sections.intro: Owners challenge the assessment, not the budget: informal review, then grievance, then court.
points: Four grounds for a challenge: excessive, unequal, unlawful and misclassified (RPTL §§522, 524). A disliked budget isn't one.
**Excessive**: above full value, or a partial exemption denied. **Unequal**: a higher level of assessment than comparable property.
**Unlawful**: for example, exempt property assessed as taxable.
**Grievance**: Form RP-524 must be **received** by the assessor before Grievance Day, or by the Board of Assessment Review (BAR) on Grievance Day. Mailing in time isn't enough.
Grievance Day is the 4th Tuesday in May in most towns. Suffolk towns use the 3rd Tuesday in May; Westchester towns, the 3rd Tuesday in June.
The BAR has 3–5 appointed members, never the assessor or staff.
Evidence: comparable sales, an appraisal, similar homes' assessments, the level of assessment or RAR, condition.
The BAR may deny, grant or grant in part, but **never raise** an assessment. Taxes stay due; a win brings a refund.
**SCAR** (Small Claims Assessment Review) covers owner-occupied 1–3 family homes used only as residences, and lots too small to build on, claiming unequal or excessive assessment.
File SCAR with the county clerk within **30 days** after the final roll, or notice of its filing if later. The fee is **$30**; no lawyer is needed.
A SCAR hearing officer weighs sales, assessment and ratio evidence. Outcomes match the BAR's.

SCAR limits: equalized value of $450,000 or less (otherwise a cut of no more than 25%), and no lower assessment than was requested at the BAR. Filing SCAR waives certiorari; review is only by **Article 78**.

Nassau owners, before SCAR or certiorari

example.title: Worked example: what assessment to request
steps: A town assesses at 50%. A home is assessed at $210,000; sales support $360,000; the rate is $32 per $1,000.
Step 1: Implied value = $210,000 ÷ 0.50 = $420,000, $60,000 too high.
Answer: request $180,000. Subtracting the whole $60,000 gap ($150,000) is the trap; it ignores the 50% level.

sections.heading: Tax liens, tax sales, and in rem foreclosure
sections.intro: Unpaid property taxes survive a sale; they attach to the parcel.
points: Unpaid taxes become a **specific, involuntary lien** that outranks private liens, even earlier mortgages; lenders escrow taxes and title searches check for them.
**In rem** ('against the thing'): an **RPTL Article 11** foreclosure targets the parcel, not the owner personally, and reaches homes as well as commercial property.

**Redemption**: the owner can pay taxes, interest and charges until the period ends, generally **two years after the lien date** (longer by local law for residential or farm property; one year for listed vacant and abandoned homes). Then the court can award title to the tax district.
**Surplus**: **Tyler v. Hennepin County (2023)** held that keeping more than the tax debt is a taking.
New York's 2024 law makes the district pay any surplus into court (RPTL §§1196–1197). Lienholders, then the former owner, claim it.
The surplus is the public-sale price (or full value, if not sold publicly) minus taxes, interest and charges.

**Tax lien sale** (NYC and some other places): an investor buys the right to collect the taxes plus interest. It isn't a transfer of title: the owner keeps title and can pay off the lien until a later foreclosure.
**Agent duty**: confirm taxes are current and flag liens or pending tax sales early; delinquent taxes are paid from the seller's proceeds.

sections.heading: Transfer taxes and mortgage recording tax
sections.intro: Transfer taxes are figured on the price; the mortgage recording tax on the loan.
points: **NYS transfer tax**: **$2 per $500 or fraction** (about 0.4%) above $500 of consideration. Round partial units up (Tax Law §1402).
The seller pays the transfer tax; if the seller doesn't or is exempt, the buyer must. It's reported on Form TP-584, due within 15 days of the deed's delivery.
**Mansion tax**: the buyer pays **1% of the entire price** when a residence (1–3 family house, condo or co-op unit) sells for $1,000,000 or more. Exactly $1,000,000 owes $10,000 (§1402-a).

**NYC extras** (since July 1, 2019): the state base rate is 0.65% for NYC residences of $3 million+ and other NYC property of $2 million+ (seller); NYC residences of $2 million+ owe a **supplemental mansion tax** of 0.25% to 2.9% (buyer).
**NYC RPTT** applies to NYC transfers over $25,000. Residential: 1% at $500,000 or less; **1.425% of the whole price** above. Other property: 1.425% or 2.625%.
The seller normally pays the NYC RPTT, on top of the state tax.

No state transfer tax on gifts, inheritances, deeds that only secure a debt, or correction deeds. Co-op sales are taxed; a co-op **flip tax** is a private building fee. Some localities (Yonkers, the Peconic Bay towns) add their own transfer taxes.
**Mortgage recording tax** is on the recorded **loan**, per $100; a remainder over $50 counts as $100. Cash buyers pay none (Tax Law Article 11).
Its parts: a basic 0.50%; a special additional 0.25%, paid by the lender on 1–6 family homes; and an additional 0.25% (0.30% in the NYC-area commuter counties).
The first $10,000 of a 1–2 family loan is excluded from the additional tax. NYC, Yonkers and some counties add local taxes.

Suburban commuter counties typically total 1.05%; NYC borrowers pay 1.8% on 1–3 family or condo loans under $500,000 and 1.925% at $500,000 or more. Exam problems usually just multiply the loan by a given rate.
**Co-op share loans** pay none, because no real property mortgage is recorded.
A **CEMA** assigns the old mortgage to the new lender, so only the new money is taxed (Tax Law §255).

head: Tax
Rate
Base
Paid by
rows: Residential: 1% ($500K or less) or 1.425% of the whole price
About 1.05% in NYC suburbs; more in NYC

example.title: Worked example: closing taxes on a Brooklyn condo
steps: A Brooklyn condo sells for $1,200,000; the buyer records a $900,000 mortgage at a stated borrower rate of 1.925%.
Step 1: NYS transfer tax = 2,400 units × $2 = $4,800 (seller).
Step 3: Mansion tax = 1% × $1,200,000 = $12,000 (buyer). The NYC supplemental tax starts at $2,000,000.
Step 4: Mortgage tax = $900,000 × 1.925% = $17,325 (buyer); taxing the price is the trap.
Step 5: A later CEMA refinance from a $700,000 balance to $800,000 taxes only the $100,000 of new money.
Answer: seller $21,900; buyer $29,325.

sections.heading: Homeowner income tax: deductions and limits
sections.intro: A home affects income tax mainly through itemized deductions; state the rules accurately and refer specifics to a tax professional.
points: Mortgage interest and property taxes are **itemized deductions**, useful only when itemizing beats the **standard deduction**.

**Acquisition debt** (to buy, build or substantially improve the main home or one second home): interest on up to **$750,000** is deductible for loans after December 15, 2017 ($1,000,000 for older loans). The 2025 federal tax law (P.L. 119-21) made $750,000 permanent.

**Home equity** interest qualifies only if the money buys, builds or substantially improves the home securing it, not credit cards, tuition or a car. A refinance stays acquisition debt up to the old balance plus improvement money; a home under construction qualifies for up to 24 months.
**Points** to buy a main home are generally deductible when paid. Seller-paid points are too, but they lower the buyer's basis. Refinance points are spread over the loan.
A prepayment penalty counts as interest. **Mortgage insurance premiums** are deductible again from 2026, phased out between $100,000 and $109,000 of AGI.
The SALT cap covers property taxes plus state and local income (or sales) taxes. It was $10,000 for 2018–2024, then **$40,000** for 2025 and **$40,400** for 2026.
The SALT cap rises 1% yearly through 2029 and returns to $10,000 in 2030.
The cap is cut by 30% of MAGI over $500,000 ($505,000 in 2026), but never below $10,000. Married filing separately: half.
Sale year: the seller deducts taxes through the day before closing, the buyer from closing on, whoever paid the town; a buyer's proration credit counts as the buyer paying.

**Not deductible**: principal, homeowners insurance, HOA or condo charges, utilities, repairs, personal-home depreciation, transfer taxes and special assessments (the last two adjust basis or the amount realized).
Co-op owners deduct their share of building interest and taxes paid through maintenance (IRC §216). New York allows itemizing on the state return without itemizing federally.
**IRA first home**: up to **$10,000** lifetime avoids the 10% early-withdrawal penalty, but a traditional IRA withdrawal is still taxed; first-time means no main home owned in the prior 2 years.
**Vacation home**: interest on one second home counts within the $750,000 limit; rent for fewer than 15 days a year isn't reported.

example.title: Worked example: who deducts the property taxes in the sale year
steps: The seller paid the $7,300 calendar-year town tax in January. Closing is April 1 (not a leap year); the buyer owns the closing day.
Step 2: Seller: January 1–March 31 = 90 days = $1,800.
Step 3: Buyer: April 1–December 31 = 275 days = $5,500, credited to the seller.
Answer: each deducts its own share (if itemizing), though the seller paid the town.

sections.heading: Basis, gain, and the home-sale exclusion (§121)
sections.intro: Gain is measured against adjusted basis, not the price or the mortgage. The Taxpayer Relief Act of 1997 created today's exclusion.
points: **Basis** = price + capitalized purchase costs (owner's title insurance, recording and legal fees, survey, buyer-paid transfer tax, seller's back taxes the buyer paid). Loan costs and insurance premiums aren't added.

**Adjusted basis** = basis + **capital improvements** − depreciation. An improvement adds value, extends life or adapts the property (addition, new roof, central air, garage, sidewalk assessment); a repair (painting, fixing a leak) doesn't count.

**Amount realized** = price − selling costs (commission, legal fees, seller-paid transfer tax, which isn't deductible); **gain** = amount realized − adjusted basis. A mortgage payoff changes cash, not gain.
**§121**: exclude up to $250,000 ($500,000 joint) if the seller owned and used the home as a main home **2 of the 5 years** before the sale.
The months needn't be consecutive or the same for both tests.
The exclusion is usable once every 2 years, at any age, with no reinvestment. The age-55 one-time exclusion and rollover ended in 1997.

**Joint**: either spouse may meet ownership, but **both** must meet use and neither may have used the exclusion in the prior 2 years; otherwise each qualifying spouse gets up to $250,000. An unmarried surviving spouse keeps $500,000 for a sale within 2 years of the death.
**Reduced exclusion** (job change, health, unforeseen circumstances): maximum × qualifying months ÷ 24.
Not excluded: gain equal to depreciation taken after May 6, 1997 (home office, rental).
Also not excluded: gain allocated to post-2008 rental use before the home became the main home, and gain on a home acquired by 1031 exchange and sold within 5 years.
A **loss** on a personal home isn't deductible. An investment capital loss offsets gains plus $3,000 a year of other income.
**Inherited** property gets a **stepped-up basis** (value at death) and is automatically long-term. A gift keeps the donor's carryover basis.
**Long-term** gain (held more than 1 year) is taxed at 0%, 15% or 20%; short-term at ordinary rates.

example.title: Worked example: gain and the exclusion
steps: A single owner paid $310,000 plus $4,000 of title, recording and legal costs, added a $40,000 kitchen and $16,000 roof, and spent $5,000 repainting. Seven years later she sold for $720,000 with $42,000 of selling costs, paying off a $200,000 mortgage.
Step 1: Adjusted basis = $310,000 + $4,000 + $40,000 + $16,000 = $370,000 (painting excluded).
Step 2: Gain = ($720,000 − $42,000) − $370,000 = $308,000; the mortgage plays no part.
Step 3: She meets the 2-of-5 tests: $308,000 − $250,000 = $58,000.
Answer: $58,000 of taxable long-term gain. A qualifying married couple filing jointly would owe nothing.

sections.heading: Investment property: depreciation, taxable income, and sale
sections.intro: Rentals are taxed like a business: rent is income; expenses and depreciation are deductions; and depreciation lowers basis, raising the gain at sale.
points: Three income types: **active** (wages, commissions, a business the owner materially runs), **passive** (rentals, businesses without material participation) and portfolio (interest, dividends, securities gains).
Passive losses generally offset only passive income and carry forward until sale.

Exceptions: an actively participating landlord may deduct up to **$25,000** of rental losses, phased out between $100,000 and $150,000 of income; an IRS **real estate professional** (750+ hours and over half of working time in real estate, materially participating) isn't limited. A license alone doesn't qualify.
**Depreciation** is a yearly deduction for buildings and improvements used in business or held for income. Land and a personal residence never qualify.
Straight-line, on cost − land: **27.5 years** for residential rental, **39 years** nonresidential. Exam problems ignore the partial first year.
Residential rental means 80%+ of rents from dwelling units, so an 85% apartment building qualifies in full.
Depreciation is a non-cash **tax shelter**, lowering taxable income and basis even as the building appreciates.
**Taxable income** = NOI − interest − depreciation; principal isn't deductible. **After-tax cash flow** = NOI − debt service − tax.
At a sale, gain equal to past depreciation (**unrecaptured §1250 gain**, the recapture portion) is taxed at up to **25%**; the rest is long-term capital gain.
**Installment sale** (seller financing): gain is reported as principal arrives, at principal × (gross profit ÷ contract price); interest is ordinary income.
**LIHTC**: federal low-income housing credits, allocated by housing agencies, cut tax dollar for dollar over 10 years, with a 15-year compliance period.

example.title: Worked example: depreciation, cash flow, and gain
steps: A rental duplex costs $520,000, including $107,500 of land. NOI is $40,000; interest $20,000; principal $6,000; 24% bracket.
Step 1: Depreciation = ($520,000 − $107,500) ÷ 27.5 = $15,000 (not $18,909 on the full cost).
Step 4: After-tax cash flow = $40,000 − $26,000 debt service − $1,200 = $12,800.
Answer: $120,000 (the depreciation) is taxed at up to 25%; $120,000 is long-term capital gain.

sections.heading: Section 1031 like-kind exchanges
sections.intro: A 1031 exchange rolls gain from one investment property into another; the tax is deferred, not forgiven.
points: **Eligible**: real property held for business or investment, exchanged for like-kind real property held the same way; since 2018, only real property.

**Like-kind** is broad: rental houses, apartments, offices, industrial buildings, hotels and investment land are interchangeable, and a leasehold with 30+ years left is like-kind to ownership. U.S. and foreign property aren't.
**Not eligible**: a personal or personally used vacation home, dealer property (a builder's lots, a flipper's houses), stocks and partnership interests.
**Deadlines**: identify in writing within **45 days**. Acquire within 180 days or by the return due date (with extensions), if earlier.
Both deadlines run from the sale, concurrently, with no weekend extension. Identify up to three properties, or more under the 200% rule.

A **qualified intermediary** holds the proceeds; if the investor receives the cash, the exchange fails. The investor's agent, attorney or broker within the past 2 years can't serve; there's no advance IRS approval.

**Boot** = cash, other property or **net debt relief**; recognized gain = the lesser of boot or realized gain. Full deferral needs equal or greater value, all equity reinvested, and debt replaced or offset with cash.
**New basis** = replacement cost − deferred gain. In a **reverse exchange** the replacement is bought first and parked with an accommodation titleholder, under the same deadlines.

Rule
Trap
rows: A home or flip doesn't qualify
Both run from the sale, not one after the other
Taking the proceeds ends the exchange
Cash, other property, net debt relief
Debt relief counts even with no cash
Using full cost erases the deferred gain

example.title: Worked example: deadlines, boot, and basis
steps: A building with a $300,000 adjusted basis closes October 2, 2026 for $800,000 net; the investor buys a $750,000 replacement and keeps $50,000.
Step 1: Identify by November 16, 2026; acquire by March 31, 2027, before the April 15 return due date.
Step 3: The $50,000 boot is taxed now; $450,000 is deferred.

sections.heading: FIRPTA and nonresident sellers
sections.intro: Two rules can cut a seller's cash at a New York closing: FIRPTA for foreign sellers and NY estimated tax for nonresidents. A foreign seller can face both.
points: **FIRPTA**: when a foreign person sells U.S. real property, the buyer withholds **15% of the amount realized**, meaning the gross price, not the gain (IRC §1445).
The buyer remits it on Forms 8288 and 8288-A within 20 days. A buyer who fails to withhold can be liable.
Residence exceptions apply if an individual buyer plans to live there at least half the days it's used in each of the first two years.
Under those exceptions: **none** at $300,000 or less; **10%** at $300,001–$1,000,000. Any other foreign-seller sale: 15%.
A U.S. seller's **certification of non-foreign status** ends the duty. A foreign seller can seek an IRS withholding certificate for less; withholding is credited against the actual tax.

**NY nonresident sellers** (individuals, estates and trusts, foreign sellers included) pay estimated NY tax on the gain at closing on **Form IT-2663** (IT-2664 for co-ops), filed with the TP-584; the clerk won't record the deed without it. It's the seller's payment, not withholding, and a fully qualifying §121 sale is exempt.
**Agent duty**: ask early whether the seller is foreign or a nonresident.

example.title: Worked example: FIRPTA on a condo sale
steps: A foreign individual sells a condo for $650,000.
Step 1: To an investor: 15% × $650,000 = $97,500.
Step 2: To a buyer who will live there: 10% × $650,000 = $65,000.
Step 3: At $290,000, such a sale owes nothing.
Answer: $97,500 to an investor; $65,000 to an occupying buyer. Taking 15% of the gain is the trap.

NYS Department of Taxation and Finance: STAR eligibility (2026 rules), senior and veterans exemption pages, ORPTS grievance booklet (checked October 2026); NYC Finance and Tax Commission guidance
Tyler v. Hennepin County, 598 U.S. 631 (2023)
