guides.title: Condos & Co-ops
guides.overview: Condos and co-ops look alike but are legal opposites. A **condo** is real property: a deeded unit plus a share of the common elements (Real Property Law Article 9-B). A **co-op** is personal property: corporate shares plus a proprietary lease. The exam stresses what the buyer owns, the common-charge lien, board approval under Levandusky, and co-op financing and taxes.

numbers.label: Condo lien ends at payment or 6 years after filing, whichever first (RPL §339-aa)
Written notice before a condo lien foreclosure (RPL §339-aa, from Oct. 16, 2025)
NYC non-eviction conversion: units bought by tenants in occupancy at AG acceptance (GBL §352-eeee)
Non-eviction threshold under GBL §352-eee (opt-in Nassau, Westchester and Rockland municipalities)
Eviction plan: 51% of tenants excluding eligible seniors and disabled; 35% including (§352-eee)
Age of an eligible senior, never evicted for not buying in a conversion
Minimum vote, by number and common interest, to amend condo bylaws (RPL §339-v)
CPS-1 market-testing period, extendable once a plan is submitted; Spada's 120 days is outdated
IRC §216 tests, pass any one: income, square footage, spending for tenant-stockholders
Earlier of these ends sponsor board control in a non-eviction conversion (eviction: 2 years)
Maximum co-op late fee on monthly maintenance, if the lease allows (RPL §238-a)
NYC co-ops of 10+ units: acknowledge application, then decide once complete (Local Law 58)
NYS mansion tax covers condo units and co-op apartments; buyer pays
NYS transfer tax on co-op share transfers and condo deeds alike; seller pays

mustKnow: A **condo** owner holds real property: a unit plus an **undivided interest in the common elements**, which normally include the land.
A co-op buyer gets **shares** (personal property) in the corporation that owns the building, plus a **proprietary lease**; no deed.
The recorded **declaration** creates the condo and fixes each unit's common interest; the **bylaws** govern elections, meetings and collections; house rules rank below both.
The **common interest** (set by fair value, floor area, equal shares or adjusted floor space) is permanent, changes only with consent of all affected owners, and can't be split from the unit.
Common elements can't be **partitioned**; a **limited common element** (private terrace) is owned by all, with use reserved to certain units.
Each condo unit is a **separate tax parcel**, so unpaid taxes lien only that unit; a co-op building gets one tax bill, passed through maintenance by shares.
The **common-charge lien** is junior only to tax liens, the **first mortgage of record** and certain agency mortgages.
The condo lien lasts **6 years** from filing and is foreclosed like a mortgage, after **90 days'** written notice to the owner.
Without unanimous owner consent, no lien can attach to condo **common elements**; a contractor can lien only the unit of an owner who ordered or consented to the work.
A condo board's resale power is normally a **right of first refusal** (buy on the same terms or waive), not a co-op-style rejection.
**Levandusky** (1990) **business judgment rule**: courts defer to good-faith board decisions within the board's authority for legitimate purposes, but never to discrimination.
The **sponsor** appoints the first board and managing agent. AG rules limit its control: in non-eviction conversions, the earlier of 5 years after the first closing or unsold interests below 50%.
Eviction conversions and new co-ops cap sponsor control at **2 years**.
Co-op **maintenance** = share of operating costs + building real estate taxes + **underlying mortgage**; the buyer's own share loan is separate.
A default on the **underlying mortgage** endangers every shareholder; also check **fee vs ground lease** ownership.
**Board package**: application, signed contract, verified financials, tax returns, employment letter, references, credit authorization, disclosures; managing agent screens, board decides.
**Share loan** collateral = stock certificate + stock power + assigned proprietary lease, perfected by **UCC-1**; default → nonjudicial UCC sale.
**Recognition agreement** (lender, co-op, shareholder): the co-op recognizes the lender's lien and gives it notice and a chance to cure defaults.
A **co-op lien search** (UCC filings, judgments, tax liens) replaces the condo's title search and title insurance.
**Flip tax** = private transfer fee paid to the co-op (gross %, profit %, per share or flat), usually by the seller.
Co-op sales pay NYS transfer tax (seller), NYC RPTT in the city and the **mansion tax** at $1M+ (buyer), but no **mortgage recording tax**.
**IRC §216**: deduct your share of the co-op's **real estate taxes and mortgage interest** if it meets one test (80% income, 80% square footage, 90% expenditures).
**RPL §226-b** sublet rights don't apply to **proprietary leases**; a subletting shareholder stays liable.
The sponsor and **holders of unsold shares** usually sell and sublet without board approval; resale investors aren't holders of unsold shares.
Offering plans go to the AG's **Real Estate Finance Bureau** (Martin Act); acceptance is disclosure review only, and owner resales need no plan.
**CPS-1**: 12 months (extendable) of AG-cleared ads and nonbinding interest only, with **no deposits and no reservations**, binding or nonbinding.
**Non-eviction plan**: non-buyers can't be evicted for not buying; NYC requires **51%** tenant purchases and bars new eviction plans.
Eligible seniors (62+) and disabled tenants are protected from eviction for not buying under any plan.
A **condop** is a condo whose residential unit is owned by a co-op.
An **HOA** owner holds a fee-owned house and lot; the association owns the common areas under recorded **CC&Rs**.
The condo **master policy** is a common expense; the owner's **HO-6** covers interior improvements, contents, liability and loss assessment.

traps.trap: A condo owner owns only air space, never land.
traps.truth: Unless the declaration says otherwise, the land is a common element owned by all unit owners in undivided shares (RPL §339-e(3)).

traps.trap: A co-op buyer gets a deed and a recorded mortgage, so mortgage recording tax applies.
traps.truth: Shares are personal property financed by a share loan perfected by UCC filing; nothing is recorded and no mortgage recording tax is due. Transfer taxes and the mansion tax still apply.

traps.trap: A flip tax is a city or state tax.
traps.truth: A flip tax is a private fee the co-op charges under its proprietary lease or offering plan (BCL §501(c)); government transfer taxes are separate.

traps.trap: During CPS-1, a fully refundable deposit or a nonbinding reservation is fine.
traps.truth: CPS-1 bars all deposits and all reservations, binding or nonbinding, until the plan is accepted; only nonbinding indications of interest are allowed.

traps.trap: A share-loan commitment obliges the co-op board to approve the buyer.
traps.truth: The approvals are independent; the board can lawfully reject, and the board-consent contingency then lets either side cancel with the down payment returned.

traps.trap: The business judgment rule lets a co-op board reject a buyer for any reason.
traps.truth: Rejecting on a protected basis (familial status, lawful source of income, military status and more) is illegal; business judgment never covers discrimination. Boards usually needn't give a reason.

traps.trap: A condo board can reject a buyer just like a co-op board.
traps.truth: A condo board normally has only a right of first refusal: buy on the same terms or waive. If its deadline passes, the sale proceeds.

traps.trap: An owner who never uses the gym, or who abandons the unit, can stop paying that share of common charges.
traps.truth: Neither waiver of use nor abandonment ends liability (RPL §339-x); only conveying the unit to the board, if the bylaws allow, stops future charges.

traps.trap: The common-charge lien ranks behind every mortgage recorded before it.
traps.truth: It ranks behind only tax liens, the first mortgage of record and certain agency mortgages; a second mortgage or HELOC is behind it even if recorded first.

traps.trap: The 80/20 rule was repealed, so a co-op's commercial income no longer matters.
traps.truth: The co-op must still pass one of three alternative §216 tests. Since 2007 the 80% income test sits alongside 80% square footage and 90% expenditures.

traps.trap: NYC sponsors can still choose eviction plans, and outside buyers count toward the percentage.
traps.truth: Since the 2019 HSTPA, new NYC plans must be non-eviction, with 51% of units bought by tenants in occupancy on the acceptance date; new eviction plans are possible only outside NYC (for example under §352-eee).

traps.trap: The $20 application-fee cap and $50/5% late-fee cap protect co-op buyers and shareholders.
traps.truth: A co-op may charge applicants managing-agent processing fees and actual-cost credit checks, and a late fee up to 8% of monthly maintenance if the lease allows (RPL §238-a). Those caps are rental rules.

traps.trap: CPS-1 market testing lasts 120 days, plus a 60-day extension.
traps.truth: The current CPS-1 runs 12 months from the AG's acceptance and can be extended once the sponsor has submitted an offering plan. Spada's 120-day rule is outdated.

traps.trap: Under §216 a shareholder deducts the whole maintenance payment.
traps.truth: The shareholder deducts only the proportionate share of the co-op's real estate taxes and mortgage interest; operating costs and principal are not deductible.

mnemonics.name: Deed vs. stock + lease
mnemonics.meaning: Condo = deed to a unit (real property, mortgage, own tax bill, title insurance). Co-op = stock + proprietary lease (personal property, share loan, UCC filing, lien search, board approval).

mnemonics.name: Red before black
mnemonics.meaning: Red herring (preliminary plan) → black book (accepted plan) → plan declared effective → closings.
IRC §216: 80% of income from tenant-stockholders, OR 80% of square footage for their use, OR 90% of spending for their benefit.

formulas.name: Common interest (floor-area method)
formulas.formula: Unit floor area ÷ total floor area of all units

formulas.name: Monthly condo common charges
formulas.formula: Annual budget × common interest ÷ 12

formulas.name: Special assessment share
formulas.formula: Total assessment × common interest

formulas.name: Monthly co-op maintenance
formulas.formula: (Annual budget ÷ total shares) × apartment's shares ÷ 12

formulas.name: IRC §216 deduction
formulas.formula: (Apartment's shares ÷ total shares) × (co-op's real estate taxes + mortgage interest)

formulas.name: Flip tax
formulas.formula: Gross: price × rate. Profit: (sale price − purchase price) × rate

formulas.name: NYS transfer tax (co-op or condo)
formulas.formula: Price ÷ $500, rounded up, × $2 (seller)

formulas.name: Largest share loan
formulas.formula: Price × (1 − minimum down-payment %)

formulas.name: Post-closing liquidity
formulas.formula: (Monthly maintenance + monthly loan payment) × months required

formulas.name: NYC non-eviction threshold
formulas.formula: Dwelling units × 51%, rounded up

sections.heading: What the buyer owns: condo, co-op and HOA compared
sections.intro: Identical-looking homes can be different legal interests, and building style never decides the form. Ask what is conveyed, by what document, and who owns the land.
points: **Condominium**: the owner holds a unit, usually in fee simple, plus an appurtenant (attached and inseparable) **undivided interest in the common elements**. These include the structure, lobby, roof and normally the land.
Each condo unit, with its common interest, is real property: deeded, mortgaged and taxed on its own (RPL §§339-g, 339-y). Units can be residential or commercial.

**Cooperative**: a corporation owns the building in fee or under a ground lease. The buyer purchases the shares allocated to an apartment and receives a proprietary lease, making the corporation the landlord.
Co-op shares are **personal property**: no deed and no recorded mortgage.
**HOA community**: each owner holds fee title to a house and lot; the association owns the common areas and charges assessments.
Test: a deed to a lot, with the association owning the green, is an **HOA**. A unit plus a percentage of all the land, green included, is a **condo**.

head: Feature
Condo
Co-op
HOA
rows: House and lot; association owns common areas
Share loan, UCC filing (no recording tax)
One building bill, paid through maintenance
Usually a right of first refusal only

sections.heading: Condominium Act essentials (RPL Article 9-B)
sections.intro: A property becomes a condominium when its owner records a declaration submitting it to the Condominium Act.
points: The **declaration** describes the land and building, each unit's designation, the common elements, each unit's **common interest** and permitted uses, and how it may be amended (§339-n). Floor plans are filed with it.
The declaration outranks the bylaws, which outrank board-adopted house rules. A rule that conflicts with the declaration fails.

The **bylaws** are annexed to the declaration. They cover electing the board of managers, meetings and collecting common charges, and may regulate sales and leasing, subject to fair housing law (§§339-u, 339-v).
At least one-third of the board seats expire each year.
Amending the bylaws takes at least **66⅔%** of owners by number and common interest, recorded as an amendment to the declaration (§339-v). The rule doesn't apply if every unit is nonresidential.

**Common elements**, unless the declaration says otherwise, include the land, foundations, main walls, roof, halls, lobbies, stairs, elevators, basements, yards, parking and central systems (§339-e(3)); the space inside a unit's boundaries is the unit itself.
A **limited common element**, such as a terrace reachable from one unit, is still owned by all; the declaration reserves its use.
The **common interest** is fixed by approximate fair value, floor area, equal percentages, or floor space adjusted for location and similar factors (§339-i(1)).
The common interest is permanent, changes only by amended declaration with consent of all affected owners, and can never be separated from the unit (§339-i(2)).
Common elements can't be **partitioned**, but a unit may be owned by the entirety, jointly or in common (§339-i(3)).
The board has an irrevocable **right of access** to units for operations and emergency repairs (§339-i(5)).

Consent of **all affected unit owners** is needed to add a material structure, excavate a new basement or cellar, or do work that threatens soundness or safety, lowers the property's value or impairs an easement. A building permit is no substitute (§339-k).
A **unit deed** states the declaration's recording data, the unit designation, its use and its common interest (§339-o).
Owners may inspect the books (§339-w). Rule-breakers can be sued for damages or an injunction (§339-j).

sections.heading: Common charges, assessments and the condo lien
sections.intro: Condo expenses are shared by common interest, not by head count or amenity use.
points: **Common charges** and special assessments are allocated by common interest (§339-m).

The declaration and bylaws may authorize **special allocation** based on exclusive use, such as roof-deck upkeep billed only to the penthouses that reach it. They may also specially allocate to nonresidential units.
Waiving use of common elements or **abandoning** the unit never ends liability. Subject to the bylaws, conveying the unit to the board stops charges accruing afterward (§339-x).
The board's **lien** for unpaid charges plus interest outranks every lien except real estate tax liens, the unpaid **first mortgage of record**, and certain government housing-agency mortgages.
A second mortgage or home equity line (HELOC) is junior to the board's lien even if recorded first (§339-z).
The lien takes effect when a **notice of lien** is filed and lasts until paid or **6 years** from filing, whichever is sooner.
The board may foreclose the lien like a mortgage or sue for a money judgment (§339-aa). Since Oct. 16, 2025 it must first give the owner at least **90 days' written notice**.
The foreclosure notice must be in 14-point type, sent to the unit and any other address of record, and state the amount due.
A seller or buyer who obtains the board's **statement of unpaid common charges** isn't liable, and the unit isn't liened, for pre-sale charges above the stated amount (§339-z).
**Mechanic's liens** can't attach to common elements once the declaration is recorded.

Unit work supports a lien only on the unit of an owner who ordered or consented to it, except for emergency repairs. For board-ordered work, common charges are **trust funds** to pay the contractor (§339-l).
At each unit's first sale the sponsor's **blanket mortgage** must be satisfied or the unit released by recorded partial release (§339-r).

example.title: Worked example: common interest, common charges and an assessment
steps: Floor-area common interest: 1,400 ÷ 56,000 sq ft = **2.5%**.
Annual charges: $612,000 budget × 1.75% = $10,710 a year.
Trap check: $1,250,000 ÷ 100 units = $12,500 ignores the percentages; $10,710 is annual, not monthly.
Answer: 2.5% common interest, $892.50 a month in charges, and a $10,000 assessment share.

sections.heading: Boards, sponsors and the business judgment rule
sections.intro: A condo has a board of managers and a co-op a board of directors; both usually hire a managing agent.
points: The **sponsor** (developer or converting owner) appoints the first board and **managing agent**. Owners later elect the board under the bylaws.
The managing agent collects charges, pays bills, supervises staff and keeps records for the board.

Attorney General (AG) regulations limit sponsor control. In a **non-eviction conversion**, the sponsor and other holders of unsold interests must give up voting control of the board by the earlier of **5 years** after the first closing or when unsold interests fall below 50%.
In an eviction plan, the sponsor-control limit is 2 years (13 NYCRR 18.3, 23.3).
New co-op plans also cap control at 2 years or 50% of units closed. A new-construction condo plan must flag control past 2 years or the 50% mark as a special risk (13 NYCRR 21.3, 20.3).

**House rules** govern daily life (pets, noise, moves). An **alteration agreement** sets renovation conditions, such as approved plans, insured contractors and deposits. Board consent never replaces a building permit.
**Levandusky v. One Fifth Avenue Apartment Corp.** (1990) upheld a co-op's stop-work order over a moved steam riser.

In Levandusky, the Court of Appeals adopted the **business judgment rule**: courts defer to board decisions made in good faith, within the board's authority, for legitimate building purposes. It applies to condo boards and HOAs too.

Courts won't substitute their own choice (no lowest-bid rule). Review opens only if the owner shows the board exceeded its authority, lacked a legitimate purpose, or acted in bad faith (self-dealing, favoritism, discrimination).
Co-op boards may reject a purchaser, generally without stating a reason, but never on a **protected basis**.

Protected bases include the federal classes plus NY additions such as age, marital status, military status, sexual orientation, gender identity and **lawful source of income**. A uniform financial standard is lawful.
Some counties outside NYC, such as Westchester and Suffolk, add decision deadlines and written reasons.
A new NYC law covers applications made from July 28, 2026, in co-ops of 10 or more units. Housing Development Fund Corporation (HDFC) co-ops are excluded (Local Law 58 of 2026).

Under it, the board must acknowledge the package in writing within **15 days**, saying whether it is complete. It must decide within **45 days** after the package is complete, but still needn't give reasons.
A condo board usually has only a **right of first refusal** on resales: buy on the contract's terms or waive, usually in writing before closing.
If the bylaws' deadline passes, the right lapses for that sale. The condo board can't reject the buyer or add conditions the governing documents don't authorize.

sections.heading: Co-op ownership, maintenance and due diligence
sections.intro: In a co-op the corporation owns the property and is the landlord; each shareholder is a tenant-owner.
points: The corporation owns in **fee** or holds a **ground lease**. In a leasehold co-op, check the remaining term, rent resets and end-of-term rights: the corporation's rights end with the lease, and a reset can sharply raise maintenance.
The **stock certificate** shows the apartment's shares; the **proprietary lease** grants occupancy and governs maintenance, alterations, subletting, assignment and default.

**Maintenance** is the apartment's share (by shares) of operating costs, reserves, the building's real estate taxes and the **underlying mortgage**. That is why it usually exceeds condo common charges on a similar unit.
Shares also allocate assessments and §216 deductions. The buyer's own share loan is paid separately.

The **underlying mortgage** is a lien on the whole building. A corporate default (for example, after a big sponsor stops paying maintenance) endangers even shareholders who paid on time, though they aren't personally liable for it.

Due diligence: **financial statements** (reserves, surplus or deficit, arrears, commercial income), **board minutes** (assessment history, planned work, litigation), the underlying mortgage's rate and maturity, and sponsor holdings.
Unpaid maintenance: the co-op holds a **lien on the shares**. As landlord, it can also terminate the lease or bring a **summary nonpayment proceeding** (RPAPL Article 7).
If the proprietary lease allows, the late fee may reach **8%** of monthly maintenance (RPL §238-a). Housing Development Fund Corporation (HDFC) and Mitchell-Lama co-ops are excepted.

example.title: Worked example: maintenance and the tax portion
steps: Per share: $2,400,000 budget ÷ 50,000 shares = $48 a year.
625 shares × $48 = $30,000 a year.
Tax per share: $1,200,000 taxes ÷ 60,000 shares = $20.
750 shares × $20 = $15,000 a year.
Trap check: $30,000 and $15,000 are annual figures.
Answer: $2,500 a month in maintenance; $1,250 a month in taxes.

sections.heading: Buying a co-op: board package, interview and approval
sections.intro: A co-op resale needs two independent approvals: the lender's and the board's.
points: Sequence: accepted offer; contract signed, with the down payment held in escrow by the seller's attorney; loan application; **board package** to the managing agent; completeness check; board review; **interview**; decision; closing, where stock and lease are transferred.

Board package: purchase application, **fully executed contract of sale**, financial statement with verification of assets, tax returns (3 years recommended), employment verification letter, personal and business references, signed credit-check authorization, and required disclosures such as lead paint. No title policy.
Boards test **debt-to-income** against building policy, the minimum down payment (often stricter than the lender's) and post-closing **liquidity**.
Income may include wages, bonuses, commissions, business, rental and investment income, trusts, alimony and Social Security. Liquid assets count most.
Rejecting a buyer because lawful income comes from Social Security or a subsidy violates NY law.

Many boards meet monthly, so submit a complete package early and time the interview against contract dates and the **rate lock**. Prepare the buyer to know the package and disclose fully; never coach concealment.

A loan commitment doesn't bind the board. Standard NY co-op contracts are contingent on **board consent**; after a rejection either party may cancel and the down payment is returned. There is no appeal to the AG.

A co-op may charge purchase applicants managing-agent processing fees and actual-cost credit checks. The $20 cap is a rental rule. Housing Development Fund Corporation (HDFC) and Mitchell-Lama co-ops face tighter limits.
Co-op and condo sales require agency disclosure (RPL §443). Federal lead-paint disclosure (pre-1978) also applies. The Property Condition Disclosure Statement (PCDS) does not.

example.title: Worked example: board financing tests
steps: Price $750,000 with 25% down required: down payment $187,500, leaving the rest to finance.
Largest loan: $750,000 − $187,500 = **$562,500** (a 75% loan-to-value cap).
Liquidity of 24 months of maintenance plus loan: ($2,100 + $3,400) × 24 = **$132,000**.
Trap check: $187,500 is the down payment; 12 months gives $66,000; the loan payment alone gives $81,600.
Answer: the largest loan is $562,500, and the buyer needs $132,000 liquid after closing.

sections.heading: Share loans, recognition agreements and lien searches
sections.intro: Co-op shares are personal property, so financing follows Uniform Commercial Code (UCC) Article 9, not mortgage law.
points: A **share loan** is secured by the shares and proprietary lease. The lender holds the stock certificate, a signed stock power and an assignment of the proprietary lease, and files a **UCC-1** financing statement. Nothing is recorded against the apartment.

The **recognition agreement** (lender, co-op and shareholder) acknowledges the lender's security interest. The co-op must notify the lender of defaults and allow a cure before cancelling the lease; it keeps its own lien for unpaid maintenance.
A **co-op lien search** checks UCC filings, judgments and tax liens against the seller and the shares, replacing the condo's title search and title insurance.
On default the lender holds a **nonjudicial UCC sale** of the shares and lease after notice, not a judicial foreclosure (UCC §9-610).
Share-loan interest counts as home mortgage interest for federal income tax, within the usual limits.

sections.heading: Flip taxes, transfer taxes and closing costs
sections.intro: Keep private building charges separate from government taxes, and know who pays each.
points: A **flip tax** is a transfer fee paid to the co-op on a sale, usually by the seller and often credited to reserves.
A flip tax may be a percentage of price, a percentage of profit, an amount per share or a flat fee.
Flip taxes provided for in the proprietary lease, occupancy agreement or offering plan are valid (Business Corporation Law §501(c)).
**NYS transfer tax** ($2 per $500 or fraction, seller) applies to co-op shares and condo deeds alike.
In NYC the city's **Real Property Transfer Tax (RPTT)**, customarily seller-paid, also applies: 1% at or below $500,000 and 1.425% of the full price above $500,000.
The 1% **mansion tax** at $1,000,000 or more expressly covers condo units and co-op apartments; the buyer pays.
Condo buyers pay title insurance, **mortgage recording tax** and recording fees.
Co-op buyers pay the **lien search**, recognition agreement, UCC and managing-agent fees, but no mortgage recording tax.
Co-op sellers typically add the flip tax and transfer fees to the usual commission, legal fees and transfer taxes.
Sponsor contracts often shift costs to buyers, such as the sponsor's transfer taxes and attorney fees or a working-capital contribution. Read the plan's closing-cost section.
Condo title checklist: recorded declaration, release from any blanket mortgage, **statement of unpaid common charges** and the board's **right-of-first-refusal waiver**.

example.title: Worked example: flip taxes and the NYS transfer tax
steps: Trap check: 15% of the price ($135,000) is the wrong base.
NYS transfer tax on an $850,000 co-op sale: $850,000 ÷ $500 = 1,700.
1,700 × $2 = **$3,400**, paid by the seller.
Mansion tax: none at $850,000; at exactly $1,000,000 the buyer owes $10,000.
Answer: flip tax $23,000 (gross) or $45,000 (profit); transfer tax $3,400 from the seller.

sections.heading: Income taxes: IRC §216 and condo owners
sections.intro: Federal law treats a co-op shareholder like a homeowner, but only for the tax and interest pieces of maintenance.
points: Under **IRC §216**, a tenant-stockholder deducts a proportionate share (by shares) of the co-op's **real estate taxes and mortgage interest**.
Operating costs, reserves and mortgage principal aren't deductible.

The co-op must meet **one test** each year: 80%+ of gross income from tenant-stockholders, 80%+ of square footage for their residential use, or 90%+ of expenditures for their benefit (§216(b)(1)(D), as amended in 2007).
Before 2007 only the income test existed (the **80/20 rule**), so store rents could disqualify a building, which drove many condops. The income test wasn't repealed; alternatives were added.
Shareholders also deduct their own **share-loan interest**.
**Condo owners** deduct their own unit's taxes and mortgage interest; common charges on a home aren't deductible. Normal itemizing limits apply, including the state-and-local-tax cap.
The §216 test is federal: an AG-accepted plan doesn't make a co-op qualify.

example.title: Worked example: §216 deduction
steps: The co-op paid $900,000 taxes, $600,000 interest, $500,000 principal and $1,000,000 operating costs.
Trap check: adding principal gives $20,000; taxes alone give $9,000.
Answer: the shareholder deducts $15,000.

sections.heading: Subletting, primary residence and unsold shares
sections.intro: Check sublet rules and the seller's share status before marketing a co-op as a rental investment.
points: The sublet statute lets tenants in buildings of 4 or more units request a sublet, but it expressly excludes **proprietary leases** (RPL §226-b).
Co-op sublet rights come only from the lease, bylaws and house rules. Many co-ops require primary residence and limit sublets.
An approved sublet may carry time limits and fees, and the shareholder stays liable for maintenance and the subtenant's conduct.
**Unsold shares** are those not bought by tenants or outsiders when the co-op is formed. They are held by the sponsor or a **holder of unsold shares** (HUS) it designates.
Plans typically let holders of unsold shares sell and sublet without board approval, and the sponsor guarantees their maintenance.
Shares stop being unsold once sold to a buyer for occupancy, or once the holder or a relative moves in. A resale investor is not a holder of unsold shares.
Offering plans warn that lenders may refuse financing where the sponsor or HUS keep more than 49% of units. A sponsor that stops paying maintenance strains the budget.
Condo owners can usually lease subject to the bylaws (notice, minimum terms, sometimes a board right of first refusal).

head: Share status
Held by
Board approval to sell or sublet?
rows: Unsold shares held by a HUS

sections.heading: Offering plans, the Martin Act and CPS-1
sections.intro: Unless the AG grants an exemption, sponsors may sell condo, co-op, HOA and timeshare interests to the public only through an offering plan filed with the Attorney General.
points: The **Martin Act** is General Business Law (GBL) Article 23-A.
No public offering may be made until the AG's Real Estate Finance Bureau accepts the **offering plan** for filing (GBL §352-e); DOS doesn't review plans. An owner's resale needs no plan.
Acceptance is a disclosure review, not an endorsement of price, value or quality; claiming otherwise is a misrepresentation.
Read the **special risks** and the description of property. The sponsor owes what the plan describes; an amenity shown only in a brochure or rendering isn't a plan obligation.

Also read the floor plans and square footage, the budget, real estate tax projections and abatement phase-outs (**tax validation**), fees shifted to buyers, and the estimated closing date with rights if it slips.
**Price increases** and other changes require filed **amendments**. New prices bind only new contracts, and a material adverse change can give purchasers a right to rescind.
Deposits are trust funds held in escrow (GBL §352-h).
**Red herring** = preliminary plan under AG review, named for its red legend. In a conversion, tenants get a copy.
**Black book** = accepted plan. The sponsor then declares the plan effective by amendment, and closings follow.

**CPS-1** covers new, vacant or nonresidential projects. Once the AG accepts the application, the sponsor may run AG-cleared ads with a required legend and collect **nonbinding indications of interest**.
The CPS-1 period lasts **12 months**, extendable once an offering plan has been submitted. Spada's 120 days plus 60 is outdated. Occupied rentals use **CPS-11** instead.
CPS-1 allows **no deposits** and **no reservations**, binding or nonbinding; refundability or escrow doesn't cure it.

The syllabus and Spada define a **letter of intent** as a written offer to reserve a specific unit, nonbinding as to purchaser or price. Before plan acceptance, such a letter can only record nonbinding interest, never reserve a unit or carry a deposit.
New construction: the sponsor must have a temporary or permanent **certificate of occupancy** before closing a unit, and lenders require one too.
Sponsors may restrict **flipping** with resale or rental limits, buyback rights or extra closing costs.
A **simultaneous closing** isn't fraud in itself, but hiding it from a lender or inflating the price can be.
Units in buildings of 5 stories or less carry the **housing merchant implied warranty** unless a compliant limited warranty is substituted (GBL §777-a).
The implied warranty covers workmanship for 1 year; plumbing, electrical, heating, cooling and ventilation for 2 years; and material structural defects for **6 years** (GBL §777-a).

head: Stage
What the sponsor may do
rows: Circulate the preliminary plan; no sales or deposits
Sign purchase agreements; deposits held in trust

sections.heading: Conversions: eviction vs non-eviction plans
sections.intro: Converting an occupied rental building adds tenant protections: GBL §352-eeee in New York City, GBL §352-eee in Nassau, Westchester and Rockland municipalities that opt in, and elsewhere GBL §352-e(2-a), which protects eligible senior and disabled tenants.
points: **Non-eviction plan**: non-buyers can't be evicted for not buying or because their lease ends, only for ordinary cause such as nonpayment.
Under a non-eviction plan, a new owner can't evict non-buyers to move in. Rent-regulated tenants keep regulation and renewals; others are protected from unconscionable increases.
**Eviction plan**: other non-buyers can eventually be removed; under §352-eee, not before the later of lease expiration or **3 years** after the plan is declared effective.
In NYC, the 2019 Housing Stability and Tenant Protection Act (HSTPA) bars eviction plans for new submissions.
NYC non-eviction plans need purchase agreements for **51%** of units from **bona fide tenants in occupancy** on the AG acceptance date. Outside buyers and investors don't count.

In an NYC building of 5 or fewer units, 15% suffices, counting outside buyers who will occupy. This applies only if the sponsor offers the unit it or an immediate family member has occupied for at least 2 years.
**§352-eee suburbs**: non-eviction plans need only **15%** of bona fide tenants in occupancy, and eviction plans remain available with the double threshold shown in the table.
**Eligible senior citizens** (62+, plus spouses) and **eligible disabled persons** can never be evicted for not buying, even under an eviction plan.
Eligible seniors and disabled persons are also shielded from unconscionable rent increases. NYC requires a written election of that status within 60 days.

In NYC plans and §352-eee eviction plans, tenants in occupancy get a **90-day exclusive right** to buy after acceptance. For 6 months after that, they can match any outside contract within 15 days of notice.
Sponsors usually offer an **insider price** below the outsider price.
A plan is void if not effective within **15 months** of acceptance (NYC) or **12 months** (§352-eee). Lease waivers of these rights are void, and harassment such as cutting services is unlawful.

head: Rule
NYC (§352-eeee)
Opt-in suburbs (§352-eee)
rows: Allowed: 51% excluding + 35% including seniors and disabled
51% of units, bought by tenants in occupancy

example.title: Worked example: the NYC 51% count
steps: 80 apartments, all occupied by bona fide tenants when the AG accepts the plan.
80 × 0.51 = 40.8 → **41** purchase agreements (40 is only 50%).
Sales of vacant units to outsiders add nothing.
Trap check: 12 (80 × 15%) is the old NYC rule, still the §352-eee non-eviction figure.
Answer: the sponsor needs 41 tenant purchase agreements.

sections.heading: Condops and homeowners' associations
points: A **condop** is a building submitted to the Condominium Act and split into at least two units: typically a residential unit owned by a co-op corporation and commercial units owned by others, often the sponsor.
Condop residential buyers get **shares and a proprietary lease**, usually with board approval. They use share loans (no mortgage recording tax) but still pay transfer taxes and any mansion tax.
The condop's commercial unit is condo real property, sold or mortgaged separately.
Why condops exist: walling off store income protected the co-op's §216 **80/20** income test, and the sponsor can keep or sell the commercial space. A co-op with relaxed sublet rules is not a condop.

**HOA**: owners hold fee title to homes and lots; the association owns the common areas and enforces the recorded **covenants, conditions and restrictions (CC&Rs)**. These run with the land (for example, a fence ban) and are separate from zoning.
HOA assessment and lien rights come from the recorded declaration and bylaws, not the Condominium Act lien.
Since Oct. 16, 2025 an incorporated HOA must also give **90 days' notice** before foreclosing its lien (RPAPL §2010). HOA offerings to the public are also filed with the AG.

sections.heading: Insurance for condos and co-ops
sections.intro: Two layers of coverage: the building's master policy and each owner's own policy.
points: The **condo board** insures the building when the declaration, bylaws or a majority of owners require it. It notifies owners and pays premiums as a **common expense** (§339-bb).
A co-op corporation insures its whole building through maintenance.
A **bare walls** master policy skips unit interiors, so the owner insures cabinets, fixtures and finishes. Broader policies may cover original fixtures but rarely upgrades.
**HO-6** (unit-owners form) is the condo owner's policy: improvements, personal property, loss of use, liability and **loss assessment** coverage.
Loss assessment coverage pays the owner's share of an assessment from a covered loss, such as a master-policy deductible, up to an often-low limit.
The DOS syllabus and the Department of Financial Services (DFS) list **HO-4** as the tenants or cooperative owners form. Many insurers write co-op shareholders on HO-6.
Exam default: renter or co-op owner = HO-4, condo owner = HO-6.
Injuries inside a unit fall mainly on the owner's liability coverage; the master policy targets common areas. Standard forms exclude flood.

Bought by

rows: Condo owner (some insurers also use it for co-op shareholders)
Contents, loss of use, liability; no building

guides.title: Commercial Real Estate
guides.overview: Commercial and investment property: why investors buy, property types, how space is measured and leased, lender documents, income analysis, 1031 exchanges, due diligence and brokerage rules. The exam hits three ideas hardest: the lease clause beats the label; every ratio (cap rate, cash-on-cash, loss factor) has its own denominator; and debt service and depreciation never come out of NOI.

numbers.label: 1031: identify replacement property in writing after the old property transfers
1031: close within 180 days or by the tax-return due date, if earlier
1031 three-property rule: identify up to three of any value
1031: identify over three if total value is at most twice the old property's
Leasehold with 30+ years left is like-kind to owned real estate (§1031)
Depreciation for residential rental buildings of any size
Depreciation for nonresidential buildings (office, retail, warehouse)
Mixed-use is residential rental only if 80%+ of gross rents come from dwelling units
Top federal rate on depreciation-related gain on real property (unrecaptured §1250 gain)
Debt service coverage ratio (DSCR) break-even: below 1.0, NOI doesn't cover the mortgage
Apartment buildings financed as commercial multifamily (income) property
Leases longer than one year must be in writing
Typical ground-lease terms
Low-rise office building (texts disagree on mid- and high-rise cutoffs)
NY bulk-sale notice (Form AU-196.10) before paying for or taking possession of business assets
NYS transfer tax, on the real-property share of the price only
NYC transfer tax on commercial property over $500,000 (1.425% at $500,000 or less)
Residential deposit cap; doesn't apply to commercial leases

mustKnow: **Gross lease**: landlord pays taxes, insurance and maintenance from a fixed rent. **Net lease**: tenant pays some or all of them on top of base rent.
Single net = taxes; double net = + insurance; **triple net** = + maintenance. The lease clauses, not the label, decide capital items like a roof.
**Modified gross**: landlord carries major costs; tenant pays listed items such as its own electric or janitorial.
**Percentage rent** is figured on **gross sales**, not profit, and is used mainly for retail.
**Natural breakpoint** = annual base rent ÷ percentage rate; a **negotiated (artificial) breakpoint** in the lease overrides it.
Commercial rent is usually quoted **per rentable square foot per year**; divide by 12 for monthly.
**Rentable** = usable + share of common areas, so rentable is normally larger than **usable**.
**Loss factor** = (rentable − usable) ÷ rentable; **add-on factor** = (rentable − usable) ÷ usable.
Usable to rentable: **divide by (1 − loss factor)** or **multiply by the load factor**.
**CAM** (common area maintenance) is a charge split by **pro-rata share** = tenant's sq ft ÷ total leasable sq ft. Estimates are reconciled at year-end.
**Expense stop**: landlord pays up to the stop, tenant pays the excess; a **base year** uses one year's actual costs as the stop.
**Porter's wage formula** (NYC office leases): rent per sq ft rises with the porters' hourly wage × a multiplier; no audit of the books.
**CPI escalation** uses the % change, (new − old) ÷ old, then any cap; a **graduated lease** fixes increases in advance.
**Subordination**: the lease ranks below the mortgage. **Nondisturbance**: the lender won't evict a tenant that isn't in default.
**Attornment**: the tenant accepts the new owner as landlord.
An **estoppel certificate** is the tenant's signed statement of lease facts; buyers and lenders rely on it, and the tenant can't later contradict it.
**Assignment** transfers the whole remaining lease; a **sublease** transfers less. The original tenant stays liable unless released.
A **personal guaranty** must be in writing; a **good guy guaranty** ends when the tenant gives notice, pays through surrender and leaves.
A **holdover** whose rent the landlord accepts becomes **month-to-month** (RPL §232-c).
Holdover premiums like 150% come from the lease. By statute, a tenant that gave notice it would leave and then stays owes **double rent** (RPL §229).
Commercial tenants get **no statutory renewal right**, deposit cap or warranty of habitability; deposits are still held in trust (GOL §7-103).
**Trade fixtures** remain the tenant's property and may be removed by lease end, with damage repaired.
**Ground lease**: land only, long term; the tenant builds, and the building usually reverts to the landowner.
**Office classes** are relative to the local market: Class A = newest, best located, top rents; Class B = older, well kept; Class C = dated, lowest rents.
An **anchor tenant** draws traffic for the smaller stores; it doesn't guarantee their rent.
**NOI** = EGI − operating expenses; debt service, depreciation, income tax and capital improvements are **not** operating expenses.
**Value = NOI ÷ cap rate** (IRV); higher cap rate = more risk = lower value.
**Cash-on-cash** = (NOI − debt service) ÷ total cash invested; **DSCR** = NOI ÷ debt service.
**Positive leverage**: the property earns more than the debt costs; leverage magnifies losses too.
**Taxable income** = NOI − interest − depreciation; principal isn't deductible.
A **1031 exchange** covers business or investment real property only. A qualified intermediary holds the cash, and **boot** is taxable.
1031 deadlines: **45 days** to identify, **180 days** to close.
**Phase I** = records, site visit, interviews, no sampling; **Phase II** tests; III remediates; IV manages.
**ADA Title III**: landlord and tenant of a public accommodation must both remove barriers where **readily achievable**.
The **§443 agency form** doesn't apply to commercial deals. The **fair housing notice** applies to all real property (19 NYCRR §175.28).
**Net listings** are illegal for commercial too. Salespeople are paid only by their **sponsoring broker**, and brokers can't share fees with unlicensed people.
Buyers of business assets file the **bulk-sale notice** at least **10 days** before paying or taking possession.

traps.trap: Triple net means the tenant pays everything, including a new roof.
traps.truth: NNN conventionally means taxes, insurance and maintenance; capital items depend on the lease's repair clauses.

traps.trap: No profit, no percentage rent.
traps.truth: Percentage rent is based on gross sales above the breakpoint, not profit.

traps.trap: Total rent = base rent + rate × all sales.
traps.truth: Apply the rate only above the breakpoint. Past the natural breakpoint, total rent equals rate × all sales, so adding base rent double-counts.

traps.trap: Base rent ÷ rate is the breakpoint even when the lease names one.
traps.truth: A negotiated breakpoint in the lease controls.

traps.trap: A 20% loss factor means rentable = usable × 1.20.
traps.truth: Rentable = usable ÷ 0.80. Multiplying by 1.20 is the add-on method (7,200 vs. 7,500 sq ft on 6,000 usable).

traps.trap: The lower quoted rent is the cheaper space.
traps.truth: Compare cost per usable sq ft (rate × load factor) plus net charges.

traps.trap: A CPI move from 250 to 260 is a 10% raise.
traps.truth: Divide the change by the starting index: 10 ÷ 250 = 4%. Then apply any cap.

traps.trap: NOI is what's left after mortgage payments and depreciation.
traps.truth: NOI comes before debt service, depreciation and income tax.

traps.trap: Cash-on-cash = NOI ÷ price.
traps.truth: Cash-on-cash = (NOI − debt service) ÷ cash invested, including closing costs. NOI ÷ price is the cap rate.

traps.trap: A higher cap rate means a more valuable property.
traps.truth: A higher cap rate means lower value and more risk: the same NOI ÷ a higher rate = a lower value.

traps.trap: Landlord consent to an assignment releases the original tenant.
traps.truth: The original tenant stays liable. Only an express release or novation frees it.

traps.trap: A holdover who pays rent gets a new full term.
traps.truth: In New York it becomes month-to-month unless agreed otherwise (RPL §232-c).

traps.trap: Large apartment buildings depreciate over 39 years.
traps.truth: Residential rental is 27.5 years at any size; 39 is for nonresidential.

traps.trap: Equipment, a personal home or flip houses can go into a 1031.
traps.truth: Only real property held for business or investment qualifies; the 2017 Tax Cuts and Jobs Act dropped equipment and other personal property for exchanges after 2017.

traps.trap: No §443 form means no agency rules in commercial deals.
traps.truth: Agency rules still apply: fiduciary duties, dual-agency consent, the net-listing ban, fee rules and the fair housing notice.

mnemonics.name: IRV
mnemonics.meaning: Income = Rate × Value. Cover the unknown: Value = Income ÷ Rate; Rate = Income ÷ Value. Income means NOI.

mnemonics.name: T-I-M (net leases)
mnemonics.meaning: Each 'net' adds one cost: single = Taxes; double = Taxes + Insurance; triple = Taxes + Insurance + Maintenance.

mnemonics.name: SNDA
mnemonics.meaning: Subordination, Non-Disturbance, Attornment: lease below mortgage; lender won't evict a tenant in good standing; tenant accepts the new owner.

sections.heading: Investment basics: risk, liquidity and leverage
sections.intro: Every later formula measures one of these trade-offs.
points: An **owner-user** (also called an 'amenity purchaser') wants space for its own business. An **investor** wants income and appreciation from other people's use of the property.
Leasing keeps a business's cash and flexibility but builds no equity.
**Risk** is uncertainty about returns. Higher risk demands a higher return, so riskier buildings sell at higher cap rates.

Three main risk types: space-market risk (supply and demand for space move rents and vacancy), capital-market risk (loans get harder or costlier, hurting resale prices) and default risk (debt must be paid even when income drops).
Vacant land is the most speculative: no income, uncertain approvals. Office, retail and industrial income swings with the economy. Apartments are usually steadier because people always need housing.
**Liquidity** is how fast an asset becomes cash without a price cut. Real estate is **illiquid**, so investors need cash reserves.

**Leverage** is using borrowed money to buy more property with less cash. It is **positive** when the property earns more than the debt costs and negative when the debt costs more. Either way, it magnifies results.
Quick test: a **loan constant** (annual debt service ÷ loan) above the cap rate means negative leverage.
A $750,000 loan on a $1,000,000 property is 75% loan-to-value but 3:1 debt-to-equity.
**Time value of money**: at 10%, $1,000 due in a year is worth about $909 today.
**IRR** (internal rate of return) is the discount rate at which the present value of all cash flows, including the purchase price, nets to zero.
A **pro forma** projects income and expenses; **actuals** report past results.
**Contract rent** comes from signed leases; **market rent** is today's going rate. A rent roll lists tenants, rents and lease dates.

example.title: Worked example: positive vs. negative leverage
steps: A $1,000,000 building earns $70,000 of NOI: a 7% all-cash return.
Borrow $750,000 interest-only at 5%: ($70,000 − $37,500) ÷ $250,000 cash = 13%. Positive leverage.
Same loan at 8.5%: ($70,000 − $63,750) ÷ $250,000 = 2.5%. Negative leverage.
If NOI falls 20% to $56,000, the 5% loan still returns 7.4%.
The 8.5% loan now runs $7,750 short every year.
Answer: debt helps only when the property out-earns its cost, and it magnifies losses.

sections.heading: Property types, office classes and ownership
sections.intro: These are the property types an investor can buy, plus the difference between owning land and leasing it.
points: **Office classes** are relative to the local market, not set by law.
**Class A** is newest or best renovated, best located, with top rents. **Class B** is older but well maintained, with lower rents.
**Class C** is older, needs upgrades and rents lowest, making it a value-add target.
Low-rise usually means 1–3 stories. Texts disagree on the higher cutoffs (high-rise at 11+ vs. 20+ stories).

Retail centers, small to large: strip center (a row of convenience stores serving the immediate area), neighborhood center (supermarket or drugstore anchor), regional mall (department-store anchors, wide trade area) and mega mall.
An **outlet center** (manufacturers' discount stores) draws shoppers from far away.
An **anchor tenant** draws the traffic that supports smaller satellite stores but doesn't guarantee their rent.
**Industrial** users (manufacturing, warehouse and distribution, loft buildings) check clear height, floor load, loading docks, truck access and power, not foot traffic or lobby finishes.

Apartment buildings with **5 or more units** are underwritten as commercial multifamily, mainly on NOI and debt coverage rather than the buyer's salary. A single-family rental's vacancy is all-or-nothing.
**Mixed-use** buildings diversify income but complicate management and financing.
**Fee simple** means owning land and building.
In a **ground lease** the tenant rents only land, often for 49 or 99 years, builds and pays the costs. The building usually goes to the landowner at the end.
No statute sets a minimum ground-lease term. The long term lets the tenant finance and recover its building.
In a **sale-leaseback**, an owner-user sells to an investor and leases the building back, freeing its equity.

head: Type

sections.heading: Measuring space: rentable, usable, loss and add-on factors
sections.intro: Rent is charged on rentable area, but the tenant uses only the usable area. The gap is common area, and the exam tests both ways of expressing it.
points: **Usable area** is the space the tenant alone occupies. **Rentable area** adds its pro-rata share of common areas (lobby, corridors, restrooms).
Carpetable area, the unobstructed floor inside the walls, is usually smallest.
Rent is normally quoted per rentable square foot per year, and tenant improvement (TI) allowances per rentable square foot.
**Loss factor** (the owner's view) = (rentable − usable) ÷ rentable. **Add-on factor** (the tenant's view) = the same gap ÷ usable.
Load factor = rentable ÷ usable. So 10,000 usable billed as 11,500 rentable is a 15% add-on but only a 13% loss factor.
To convert usable to rentable, divide by (1 − loss factor) or multiply by the load factor.
One course math sheet figures 'rent using loss factor' as usable × (1 + loss factor). That is really the add-on method.
Follow the question's wording. If it just says loss factor, divide.
Compare spaces by **cost per usable square foot** = quoted rate × load factor: $50 × 1.15 = $57.50 beats $47 × 1.25 = $58.75.

head: Term
Formula (R = rentable, U = usable)
Use
rows: Cost per usable sq ft = rate × load

example.title: Worked example: loss factor vs. add-on factor
steps: A tenant needs 6,000 usable sq ft; the loss factor is 20%; rent is $48 per rentable sq ft per year.
Rentable = 6,000 ÷ 0.80 = 7,500 sq ft.
As an add-on, the same gap is 1,500 ÷ 6,000 = 25% (load 1.25). Efficiency is 80%.
Cost per usable sq ft = $48 × 1.25 = $60.
Trap: 6,000 × 1.20 = 7,200 sq ft ($345,600) treats the loss factor as an add-on.
Answer: 7,500 rentable sq ft; $360,000 a year.

sections.heading: Commercial lease types
sections.intro: Lease names describe who pays operating costs and how rent changes, but the clauses always control.
points: Labels are shorthand. **Triple net** doesn't settle who replaces a roof or structure; read the repair and capital-cost clauses.
To compare quotes, add the net charges: $40 gross vs. $28 NNN + $10 of charges = $38, so on 3,000 sq ft the NNN space saves $6,000 a year, not $36,000.
A **loft lease** covers open, undivided floor space and usually allows only nonstructural changes approved in writing; it isn't permission to live there.
Commercial rent is usually stated annually, and a lease over one year must be in writing.
New York gives commercial tenants **no statutory renewal right**. Renewal comes only from a lease option exercised on time.

head: Lease
How it works
Typical use
rows: Fixed rent; landlord pays taxes, insurance, maintenance
Landlord pays major costs; tenant pays listed items
Landlord pays up to a stop; tenant pays excess
Base rent + % of gross sales over a breakpoint
Rent tracks an index such as the CPI
Land only; tenant builds; long term

sections.heading: Percentage leases and breakpoints
sections.intro: Percentage rent lets a retail landlord share in a strong store's sales. Find the breakpoint, then apply the rate only above it.
points: A **percentage lease** charges base rent plus a percent of **gross sales** above a breakpoint. It's based on sales, not profit, and is used mostly in shopping centers.
**Natural breakpoint** = annual base rent ÷ rate: the sales level where the percentage equals base rent. Above it, total rent = rate × total sales.
An **artificial (negotiated) breakpoint** is any other threshold the lease sets; when the lease names one, use it.
The syllabus calls it the 'natural break-even.' One New York textbook loosely describes it as the point where an investment starts producing a positive return.
For calculations, use base rent ÷ rate. It isn't the tenant's profit break-even.
Annualize monthly base rent first.
Working backward: (total rent − base rent) ÷ rate = sales above the breakpoint.

example.title: Worked example: natural and negotiated breakpoints
steps: Base rent is $6,000 a month plus 5% of gross sales over the natural breakpoint; sales were $1,800,000.
Natural breakpoint = $72,000 ÷ 0.05 = $1,440,000.
Total = $72,000 + $18,000 = $90,000, which is 5% of all sales.
With a negotiated $1,200,000 breakpoint: $600,000 × 0.05 = $30,000.
Total with the negotiated breakpoint = $72,000 + $30,000 = $102,000.
Backward (natural breakpoint): total rent of $80,000 means $8,000 ÷ 0.05 = $160,000 above $1,440,000.
Trap: $72,000 + 5% of all sales ($90,000) = $162,000 double-counts.
Answer: $90,000 total (natural); $102,000 (negotiated).

sections.heading: CAM charges and expense pass-throughs
sections.intro: Multi-tenant leases pass operating costs to tenants by pro-rata share.
points: **Common area maintenance (CAM)** charges share the cost of parking lots, landscaping, snow removal, lighting and hallways. CAM is a charge, not a measurement, and is **additional rent**.
**Pro-rata share** = tenant's square feet ÷ total leasable square feet as the lease defines them. Dividing by occupied space instead shifts vacant-space costs to tenants.
Apply any **administrative fee** (for example 10% or 15%) to the whole CAM pool first, then take the tenant's share.
Monthly estimates are **reconciled** at year-end: the tenant pays any shortfall or gets a credit. Leases often exclude capital costs and give audit rights.
An **expense stop** has the landlord pay up to the stop and the tenant pay the excess. A **base year** uses a chosen year's actual costs as the stop.
Free base rent doesn't free CAM or taxes unless the lease says so.

example.title: Worked example: CAM share, fee and reconciliation
steps: Tenant: 4,000 sq ft in an 80,000-sq-ft center; CAM is $320,000 plus a 10% fee; estimates paid were $1,400 a month.
Owed at reconciliation = $17,600 − $16,800 = $800.
Expense stop: actual $9.50 vs. an $8.00 stop on 5,000 sq ft = $7,500 owed.
Answer: $17,600 a year; $800 due.

sections.heading: Escalation clauses
sections.intro: Escalation clauses protect the landlord from rising costs and inflation over a long lease.
points: Tax and operating-cost escalation clauses name a **base year**: the tenant pays its **proportionate share** (its percentage of the building) of increases above the base, and nothing for the base year itself.

The **porter's wage formula**, common in NYC office leases, raises rent per square foot as the porters' hourly union wage rises, times a multiplier such as 'penny for penny.' Porters are the building's cleaning staff.
The porter's wage formula is simple and needs no audit of the owner's books, but it tracks a wage, not actual costs.
**CPI** (Consumer Price Index) escalations use the percentage change, (new − old) ÷ old, then any cap or partial pass-through.
Fixed percentage increases compound: 3% a year on $25 gives $26.52 in year 3.
For dollar step-ups, add each year's rent: $5,000 a month rising $250 a year for four years = ($5,000 + $5,250 + $5,500 + $5,750) × 12 = $258,000.

head: Clause
How it works
Watch for
rows: Divide by the starting index; caps
Tenant pays costs above a dollar stop
Share of tax increases over base
Rent rises with porters' wage × multiplier

example.title: Worked example: three escalations
steps: Tenant leases 5,000 sq ft (5% of the building) at $200,000 a year.
CPI change: 250 to 260 = 4%.
A 50% pass-through instead would give 2%: $204,000.
Porter's wage, penny for penny: wage rises $0.90 an hour, so rent rises $0.90 × 5,000 = $4,500.
Answer: rent $206,000, plus $3,000 and $4,500 of escalations.

sections.heading: Key lease clauses, concessions and fixtures
sections.intro: These clauses decide what the tenant may do, who pays for power and build-out, and what the tenant may take when it leaves.
points: The **use clause**: landlords want narrow wording ('for no other purpose'), tenants broad ('any lawful purpose'). Landlord consent can't authorize a use zoning forbids.
An **assignment** transfers the whole remaining lease; a **sublease** transfers less, so the tenant keeps a reversion.
Most commercial leases require landlord consent. The residential sublet right doesn't apply (RPL §226-b).
After an assignment the original tenant **stays liable** unless released or replaced by **novation**. Consent isn't a release.
In a sublease the tenant stays fully liable to the landlord and collects from the subtenant. The subtenant's rent obligation runs to the tenant, not the landlord.
A **tenant improvement (TI) allowance** is the landlord's build-out contribution, usually per rentable square foot. The tenant pays any excess.
**Free rent** lowers the **effective rent** (rent actually paid ÷ months in the term); additional rent stays due unless also abated.
**Trade fixtures** a tenant installs for its business stay its personal property and may be removed by lease end, with damage repaired.

head: Electric
How it works
Note
rows: Landlord buys through a master meter and bills measured use
May resell at the lease rate

example.title: Worked example: TI allowance and effective rent
steps: Five-year lease: 6,000 rentable sq ft at $42; TI allowance $50 per sq ft; build-out $360,000; 4 months free.
Effective rent = $1,176,000 ÷ 60 = $19,600 a month.
Answer: $60,000 out of pocket; $19,600 effective monthly rent.

sections.heading: SNDA, estoppel certificates and attornment
sections.intro: Lenders and buyers need to know whether the mortgage or the lease comes first and exactly what each lease says.
points: **Subordination** puts the lease behind the mortgage, so a foreclosure could end it. It doesn't make the tenant pay the debt or the lender the landlord.
**Nondisturbance** is the lender's promise, binding on a foreclosure buyer, to leave a tenant in place while it isn't in default. Tenants trade subordination for it.
**Attornment** is the tenant's promise to accept a successor owner as landlord.
All three usually sit in one **SNDA** signed by lender, landlord and tenant. Its protection is only what it says.

An **estoppel certificate** is the tenant's signed statement of lease facts (term, rent, deposit, prepaid rent, options, defaults) for a buyer or lender. The tenant is **estopped** from later asserting contrary facts, such as an undisclosed rent prepayment.
A sale doesn't let the tenant void its lease.
A **rent roll** is only the landlord's summary, so verify it against the leases and estoppels.

head: Document
Who promises
Effect
rows: Tenant in good standing stays after foreclosure
Pays rent to the new owner
Bound by the facts it certified

sections.heading: Guaranties, holdovers and residential-only rules
sections.intro: Commercial landlords rely on guaranties and holdover clauses, and many New York tenant protections are residential only.
points: A **personal guaranty** makes an owner personally liable if its entity tenant defaults. It must be in writing (General Obligations Law §5-701).
With a guaranty, the entity still signs as tenant. The guaranty changes neither the lease type nor ownership.

A NYC **good guy guaranty** releases the guarantor from future rent once the tenant gives the required notice, pays through surrender and leaves the space vacant. A default first keeps the guarantor liable.
Alternatives to a guaranty include a larger deposit or a **letter of credit**.
A tenant who stays after expiration without consent is a **holdover** (tenant at sufferance). The landlord can remove it in a holdover proceeding.
If the landlord accepts rent for a later period, the tenancy becomes **month-to-month** unless otherwise agreed, not a new full term (RPL §232-c).
**Holdover rent** premiums (such as 150% or 200%) come from the lease.
One statute adds a penalty: a tenant that gives notice it will leave on a set date and then stays owes **double rent** while it remains (RPL §229).
Commercial deposits have no statutory cap or 14-day deadline but must be held in trust without commingling (GOL §7-103).

head: Rule
Residential (NY)
Commercial
rows: 1 month max; returned within 14 days, itemized
Rent stabilization or Good Cause may apply

example.title: Worked example: holdover rent
steps: Rent is $12,000 a month; the lease sets holdover rent at 150%; the tenant stays 3 extra months.
Holdover rent = $12,000 × 1.5 = $18,000 a month.
Answer: $18,000 × 3 = $54,000 for the three months.

sections.heading: Investment analysis: from gross income to after-tax cash flow
sections.intro: The syllabus calls this the reconstructed income and expense statement: the 'cash world' top to bottom, then the 'tax world.'
points: A **reconstructed operating statement** strips out non-operating items (mortgage payments, depreciation, the owner's taxes and personal costs, capital improvements) and adds realistic vacancy, management and reserves.
**Potential gross income (PGI)** − vacancy and collection loss + other income (laundry, parking) = **effective gross income (EGI)**.
EGI − operating expenses (taxes, insurance, utilities, repairs, management) = **net operating income (NOI)**.
Property taxes and insurance always come out of NOI. Debt service, depreciation and income tax never do.
**IRV**: Value = NOI ÷ cap rate. Higher cap rate = more risk = lower value: $100,000 ÷ 6% = $1,666,667 but ÷ 9% = $1,111,111.
**Before-tax cash flow (BTCF)** = NOI − debt service.
**Cash-on-cash** (equity dividend rate) = BTCF ÷ cash invested (down payment + closing costs). It ignores appreciation, principal paydown and taxes.
NOI ÷ price is the cap rate, not cash-on-cash.
**DSCR** (debt service coverage ratio) = NOI ÷ debt service. A lender requiring 1.25 allows at most NOI ÷ 1.25 in annual payments.
Tax world: **taxable income** = NOI − interest − depreciation; **after-tax cash flow (ATCF)** = BTCF − tax.
The **gross rent multiplier** (price ÷ gross rent) ignores expenses.

example.title: Worked example: NOI to after-tax cash flow
steps: Office building: price $2,000,000 (land $440,000); PGI $250,000; vacancy 8%; parking $6,000; expenses $86,000; cash invested $625,000 (down payment plus closing costs); debt service $90,000 ($80,000 interest).
Cash-on-cash = $60,000 ÷ $625,000 = 9.6%. That beats the 7.5% cap rate, so leverage is positive.
Tax at an assumed 30% rate = $9,000.
Answer: NOI $150,000; 7.5% cap; 9.6% cash-on-cash; ATCF $51,000.

sections.heading: Tax angles: depreciation, recapture and 1031 exchanges
sections.intro: Investment questions lean on four tax ideas: depreciation, passive losses, recapture and the like-kind exchange.
points: **Depreciation** is a non-cash deduction for buildings, never land. Depreciable basis = cost − land + capital improvements.
Recovery periods: **27.5 years** for residential rental of any size; **39 years** for nonresidential.
A mixed-use building is residential only if 80%+ of gross rents come from dwelling units.
**Tax shelter**: depreciation can show a taxable loss while cash flow is positive.
Rental income is usually **passive**. The other income classes are active and portfolio.
Passive losses offset passive income, except up to $25,000 for active participants. That allowance phases out between $100,000 and $150,000 of modified adjusted gross income (AGI).
**Adjusted basis** = basis + improvements − depreciation; **gain** = (price − selling costs) − adjusted basis.
Depreciation-related gain on real property is taxed at up to 25%. Gain on property held over a year is long-term.
A **§1031 exchange** defers gain when business or investment real property is swapped for like-kind real property.
The **2017 Tax Cuts and Jobs Act** limited §1031 to real property. For exchanges after 2017, equipment and other personal property don't qualify.
A personal residence doesn't qualify either; it has the $250,000/$500,000 exclusion. Neither does dealer inventory such as flips.
Like-kind is broad: investment land for a building, an apartment house or hotel for a warehouse, or a fee for a leasehold with 30+ years to run.
A **qualified intermediary** holds the cash. **Boot** (cash, other non-like-kind property, net debt relief) is taxable up to the gain.
In a reverse exchange, the replacement is bought first and parked with an accommodation titleholder.

head: 1031 rule
Requirement
Note
rows: Within 180 days or by the tax-return due date (with extensions), if earlier
3 of any value, or more within 200%

example.title: Worked example: depreciation and gain on sale
steps: Apartment building bought for $1,400,000 (land $300,000), held 8 years, sold for $1,900,000 with $100,000 of selling costs.
Depreciation = $1,100,000 ÷ 27.5 = $40,000 a year.
Total depreciation = $40,000 × 8 = $320,000.
Of that, $320,000 is depreciation-related (taxed at up to 25%) and $400,000 is long-term capital gain.
Answer: $720,000 gain, all deferrable in a proper 1031 with no boot.

sections.heading: Due diligence and selling a business with its building
sections.intro: Commercial buyers verify income, condition, zoning and environmental status, and business sales add personal-property and sales-tax rules.
points: **Verify income**: rent roll vs. leases and **estoppels**, deposits, arrears, CAM reconciliations, and actual statements vs. the pro forma.
**Verify the property**: title and survey, condition, code violations, the certificate of occupancy, taxes and any pending tax certiorari, which is a court challenge to an assessment.
A **special use permit** allows a use the ordinance permits once listed conditions such as parking, hours and traffic are met (Town Law §274-b, Village Law §7-725-b).
A **use variance** covers a prohibited use and requires unnecessary hardship.
A **legal nonconforming use** may continue and pass to a buyer but usually can't expand without relief.
A Phase I environmental review done to ASTM E1527-21 meets EPA's all-appropriate-inquiries rule. Buyers need it for federal (CERCLA) landowner defenses.
Environmental red flags: gas stations, dry cleaners and underground storage tanks.
**ADA Title III**: public accommodations (stores, restaurants, a leasing office) must remove barriers where **readily achievable**, such as adding a ramp. Older buildings aren't exempt.
Full ADA standards apply to new construction and alterations.
Landlord and tenant are both liable under the ADA; the lease only splits the cost.
Private apartments fall under the Fair Housing Act.
In a business sale, a deed conveys the land and building; a **bill of sale** transfers equipment, inventory and goodwill.
The buyer must file the **bulk-sale notice** (Form AU-196.10) at least 10 days before paying or taking possession (Tax Law §1141(c)).
A buyer that skips the bulk-sale notice may owe the seller's sales tax. The seller's assurances don't protect it.
**Transfer taxes**: the NYS $2 per $500 applies only to the real-property consideration.
The 1% mansion tax covers only 1–3 family homes and condo or co-op units, not commercial sales.
NYC's commercial real property transfer tax (RPTT) is 1.425% at $500,000 or less and 2.625% above.
In NYC only, the state rate rises to 0.65% ($3.25 per $500) on commercial sales of $2 million or more. Elsewhere it stays $2 per $500.

example.title: Worked example: transfer tax on a building-plus-business sale
steps: Building and restaurant sell for $2,000,000 outside NYC; $250,000 is allocated to equipment and goodwill.
Real property consideration = $2,000,000 − $250,000 = $1,750,000.
Tax = 3,500 × $2 = $7,000, paid by the seller.
Answer: $7,000 (taxing the full $2,000,000 would wrongly give $8,000).

sections.heading: Commercial brokerage rules in New York
sections.intro: A New York license covers commercial work, and nearly every license-law rule applies; mainly the paperwork differs.
points: A New York real estate license covers commercial sales and leasing; there's no separate commercial license.
The **§443 agency form** covers only 1–4 family homes and condo or co-op units. It isn't required for commercial space, vacant land or a 12-unit building sale.
The **fair housing notice** covers all real property and must be given in writing or electronically at first substantive contact (19 NYCRR §175.28).
New York's Human Rights Law also bars discrimination in land and commercial space (Executive Law §296(5)).
Common-law duties still apply: **dual agency** needs both principals' informed consent (no DOS approval), and pay from more than one party needs the client's knowledge and consent (19 NYCRR §175.7).
**Net listings** are banned for commercial property too, even in writing or with a fee cap (19 NYCRR §175.19).
Salespeople are paid only by the **sponsoring broker**, even if the tenant consents (RPL §442-a).
Brokers can't share fees with **unlicensed** people such as a tipster super. There's no small-referral exception (RPL §442).
Commissions are negotiable; competitors agreeing on rates or floors is **price fixing** (Sherman Act, Donnelly Act). Lease commissions are often a percentage of **aggregate rent** for the term.

example.title: Worked example: commission on aggregate rent
steps: 4% of aggregate rent; 5-year lease of 3,000 sq ft at $40, rising $1 a year.

guides.title: Property Management
guides.overview: Property management is running real estate for its owner for a fee: leasing, screening, rent collection, maintenance, risk control and reporting. Most tested: the manager as a **general agent** under a written **management agreement**; strict handling of **trust money**; New York's post-2019 deposit, fee, notice and eviction rules; fee and budget math; and NYC landlord duties.

numbers.label: Cap on any residential deposit or advance; first month's rent is separate (GOL §7-108)

Deposits must sit in an interest-bearing account at a New York bank
