mustKnow: The manager is a **general agent**, but only within the **management agreement**. Selling or mortgaging the building needs specific authority.
A **management proposal** creates no authority; the signed **management agreement** does.
In New York, negotiating leases or **collecting rent for another for a fee** requires a **broker's license** (RPL §440).
**No license** is needed by owners managing their own property or by maintenance-only staff.
A **salesperson** manages only through the sponsoring broker and is paid only by that broker.
Duties are **OLD CAR**. **Obedience** covers only lawful orders, so refuse to discriminate or misrepresent.
Keep the owner's bottom-line rent **confidential**. Tenants are **customers** owed honesty, not loyalty.
No vendor **rebate or profit on owner expenditures** without the owner's **full knowledge and consent** (19 NYCRR §175.3).
Fees are **negotiable**; competitors fixing a minimum fee is price fixing. Percentage fees are usually on rent **actually collected**.
**Operating budget** = one year of routine income and expenses. **Capital reserve budget** = big replacements.
**Stabilized budget** = normal operations over about 5 years, minus one-time items.
**Fixed expenses** (taxes, insurance premium) don't vary with occupancy; **variable expenses** (supplies, repairs) do.
**NOI = EGI − operating expenses**. Debt service is not an operating expense, but the **management fee** is.
A **rent roll** shows what each unit owes; the **property management report** shows money in, money out and the ending balance.
Client money goes in a **separate, special, federally insured account within 3 business days**. No commingling, no conversion, and **remit unspent funds within a reasonable time**.
Deposits are the **tenant's money in trust** in every building. Give written notice of the bank's name, address and amount; the bank needs a **New York** place of business.
**6+ units**: interest-bearing account. The landlord keeps **1% a year of the deposit**, and the tenant gets the rest of the interest.
Deposit cap is **one month's rent**. Offer a move-in inspection and notice of the right to a **pre-move-out inspection** (GOL §7-108).
Deduct only unpaid rent, unpaid landlord-billed utilities, damage beyond **normal wear and tear**, and moving or storage costs. **Itemize and return in 14 days** or forfeit.
Use the **same written criteria** for every applicant. New York protects **lawful source of income** (vouchers) and more classes than federal law.
Never deny an applicant for a **past or pending landlord-tenant case** (RPL §227-f).
The only rental application charge is a background/credit check at **actual cost or $20, whichever is less**. Co-op purchase applications may cost more.
Give a written **receipt** for rent paid in cash or by money order, and send a **certified-mail** late notice at 5 days.
Late fee max is the **lesser of $50 or 5%**. A bounced-check fee needs a lease clause and is capped at the **greater of actual bank cost or $20**.
Nonrenewal or a **5%+ increase** needs **30/60/90 days'** notice based on length of occupancy or lease (RPL §226-c).
**Good Cause** (NYC and opt-in localities): removal needs a legal ground. Raises above the lower of **5% + CPI or 10%** are presumed unreasonable.
Evict only through a **court summary proceeding**. A sheriff, marshal or constable removes the tenant after **14 days'** notice; self-help is a crime.
**Constructive eviction**: the landlord makes the unit unusable and the tenant **moves out**.
Maintenance: **preventive** (before failure), corrective (fix what broke), routine (cleaning), construction (build-outs). **Deferred** work costs more later.
Risk responses (**ACTOR**): **avoid, control, transfer or retain**. Insurance transfers; deductibles retain.
**Fidelity bond** = employee theft; **equipment breakdown** = boiler failure; rent loss = rent lost after a covered loss.
ADA Title III: existing public accommodations, including leasing offices, remove barriers if **readily achievable**. Buildings first occupied after Jan 26, 1993 must be **readily accessible**.
NYC: annual **HPD registration** or no nonpayment evictions; annual **DHCR registration** for stabilized units or the rent freezes.

traps.trap: A general agent can do anything the owner could do.
traps.truth: Authority covers only the management business in the agreement. Purchase offers go to the owner.

traps.trap: The percentage fee applies to scheduled rent.
traps.truth: Use rent actually collected unless the agreement says otherwise: 5% × $37,500 = $1,875, not 5% × $40,000 = $2,000.

traps.trap: Mortgage payments reduce NOI.
traps.truth: Debt service comes after NOI. Subtracting it gives cash flow, not NOI.

traps.trap: The landlord's 1% fee is 1% of the interest.
traps.truth: It is 1% a year of the deposit, paid out of the interest: $20 on a $2,000 deposit.

traps.trap: Buildings under 6 units can mix deposits with operating cash.
traps.truth: Every deposit is trust money. The 6-unit line only triggers the interest requirement.

traps.trap: First month, last month and security is a normal move-in package.
traps.truth: Any deposit or advance is capped at one month's rent, so first month plus one month's security is the most.

traps.trap: The rent demand is 3 or 5 days, and a marshal gives 72 hours' notice.
traps.truth: Both are 14 days since the 2019 HSTPA. Five days is the late-fee and late-notice trigger.

traps.trap: A lockout clause or long nonpayment lets the landlord change the locks.
traps.truth: Only an officer acting on a court warrant removes a tenant. Self-help is a class A misdemeanor with $1,000–$10,000 civil penalties per violation.

traps.trap: Postponed facade repairs are rescheduled preventive maintenance.
traps.truth: That is deferred maintenance. Preventive work happens before anything fails.

traps.trap: Once insured, a known hazard can wait.
traps.truth: Control (repairs) is still required. Insurance transfers the cost but doesn't reduce the risk. Deductibles are retention.

traps.trap: The ADA makes existing buildings rebuild to new standards, and only if federally funded.
traps.truth: Existing places remove barriers where readily achievable, funding or not. Readily accessible is the standard for buildings first occupied after Jan 26, 1993.

traps.trap: NYC window guards protect children under 6, and NYC's lead law uses 1978.
traps.truth: Window guards: 10 or younger, or on request. NYC lead law: under 6 and pre-1960. 1978 is the federal cutoff.

traps.trap: NYC heat must be 68°F all night in heat season.
traps.truth: Overnight (10 p.m.–6 a.m.) the minimum is 62°F regardless; 68°F applies 6 a.m.–10 p.m. when it is below 55°F outside.

traps.trap: Tenants get the buyer's 10-day lead inspection period.
traps.truth: That is a purchaser's right. A landlord gives the EPA pamphlet, discloses known lead paint and puts the lead warning in the lease.

mnemonics.name: OLD CAR
mnemonics.meaning: Obedience (lawful orders only), Loyalty, Disclosure, Confidentiality, Accounting, Reasonable care.

mnemonics.name: ACTOR
mnemonics.meaning: Avoid, Control, Transfer, Or Retain: eliminate the risk (fill in the pool), reduce it (handrails, lighting), shift it (insurance, additional-insured and hold-harmless clauses) or absorb it (deductibles, self-insurance).

mnemonics.name: The New York 14s
mnemonics.meaning: 14-day rent demand (RPAPL §711), 14-day officer's notice before an eviction (RPAPL §749), 14 days after move-out to itemize and return a deposit (GOL §7-108). The odd one out is 5 days: the late-notice and late-fee trigger.
Notice for nonrenewal or a 5%+ raise, month-to-month tenants included: under 1 year 30 days, 1–2 years 60, 2+ years 90, using the longer of occupancy or lease term (RPL §226-c).

mnemonics.name: 68 by day, 62 by night, 120 all year
mnemonics.meaning: NYC heat season Oct 1–May 31: 68°F from 6 a.m. to 10 p.m. when it is below 55°F outside, 62°F from 10 p.m. to 6 a.m. whatever the weather; hot water 120°F year-round.

formulas.name: Effective gross income (EGI)
formulas.formula: EGI = potential gross rent − vacancy and collection loss + other income

formulas.name: Net operating income (NOI)
formulas.formula: NOI = EGI − operating expenses (never debt service)

formulas.name: Before-tax cash flow
formulas.formula: Cash flow = NOI − annual debt service

formulas.name: Management fee
formulas.formula: Fee = base fee + (fee % × rent collected) + leasing fees

formulas.name: Owner remittance
formulas.formula: Remittance = collections − expenses paid − fee − reserve transfer

formulas.name: Capital reserve per unit
formulas.formula: Monthly reserve per unit = cost ÷ years ÷ 12 ÷ units

formulas.name: Tenant's deposit interest
formulas.formula: Tenant's share = interest earned − (1% × deposit)

formulas.name: Late fee cap
formulas.formula: Maximum late fee = lesser of $50 or 5% of monthly rent

formulas.name: Retained loss (per-occurrence deductible)
formulas.formula: Owner pays each loss up to the deductible

formulas.name: Rent loss coverage
formulas.formula: Units out × monthly rent × months

sections.heading: Property management basics and licensing
sections.intro: A property manager runs real estate for its owner (the principal) for a fee. The goal is the best net return consistent with the owner's goals, while preserving the property.
points: **Functions**: leasing and marketing, screening, collecting rent, paying bills, hiring and supervising staff and contractors, maintenance, risk and insurance, records, legal compliance and owner reports.
A **building manager** runs one large property.
A **resident manager** lives on site as a salaried employee of the owner, a broker or a management firm.
An **asset manager** handles long-term investment strategy rather than daily operations.

Office management means tenant improvements and space planning. Retail means tenant mix, common-area maintenance and **anchor stores** that draw shoppers to smaller tenants. Residential means screening, turnover and habitability.
In condo, co-op and **planned unit development (PUD)** communities, the manager answers to a board or owners' association. The manager collects charges or assessments rather than rent.
In New York, negotiating leases or **collecting rent for another for a fee** is brokerage, so a management firm needs a **broker's license** (RPL §440). Its salespersons act under that broker.
A salesperson can't take management fees directly from owners (RPL §442-a).

**No license** is needed for an owner managing his or her own buildings (any number) or for staff who only clean, maintain and repair. Calling the work 'consulting' doesn't matter; the activity decides.
**Skills** the syllabus lists: supervising staff, accounting and reports, building systems, landlord-tenant law, leasing, marketing, codes, union negotiations, purchasing, finance and construction.
A management office must also win and service accounts, staff efficiently and stay profitable.
Many managers start on site or come from brokerage. Designations such as IREM's Certified Property Manager (CPM) show training but never replace a license.

sections.heading: The management proposal and the management agreement
points: A **management proposal** is the manager's plan to win the account. It covers the property description, maintenance needs, accounting methods, inspection schedule, market analysis, proposed budgets and fee.
A proposal creates **no authority**, even if the owner praises it.
The signed, written **management agreement** creates the agency. The owner is the principal and the manager a **general agent**, with ongoing authority over a range of tasks for one business.
A **universal agent** handles all of a principal's affairs (broad power of attorney). A **special agent** handles one transaction, like a typical listing.

The agreement's **contents**, per the syllabus: property description, term, the manager's authority and reporting duties, the fee, accounting for rents, deposits and expenses, insurance and risk management, the owner's responsibilities and objectives, and how the agreement can end.
**Spending limits**: planned work above the dollar cap needs owner approval. An emergency clause lets the manager act at once to protect people or property.
**Limits of general agency**: no selling, mortgaging or signing a sale contract without specific authority. Purchase offers go to the owner.
**Obligations to the owner**: pursue the owner's goals, set maintenance standards, plan for the property's future and report regularly.
Agreements also assign insurance, require **fidelity bonds** for staff who handle money, and require turnover of funds and files when the agreement ends.

head: Clause
Settles
Exam angle
rows: Notice and handoff of funds and files

example.title: Worked example: does the manager need approval?
steps: Facts: the manager may approve repairs up to $1,500 without the owner, except in emergencies.
A $600 pipe repair is within the limit: order it and document it.
A 2 a.m. burst pipe is an emergency: act now, report after.
A $14,000 quote to replace a working but aging boiler next spring is planned capital work over the limit.
Splitting it into ten $1,400 invoices would evade the limit, and tenant security deposits can never fund it.
Answer: the boiler job needs the owner's approval.

sections.heading: Fiduciary duties and conflicts of interest
sections.intro: A **fiduciary** acts for another with the highest loyalty and care. The owner is the client; tenants and vendors are customers or third parties.
points: **Obedience** covers only lawful instructions. Refuse orders to discriminate or to lie, such as denying a known bedbug history. The owner's order is no defense.
**Confidentiality**: never reveal the owner's lowest acceptable rent. Tenants still get **honesty**: no misrepresentation and all required disclosures.
**No secret profits**: no commission, rebate or profit on the owner's expenditures without the owner's full knowledge and consent, even at a fair price (19 NYCRR §175.3).
Pay from more than one party needs the knowledge and consent of the broker's **client** (§175.7).
**Antitrust**: competing firms must set fees independently. Agreeing on a minimum fee is price fixing under the Sherman Act and New York's Donnelly Act, disclosed or not.
Agents leasing 1–4 family homes or condo or co-op units give the **NYS Disclosure Form for Landlord and Tenant**. It is an agency disclosure, not a contract.
All licensees give the **Housing and Anti-Discrimination Disclosure** at first substantive contact.
DOS can suspend, revoke or fine up to $2,000 (RPL §441-c).

head: Duty
Manager's version
Example
rows: All material facts to the owner

sections.heading: Management compensation
sections.intro: Fees are negotiated; no law, board or trade group sets them.
points: **Percentage of collections** (most common): fee % × rent **actually collected**, not scheduled rent, unless the agreement says otherwise.
**Base fee**: a fixed monthly amount, alone or plus a percentage.
**Leasing fees** pay for new leases or renewals, often a fraction of a month's rent. Some agreements add construction-supervision fees.
The management fee is an **operating expense** in NOI.
Vendor rebates aren't compensation without the owner's informed consent.

example.title: Worked example: three fee calculations
steps: A. 5% of collections; scheduled rent $40,000, uncollected $2,500. Fee = ($40,000 − $2,500) × 0.05 = $1,875.
B. $600 base plus 4% of $28,750 collected. Percentage part = $28,750 × 0.04 = $1,150.
C. 5% of $30,000 collected = $1,500.
C leasing fees: half a month's rent for each of three new $2,400 leases = 3 × $1,200 = $3,600.

sections.heading: Budgets, expenses and the operating statement
points: **Operating budget**: one year of rent, other income and recurring expenses, usually built from last year's actuals.
**Capital reserve budget** (replacement reserve): set-asides over the building's economic life for big, irregular items such as roofs, boilers and remodeling.
New York textbooks list repairs, decorating and remodeling as the capital reserve budget's variable items. Pick it when a question pairs those with capital expenses.
**Stabilized budget**: income and expenses under normal operation over a short term (typically about 5 years). It excludes one-time items like lease-up costs or a temporary tax abatement.

**Fixed expenses** stay put regardless of occupancy (real estate taxes, insurance premium, fixed-price contracts). **Variable expenses** move with use or needs (cleaning supplies, utilities, repairs).
**Capital expenses** replace or improve long-lived parts (a new roof), unlike patching a leak.
**EGI** (effective gross income) = potential gross rent − vacancy and collection loss + other income. **NOI** (net operating income) = EGI − operating expenses. Cash flow = NOI − debt service.
Mortgage payments, depreciation and income taxes are never operating expenses.
**Setting rents**: cover expenses plus a fair return and match comparable space. Very high occupancy (say 98%) hints rents are below market.

head: Term
Meaning
Example
rows: One year of routine income and expenses

example.title: Worked example: a 20-unit building's budget
steps: Rent roll: 20 units × $750 × 12 = $180,000 potential gross income.
Plus $2,000 laundry = EGI of $173,000.
Less $70,000 operating expenses = NOI of $103,000.
Subtracting the $40,000 mortgage too gives $63,000 cash flow, not NOI.
Roof reserve: $96,000 due in 8 years ÷ 8 = $12,000 a year.
Answer: NOI is **$103,000**, and the roof reserve is $1,000 ÷ 20 units = **$50 per unit per month**.

sections.heading: Trust accounts, accounting and owner reports
points: No **commingling** of client money with the broker's own (19 NYCRR §175.1).
Deposit client money in a **separate, special, federally insured account within 3 business days**, kept secure until then.
**Conversion** is spending trust money on anything unauthorized (payroll, the manager's bills, another owner's shortfall), even briefly and with intent to repay.
If Owner A is short, ask Owner A for funds.
Account to the client and **remit unspent funds within a reasonable time**, not only when the agreement ends or on written request (19 NYCRR §175.2).
**Rent roll**: units, tenants, lease dates, scheduled rents and arrears. It shows what's owed, not proof of collection.
**Property management report** (usually monthly): receipts, expenses, disbursements and the ending balance against the budget.

head: Report
Shows
Not the same as
rows: Units, tenants, leases, rents, balances owed
Who owes what and for how long

example.title: Worked example: monthly owner remittance
steps: Collected $52,300 (scheduled $54,000); expenses paid $18,450; fee 6% of collections; $2,000 to the capital reserve.
Traps: a fee on scheduled rent gives $28,610; skipping the reserve gives $30,712; skipping the fee gives $31,850.
Answer: remit **$28,712** to the owner.

sections.heading: Security deposits under GOL §7-103 and §7-108
sections.intro: In New York, trust and interest rules cover any rental of real property (GOL §7-103). Cap, inspection and return rules cover residential units (GOL §7-108), and rent-stabilized units follow the same rules (GOL §7-107).
points: **Trust**: a deposit stays the **tenant's money**. It is never commingled with the landlord's or manager's funds, whatever the building size and whatever the owner says.
Tell each tenant in writing the **bank's name and address and the amount**.
The bank must have a **New York** place of business; an out-of-state online bank won't do.
**6+ units**: the deposit earns interest at the prevailing rate, and the landlord keeps **1% a year of the deposit**. The tenant's interest is paid yearly, credited to rent or paid at the end.
Under 6 units, the trust rules still apply but no interest is required.
The cap is **one month's rent** for any deposit or advance.
Cap exceptions include rent-controlled units, registered seasonal rentals, some senior housing and owner-occupied co-ops.
Offer a **move-in inspection**, with a signed condition report if the tenant wants one.
Before move-out, tell the tenant in writing of the right to an inspection 1–2 weeks before the end, on 48 hours' notice, with a chance to fix listed items.
Deduct only unpaid rent, landlord-billed utilities, damage beyond **normal wear and tear**, and moving or storage.
Return the itemized balance within **14 days** of move-out or forfeit it all.
The landlord bears the burden of proof. Willful violations risk punitive damages up to twice the deposit.
**No waivers**: lease clauses giving up these rights are void.
On a sale, deposits go to the buyer within **5 days**, with registered or certified-mail notice to tenants (§7-105).

head: Topic
GOL §7-103
GOL §7-108
rows: Residential units (§7-107 copies the rules for rent-stabilized units)
NY bank, notice, interest at 6+ units, 1% fee
Inspections; itemize and return in 14 days

example.title: Worked example: deposit cap and interest
steps: Cap: rent is $1,950. Most collectible at signing = $1,950 first month + $1,950 security = $3,900.
Adding last month's rent would break the cap.
Interest: $2,000 deposit in a 12-unit building at 3.2% = $64.
Landlord's fee = 1% of $2,000 = $20 (not 1% of $64).
Answer: tenant's share = $64 − $20 = **$44**; the most collectible at signing is **$3,900**.

sections.heading: Marketing, tenant selection and fair housing
points: **Marketing plan**: study vacancy rates, competition and demographics, price the units, then choose channels and a budget.
**Cost per prospect** = ad cost ÷ prospects produced.
**Screening**: one written application and identical standards for everyone.
Demanding extra references only from an applicant with a foreign accent is national-origin discrimination, even if the applicant is later approved.
**Protected classes**: federal law covers race, color, religion, national origin, sex, familial status and disability.

New York adds creed, age, marital status, military status, sexual orientation, gender identity or expression, **lawful source of income**, citizenship or immigration status and domestic-violence-victim status.
Banning children from a walk-up 'for safety' is familial status discrimination. 'No vouchers' violates New York's source-of-income protection, even though federal law doesn't cover it.
The owner's order excuses neither; the manager is liable for his or her own acts.
Never deny an applicant for a past or pending landlord-tenant case, whatever its age or outcome (RPL §227-f).
Denying after checking court records raises a **presumption** of a violation.
The only rental application charge is a background/credit-check fee at **actual cost or $20, whichever is less** (RPL §238-a), with a copy of the report and a receipt.
The fee is waived if the applicant provides a background or credit check from the past 30 days.
Co-op purchase applicants differ: the co-op may charge managing-agent processing fees and the actual cost of credit checks, even above $20.
**Disability**: grant reasonable accommodations (an assistance animal despite a no-pets rule) and allow reasonable modifications (grab bars).
Under the federal FHA, the tenant usually pays for modifications in private housing. State, city and subsidy rules can differ.
**NYC FARE Act**: a tenant can't be charged the fee of a broker the landlord hired. It took effect June 11, 2025, and the Second Circuit upheld it July 13, 2026.

rows: Same income and credit standard for all

sections.heading: Rent collection, notices and rent regulation
sections.intro: The 2019 Housing Stability and Tenant Protection Act (HSTPA) rewrote most of these rules.
points: **Lessor** = landlord; **lessee** = tenant.
A **tenancy for years** has fixed start and end dates, even if under a year. A periodic tenancy renews until ended. New York's notice rules apply either way.
Give a **receipt** for rent paid in cash, by money order or by anything but a personal check. For a personal check, give one on written request (RPL §235-e).
**Late notice**: if rent isn't received within **5 days** of the due date, send a certified-mail notice. Skipping it gives the tenant a defense in a nonpayment case.
The late notice is separate from the 14-day rent demand.
A late fee is allowed only after 5 days, capped at the lesser of **$50 or 5%** (RPL §238-a).

A **bounced-check fee** is allowed only if the lease provides for it. It is capped at the greater of the landlord's actual bank charges or $20, with proof on request above $20. This rule was added Oct 16, 2025 (RPL §238-a).

A **co-op** may charge shareholders a late fee of up to **8%** of monthly maintenance if the proprietary lease allows. This 2021 amendment doesn't cover Mitchell-Lama, HDFC or similar supervised co-ops.
Nonrenewal or a **5%+ increase** needs 30, 60 or 90 days' written notice: under 1 year, 1–2 years, 2+ years, using the longer of occupancy or lease (RPL §226-c).
If notice is late, the tenant stays at the old rent until the period runs.

**Good Cause Eviction Law (2024)** covers NYC and opt-in localities. Covered tenants can be removed only on a legal ground, and raises above the lower of **5% + CPI or 10%** are presumed unreasonable.

Good Cause exemptions: landlords with 10 or fewer units, owner-occupied buildings of 10 or fewer units, regulated and subsidized units, co-ops and condos, buildings with a 2009-or-later certificate of occupancy (for 30 years) and high-rent units.
**Rent stabilization**: tenants have renewal rights, and the NYC Rent Guidelines Board sets renewal increases.
Owners of stabilized units register yearly with DHCR (the state Division of Housing and Community Renewal). HSTPA ended high-rent and high-income deregulation.
**Retaliation** is presumed if the landlord acts within **1 year** of a good-faith complaint (RPL §223-b).
The **warranty of habitability** can't be waived (RPL §235-b).
A landlord must try to re-rent if a tenant leaves early (RPL §227-e).

example.title: Worked example: late fee and notice periods
steps: Rent $1,800, paid more than 5 days late: 5% = $90, so the fee is capped at $50.
Month-to-month tenant in a non-regulated unit for 7 months: under 1 year, so 30 days' notice to end it.
Tenant of 15 months offered a 6% renewal increase: 5%+ and 1–2 years, so 60 days' notice.
Answer: late fee **$50**; notice periods **30 days** and 60 days.

sections.heading: Evictions: court process, self-help and constructive eviction
points: A **nonpayment** case is brought after a **14-day written rent demand**.
A **holdover** case is for a tenant who stays after the lease ends or after proper termination. Good Cause units need a legal ground.

**Order**: rent demand → petition (served 10–17 days before the hearing) → judgment of possession → warrant → officer's **14-day written notice** → removal on a business day between sunrise and sunset.
Only a **sheriff, marshal or constable** executes the warrant. A judgment doesn't let the owner, manager or a locksmith remove anyone.
In a nonpayment case, paying all rent due before execution generally voids the warrant.
**Unlawful eviction** means lockouts, utility shutoffs, or removing belongings or doors against an occupant of 30+ days or with a lease.
Unlawful eviction is a **class A misdemeanor** with $1,000–$10,000 civil penalties per violation (RPAPL §768). No lease clause can authorize it.
**Actual eviction** is removal by legal process.
**Constructive eviction** happens when the landlord's act or neglect makes the unit unusable and the tenant moves out.

head: Term
Meaning
Exam angle
rows: Tenant must vacate to claim it

sections.heading: Maintenance types and building operations
points: **Preventive (preventative)**: scheduled servicing before failure, such as quarterly filter changes.
**Corrective**: fixing a reported defect, such as a dripping faucet.
**Routine (custodial)**: daily housekeeping such as mopping halls, trash removal and sweeping.
**Construction**: budgeted remodeling, tenant improvements (build-outs for a new tenant) and capital improvements.
**Deferred**: needed work postponed, such as skipping facade repairs to boost NOI before a sale. Deterioration continues and costs rise.
**Cosmetic** work improves appearance more than function.
Use inspections, an annual schedule, work orders and purchasing controls. Know when licensed trades, engineers or code officials are needed.
For a gas smell, get people out and call 911 and the utility from a safe place. Don't send the super to find the leak first.

sections.heading: Risk management and insurance
sections.intro: **Risk management** means identifying what could go wrong and choosing how to handle it.
points: **Avoid**: eliminate the activity (fill in the pool).
**Control**: reduce the odds or size of a loss (handrails, anti-slip treads, lighting, inspections).
**Transfer**: shift the cost to others through insurance, contractor insurance naming the owner and manager as additional insureds, and **hold-harmless (indemnification)** clauses.
**Retain**: absorb a layer of loss through deductibles or self-insurance. A per-occurrence deductible applies to each loss separately.
**Coinsurance**: say a policy requires coverage of 80% of value and the owner carries less. A partial loss then pays loss × (carried ÷ required), minus the deductible.
**Workers' compensation** is required in New York for employees such as building staff.

head: Coverage
Pays for
Exam angle
rows: Rent lost after a covered loss
Employee theft of rents or deposits

example.title: Worked example: deductibles and rent loss
steps: Deductible: $5,000 per occurrence; losses of $3,200 and $14,500.
The owner pays all of the $3,200 loss.
The owner pays $5,000 of the $14,500 loss.
Rent loss: fire closes 6 of 20 apartments for 5 months at $2,250 each.
Answer: retained loss **$8,200**; rent loss = 6 × $2,250 × 5 = **$67,500**.

sections.heading: Accessibility: ADA Title III and Fair Housing Act design rules
points: **ADA Title III** covers places of public accommodation, including a **leasing or sales office** open to the public, even when privately owned and with no federal funding.
**Existing facilities**: remove barriers where **readily achievable**, meaning easily done without much difficulty or expense (ramps, for example).
The barrier-removal duty is ongoing, needs no complaint, and doesn't require a full rebuild.
New construction first occupied after **January 26, 1993** must be **readily accessible to and usable by** people with disabilities.
**Landlord and tenant are both responsible** for a public accommodation in leased space. The lease can divide the work, but neither escapes liability.
The apartments themselves fall under the Fair Housing Act (FHA).

sections.heading: New York City landlord obligations
sections.intro: HPD (Housing Preservation and Development) enforces most housing rules. The Department of Buildings handles facades and energy, and the state's DHCR (Division of Housing and Community Renewal) handles rent stabilization.
points: **Window guards**: windows onto a fire escape are exempt.
The combined lead and window-guard notice goes out each January. If a tenant hasn't returned it by **February 15**, the owner must try to inspect, because silence isn't a 'no.'
**Lead (Local Law 1 of 2004)**: pre-1960 paint is presumed lead-based (1960–1978 if the owner knows of lead).
Lead duties attach where a **child under 6** lives or regularly spends 10+ hours a week.
At **turnover**, fix lead hazards, including door and window friction surfaces. Make floors, sills and window wells smooth and cleanable, child or no child.
Federal rules for leases of pre-1978 housing apply too: EPA pamphlet, disclosure of known lead paint and reports, and a lead warning in the lease. The 10-day inspection right is for buyers only.
**Bedbugs**: give the 1-year history (HCR form DBB-N) with a vacancy lease.
File a bedbug report with HPD every December for each multiple dwelling, **even with zero infestations**, then share it with tenants.
**Detectors**: the owner installs smoke and CO alarms and replaces missing or broken ones before a new tenancy. The tenant changes batteries.
The owner replaces a detector that fails within 1 year from a manufacturing defect.
Battery-only smoke alarms sold in New York since April 1, 2019 need sealed 10-year batteries (GBL §399-ccc).
Without **HPD registration**, an owner can't recover possession for nonpayment and faces penalties.
A missed **DHCR filing** freezes the rent at the last registered amount until the owner files. The cure is prospective only.
**Janitor**: a building of 9+ units whose owner doesn't live there needs a janitor in the building or within one block or 200 feet (whichever is greater), unless a 24-hour service is used.
Janitorial services cover cleaning, minor repairs, heat, hot water, garbage and sidewalk snow, not rent collection or leasing.
**Energy**: Local Law 84 requires annual energy and water benchmarking. Local Law 33 (amended by LL95) requires posting the energy letter grade near each public entrance.
Local Law 97 emission caps began in 2024 and tighten in 2030.

guides.title: Rentals & Deal Sheets
guides.overview: New York residential leasing and the paperwork after an accepted sale offer. The exam hits hardest on the 2019 **Housing Stability and Tenant Protection Act (HSTPA)** limits on deposits, fees, late charges and notices; habitability, the self-help ban and Good Cause; and NYC's **FARE Act**. For sales, know that a **deal sheet** isn't the contract and how commissions split.

numbers.label: Cap on security deposit plus any advance; 'last month's rent' counts toward it
After move-out, itemized statement and refund due, or landlord forfeits right to keep any
Screening-fee cap, whichever is less; waived for a report from the past 30 days
Late-fee cap, whichever is less, only once rent is more than 5 days late
Rent not received by then: landlord must send a certified-mail nonpayment notice
Rent demand before a nonpayment case (was 3 days); also marshal's eviction notice
Nonrenewal or 5%+ increase notice: under 1, 1 to under 2, 2+ years (§226-c)
Retaliation presumption window after a good-faith complaint (was 6 months)
Building size for the right to sublet with consent not unreasonably withheld
Sublet request silence = consent; also release notice after unreasonably refused assignment
Deposits must earn interest; the landlord keeps 1% per year of the deposit
Occupancy after which only a court warrant can remove someone, lease or no lease
Civil penalty per unlawful eviction, plus a class A misdemeanor
Good Cause: renewal increases above the lower of these are presumptively unreasonable
Good Cause small-landlord exemption: 10 or fewer units statewide; opt-in localities may differ
Stabilized renewal offer window; tenant accepts within 60 days, choosing 1 or 2 years
NYC FARE Act effective date (upheld by the 2d Circuit July 13, 2026)
Keep DOS-1735 acknowledgments or sworn refusal declarations and signed FARE fee disclosures
Typical income screens: tenant 40× the monthly rent, guarantor 80× (landlord policy, not law)
Customary NYC contract deposit on a sale; also a stabilized tenant's furnished-sublet surcharge

mustKnow: **HSTPA** (2019) rules cover nearly every New York residential tenancy, and no lease clause can waive them.
Deposit plus advances can't exceed **one month's rent**. A 'last month's rent' counts, so first month's rent plus one month is the most due at signing.
No application, processing or move-in fees. The only allowed up-front fee is a screening fee of the lesser of **actual cost or $20**, waived for a report from the past **30 days**.
A late fee is allowed only after rent is more than **5 days** late and is capped at the lesser of **$50 or 5%** of the rent.
Deposits are trust money, never commingled. **6+ unit** buildings must use an interest-bearing New York account, and the landlord keeps **1% per year of the deposit**.
Return the deposit with an itemized statement **within 14 days after move-out** or **forfeit** the right to keep any of it. Never deduct ordinary wear and tear or a prior tenant's damage.
If rent isn't received within **5 days**, send a certified-mail notice. Before suing for nonpayment, serve a written **14-day rent demand**.
Not renewing, or raising rent 5% or more, needs **30/60/90 days'** written notice based on the **longer** of occupancy or lease term (RPL §226-c). Late notice delays, not voids, the change.
The **warranty of habitability** is implied in every residential lease, covers common areas, and **can't be waived**. It excludes conditions the tenant caused.
Landlord action within **1 year** after a good-faith complaint (to the landlord or a government agency) or an effort to enforce lease or habitability rights is **presumed retaliatory**.
Tenant organizing is also protected from retaliation, but without the 1-year presumption.
**Assignment** transfers the whole remaining term; an unreasonable refusal's **only remedy is release on 30 days' notice**. A sublease transfers less. Neither releases the original tenant.
In **4+ unit** buildings, sublet consent can't be unreasonably withheld, and **30 days' silence** after a proper request is consent.

Roommate law: a sole tenant may live with immediate family plus **one occupant** and that occupant's dependent children; the occupant has **no right to stay** after the tenant leaves without written consent.
Self-help is banned: lockouts or utility shutoffs against anyone with a lease or **30+ days** of occupancy are **unlawful eviction**, a class A misdemeanor.
Only a **marshal, sheriff or constable** executes an eviction warrant, after **14 days'** written notice.
Good Cause applies automatically in **NYC** and elsewhere only by **opt-in**. A lease simply ending is not a ground for removal.
Good Cause exempts owners of **10 or fewer units** (opt-in localities may differ), rent-regulated units, condo/co-op units, and buildings first certified on or after **Jan 1, 2009**, for 30 years.
**Rent stabilization** covers most NYC **6+ unit buildings built before 1974**. The Rent Guidelines Board sets renewal increases, and DHCR handles overcharge complaints.
Stabilized renewals are offered **90–150 days** before expiration, and the **tenant picks 1 or 2 years**. The HSTPA ended high-rent and high-income deregulation.
A stabilized tenant may sublet only **2 years in any 4**, charging at most the legal rent plus **10%** if furnished.
Rejecting an applicant for a past or pending landlord-tenant case (**blacklisting**) is illegal, whatever the outcome.
Lawful **source of income** is protected statewide: no 'No Section 8,' and any income test applies only to the tenant's **own share** of the rent.
In NYC, no income test applies at all when the voucher sets the tenant's share from her income (Section 8, CityFHEPS).
The **40×** income and **80×** guarantor rules are landlord policy, not law. A guarantor pays if the tenant defaults but has no right to live there.
**DOS-1735** goes to a prospective tenant at the **first substantive contact**. It covers rentals of 1–4 family homes and condo/co-op units.
DOS-1735 is **not a contract**. If the person refuses to sign, the agent makes a **sworn declaration** and keeps it 3 years.
FARE Act: the landlord's agent can't charge the tenant, and a listing is **presumed** to have landlord permission. A tenant may still **hire and pay her own broker**.
FARE bans conditioning a rental on hiring any agent and requires an **itemized fee disclosure signed before the lease**. It is **NYC-only**.
Rent and deposits a broker collects go into a special **escrow account within 3 business days**.
A **deal sheet** summarizes accepted terms so the seller's attorney can draft the contract. It is **not the contract**; parties generally aren't bound until both sign the contract of sale.
Deal sheet essentials: **price, deposit, mortgage amount, contingencies, closing date, commission split, both attorneys' contacts**. Never include protected-class details or client secrets.
NYC's **10% deposit** is custom, usually held by the seller's attorney. Commissions are negotiable, and a salesperson is paid **only by her own broker**.

traps.trap: First month, last month and a full month's security is a lawful move-in package.
traps.truth: Last month's rent is an advance under the one-month cap; first month plus one month is the maximum.

traps.trap: The late fee is always $50.
traps.truth: It's the lesser of $50 or 5% ($42.50 on $850 rent), and only after rent is more than 5 days late.

traps.trap: The deposit must be returned two weeks before move-out.
traps.truth: It's due within 14 days AFTER move-out; the 1–2 weeks before move-out is the inspection window.

traps.trap: The landlord keeps 1% of the interest.
traps.truth: It's 1% of the deposit: $3,000 earning 2% makes $60, so the landlord keeps $30 and the tenant gets $30.

traps.trap: A 3-day rent demand starts a nonpayment case.
traps.truth: Since 2019 the demand must allow 14 days; the 5-day rule is the separate certified-mail late notice.

traps.trap: Retaliation is presumed only for 6 months after a complaint.
traps.truth: The HSTPA made it 1 year.

traps.trap: A tenant 8 months into a one-year lease gets 30 days' nonrenewal notice.
traps.truth: Use the longer of occupancy or lease term; a lease of at least one year means 60 days.

traps.trap: A habitability waiver traded for lower rent is valid.
traps.truth: Any waiver is void as against public policy; consideration doesn't save it.

traps.trap: If an assignment is unreasonably refused, the tenant may assign anyway.
traps.truth: The sole remedy is release on 30 days' notice. 'Sublet anyway' is the remedy for an unreasonably refused sublet.

traps.trap: Good Cause caps every New York rent increase at 10%.
traps.truth: It covers only non-exempt units in NYC and opt-in localities, uses the lower of 5% + CPI or 10%, and a bigger increase is only presumed unreasonable.

traps.trap: The FARE Act bans tenant-paid broker fees statewide.
traps.truth: It's NYC-only, and even there a tenant may pay a broker she hires herself.

traps.trap: Without a written listing agreement, the broker advertising an NYC apartment may charge the tenant.
traps.truth: Publishing a listing creates a presumption of landlord permission, so no tenant fee.

traps.trap: A signed DOS-1735 or a signed deal sheet binds the signer.
traps.truth: DOS-1735 only acknowledges receipt. A deal sheet is a summary; a sale binds once both parties sign the contract.

traps.trap: Luxury decontrol at $2,000 rent and $175,000 income still applies.
traps.truth: The HSTPA abolished high-rent and high-income deregulation in 2019; the syllabus figures are obsolete.

mnemonics.name: Who hires, pays
mnemonics.meaning: FARE Act: whoever engages the broker pays the broker. Landlord's agent → landlord pays; tenant's own broker → tenant may pay.

formulas.name: Late-fee cap
formulas.formula: Lesser of $50 or 5% × monthly rent (only after 5 days)

formulas.name: Most due at signing (no broker fee)
formulas.formula: First month + deposit (≤ 1 month) + screening fee (≤ lesser of cost or $20)

formulas.name: Tenant's deposit interest
formulas.formula: Interest earned − (1% × deposit)

formulas.name: Good Cause threshold
formulas.formula: Rent × (1 + lower of [5% + CPI] or 10%)

formulas.name: 40× and guarantor tests
formulas.formula: Income needed = rent × 40 (guarantor × 80); max rent = income ÷ 40

formulas.formula: (Rent − voucher payment) × 40; none in NYC when the voucher sets the tenant's share (Section 8, CityFHEPS)

formulas.name: Salesperson's commission
formulas.formula: Price × rate × firm's side % × agent's split

formulas.name: LTV and cash at closing
formulas.formula: LTV = loan ÷ lower of price or appraisal; down-payment balance at closing = (price − loan) − contract deposit (before closing costs)

sections.heading: Lease basics and leasehold estates
sections.intro: A lease transfers possession, not ownership, for a term in exchange for rent. Contract law governs it, subject to tenant protections no lease can waive.
points: The **lessor** is the landlord, and the **lessee** is the tenant.
The **demising clause** grants possession. A valid lease also needs parties with capacity, a description of the premises, the term, and the rent and how it's paid.
Both parties sign. Notarization is needed only if the lease will be recorded.
**Statute of frauds**: a lease longer than **one year** needs a signed writing; one year or less may be oral (GOL §5-703).
The **plain language law** requires clear, everyday wording in residential leases, for agreements up to $250,000 (GOL §5-702). Older books say $50,000.
If the lease is silent, the common-law default (repeated in the syllabus) is rent due **in arrears**. Standard leases make it due in advance.
A **gross** lease has the landlord pay operating costs; it's typical for residential.
A **net** lease has the tenant pay taxes, insurance and/or maintenance. Triple net = all three.
A **percentage** lease is base rent plus a share of sales. A **graduated** lease has scheduled step-ups.
An **index** lease is tied to an index such as the consumer price index (CPI).
A **ground or land lease** covers land only. A **proprietary lease** is for co-op occupancy.
The **use clause** limits permitted uses. In commercial leases, 'for no other purpose' is narrow and 'any lawful purpose' is broad.
There's no general statutory renewal right. Renewal comes from rent stabilization, Good Cause, or an **option to renew**.
Attached tenant improvements usually stay with the property. Commercial **trade fixtures** may be removed if the damage is repaired.
If possession isn't delivered at the start, the tenant may rescind (RPL §223-a). A sale, or the death of either party, doesn't end a lease.

sections.heading: Move-in money: deposits, fees and late charges
sections.intro: These HSTPA rules cover market-rate (GOL §7-108) and rent-stabilized (GOL §7-107) units statewide. Rent-controlled units follow their own rules.
points: **Deposit cap**: deposit plus advances can't exceed **one month's rent** (GOL §§7-107, 7-108).
Narrow exceptions to the cap cover registered seasonal rentals, owner-occupied co-op purchases, and some senior and care housing.
**Fee ban**: no application, processing, move-in or other fee before or at the start of a tenancy (RPL §238-a).
Calling a charge 'refundable' just makes it an illegal extra deposit.
The sole exception is a **background/credit check**: the lesser of actual cost or **$20**, only with a copy of the report and the receipt.
The screening fee is **waived** if the applicant brings a report from the past 30 days.
A **late fee** is allowed only if rent isn't paid within 5 days of the due date. It's capped at the lesser of **$50 or 5%**; $50 controls only above $1,000 rent.
A bounced-check fee needs a lease clause and is capped by statute.
Co-op purchases differ: a co-op may charge a buyer its actual screening cost, even above $20, plus managing-agent processing fees.
A co-op may charge shareholders a late fee of up to 8% of monthly maintenance if the proprietary lease provides for it.

head: Charge
Rule
Quick check
rows: A $300 'processing fee' is illegal even if disclosed

example.title: Worked example: late fee
steps: Rent of $850 is due on the 1st and paid on the 10th, more than 5 days late.
Cap: 5% × $850 = $42.50, which is less than $50.
Compare: on $1,400 rent, 5% is $70, so the $50 cap would control.

sections.heading: Holding and returning the security deposit
points: **Trust money**: the deposit stays the tenant's and is never commingled (GOL §7-103).
If banked, the deposit must be in a bank with a New York office. The tenant gets written notice of the bank's name and address and the amount.
**6+ units**: an interest-bearing account is required. The landlord keeps **1% per year of the deposit**; the rest of the interest is the tenant's (paid yearly, credited to rent, or paid at the end).
**Move-in inspection**: the landlord must offer a joint inspection. Defects listed in a signed condition report can't be deducted later.
Before move-out, the landlord must tell the tenant of the right to an inspection 1–2 weeks before the end, on **48 hours' written notice**.
After that inspection, the landlord lists proposed deductions so the tenant can cure.
**Refund**: an itemized statement and the balance are due within **14 days after the tenant vacates**.
Missing the refund deadline forfeits any right to keep money, even for real damage.
**Deductions** are allowed only for unpaid rent, damage beyond normal wear and tear, landlord-billed utilities, and moving/storage of belongings.
Never deduct faded paint, normally worn carpet, or a prior tenant's damage.
The landlord bears the burden of proof. A willful violation risks punitive damages up to twice the deposit.
**Building sale**: deposits go to the buyer within 5 days, and tenants are notified by registered or certified mail (GOL §7-105).
After a building sale, the buyer owes the refunds. This is a seller debit and buyer credit at closing.

example.title: Worked example: deposit interest in a 20-unit building
steps: Landlord's fee is 1% of the deposit, not of the interest: $3,000 × 1% = $30.
Answer: the tenant gets $60 − $30 = **$30**.

sections.heading: Notices: renewals, nonrenewals and late rent
points: A landlord who won't renew, or will raise rent **5% or more**, must give written notice measured by the **longer** of occupancy or lease term (RPL §226-c).
An increase under 5% needs no §226-c notice, though Good Cause may still apply.
**Late notice** doesn't cancel the change. The old terms continue from the date notice was actually given until the full period runs.
Month-to-month terminations use the same tiers. A tenancy at will or sufferance needs **30 days'** notice.
Statewide, every landlord must attach the **Good Cause notice** to new leases, renewals, §226-c notices, 14-day rent demands and eviction petitions (RPL §231-c).
The Good Cause notice states whether the unit is covered and, if not, why. Outside NYC, 'locality hasn't opted in' is one listed reason.
Landlords give receipts for cash or money-order rent, and for personal checks only on request.
If rent isn't received within **5 days**, the landlord sends a certified-mail notice (RPL §235-e).
Before a nonpayment case, the landlord serves a **14-day rent demand** (RPAPL §711).
If a tenant leaves early, the landlord must try to re-rent: the **duty to mitigate** (RPL §227-e).
Tenants 62+ or disabled moving to care, senior or subsidized housing or a relative's home may end a lease early (RPL §227-a). Domestic-violence victims and service members have similar rights.

head: Longer of occupancy or lease term
Notice required
rows: 1 year to under 2 years (incl. a 1-year lease)

example.title: Worked example: late notice of an increase
steps: A 4-year tenant gets written notice of a 10% increase 40 days before the lease ends.
Two-plus years requires 90 days, so the notice is short.
Answer: the old rent continues until 90 days after the notice date; the increase is delayed, not void.

sections.heading: Habitability, safety and required lease disclosures
points: The **warranty of habitability** is implied in every written or oral residential lease and covers the unit and common areas (RPL §235-b).
The warranty **can't be waived** but excludes conditions the tenant caused. It protects co-op shareholders but not condo owners.
The usual habitability remedy is a court-ordered rent abatement.
**Constructive eviction**: landlord fault makes the unit unusable, and the tenant must move out to claim it.
**Quiet enjoyment** protects possession from landlord interference. The landlord enters as the lease allows on reasonable notice, or anytime in an emergency.
**Window guards** in NYC buildings with 3+ units: required on every window except fire-escape windows wherever a child **10 or younger** lives or the tenant asks.
**Local Law 1** presumes lead paint in pre-1960 NYC buildings with 3+ units where a child **under 6** lives.
One January notice covers window guards and lead paint. If it isn't returned by February 15, the owner must try to inspect.
NYC owners install smoke and carbon monoxide detectors, and occupants maintain them, batteries included.
**Amanda's Law** requires CO alarms in homes with fuel-burning appliances or an attached garage.

head: Disclosure
Applies to
Key point
rows: Whether a working sprinkler system exists; if so, last inspection date
FEMA flood-zone status, known flood damage, renter's flood insurance notice
Known lead info, EPA pamphlet, warning in the lease; no 10-day test right for tenants
Prior year's infestation history, before signing
Tenant pays for heat or cooling
Two years of bills, free on written request

sections.heading: Assignment, subletting and roommates
points: An **assignment** transfers the entire remaining term. The original tenant stays liable unless the landlord releases them (a novation).
A **sublease** transfers part. The tenant keeps a reversion and stays liable for everything.
Assignment consent may be withheld without a reason (RPL §226-b(1)). If the refusal is **unreasonable**, the tenant's **sole remedy** is release on 30 days' notice.
**Sublet right** in **4+ unit** buildings: consent can't be unreasonably withheld (RPL §226-b(2)).

The tenant requests by certified mail. The request gives the term, the subtenant's name and addresses, the reason, her address during the sublet, any co-tenant or guarantor consent, and the proposed sublease.
The landlord may ask for more information within 10 days and must answer within **30 days**; **silence = consent**.
After an unreasonable refusal, the tenant may sublet anyway, with legal fees if the landlord acted in bad faith.
§226-b doesn't cover public housing or **co-op proprietary leases**, and in buildings under 4 units the lease controls. Skipping the procedure is a substantial breach.
**Stabilized sublets**: the tenant keeps a primary residence there, sublets at most **2 years in any 4**, and charges no more than the legal rent plus 10% if furnished.
**Roommate law**: one named tenant may add **one occupant** plus that occupant's dependent children, if the tenant or spouse lives there as a primary residence (RPL §235-f).
With several named tenants, the total can't exceed the number named.
The landlord gets the occupant's name within 30 days. The occupant has **no right to stay** without written consent.

head: Arrangement
Transfers
Landlord consent
Tenant still liable?
rows: Required; unreasonable refusal → release on 30 days' notice
Part of the term or space
Not unreasonably withheld; 30 days' silence = consent
Not needed; give name within 30 days

example.title: Worked example: furnished stabilized sublet
steps: Legal regulated rent is $1,800, and the unit is sublet fully furnished.
Answer: at most **$1,980** a month.

sections.heading: Evictions, retaliation and the ban on self-help
points: **Unlawful eviction**: without a court warrant, no one may remove anyone who has a lease or **30+ consecutive days** of lawful occupancy (RPAPL §768).
Banned removal methods include force, threats, lock changes, removing belongings, and cutting utilities.
Unlawful eviction penalties: class A misdemeanor, **$1,000–$10,000** per violation, and treble damages to the tenant (RPAPL §853).
Only a **marshal, sheriff or constable** executes a warrant, after **14 days' written notice**.
In a nonpayment case, paying all rent due before execution vacates the warrant unless rent was withheld in bad faith.
Nonpayment path: 5-day certified notice → 14-day demand → petition → judgment → warrant → 14-day notice → execution.
Holdover path: predicate notice (§226-c or 30 days) → petition → judgment → warrant.
**Retaliation** is banned: no notice to quit, eviction, nonrenewal or substantial change in terms because of protected activity (RPL §223-b).
Protected activity: a good-faith complaint to the landlord or a government agency, enforcing lease or habitability rights, or tenant organizing.
Retaliation is **presumed** within **1 year** after a complaint or enforcement effort, or after a resulting inspection, order or tenant judgment. Organizing gets no presumption.
The landlord must rebut the presumption, and the tenant still owes rent.
Retaliation rules exclude owner-occupied buildings under 4 units and tenant-caused conditions.
Lease violations aren't protected activity: unapproved sublets, banned pets, or blocking repairs.

example.title: Worked example: a guest with no lease
steps: A homeowner's friend has stayed 49 days, no lease, no rent; the homeowner changes the locks.
Thirty-plus days of lawful occupancy triggers RPAPL §768, lease or not.
Answer: **unlawful**; the homeowner needs notice and a court proceeding.

sections.heading: Good Cause Eviction Law
sections.intro: Enacted in April 2024 as RPL Article 6-A; scheduled to expire June 15, 2034.
points: Applies automatically in **NYC**. Elsewhere it applies only where a city, town or village **opts in**, and then only to non-exempt units.
A six-unit test belongs to rent stabilization, not Good Cause.
Covered tenants can be removed only for listed grounds. **Lease expiration alone isn't a ground.**
Grounds: **nonpayment** (not caused by an unreasonable increase), an uncured substantial lease violation, nuisance, illegal use, or unreasonably refusing access.
More grounds: good-faith **owner or family use** (not against tenants 65+ or disabled), demolition, leaving the rental market, or refusing reasonable renewal terms.
**Local rent standard**: increases above the **lower of 5% + CPI or 10%** are presumptively unreasonable. The landlord can justify more (taxes, costs, significant repairs).
HCR publishes the regional figure by August 1 each year. On the exam, use the CPI the question gives.
Leases, renewals and notices must include the Good Cause notice stating coverage or the exemption claimed.

head: Exemption
Detail
rows: Owns 10 or fewer units statewide, looking through LLCs (an opt-in locality may set another number)
Owner lives there; 10 or fewer units
First CO on or after Jan 1, 2009: exempt 30 years
Above 245% of HUD fair market rent (an opt-in locality may set its own percentage)
Condo and co-op units, seasonal rentals, employer housing, dorms, care facilities

example.title: Worked example: Good Cause threshold
steps: Covered NYC unit at $2,400; CPI change 3%.
5% + 3% = 8%, lower than 10%.

sections.heading: Rent stabilization, rent control and the HSTPA
points: **Rent stabilization** covers most NYC buildings of **6+ units built before 1974**.
Outside NYC, the **Emergency Tenant Protection Act (ETPA)** applies where localities adopt it: parts of Nassau, Westchester and Rockland. Since 2019 any municipality may opt in.
The **Rent Guidelines Board** sets yearly maximum increases for 1- and 2-year renewals.
**DHCR** (Division of Housing and Community Renewal, within NYS Homes and Community Renewal) handles registrations and overcharge complaints.
Renewals are offered on the DHCR form **90–150 days** before expiration. The tenant has **60 days** to accept and chooses 1 or 2 years.
The unit must be the tenant's **primary residence**.
A family member who lived there 2 years (1 if 62+ or disabled) before the tenant left has **succession** rights.
The **HSTPA (2019)** made the rent laws permanent. It ended high-rent vacancy and high-income deregulation, the up-to-20% vacancy bonus, and the longevity bonus.
The HSTPA also protected preferential rents, limited improvement-based increases, and extended the overcharge look-back to 6 years with treble damages.
The syllabus's **luxury decontrol** figures ($2,000 rent, $175,000 income) are obsolete: no unit deregulates that way after 2019.
**Rent control** mostly covers NYC pre-1947 buildings with tenants in place since before July 1, 1971 (Maximum Base Rent system). On vacancy the unit usually becomes stabilized or deregulated.

head: Regime
Covers
Increases
Renewal right
rows: Lower of 5% + CPI or 10% presumed limit
Pre-1947 buildings, tenant there since before July 1971

sections.heading: Agency disclosure for rentals: DOS-1735
points: The agency disclosure law covers rentals (and sales) of **1–4 family homes and condo/co-op units**, not commercial space or vacant land (RPL §443).
The definition doesn't reach apartments in larger rental buildings. DOS-1736 is the sales version.
A listing agent gives DOS-1735 to the landlord before the listing agreement.
A landlord's agent gives it to a prospective tenant at the **first substantive contact**.
A tenant's agent gives it to the tenant before the agency agreement, and to the landlord at first substantive contact.
It's headed **THIS IS NOT A CONTRACT**: signing only acknowledges receipt. Keep acknowledgments 3 years.
On a refusal to sign, the agent writes a **sworn declaration** of the facts and keeps it 3 years. The agent may keep working with the person.
A landlord's agent owes the landlord full fiduciary duties but must deal honestly with the tenant and disclose known material facts.
Owners renting directly need no form.

The separate **fair housing disclosure** (DOS-2156) goes at first substantive contact to every prospective buyer, tenant, seller or landlord (19 NYCRR §175.28), for any property type, commercial and vacant land included.

head: Relationship
Who
Key fact
rows: Another firm helping the listing or tenant's agent
No direct tie to landlord or tenant; the engaging agent is liable
Needs both parties' informed written consent
Broker assigns one salesperson per side
Also needs both parties' informed written consent

sections.heading: NYC FARE Act: who pays the broker
sections.intro: NYC Local Law 119 of 2024, effective **June 11, 2025**, upheld by the Second Circuit on July 13, 2026: whoever hires the broker pays.
points: An agent who **represents or was engaged by the landlord** can't charge the tenant any fee, and the landlord can't pass it along. Disclosing the fee doesn't cure it.
Publishing a listing creates a **rebuttable presumption** of landlord permission, which bars a tenant fee even without a written listing agreement.
No rental, tour or application may be **conditioned** on hiring an agent, including a dual agent.
A tenant may voluntarily **hire her own broker** and pay the agreed fee.
Listings must show **every tenant-paid fee**.
The tenant signs an **itemized fee disclosure before the lease**, kept 3 years.
Order: DOS-1735 → application and screening → fee disclosure → lease.
NYC's Department of Consumer and Worker Protection enforces it.
FARE is **NYC-only**. Elsewhere, RPL §238-a limits landlords' fees but, per a 2021 court ruling, not brokers' commissions.

example.title: Worked example: tenant's own broker
steps: An NYC tenant hires her own broker at 12% of the first year's rent and leases at $3,000 a month.
First year's rent: $3,000 × 12 = $36,000.
Answer: she may pay **$4,320**; a landlord's listing agent could charge her nothing.

sections.heading: Rental brokerage practice: screening, guarantors and move-in costs
points: **40× rule**: annual income of at least 40 × the monthly rent (max rent = income ÷ 40). It's landlord policy, not law, and must be applied consistently.
A **guarantor** signs a written guaranty to pay if the tenant defaults (GOL §5-701).
A guarantor is liable but has **no right to occupy**, unlike a co-tenant. Buildings often require 80×; institutional guarantors are an alternative.
**Source of income** is protected: no 'No Section 8' ads (Executive Law §296(5); NYC Admin. Code §8-107).
Income tests apply only to the tenant's share, and none apply if a voucher pays 100%.
In NYC, a landlord can't require any income minimum or guarantor when the voucher sets the tenant's share from income (Section 8, CityFHEPS).

**No blacklisting**: rejecting an applicant after checking court or screening-bureau records about past cases creates a rebuttable presumption of a violation, even if the old case was dismissed (RPL §227-f).
Rent and deposits the broker collects go into a special **escrow account within 3 business days** (19 NYCRR §175.1).
Compensation from more than one party needs the client's knowledge and consent (§175.7).
Ads must name the brokerage plus its address or phone, or they're **blind ads** (19 NYCRR §175.25).
Advertising a unit already rented is **bait advertising**, which is dishonest or misleading advertising (RPL §441-c).
Selling rental lists requires an apartment information vendor license.
NYC tenant who hires her own broker at one month's rent on a $2,750 unit: $2,750 rent + $2,750 deposit + $20 + $2,750 fee = **$8,270**.

example.title: Worked example: most due at signing (NYC, landlord's broker)
steps: Rent $3,400; the screening check costs $30; the landlord hired the broker.
First month $3,400 + one-month deposit $3,400.
Screening fee: lesser of $30 or $20 = $20.
Broker fee: $0 under FARE.
Answer: **$6,820**. Adding a last month ($10,220) or a 15% fee ($12,940) is illegal.

sections.heading: Sales deal sheets
sections.intro: After an offer is accepted, an agent circulates a deal sheet so the attorneys can prepare the contract. In NYC this is usually the listing agent. It's also called a memorandum of sale, binder or offer to purchase.
points: Downstate, the **seller's attorney** drafts the contract from the deal sheet. The buyer's attorney reviews it and negotiates riders.
Brokers may not draft contracts or riders; that's practicing law (Judiciary Law §478).
A deal sheet is **not the contract**. The statute of frauds requires a signed writing (GOL §5-703).
When parties plan a formal contract, neither is bound until both sign it, so the seller may still take other offers.
A signed binder with every essential term and no 'subject to contract' language can be binding, which is why forms include it.
**Upstate**, agents often fill in a preprinted contract with an **attorney approval clause**. They fill blanks only, and the §443 disclosure must already be done.
The attorneys (or an upstate agent filling in a form) need the seller's prior deed and title policy, survey, certificate of occupancy, tax bills, and each party's legal name and contacts.
The deed's legal description (metes and bounds or lot on a filed map) identifies the property. The street address and tax-map number are cross-checks.
Contracts are signed by exchange (mail or email) or at a sit-down signing.
**Down payment**: about **10%** in NYC by custom, negotiable.
Downstate, the seller's attorney usually holds the down payment in escrow, backed by the **Lawyers' Fund for Client Protection**. Upstate, the broker often holds it.
The **buyer signs first**, then the seller.
Never put client secrets ('buyer can go higher') or protected-class details on a deal sheet; it goes to the other side.
Brokers keep transaction records **3 years** (19 NYCRR §175.23).
Pre-1978 homes need the federal lead clause. The syllabus's 'after 1978' is backward.

head: Item
Record
Why
rows: Address or unit; every owner and buyer, with contacts
Contract must name all title holders
Accepted price; deposit (often 10%) and escrow holder
Loan amount or LTV; conventional, FHA/VA, seller purchase-money or assumed loan; lender; or all cash
Inspection, appraisal, sale of buyer's home; co-op board approval
Each becomes a dated contract clause
Target closing; appliances and fixtures included
Listing and cooperating firms, commission and split
So the draft contract goes out

example.title: Worked example: $640,000 deal sheet
steps: Price $640,000; 80% mortgage; 10% deposit; 5% commission split 60/40 listing/cooperating.
Deposit: $64,000.
Balance due at closing (before closing costs): $128,000 − $64,000 = $64,000.
Commission: $32,000.
Answer: cooperating broker 40% = **$12,800**; listing broker $19,200.

sections.heading: Commission splits
points: **Commissions are negotiable**; no law or DOS rule sets them. Agreeing on an 'area rate' risks price fixing (Sherman Act; Donnelly Act).
The listing agreement sets the total and any co-broke share the seller offers.
The co-broke share can be equal halves (5% split 50/50) or separate rates (3% + 2.5% = 5.5%).
Separate rates on $720,000: $39,600 total and $18,000 to the co-broke.
Each firm pays its salesperson under its plan. A salesperson is paid **only by her own broker** (RPL §442-a).
**Referral fees** go only to licensed brokers, including out-of-state brokers (RPL §442). They come off the firm's side first.
What the firm keeps: $1,240,000 × 6% × 50% = $37,200 side; at a 70/30 split the firm keeps **$11,160**.
Rentals: a $4,200 landlord-paid fee at 60/40 pays the agent **$2,520**.
15% of a year's rent ($5,580 on $3,100) beats one month by $2,480.
Reverse problems: **price = commission ÷ rate** ($15,000 ÷ 2.5% = $600,000).

example.title: Worked example: referral fee first
steps: 25% referral = $3,500, leaving $10,500.
Answer: at a 50% split the salesperson earns **$5,250**.
