guides.title: Closing & Settlement
guides.overview: Closing finishes the sale: the seller delivers the deed and gets paid, old liens are paid off, and the buyer's loan funds. This chapter covers New York's attorney-run closing, RESPA, TRID, prorations, New York taxes, title clearance, FIRPTA and recording. The exam hits hardest on who represents whom, which way each entry goes, who pays which tax, and deadlines.

numbers.label: Loan Estimate due after application; counts days the lender's offices are open
Loan Estimate lead time before consummation; Saturdays count, Sundays and federal holidays don't
Closing Disclosure must be received before consummation; Saturdays count, Sundays and federal holidays don't
APR error beyond this forces a corrected CD and a new 3-day wait
Cumulative TRID tolerance: recording fees plus shoppable services from the lender's list
Lender's deadline after consummation to refund a TRID tolerance overcharge
Maximum escrow cushion: one-sixth of annual disbursements (2 months of payments)
Escrow surplus that must be refunded, and the refund deadline after the analysis
Servicing-transfer notice: old servicer at least 15 days before, new within 15 after
Post-transfer window: an on-time payment to the old servicer can't count as late
RESPA §8 civil damages on the charge; criminal up to $10,000 and 1 year
NYS transfer tax; any fraction of $500 rounds up; the seller pays
Mansion tax on the whole price of a residence; the buyer pays
NYC RPTT, residential: $500,000 or less / whole price above $500,000
Special additional mortgage recording tax the lender must pay on 1–6 family homes
FIRPTA withholding on a foreign seller's gross price
FIRPTA residence breakpoints: 0% up to $300,000; 10% above that up to $1,000,000
Form 1099-S exemption for a certified main-home sale (single / married seller)
Old lender's deadline to present the satisfaction of mortgage for recording (RPAPL §1921)
Seller turns tenants' security deposits over to the buyer after deed delivery (GOL §7-105)

mustKnow: New York uses **attorney closings**: buyer, seller, and lender each have a lawyer, and a title closer represents the title insurer.
Licensees can't draft deeds or give legal advice; that is the **unauthorized practice of law**.
The **bank attorney** represents only the lender, even though the buyer usually pays the fee.
Downstate, the **seller's attorney** drafts the contract; the **buyer's attorney** orders title after it is signed.
Title passes on **delivery and acceptance**. **Recording** gives constructive notice under New York's race-notice act.
NYC records through **ACRIS**. **Staten Island** deeds go to the Richmond County Clerk, but NYC tax forms are still made in ACRIS.
**TP-584** (transfer tax return) is filed with every deed, even a gift with no tax due. **RP-5217** gives assessors sale data.
**RESPA** covers federally related mortgage loans on 1–4 family homes, including refinances and second mortgages, but not all-cash sales.
**Referral fees and kickbacks** are banned (RESPA §8). Broker-to-broker commission splits and pay for work actually done are allowed.
**Affiliated business arrangement**: disclose at or before the referral, no required use, ownership return only.
A seller can't make the buyer use a particular **title insurer** (RESPA §9).
Escrow **cushion** is capped at 1/6 of annual disbursements. A **surplus** of $50 or more is refunded within 30 days.
**Loan Estimate**: within 3 business days of application and at least 7 business days before consummation. Before intent to proceed, only a **credit report fee** is allowed.
**Closing Disclosure**: received at least 3 business days before consummation. In hand Monday → close Thursday; mailed Monday → close the next Monday.
**Zero tolerance**: lender and affiliate fees, unshoppable services, transfer taxes. **10% cumulative**: recording fees and unaffiliated providers picked from the lender's list.
**No limit**: prepaid interest, homeowner's insurance, escrow deposits, off-list providers, and services the lender doesn't require. A tolerance overcharge is cured by refund within 60 days.
**Debit** = charged to a party; **credit** = allowed to a party. Cash to close = buyer debits − buyer credits.
**Buyer credits only**: earnest money and the new loan. **Seller debits only**: the payoff and the commission.
Seller **prepaid**: seller credit, buyer debit. Seller's days **unpaid**: seller debit, buyer credit.
Collected **rent** and **security deposits**: seller debit, buyer credit.
**Fuel oil**: seller credit, buyer debit. **Assumed loan**: buyer credit, seller debit.
By New York custom the **buyer owns the closing day**; follow the question if it says otherwise.
The **seller** pays the NYS transfer tax ($2 per $500 or fraction) and NYC RPTT (1% up to $500,000; 1.425% of the whole price above).
The **buyer** pays the **mansion tax**: 1% of the whole price at $1,000,000 or more.
**Mortgage recording tax** is figured on the loan and paid by the borrower, except the 0.25% the lender pays on 1–6 family homes. None on cash deals or co-op share loans.
NY buyers customarily pay **title insurance** (owner's and lender's), lender fees, inspections, and recording the deed and mortgage.
The **final walk-through** confirms condition; it is not a new contingency, and problems go to the attorneys.
A salesperson is paid **only by her own broker**, never directly at the closing table (RPL §442-a).
**FIRPTA**: the buyer withholds 15% of the gross price from a foreign seller. A non-foreign certification ends the duty.
**Form 1099-S** reports gross proceeds and is filed by the person responsible for closing.

traps.trap: The Closing Disclosure is due 3 business days after the application.
traps.truth: The CD must be received at least 3 business days before consummation. The 3-days-after-application deadline is for the Loan Estimate.

traps.trap: Saturdays don't count when timing the CD.
traps.truth: Saturdays count. For the CD wait and the mailbox rule, only Sundays and federal holidays are skipped.

traps.trap: Any change after the CD restarts the 3-day wait.
traps.truth: Only APR, product, or prepayment-penalty changes restart it. A higher fee needs just a corrected CD.

traps.trap: Recording the deed transfers title.
traps.truth: Delivery and acceptance transfer title; recording protects the buyer against later purchasers.

traps.trap: The mansion tax applies only above $1,000,000, on the excess.
traps.truth: The mansion tax is 1% of the entire price starting at exactly $1,000,000, and the buyer pays.

traps.trap: NYC RPTT above $500,000 is 1% on the first $500,000 and 1.425% on the rest.
traps.truth: Once the price exceeds $500,000, 1.425% applies to the whole price. Exactly $500,000 is taxed at 1%.

traps.trap: NYS transfer tax is a flat 0.4% and starts above $25,000.
traps.truth: NYS transfer tax is $2 per $500 or fraction, with units rounded up, once consideration exceeds $500.

traps.trap: The earnest money deposit is a seller debit.
traps.truth: Earnest money is a buyer credit only; the price credited to the seller already includes it.

traps.trap: The new mortgage is a buyer credit and a seller debit.
traps.truth: The new mortgage is a buyer credit only. Only an assumed loan or seller financing also hits the seller's side.

traps.trap: Taxes the seller hasn't paid are a seller credit.
traps.truth: Unpaid taxes are a seller debit and buyer credit: the seller used those days without paying.

traps.trap: FIRPTA is 15% of the gain, withheld by the broker.
traps.truth: FIRPTA is 15% of the gross amount realized, and the buyer withholds.

traps.trap: A Florida resident selling NY property triggers FIRPTA.
traps.truth: FIRPTA covers foreign persons. A nonresident U.S. seller pays NY estimated tax on Form IT-2663.

traps.trap: An exempt seller, such as a state agency, makes the sale transfer-tax-free.
traps.truth: When the grantor is exempt, the grantee must pay the NYS transfer tax.

traps.trap: To confirm new wiring instructions, call the number in the email.
traps.truth: Use an independently known, previously verified number. The number in the email may reach the criminal.

mnemonics.name: APP
mnemonics.meaning: The only post-CD changes that restart the 3-business-day wait: APR beyond tolerance, loan Product change, Prepayment penalty added

mnemonics.name: Paid ahead, paid back
mnemonics.meaning: Seller paid ahead (prepaid taxes, oil, maintenance): the buyer pays the seller back, so seller credit, buyer debit. Seller owes for days used or holds the buyer's money (unpaid taxes, collected rent, deposits): seller debit, buyer credit.

formulas.name: NYS transfer tax
formulas.formula: Tax = (price ÷ $500, rounded up) × $2

formulas.name: Mansion tax
formulas.formula: Tax = 1% × entire price (residence at $1,000,000 or more)

formulas.name: NYC RPTT (residential)
formulas.formula: Price × 1% if $500,000 or less; price × 1.425% if more

formulas.name: Daily proration
formulas.formula: Annual amount ÷ 365 (or 360) × days in the period

formulas.name: Buyer's cash to close
formulas.formula: Total buyer debits − total buyer credits

formulas.name: Seller's net proceeds
formulas.formula: Total seller credits − total seller debits

formulas.name: Mortgage payoff
formulas.formula: Good-through amount + (per diem × extra days)

formulas.name: Escrow cushion cap
formulas.formula: Annual escrow disbursements ÷ 6

formulas.name: FIRPTA withholding
formulas.formula: Amount realized × 15% (10% or 0% under the residence rules)

formulas.name: Mortgage recording tax
formulas.formula: Loan amount, rounded to the nearest $100, × the borrower's rate. Borrower's rate = local total − the 0.25% the lender pays on 1–6 family homes.

sections.heading: What a closing is and who is at the table
sections.intro: A **title closing** (settlement) completes the sale. The seller delivers the deed and is paid the balance, existing liens are paid off, and the buyer's loan funds. New York is an attorney-closing state.
points: Several deals close at once: buyer and seller (deed for price), buyer and lender (loan), buyer and title insurer (policy), seller and broker (commission), and seller and old lender (payoff).
The buyer pays with **acquisition mortgage** money plus her own funds. The seller's mortgage, judgments, and unpaid taxes are paid from the seller's proceeds.
New York usually uses a **table closing**: the parties meet and exchange papers and checks.
In an **escrow closing**, a neutral escrow agent holds the deed and funds until every condition is met, so no one needs to meet.
A seller who can't attend may sign the deed in advance for her attorney to hold in escrow, or act through an attorney-in-fact.

Closings are held at an attorney's office (often the lender's attorney's), the lender, a title company, or in some areas the county clerk's office. The clerk never runs the closing; it only records documents afterward.
Licensees may attend and coordinate. Drafting the deed or giving legal or tax advice is the **unauthorized practice of law** (Judiciary Law §§478, 484).
Co-op closings have no deed. The seller assigns the stock and proprietary lease, and the managing agent attends.
In a co-op sale, a **lien search** replaces the title search, and the share lender files a UCC-1.

head: Participant
Represents
Typical job at a New York closing
rows: Signs the deed and seller forms (TP-584, RP-5217); receives net proceeds
Brings good funds, signs the loan papers, accepts the deed
Drafts the contract downstate, holds the down payment, prepares the deed, orders payoffs, clears objections
Negotiates the contract, orders and reviews title and survey, checks the loan and closing figures
Lender only, though the buyer pays the fee
Prepares and supervises the loan documents, confirms the lender's conditions, funds the loan
Collects the premium, fees, and taxes; handles payoffs; runs the bring-down; takes documents for recording
Coordinate, attend, account for deposits, present the commission bill; no legal advice

sections.heading: From accepted offer to recording: the New York timeline
sections.intro: Who writes the contract varies by region, but the checkpoints don't, and recording always comes last.
points: Downstate, the licensee's paperwork ends with a memorandum of sale, and attorneys write the contract.
In much of upstate, licensees fill in preprinted contracts. They may only fill in blanks, never draft legal terms.
To avoid the unauthorized practice of law, they make the contract subject to each party's attorney's approval with an **attorney-approval clause** (Duncan & Hill Realty v. Department of State).
The **down payment** (often 10% downstate) is held in escrow, usually by the seller's attorney, and credited to the buyer at closing.
The **buyer's attorney** orders title after the contract is signed. That way the buyer's own advocate reviews the exceptions and demands that the seller clear them.

head: Stage
What happens
Who drives it
rows: Memorandum of sale downstate; form contract with attorney approval in much of upstate
Seller's attorney drafts; buyer signs and pays the down payment into escrow
Application, Loan Estimate, appraisal, mortgage commitment
Title report ordered; seller clears objections
CD received 3 business days ahead; payoff letters ordered
Usually within a day of closing
Deed delivered, loan funded, funds disbursed
Deed and mortgage recorded; satisfaction within 30 days; 1099-S filed

sections.heading: Title clearance before closing
sections.intro: The seller must deliver **marketable, insurable title**. Each exception on the buyer's title report must be cleared, insured over, or accepted before the deed passes.
points: A title search traces the **chain of title** (the unbroken line of owners) through the public records.
An **abstract of title** condenses that history. Title insurance pays for covered defects.
**Marketable title** is title a reasonable buyer would accept. It may stay subject to easements the contract allows.
The buyer's attorney sends the report's objections to the seller's attorney, and the seller pays to clear its own defects.
A **payoff letter** states the amount needed to retire a loan through a stated date, plus a **per diem** for later days.
Don't use a monthly-statement balance as the payoff. It leaves out accrued interest and would leave the lien open.
Recorded judgments survive a sale and must be paid, bonded, or satisfied.
A paid mortgage with no recorded satisfaction stays a cloud until one is recorded or the insurer accepts other proof. It doesn't expire on its own.
A **survey** reveals encroachments, which can make title unmarketable. Without a survey, the policy excepts survey matters.
A **bring-down search** just before closing catches anything recorded since the original search.
Title insurance costs a one-time premium at closing and covers defects that exist on the policy date.
The **owner's policy** protects the buyer and the **lender's policy** protects the lender. New York buyers customarily pay for both.

head: Title problem
Usual cure
rows: Payoff at closing; the lender records a satisfaction within 30 days
Paid mortgage with no satisfaction of record
Record a satisfaction, or give proof of payment the insurer accepts
Pay it from the proceeds, bond it, or obtain a satisfaction
Disputed lien that can't be cleared in time
Title company escrow holdback from the seller's proceeds, insured over
Negotiate a fix, insure over it, or object under the contract
Missing link in the chain of title
Corrective deed, quitclaim deed, or quiet title action

example.title: Worked example: payoff with per diem interest
steps: The payoff letter shows $187,600 due through August 10, plus $28.40 per diem.
Funds reach the lender August 18, 8 days later: 8 × $28.40 = $227.20.
Answer: $187,827.20, a debit to the seller only.

sections.heading: Walk-through, insurance, possession, and commission
sections.intro: Three licensee-facing steps sit just before and at the closing: the walk-through, homeowner's insurance, and getting paid.
points: The **final walk-through**, usually within a day of closing, confirms the condition the contract requires: no new damage, repairs done, included fixtures still there, and vacant and broom-clean if required.
The walk-through is not a new contingency or a chance to renegotiate the price.
Problems, such as a missing dishwasher the contract included, go straight to the buyer's attorney. The attorney can negotiate a credit, repair, or escrow holdback.
The licensee shouldn't promise money, advise suing, or tell the buyer to walk away.

If the seller must stay after closing, use a written **post-closing possession agreement** with a daily charge and an escrow holdback released at move-out. Delaying recording would only expose the buyer's title.

**Risk of loss**: if a material part is destroyed before title or possession passes, without the buyer's fault, the seller can't enforce the contract and the buyer gets the deposit back (General Obligations Law §5-1311).
Once title or possession passes, the risk of loss is the buyer's.
Before closing, the buyer shows **homeowner's insurance**: a policy or binder naming the lender as mortgagee. Homes in a flood zone generally need flood insurance too.
The seller usually pays the **commission** at closing with one check to the listing broker, who pays cooperating brokers and its salespersons.
A salesperson may be paid **only by her own broker**, never directly at the table, even with the broker's approval (Real Property Law §442-a).
The **Commission Escrow Act** covers 1–4 family homes, condos, and co-ops (RPL §294-b).

Under that act, if the listing has the required notice and the broker records an affidavit of entitlement before closing, a seller who won't pay must deposit the disputed commission with the county clerk. If the net proceeds are less, the seller deposits those.

sections.heading: RESPA: kickbacks, affiliated businesses, and escrow accounts
sections.intro: The **Real Estate Settlement Procedures Act** (RESPA, 1974) makes settlement costs visible, bans kickbacks that inflate them, and limits escrow accounts. The Consumer Financial Protection Bureau (CFPB) enforces it through Regulation X.
points: RESPA covers **federally related mortgage loans** on 1–4 family residential property: purchases, refinances, home equity and second mortgages, and condo and co-op units.
Not covered: all-cash sales, business or agricultural loans, temporary construction loans, most vacant-land loans, assumptions without lender approval, and secondary-market loan sales.
**Kickbacks**: RESPA bans any fee or thing of value (cash, gift cards, parties) for referring settlement business (Section 8).
Section 8 also bans fee splits for work not performed. Labels don't matter, and disclosure doesn't cure a kickback.
Allowed: payment for goods or services actually provided, bona fide salaries, and **commission splits between brokers and agents**.
Penalties for Section 8 violations: fines up to $10,000 and up to 1 year in prison, plus civil liability for **3 times** the settlement charge, costs, and attorney's fees.
**Affiliated business arrangement**: written disclosure **at or before the referral**, no required use, and only a return on ownership.
One exception to no required use: a lender may require its own attorney, credit bureau, or appraiser.
A seller **can't require** the buyer to buy title insurance from a particular company. The seller is liable for 3 times the title charges (Section 9).
Lenders often require an **escrow (impound) account** for taxes and insurance. The buyer's **initial escrow deposit** at closing is a buyer debit only, since it goes to the buyer's own lender.
The escrow account is capped at what the bills need plus a **cushion** of at most **1/6 of annual disbursements**, which is 2 months of payments (RESPA §10).
After the yearly analysis, a **surplus of $50 or more** goes back to a current borrower within **30 days**.
**Servicing transfers**: the old servicer gives notice at least **15 days before** the transfer, and the new servicer within 15 days after (RESPA §6).
For **60 days** after a servicing transfer, an on-time payment sent to the old servicer can't be treated as late.

example.title: Worked example: maximum escrow cushion
steps: Taxes $8,400 + insurance $2,040 = $10,440 a year, or $870 a month.
Maximum cushion: $10,440 ÷ 6 = $1,740, which is 2 months of payments.
Answer: $1,740; demanding 3 months ($2,610) violates RESPA.

sections.heading: TRID: Loan Estimate, Closing Disclosure, and tolerances
sections.intro: The **TILA-RESPA Integrated Disclosure** rule (TRID, effective October 3, 2015) uses two forms: the Loan Estimate (LE) after application and the Closing Disclosure (CD) before consummation.
points: TRID covers most closed-end consumer mortgages on real property or a **co-op unit** (since the 2017 amendments).
TRID excludes home equity lines of credit (HELOCs), reverse mortgages, mobile homes not attached to land, and business-purpose loans.
An **application** is six items: name, income, Social Security number, property address, estimated value, and loan amount. The lender can't hold up the LE to demand tax returns first.
The **LE** is delivered or mailed within **3 business days** of application. For this deadline, a business day is a day the lender's offices are open for substantially all business.
The LE must also be delivered or mailed at least **7 business days before consummation**, counting Saturdays as for the CD.
Until the borrower receives the LE and signals intent to proceed, only a reasonable **credit report fee** may be charged.
The **CD** must be received at least **3 business days before consummation**. Consummation is when the borrower becomes bound on the loan, usually by signing the note.
For the CD wait and the mailbox rule, a business day is every calendar day except **Sundays** and **federal legal public holidays**, so Saturdays count (Regulation Z §1026.2(a)(6)).
Federal holidays include Columbus Day, Veterans Day, and Juneteenth. In hand Monday → consummation Thursday.
A mailed or emailed CD is presumed received **3 business days after it is sent**: mailed Monday → received Thursday → consummation the next Monday.
Only three changes force a corrected CD plus a new 3-day wait: an inaccurate **APR** (off by more than 1/8 point, or 1/4 on irregular loans), a product change, or an added prepayment penalty.
Any other change needs only a corrected CD at or before consummation.
Only the borrower can waive the wait, for a **bona fide personal financial emergency**. It takes a dated written statement, signed by every borrower, that isn't a preprinted form.
A tolerance overcharge is cured by refunding the excess **within 60 days after consummation**. Treble damages belong to RESPA §8, not TRID.

example.title: Worked example: counting CD days (no federal holidays)
steps: Handed over Tuesday: count Wednesday, Thursday, Friday. Earliest consummation: Friday.
Mailed Tuesday: presumed received 3 business days later, on Friday.
Count from Friday: Saturday (1), Monday (2, Sunday skipped), Tuesday (3).
Answer: Friday if handed over; the following Tuesday if mailed.

sections.heading: The closing statement: debits and credits
sections.intro: The closing statement lists every item and shows who is charged (debit) and who is allowed (credit). Each side must balance.
points: A **debit** is an amount charged to a party; a **credit** is an amount allowed to a party or already paid by it.

**Double entries** move money between buyer and seller (price, prorations, concessions, assumed loans, tenants' security deposits, fuel). **Single entries** involve an outsider (new loan, earnest money, payoff, commission, title insurance, escrow deposit).
Earnest money is a buyer credit only, because the price credited to the seller already includes it.
An **assumed mortgage** is a buyer credit and seller debit. A new bank loan never touches the seller's side.
**Cash to close** = buyer debits − buyer credits, paid in good funds. **Seller's net** = seller credits − seller debits.
**Reconciliation** confirms both sides balance and money in equals money out.

example.title: Worked example: buyer's cash to close
steps: Debits: price $610,000 + closing costs $15,900 = $625,900.
Credits: earnest money $61,000 + new loan $488,000 + unpaid-tax credit $1,140 = $550,140.
Answer: $625,900 − $550,140 = $75,760, by wire or certified or official bank check.

sections.heading: Prorating taxes
sections.intro: **Proration** splits a recurring expense or income item so each party bears only its own days of ownership. Taxes are the most tested item.
points: **Accrued** (paid in arrears): the seller used days that are unpaid, and the buyer will pay the bill. It is a **seller debit, buyer credit** for the seller's days.
**Prepaid** (paid in advance): the seller paid for days the buyer will own. It is a **seller credit, buyer debit** for the buyer's days.
New York contracts customarily apportion as of midnight before closing, so the **buyer owns the closing day**. Some textbooks give it to the seller; follow the question.
**365-day** method: annual amount ÷ 365 (366 in a leap year) with actual calendar days. **360-day** method: annual ÷ 360 with 30-day months. Don't switch midway.
Count from the bill's own start date. **School taxes** and NYC property taxes run July 1–June 30, while many town and county bills follow the calendar year.
**Special assessments** are charges for local improvements such as sewers or sidewalks.

Under the standard New York residential contract, if the first installment of an installment assessment is already a lien or has been paid, all unpaid installments count as due. The seller pays them at or before closing.

example.title: Worked example: three tax prorations
steps: Unpaid calendar-year tax of $13,140; closing June 10; buyer owns the closing day; 365-day year: $13,140 ÷ 365 = $36 a day.
Seller's days, January 1–June 9: 31 + 28 + 31 + 30 + 31 + 9 = 160. 160 × $36 = $5,760, seller debit and buyer credit.
Same bill on a 360-day year: $36.50 a day × 159 days (5 × 30 + 9) = $5,803.50. The convention changes the answer.
School tax of $7,300 for July 1–June 30 already paid by the seller: $20 a day × 21 buyer days (June 10–30) = $420, seller credit and buyer debit.
Answer: $5,760 seller debit/buyer credit (365-day basis); $420 seller credit/buyer debit.

sections.heading: Prorating rent, deposits, fuel, and interest
sections.intro: For every other item, ask the same two questions: who paid, and whose days were they?
points: **Rent collected in advance** for the closing month: seller debit, buyer credit for the buyer's days. Overdue rent usually isn't credited to the seller.
**Security deposits**, plus any interest owed, are the tenants' money: seller debit, buyer credit for the full amount.
The seller turns the deposits over at closing or within 5 days after, and notifies tenants by registered or certified mail (General Obligations Law §7-105).
**Fuel oil** left in the tank: seller credit, buyer debit at the contract price.
**Insurance** is rarely prorated today because the buyer buys a new policy. If a transferable prepaid policy were assigned, the unused premium would be a seller credit and buyer debit.
**Interest on an assumed mortgage** is paid in arrears: seller debit, buyer credit for the interest accrued since the last payment.
**Co-op maintenance or condo charges** paid for the closing month: seller credit, buyer debit for the buyer's days. Water and sewer charges are settled from a final meter reading.

example.title: Worked example: closing on a two-family rental
steps: Closing April 19; buyer owns the closing day; 30-day month. The tenant paid April rent of $2,100 and has a $2,100 deposit; 180 gallons of oil are priced at $3.75.
Rent: $2,100 ÷ 30 = $70 × 12 buyer days (April 19–30) = $840, seller debit and buyer credit.
Deposit: $2,100, seller debit and buyer credit.
Oil: 180 × $3.75 = $675, seller credit and buyer debit.
Answer: the buyer nets $840 + $2,100 − $675 = $2,265 in credits.

sections.heading: Who pays what in New York
sections.intro: Custom sets the defaults below, but the contract controls, and tax law decides who is primarily liable for transfer taxes.
points: Contracts can shift costs: NYC sponsors often make new-condo buyers pay the transfer taxes, and seller concessions can cover a buyer's closing costs.
Co-op and condo sellers must bring maintenance or common charges current.
A co-op **flip tax** is a private transfer fee under the co-op's own documents, not a government tax. The seller usually pays it.
Managing agents charge each side processing fees, and the co-op buyer pays application and UCC-1 filing fees.
Co-op sales still owe the NYS transfer tax, the mansion tax at $1,000,000 or more, and in NYC the RPTT.
Only the mortgage recording tax drops out of a co-op sale, because a share loan is perfected by a UCC filing, not a recorded mortgage.

sections.heading: Transfer taxes and the mortgage recording tax
sections.intro: Transfer taxes are charged on the deed and based on the price. The mortgage recording tax is charged on the mortgage and based on the loan.
points: **NYS transfer tax**: $2 per $500 **or fraction** once consideration exceeds $500, so round units up (Tax Law §1402). Example: $412,300 → 824.6 → 825 units → $1,650.
The **seller** pays the NYS transfer tax with the TP-584; the **buyer** pays if the seller fails to or is exempt. Co-op share sales are taxed too.
Use the full price: a payoff isn't subtracted. A lien that stays on the property, such as an assumed mortgage, is excluded only for 1–3 family houses, residential condos, or sales under $500,000.
**Mansion tax**: 1% of the **whole** price of a 1–3 family house, condo, or co-op at $1,000,000 or more, paid by the buyer (§1402-a). $999,999 → $0; $1,000,000 → $10,000.
The **NYC Real Property Transfer Tax** (RPTT) is paid by the seller on top of the state tax (NYC Administrative Code §11-2102).
RPTT rates: residential (1–3 family, condo, co-op) 1% at $500,000 or less and 1.425% of the whole price above. Other property: 1.425%, or 2.625% above $500,000.

NYC-only extras: a state **additional base tax** (0.65% in total) at residential $3 million+ or other $2 million+, paid by the seller. A graduated **supplemental mansion tax** applies at residential $2 million+, paid by the buyer.
Some towns, such as those in the Peconic Bay region, add buyer-paid local taxes.
**Mortgage recording tax**: local rate × loan amount, rounded to the nearest $100 (Tax Law Article 11). It is paid to the county clerk or NYC City Register when the mortgage is recorded.
Form MT-15 is needed only when the property spans localities with different rates.
Mortgage recording tax totals run 0.75%–1.30% outside NYC (1.80% in Yonkers). NYC charges 2.05%, or 2.175% on 1–3 family and condo loans of $500,000 or more. Other NYC loans that size pay 2.80%.
The borrower pays, except the **0.25% special additional tax**, which the lender must pay on 1–6 family homes.
On a one- or two-family home or condo unit, the first $10,000 is exempt from the 0.25–0.30% additional tax.
No mortgage recording tax applies to cash deals or co-op share loans. A **CEMA** (consolidation, extension and modification agreement) limits the tax to new money.

example.title: Worked example: Brooklyn condo resale for $1,150,000
steps: Mansion tax: 1% × $1,150,000 = $11,500, buyer. Neither NYC add-on applies at this price.
Mortgage recording tax if the buyer borrows $920,000: NYC's rate on a condo loan of $500,000 or more is 2.175%.
The lender pays 0.25% ($2,300). The buyer pays 1.925% ($17,710).
A condo unit's first $10,000 is exempt from the 0.30% additional tax, so the buyer saves $30: $17,710 − $30 = $17,680.

sections.heading: Recording and the New York closing forms
sections.intro: Delivery transfers title; recording protects it. Right after closing, the title closer takes the deed, mortgage, tax returns, and checks for recording.
points: Title passes when the signed deed is **delivered and accepted** during the grantor's lifetime. An unrecorded deed is still valid between the parties.
**Recording** gives **constructive notice** to everyone (Real Property Law §291). Actual notice is real knowledge.
Under New York's **race-notice** rule, an unrecorded deed loses to a later good-faith purchaser for value who records first.
A deed must be acknowledged, or proved by a subscribing witness, to be recorded.
Outside NYC, record with the **county clerk**. For Manhattan, the Bronx, Brooklyn, and Queens, record with the City Register through **ACRIS**.
Staten Island deeds go to the Richmond County Clerk, though NYC tax forms are still prepared in ACRIS.
The old lender must present a **satisfaction of mortgage** for recording within **30 days** of payoff (RPAPL §1921).
A late lender owes the owner $500, rising to $1,000 at 60 days and $1,500 at 90 days.

sections.heading: FIRPTA and Form 1099-S
sections.intro: Two federal tax rules ride along with most closings: withholding under the Foreign Investment in Real Property Tax Act (FIRPTA) when the seller is foreign, and 1099-S reporting of the sale.
points: Under **FIRPTA**, the buyer must withhold when buying U.S. real property from a **foreign person**, and can be liable if it doesn't (IRC §1445).
Rate: **15% of the amount realized** (the gross price), not of the gain.
Residence rule: if the buyer is an individual who will live there, there is no withholding at $300,000 or less, and **10%** over $300,000 up to $1,000,000.
To qualify, the buyer or a family member must have definite plans to live there at least 50% of the days anyone uses it in each of the first two 12-month periods.
A signed **non-foreign certification** with the seller's taxpayer ID ends the duty unless the buyer knows it is false. An IRS **withholding certificate** can reduce or eliminate it.
The buyer sends the tax with Forms 8288 and 8288-A within 20 days.
FIRPTA isn't about Americans who live in other states. A nonresident U.S. seller of NY property pays estimated NY tax on **Form IT-2663**.
**Form 1099-S** reports **gross proceeds**, not gain.
1099-S filer order: the person responsible for closing (such as the closing attorney), then the buyer's mortgage lender, the seller's broker, the buyer's broker, and the buyer.
No 1099-S is needed for a main-home sale of **$250,000 or less ($500,000 if married)** when the seller certifies in writing that the whole gain is excludable.

example.title: Worked example: FIRPTA on a rental
steps: A foreign investor sells a rental duplex for $640,000 with a $210,000 gain; the buyer will keep renting it out.
No residence rule applies: $640,000 × 15% = $96,000, sent to the IRS within 20 days.
Answer: $96,000. Taking 15% of the gain ($31,500) or using 10% ($64,000) is wrong.

sections.heading: Closing funds and wire fraud
sections.intro: Closings move large sums by wire, which makes them a top target for email fraud.
points: The buyer pays the balance in **good funds**: a wire or a certified or official bank check. A personal check isn't accepted for the balance.
The scam: criminals hack or imitate the email of an attorney, agent, or title company and send 'updated' wiring instructions near closing.
Red flags: last-minute changes, pressure, a slightly altered address, or new bank details.
Verify any wiring instructions by phone using an **independently known, previously verified number**, never the number or link in the message. Don't reply to the email to ask.
After wiring, confirm receipt by phone.
If money went out, call the sending bank at once to request a recall, and report it at ic3.gov.
Licensees should warn clients early, in writing, that wiring instructions will never change by email.
